Uniform Title: Puraścaryārṇava, Volume 2 Main Title: Puraścaryārṇavaḥ, Volume 2 Editor: Muralidhara Jhā
Description: Compiled by His Highness the Maharaja Pratapa Simha Shah Bahadur of Nepal.
Notes: The texts were transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0, January 28, 2007.
Publisher: Prabhakari and Co.
Year of publication: 1901 City of publication: Benares Country of publication: India
Now, the practical application of initiation (dīkṣā) is being elucidated.

P. 319) There, at the outset, the disciple endowed with devotion, having performed the shaving of the head and other rites on the first day, and having bathed in a sacred ford or similar place for the sake of bodily purification, should mutter the *gāyatrī* a thousand times, eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) once, and observe a fast on the second day. On the third day, having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*), having adorned his body with garments, ornaments, and so forth, and having worshipped Gaṇeśa in his own home to ward off obstacles, he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) and perform the *nāndī-śrāddha*. Then, taking the materials required for the formal invitation (*varaṇa*) as prescribed, he should go to the teacher’s house preceded by the five musical instruments. There, having washed his hands and feet, with palms joined in reverence and bowed low with devotion—
"O Blessed One, O Embodiment of the Supreme Self, O Most Compassionate Śrī Guru, please favor me by bestowing the great mantra that accomplishes all human goals.

Having spoken thus, he should prostrate before the Guru with the eight limbs of the body. Then, by the Guru’s command, sitting upon a seat facing either east or north, and taking three blades of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water, he should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) preceded by the recitation of the *svasti-vācana*.
It is as follows:

Oṃ Viṣṇurviṣṇuḥ. Oṃ, beginning with "Today," etc.—having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "I, [Name], born of the [Name] lineage (*gotra*), desiring the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, shall perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the [Name] mantra of the venerable deity [Name]," he should choose a guru.
As follows:
"Oṃ, may you be gracious"—thus the disciple should say.
"Oṃ, I am worthy," says the Guru.
"Oṃ, we shall worship you," says the disciple.
"Oṃ, worship," says the Guru.

Then the disciple, having offered a seat to the Guru with the mantra "Obeisance to the Śrī Guru," and having worshipped the Guru with that same mantra using water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, as well as sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, ornaments, and so forth, should place his right knee upon the ground and recite:
"Oṃ, today... [etc. ...I, Amukadevaśarman, born of the Amuka lineage, for the sake of Dharma... [the mantra] of the deity... and so on.

p. 320) "I choose you—of such-and-such lineage, of such-and-such family, a student of such-and-such Veda, named such-and-such Devaśarmā—who have been honored with these offerings beginning with water for the feet—to be my preceptor.
The response is: "Om, I am chosen.
Again, with palms joined in reverence:
"Oṃ, from this day forward—and so on—in this rite of initiation into the mantra named [so-and-so], may you be the preceptor.
"Oṃ, I shall be," is the reply.
"O Blessed One, O Illustrious Guru, perform the rite as prescribed," the disciple should say.
"I shall do as you have commanded"—this is the reply.

Thereafter, the disciple should perform a salutation to the guru. Then, having presented the remaining materials for the selection (*varaṇa*) to the guru and having prostrated at his feet, he should select the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) by the guru's command. Having honored each of them individually with the aforementioned services and in the manner prescribed, he should recite:

Oṃ, beginning with "Today," etc.—I, [Name], born of the [Name] lineage (*gotra*), desiring the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life, choose you, [Name], who belongs to the [Name] lineage, the [Name] *pravara*, a student of the [Name] Veda, and who has been honored by me with these offerings such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, as my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) for the ritual of initiation (*mantra-dīkṣā*) into the mantra of the glorious [Name] deity.
"Oṃ, I am chosen"—this is the reply.
"Perform the ritual according to the injunctions"—thus says the disciple.
"I shall do as you have commanded"—this is the reply.
In this manner, one should appoint each of the eight officiating priests (ṛtvij). Then, having given them the materials required for the ritual, one should bow down to them.

Then the Guru, accompanied by the disciple and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), shall go to the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) and, having sat at its entrance, perform the examination of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*). The examination of the tooth-stick must be performed immediately after the meal of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). [According to their opinion, it should be performed at that very time. It is as follows:

the Guru, having consecrated with the root mantra a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, produced from a milky tree such as the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, or *plakṣa*, should give it to the disciple.

The disciple, having washed his hands and feet, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and bowed to the Guru, takes the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and cleanses his teeth. Having discarded the tooth-stick upon a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) one cubit in size, constructed from sand or similar materials, he performs the ritual sipping of water preceded by rinsing the mouth with pure water. Then the Guru, observing the tip of the tooth-stick as it falls toward the eastern or other directions, shall deliberate upon the auspicious or inauspicious results.
As follows:

If the tip of the tooth-stick falls toward the eastern direction, there is the attainment of sovereignty; if it falls toward the south-eastern direction, there is distress of the heart; if it falls toward the southern direction, there is the loss of kinsmen; if it falls toward the southwestern direction, death; if it falls toward the western direction, grief; if it falls toward the northwestern direction, agitation; if it falls toward the northern direction, happiness; and if it falls toward the northeastern direction, the attainment of knowledge—having thus considered these results, if it falls toward an inauspicious direction, then for the purpose of warding off the resulting defects:
With the mantra "phaṭ amukadoṣaṃ jahi 2 phaṭ svāhā," one should perform a fire offering (*homa*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.

Then, the preceptor, having sat upon a seat at the entrance of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), should establish the general water-offering (*sāmānyārgha*).
It is as follows:
Having sprinkled the ground with water consecrated by mantras and having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square—
having worshipped the mandala with "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti"— and having placed the support (ādhāra) upon it:

Having worshipped the support (ādhāra) with "Ra! Obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās," and having washed the arghya vessel with the mantra "Phaṭ" and placed it upon the support, one worships the arghya vessel with "A!
Obeisance to the sun-mandala consisting of twelve kalās."
Saying "Namas," fill it with water;
then, having worshipped the water with "Namas to the lunar mandala consisting of sixteen kalās," [recite] within that water:
"Oṃ, O Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Godāvarī and Sarasvatī..."
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! || 5-1 ||

Thus, having invoked the *tīrtha* from the solar disc by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, and having placed fragrance and flowers with the *praṇava*, one should worship it with that same [mantra]. Having consecrated it eight or ten times with that same [mantra], one should display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Then, having sprinkled the door with that water while reciting "phaṭ," one should perform the worship of the door.
Namely:
"Oṃ [omitted] namaḥ" at the door on the upper part of the udumbara tree;
and "ma/ Mahālakṣmyai namaḥ" to its right.

He should worship these deities of the door, starting from the upper part down to the base, on the right and left branches of the door: "Salutation to Sarasvatī" on its left; "Salutation to Dvāraśrī" in the middle.
Namely:
"Gaṃ, homage to Gaṇapati"—thus on the right;
"Kṣaṃ, homage to Kṣetrapāla"—thus on the left.
"Obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi, joined with Vasundharā"—thus again on the right. "Obeisance to Padmanidhi, joined with Vasumatī"—thus on the left. "Obeisance to Māyāśakti"—thus on the right.
Ca / *Cicchaktaye namaḥ*—thus on the left.
Ga / *Gaṅgāyai namaḥ*—thus on the right.
Ya / *Yamunāyai namaḥ*—thus on the left.
"Dha/ To Dhātṛ, salutation"—thus on the right; "Va/ To Vidhātṛ, salutation"—thus on the left;
"Da/ To the threshold (dehalī), salutation" and "A/ To the weapon (astra), salutation"—thus on the threshold.
Thus, beginning from the western gate and having worshipped at each gate, one should worship the door-keepers.
In that regard, for the special worship of Śiva, [one worships] Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣabha, Bhṛṅgin, Skanda, Bhavānī, and Caṇḍeśvara.
Beginning from the western gate, one should worship two [deities] at each gate in succession.
The mantra for their worship is:
"Naṃ, obeisance to Nandin," and so forth.
In the worship of Viṣṇu—[the attendants] named Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bala, Prabala, Bhadra, and Subhadra;
in the worship of Gaṇeśa—(p. 323).
One should worship Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajānana, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnarāja, and Dhūmravarṇa.
In the worship of the Sun and in the worship of the Goddess,
one should worship Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī.
In the worship of Tripura and other deities, however, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.

Then, having dispelled the celestial obstacles by beholding with divine vision while reciting the *deya-mantra*, one should dispel the obstacles moving through the atmosphere by sprinkling water while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ. With that same mantra, one should dispel the terrestrial obstacles by striking the ground three times with the left heel.

Then, slightly contracting the right limb and touching the left threshold of the door, one should enter the interior of the pavilion with the right foot leading, thereby providing a path for the departed spirits to exit.

On the left-hand path (vāmamārga), however, entry into the pavilion is preceded by the left foot of the Śakti; the same applies to initiation performed by a female officiant. Then, in the south-western direction:
"Oṃ, salutation to Vāstupuruṣa, the lord of the site, Brahmā."

Having thus worshipped with flowers and consecrated rice (*akṣata*) and having prostrated, one should sprinkle the interior of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the water for the general offering (*sāmānyārgha*), and then perform the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). They are as follows:
while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should gaze upon the interior of the pavilion.

With the syllable *phaṭ*, one should perform the sprinkling with the general *argha* water. With that same mantra, one should strike [the site] with *darbha* grass. With the mantra *huṃ*, one should sprinkle it.

Then, having thoroughly perfumed the interior of the pavilion with incense such as *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *aguru*, and camphor, one should combine the seven scattering materials—fried grain (*lāja*), sandalwood, white mustard, ashes, *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice—and [scatter them].
Having consecrated [the water] seven times with the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*:
*Oṃ, may those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.* (5.2)
Thus, one should scatter [the offerings] in three ways.

Then, while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should sweep those scattered offerings with a handful of *darbha* grass, heap them into a pile in the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*) upon the seat of the *vardhanī* vessel, and set them there.
Thereafter, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having gratified the Brahmins—
"Oṃ, salutation to Dīpanāthabhairava"—having thus worshipped the Bhairava bearing that name, one should pray with palms joined in reverence:
"O Dīpanātha, in this sacred field, for the sake of unimpeded accomplishment and for the success of the initiation sacrifice, you should grant me your permission. (5.3)
O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon—homage to you, Bhairava; you should grant me permission. || 5-4 ||

Having thus taken up the *anuśāsana*, while reciting the mantra "phaṭ," he should go to the altar (*vedikā*). Having fashioned a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the altar out of clay, and having drawn the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala upon it, he should arrange the articles for worship in their proper places, spread out a seat, take the water vessel located on his left side, and perform the purification of the water.
It is as follows:
Having purified with the seed-syllable of air, *ya*;
having incinerated with the seed-syllable of fire, *ra*;
and having flooded with the seed-syllable of water, *va*.
Having sprinkled [the water] with the *prāyatryā* [mantra] and rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*,
one should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) three times with that water, reciting: *oṃ ātmatattvāya svāhā*, *oṃ vidyātattvāya svāhā*, and *oṃ śivatattvāya svāhā*.
Having sprinkled the seat with "Astrāya Phaṭ" and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus upon it:
"The Earth, Meru’s summit is the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is the meter (chandaḥ), Kūrma is the deity; the application (viniyoga) is for the acceptance of the seat.
Having thus taken hold of the seat—
Oṃ, O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.

Hrīṃ! *Namaḥ* to the lotus-seated Ādhāraśakti—having thus worshipped the seat, and having sat upon it in the sequence of the svastika, lotus, or other postures while reciting the *ātman-mantra*, one should perform the *saṃkalpa* as follows:

*Oṃ*, beginning with "Today," and so forth: "I, [Name] Devaśarman, of the [Name] Gotra, shall perform the worship of the deity [Name], the agent of the initiation rite for the mantra of the deity [Name], with whatever offerings are available. This is the *saṃkalpa*. Having offered the *argha* to the Sun with: *Oṃ hrāḥ hrīḥ saḥ, to the venerable Sūrya, seated upon a throne surrounded by planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, yogas, and karaṇas; this is your *argha*, svāhā*, one should consecrate the materials for worship.
That is as follows: having formed the *nārāca-mudrā*—
Reciting the mantra *hrāḥ huḥ phaṭ*, one should gaze with an even vision upon the perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth. With the mantra *raḥ*, one should touch the tip of the lamp flame.
Then—
Uttering the seed-syllable *auṃ*, touching water with the *devatīrtha* [part of the hand], and holding the water vessel with the left hand, one should recite the mantra:
*jaṃ jalādhārapātrāya namaḥ*.
Then, placing the joined palms (*añjali*) upon the head to the left—

Oṃ, homage to the gurus; Oṃ, homage to the supreme gurus; Oṃ, homage to the gurus who are both supreme and subordinate—having thus bowed to the three gurus, and having prostrated to Gaṇapati on the right and to [the deity named] Amukadevatā in the center—
Of unbroken circular form, by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
"Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state has been revealed.
Having thus bowed again to the Guru, one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) as follows:
Taking a flower smeared with sandalwood paste while reciting the mantra *hsauḥ*,

crushing it between both hands while reciting the mantra *phaṭ*, taking that flower with the left hand, whirling it around one’s head while muttering the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and then smelling it— [one should recite]:
*hauḥ | oṃ | May all those who harm me and all those who seek to do me injury go to destruction.* (5–6)

Having recited, "May death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the head of the enemy," one should cast [the offering] toward the northeast with the mantra *phaṭ* while employing the *nārāca-mudrā*. Then,

having performed the binding of the ten directions (*digbandhana*) by means of the *astra-mantra* preceded by three *tāla*-claps and finger-snaps (*choṭikā*) in an upward sequence, and having protected that generated splendor with the *vahni-prākāra-mudrā*, one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) using either the root mantra, its seed-syllable, or the *praṇava* (oṃ), and then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
For example—having placed both hands palms-upward upon one's own lap—

Thinking "I am He," one should unite the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which has the form of a lamp-flame, with the *kuṇḍalinī* situated at the *mūlādhāra*—the seat of the heart-lotus—by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*. Having pierced the six wheels known as *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūra*, *anāhata*, *viśuddha*, and *ājñā*, one should join it with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) located within the pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus at the head, which faces downward. Therein, the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*)—namely earth, water, fire, air, ether; smell, taste, form, touch, sound; nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear; speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals; and nature (*prakṛti*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*)—are dissolved in the aforementioned order.

Having visualized—*ya*—that is, having contemplated the smoke-colored seed-syllable *ya*, the seed of wind, in the left nostril, one should fill the body with air by reciting it sixteen times; then, holding the nostrils, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention) by reciting it fifty or sixty-four times. Having purified the body along with the black-colored personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) residing in the left abdomen, one should exhale the air through the right nostril by reciting it fifty or thirty-two times. In the same way, the options regarding the number of recitations should be understood for what follows as well.
Then, in the right nostril—

Having meditated on *raḥ*—the seed-syllable of fire (*vahni-bīja*)—which is red in color, one should fill the body by reciting it sixteen times; then, holding the nostrils and performing *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) by reciting it sixty-four times, one burns away [impurities] along with the sin; finally, by reciting it thirty-two times, one should exhale the air through the left nostril along with the ashes.

Then, having held *ṭhaḥ*—the seed-syllable of the moon (*candra-bīja*)—which is white in color, at the left nostril, one should lead the moon to the forehead by reciting it sixteen times, and visualize the Supreme Self in the form of the moon within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus.
Having bathed the entire body with the nectar flowing from that moon on the forehead—consisting of the letters of the Mātṛkā—by reciting the seed-syllable of Varuṇa (*va*) sixty-four times;

and having contemplated the body as very firm by reciting the seed-syllable of Earth (*la*) thirty-two times; then, having dissolved the five elements into the Supreme Self and re-established them in their respective places according to the stated sequence, one should visualize a body produced in the form of radiant energy (*tejas*), fit for the worship of the Deity.

"Haṃsa"—having thus drawn the individual soul (jīvātman) from the Supreme Soul (paramātman) and established it within the lotus of the heart, one should contemplate the Self as having the form of the Deity.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi):
"Ā! So 'ham; my vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are here, my vital breaths are established here, Ā! So 'ham."
"O my life-force, live here, remain here! May I, and all my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, and smell—having come here, remain happily for a long time, Svāhā!
Having thus performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) in one's own heart, one should perform the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* as follows:

Of this Śrīmātṛkāsarasvatī mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Mātṛkāsarasvatī is the deity (devatā), the consonants are the seeds (bījas), the vowels are the powers (śaktis), and the manifest forms are the pegs (kīlakas). With the prior purification of the body, the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining one's desired goal through the ritual placement of the letters (lipinyāsa). On the head: *namaḥ* to Brahmā, the seer. In the mouth: *namaḥ* to Gāyatrī, the meter.
In the heart: *namaḥ* to Mātṛkāsarasvatī, the deity.
In the secret place: *namaḥ* to the half-syllable seeds.
In the two feet: *namaḥ* to the vowels, the powers (*śakti*).
In all limbs: *namaḥ* to the manifestations, the stakes (*kīlaka*).
The application for the placement of the letters (*lipinyāsa*)—thus, with palms joined in *añjali*:

Then follow the placements on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): A Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ā—salutation (*namaḥ*) with both thumbs. I Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña Ī—*svāhā* with both index fingers. U Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ū—*vaṣaṭ* with both middle fingers. E Ta Tha Da Dha Na AI—*huṃ* with both ring fingers. O Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma AU—*vauṣaṭ* with both little fingers. A Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha La Kṣa AḤ—*phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*) with both palms and backs of the hands.

p. 328) In the same manner, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs as follows: *a*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ā*; "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), and so forth.
Then follows the visualization (*dhyāna*).
For example:
[She] whose face, lips, and middle of the chest were adorned with the fifty letters;
who wore a crescent moon bound upon her radiant crown; and who possessed full, lofty breasts.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes and radiant white luster, holding in her lotus-like hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jar filled with nectar, and a sacred lore.
Having meditated thus, one should place the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, either alone or accompanied by the *visarga*, upon the locations beginning with the forehead.
For example: *aḥ namaḥ* on the forehead.
Āḥ namaḥ—to the face; Iḥ namaḥ—to the right eye; Īḥ namaḥ—to the left eye.
*uḥ* namaḥ—to the right ear;
*ūḥ* namaḥ—to the left ear;
*ṛḥ* namaḥ—to the right nostril.
Ṛḥ namaḥ—to the left nostril; Ḷḥ namaḥ—to the right cheek; Ḹḥ namaḥ—to the left cheek.
*Eiḥ* namaḥ—to the upper lip;
*Aiḥ* namaḥ—to the lower lip;
*Oḥ* namaḥ—to the upper teeth.
Auḥ, obeisance—to the lower teeth;
aḥ, obeisance—to the mouth;
kaḥ, obeisance—to the base of the right arm.
Khaḥ namaḥ—at the right elbow;
Gaḥ namaḥ—at the right wrist;
Ghaḥ namaḥ—at the bases of the fingers of the right hand.
ṄAḤ NAMAḤ—at the tips of the right fingers; CAḤ NAMAḤ—at the base of the left arm;
CHAḤ NAMAḤ—at the left elbow.
Jaḥ namaḥ—at the left wrist;
Jhaḥ namaḥ—at the bases of the left fingers;
Ñaḥ namaḥ—at the tips of the left fingers.
Ṭaḥ namaḥ—at the base of the right foot; Ṭhaḥ namaḥ—at the right knee;
Ḍaḥ namaḥ—at the right ankle.
Ḍhaḥ Namaḥ—at the bases of the toes of the right foot. (p. 329) Ṇaḥ Namaḥ—at the tips of the toes of the right foot. Taḥ Namaḥ—at the base of the left foot.
Thaḥ namaḥ—at the left knee;
daḥ namaḥ—at the left ankle;
dhaḥ namaḥ—at the bases of the toes of the left foot.
*Naḥ* namaḥ—at the tips of the left fingers;
*paḥ* namaḥ—on the right side;
*phaḥ* namaḥ—on the left side.
Baḥ namaḥ—on the back; Bhaḥ namaḥ—at the navel;
Maḥ namaḥ—at the abdomen.
Yaṃ namaḥ—to the heart; Raṃ namaḥ—to the right shoulder; Laṃ namaḥ—to the crown of the head.
*Vaḥ* namaḥ—to the left shoulder. *Śaḥ* namaḥ—to the heart and the right hand. *Ṣaḥ* namaḥ—to the heart and the left hand.
*Saḥ* *namaḥ*—from the heart to the right foot;
*haḥ* *namaḥ*—from the heart to the left foot;
*laḥ* *namaḥ*—from the heart to the abdomen.
*Kṣaḥ* *namaḥ*—this is the pervasive [mantra] from the heart to the mouth.
This is the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Now, the sequence of maintenance (*sthitikrama*).
There, having performed the rites from the invocation of the sages (*ṛṣi*) up to the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) as previously described, one should meditate as follows:
[She who possesses] the luster of vermilion, adorned with immeasurable ornaments, and three eyes.

One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady, who has the luster of gold, standing by his side, holding a book and a rosary of beads in her hands, and carrying a knowledge-mantra, a rosary, a deer-calf, and a water-pot. (5–7)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) as follows:

*oṃ namaḥ* at the right ankle, and so forth; up to *kṣa/ namaḥ* at the mouth, starting from the heart. Then again, one should place the letters from *ḍa* to *ṭha*, joined with the *visarga* and the *anusvāra*, beginning with *a/ḥ namaḥ* at the forehead, and ending with *ṭha/ namaḥ* at the right knee.
Thus is the sequence of maintenance (*sthiti*).
Now follows the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Here too, having performed the ritual placement of the sages (*ṛṣinyāsa*) and so forth as before, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*).
p. 330) For example:
[I worship] the three-eyed goddess, who incessantly holds in her hands a rosary of beads, a young deer, a lofty axe, and the sciences.
One should bow to the Mistress of Colors, who bears the crescent moon upon her head, whose luster is like that of a red lotus, and who is bent by the weight of her breasts.
Having meditated thus:
"Oṃ namaḥ," one should place the phonemes from *kṣa* down to *a*, joined with the bindu (e.g., *kṣaṃ*, *khaṃ*, etc.), at their respective locations beginning with the heart and ending with the mouth;
this is the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).

In this regard, the placement (*nyāsa*) should first be performed by ascetics (*yati*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), and others according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), then according to the order of maintenance (*sthiti-krama*), and then according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*).

For celibate students (*brahmacārin*), the placement should be performed first according to the order of maintenance, then according to the order of withdrawal, and then according to the order of emanation.

For householders (*gṛhastha*), however, the placement should be performed first according to the order of withdrawal, then according to the order of emanation, and then according to the order of maintenance. This threefold [method] constitutes the external placement of the Mother-letters (*bāhyamātṛkā-nyāsa*).

Now follows the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (antarmātṛkānyāsa). Therein, one should meditate upon the letters of the Mātṛkās as being composed of nectar, having emerged from the thousand-petaled lotus—which has been touched by Kuṇḍalinī awakened by the hearing of the sound at the Mūlādhāra—and having pervaded one’s own body via the path of the Suṣumṇā. One should mentally place the sixteen vowels, beginning with *a* and ending with *au*, along with the nasal bindu (*m*) and preceded by the Praṇava (*oṃ*), on the petals of the sixteen-petaled lotus called Viśuddha located in the throat, in the sequence starting from the eastern petal and ending with *namaḥ*. For example: *oṃ aṃ namaḥ* [to the eastern petal], and so forth.
*Oṃ a*, *namaḥ*, and so forth.
Then, one should place the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha* upon the petals of the twelve-petalled lotus called Āhata located at the heart, following that same sequence.
Next, one should place the ten letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha* upon the petals of the ten-petalled lotus called Maṇipūraka located at the navel.
Then, one should place the six syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *la* upon the petals of the six-petalled lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna at the base of the *liṅga*.
Next, one should arrange the four syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *sa* upon the petals of the four-petalled lotus called Mūlādhāra.
Then, one should place the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* upon the two petals of the two-petalled lotus called Ājñā situated between the eyebrows.
Thus ends the internal nyāsa of the Mātṛkās.
As follows: (p. 331) Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti.
Oṃ, salutation to Mūlaprakṛti;
Oṃ, salutation to Kūrma;
Oṃ, salutation to Ananta.
Oṃ, homage to Varāha; Oṃ, homage to the Earth;
Oṃ, homage to the Ocean of Milk.
Oṃ, salutation to Śvetadvīpa; Oṃ, salutation to Maṇimaṇḍapa;
Oṃ, salutation to Kalpavṛkṣa.
Oṃ, obeisance to the jeweled pedestal; Oṃ, obeisance to the jewel lion-throne;
all of this is within the heart.
Oṃ dharmāya namaḥ—on the right shoulder.
Oṃ jñānāya namaḥ—on the left shoulder. Oṃ vairājñāya namaḥ—on the left thigh.
Oṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ—on the right thigh.
Oṃ adharmāya namaḥ—on the face.
Oṃ ajñānāya namaḥ—on the left side.
Oṃ, salutation to Avairāgya—at the navel. Oṃ, salutation to Anaiśvarya—at the right side.
Oṃ, salutation to Ananta—at the heart.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Lotus; Oṃ, obeisance to the Root of Bliss;
Oṃ, obeisance to the Stem of Consciousness.
Oṃ, homage to the lotus whose essence is all reality;
Oṃ, homage to the petals consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti); Oṃ, homage to the filaments consisting of the transformations (vikāra).
Oṃ, salutation to the pericarp enriched with the fifty seed-syllables of the letters;
Oṃ A, salutation to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās;
Oṃ U, salutation to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen kalās.
Oṃ ma/ homage to the fire-maṇḍala, whose essence consists of ten kalās;
sa/ homage to sattva;
ra/ homage to rajas.
ta/ to Tamas, obeisance;
ā/ to Ātman, obeisance; a/ to Antarātman, obeisance.
*Pa*: Homage to the Supreme Self (*paramātmane namaḥ*).
*Hrī*: Homage to the Self of Knowledge (*jñānātmane namaḥ*).

Having performed the placement on the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*) with the formula, "Homage to the Yogic Seat of such-and-such deity," one should meditate upon the deity within the seat that is one's own body and worship her with mental offerings.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: having mentally worshipped within one's own body, according to the stated order of the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*), from the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) up to the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), and having meditated upon the deity as described on that seat, one should contemplate the identity [of the self] with the deity through the thought "I am He" (*so'ham*). Then, having offered mental services such as perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, one should perform the mental oblation (*mānasahoma*). For example:

Having conceptualized the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) as consisting of egoism, falsehood, backbiting, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and so forth, and having conceived the mind as the *sruva* ladle and the *suṣumṇā* nerve as the *sruk* ladle; and having meditated upon the fire-pit at the *mūlādhāra* as a four-cornered hearth representing the Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Knowledge-Self; and having visualized therein the blazing fire in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, one should utter the root mantra with the mind alone and [recite]:
"In the fire of my own self, which blazes with the oblation of merit and demerit, I daily offer the functions of the senses by means of the mental ladle through the path of the *suṣumṇā*. (5–9)
Having recited this verse,
[one offers] the first oblation with "I offer merit, svāhā.
Again, having recited that same verse at the end of the root mantra—
"I offer evil, svāhā"—this is the second oblation.
Likewise, having recited that same verse at the end of the root mantra:
"I offer action, svāhā"—this is the third oblation.
"Thus,
for what should not be done, svāhā"— this is the fourth oblation.
"I offer the intention, svāhā"— this is the fifth oblation.

"I offer conceptual construction, svāhā"—this is the sixth oblation. "I offer dharma, svāhā"—this is the seventh oblation. Having thus offered these oblations, one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
As it is said at the end of the root mantra:
"Holding the *unmanī*-ladle with the hands of Light and Impatience (*amarṣa*), I offer the oil of the portions of merit and demerit into the full fire; *svāhā*!"

Having thus performed the *pūrṇāhuti* as prescribed [on p. 333], and having recollected the Self—which is free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)—one should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times and offer that recitation to the deity. In some traditions, however, the recitation is said to precede the fire-oblation (*homa*). This concludes the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).

Then, having established the general water-offering (*sāmānyārgha*) on one's right according to the prescribed method for the worship of the door, one should perform the installation of the ritual jar (*kalaśa*).

For example, having sprinkled the ground with the general offering water while reciting "svavāme— astrāya phaṭ," and having drawn there a mandala consisting of a circle, a hexagon, and a square, one should worship it at the end of the root mantra with:
"Homage to the mandala that serves as the base for the flask of such-and-such deity."
Saying "Phaṭ," one washes the base; then, at the end of the root mantra, saying "I establish the base for the flask of [the deity named] Amuka, Namaḥ," one establishes the base.
Then, as before, one worships it with "Obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās."

Having washed the *kalaśa* and adorned it with garments, garlands, and so forth, one should install it by reciting at the end of the root mantra: "I install the *kalaśa* of [Name] Devatā; *namaḥ*. Then, having worshipped it with: "*A*, *namaḥ* to the solar disc consisting of twelve *kalās*," one should fill the *kalaśa* with pure water while reciting the root mantra. However, in the Vāmācāra tradition, one should fill it with the *hetu-dravya* (causal substance), as that is seen in the *Śyāmārahasya* and other texts.

Then, having worshipped that water with the mantra: *Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar maṇḍala consisting of sixteen digits*, one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) from the solar maṇḍala using the *Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva* verse and the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*; protect it with the *astra-mantra*, veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*, gaze upon it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), and sprinkle it with that same mantra. At the end of the root mantra—

"Salutation to the nectar of the jar of such-and-such deity"—having thus worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having covered [the jar] with the *matsya-mudrā*, one should recite "Oṃ, Viṣṇu is at the mouth of the jar," and so on; then, having muttered the root mantra eight times and displayed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should contemplate the jar as being of the nature of the deity.
This is the procedure for the installation of the jar (*kalaśa-sthāpana-vidhi*).

Then one should perform the installation of the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpana*). It is as follows: to the right of the flask (and) on one's own left, having sprinkled the ground with the water of the general *argha* while reciting "Astrāya phaṭ," one should draw there a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square using the *matsyamudrā*.

p. 334) Oṃ, homage to the mandala of the conch-vessel of such-and-such deity— having thus worshipped the mandala with fragrance and flowers, and having worshipped the four corners starting from the southeast of the square [mandala], as well as in front and in the cardinal directions, with the mantras of the six limbs—
[saying] "phaṭ," one should wash the vessel with water and, at the end of the root mantra,
saying "I establish the conch-vessel of such-and-such deity, homage," one should place the vessel.

*Ma Ra*. Having worshipped the support (*ādhāra*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the circle of fire (*vahnimaṇḍala*), whose self consists of ten digits (*kalā*), which serves as the conch-vessel for such-and-such deity," one should worship the ten digits of fire in a clockwise direction starting from the east.
As follows:
*Ya*: Obeisance to Dhūmrārcis.
Ra: Homage to Ūṣmā.
La: Homage to Jvalinī.
Va: Homage to Jvālinī.
Śa: Homage to Visphuliṅginī.
Ṣa: Homage to Suśrī. Sa: Homage to Surūpā.
Haḥ / Salutation to Kapilā. Laḥ / Salutation to Havyavāhā.
Kṣaḥ / Salutation to Kavyavāhā—thus.
If one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one should worship with: "Obeisance to the ten kalās of fire, beginning with Dhūmrārcis.
Then, the conch—

Saying "phaṭ," one should wash [the conch]. Then, at the end of the root mantra, saying "I establish the conch of such-and-such deity; namaḥ," one should place the conch upon the support (ādhāra). Having worshipped the conch with the mantra: "Obeisance to the solar disc consisting of twelve digits that bestows wealth, which serves as the vessel for the conch of such-and-such deity," one should visualize a hexagon and the earth-circle within the conch. Having worshipped the six corners with the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra), one should worship the twelve digits of the sun, beginning with *Tapinī*, starting from the east and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Namely:
Ka Bha, homage to Tāpinī; Kha Ba, homage to Tāpinī.
ga/ pha/ obeisance to Tāpinī; gha/ pa/ obeisance to Marīcī; ṅa/ na/ obeisance to Jvālinī.
ca/ dha/ salutation to Rucyā; cha/ da/ salutation to Suṣumṇā;
ja/ tha/ salutation to Bhogadā.
Jha / Ta / Salutation to Viśvā.
Ña / Ṇa / Salutation to Bodhinī. Ṭa / Ḍha / Salutation to Dhāriṇī.
"Ṭha/ Ḍa/ Kṣamāyai namaḥ"— thus [one should worship].
If one is unable [to do so],
one should worship with "Namaḥ to the twelve kalās of the Sun, beginning with Tapinī."
Then, at the end of the root-mantra, one should pronounce the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order as follows:

kṣa, ha, sa, ṣa, śa, va, la, ra, ya, ma, bha, ba, pha, pa, na, dha, da, tha, ta, ṇa, ḍha, ḍa, ṭha, ṭa, ña, jha, ja, cha, ca, ṅa, gha, ga, kha, ka, aḥ, a, au, o, ai, e, ḹ, ḷ, ṝ, ṛ, ū, u, ī, i, ā, a. Having thus recited the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order—

"Oṃ, I fill the conch of such-and-such deity with nectar; namaḥ. Having thus filled the conch with pure water, one should worship the water in the conch with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, saying: "Oṃ, saḥ, namaḥ to the lunar maṇḍala, which consists of sixteen digits and bestows all desires. Then, according to the stated sequence, one should worship the sixteen digits of the moon, beginning with Amṛtā.
For example:
a/ homage to Amṛtā;
ā/ homage to Mānadā.
i/ Homage to Pūṣā. ī/ Homage to Puṣṭi. u/ Homage to Tuṣṭi.
Ū: Homage to Ratī (Delight).
Ṛ: Homage to Dhṛti (Fortitude).
Ṝ: Homage to Śaśinī (the Moon-like One).
Ḷ / Homage to Candrikā (the Moonlight). Ḹ / Homage to Kānti (Radiance). E / Homage to Jyotsnā (Moonlight).
Ai, obeisance to Śrī; O, obeisance to Prīti; Au, obeisance to Aṅgadā.
a/ Homage to Pūrṇā.
aḥ/ Homage to Pūrṇāmṛtā. Thus [one should recite]. If one is unable—

"Obeisance to the sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon, beginning with Amṛtā. If one is capable, one should invoke each [digit] individually, perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths), and worship them with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.

Then, having cast into that [water] sandalwood paste (*gandha*), flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley (*yava*), tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds (*tila*), mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), and *dūrvā* grass, one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb using the *aṅkuśamudrā* while reciting "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva... and so forth. Having united the sacred waters within that water by means of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*)—
Having cast the flower with "vauṣaṭ," having displayed the Mālinī mudrā with "vaṣaṭ," and having rendered it nectarine by means of the Dhenu mudrā with "vam," [recite] at the end of the root mantra—

"O such-and-such deity, come here; stay here"—having thus invoked the deity from the heart [center] into that [consecrated vessel], having displayed the mudrās of mounting and so forth, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the six limb-mantras, having protected the directions with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), having veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), having gazed upon it with "vauṣaṭ," having stabilized it with the conch-mudrā (*śaṅkhamudrā*), having inflamed it with the womb-mudrā (*yonimudrā*), and having worshipped the chosen deity there with the root-mantra and offerings of perfume, flowers, and so forth, as well as worshipping the six limbs, one should cover it with the fish-mudrā (*matsyamudrā*) and recite the root-mantra eight times.
This is the procedure for the installation in the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpanavidhi*).

Then, having poured a little water from the conch into the water of the *kalaśa*, and having set aside a small space on the right side of the *sāmānyārgha* for the *pādya* vessel, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.

This is as follows: having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle within a circle with the water from the *sāmānyārgha* and worshipped it with "Namaḥ," one should wash the *prokṣaṇī* vessel along with its stand using water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, and then place it upon that [mandala].
Having filled [the vessel] with water by reciting "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune...

and so forth, having worshipped it with scents and flowers while saying "Namaḥ," having cast kusha grass, flowers, barley, and so on into it with the Praṇava (Oṃ), and having consecrated it three times with the Praṇava alone, one should display the *dhenumudrā* and pour a small amount of the ordinary *argha* water into that water.
This is the procedure for the placement of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.

Then, having placed the vessel for the *pādya* (water for washing the feet) on its left side—just as one establishes the general *argha* vessel—and having cast substances such as *uśīra*, *golocanā*, *śyāmāka*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā* into that water, one should perform the establishment of the special *argha* (*viśeṣārgha*) in front of oneself, to the left of the general *argha* situated on its own left.
As for the procedure for that:
at the place where the *gālinī* and other mudrās are displayed during the establishment of the conch, one should display the *yoni* and other mudrās.

Regarding the cult of Viṣṇu, however, the specific distinction is that one should display the *dhenumudrā* in the place where the *yonimudrā* is [otherwise] prescribed; this is the general rule. But in the case of the *Śyāmā* and other *vidyās*, there is a specific procedure:
having drawn a hexagon with a square outside it, one should worship the four seats (*pīṭha*) in the four corners of the square, starting from the eastern corner and proceeding clockwise. As follows:
Ha! Homage to the seat of Oḍḍiyāna; Ga! Homage to the seat of Jālandhara;
Ṛ! Homage to the seat of Pūrṇagiri; A! Homage to the seat of Kāmarūpa—thus [one should worship].

Then, in that same sequence, one should worship the six corners of the hexagon with the mantras of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Then, one should worship the three corners of the triangle with the three parts of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). And where a division [of the mantra] is impossible, there one should worship all three corners with the entire root mantra alone.

Then, having uttered either the root mantra or its seed-syllable alone—saying "Obeisance to the support-power (ādhāraśakti) for the specific deity [named] so-and-so"—one should worship the letter *Ī* situated in the center of the triangle. Having washed the support with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should establish the support by reciting at the end of the root mantra:
"I establish the support for the specific deity [named] so-and-so; obeisance. Thus, the support is established.

Having worshipped the base (*ādhāra*) with the mantra: *ma ra dharmapradadaśakalātmane vahnimaṇḍalāyāmukadevatāviśeṣārghādhārāya namaḥ*, one should also worship the ten digits (*kalā*) of fire, beginning with *dhūmrārcis* and so forth, according to the sequence prescribed for the placement of the conch (*śaṅkha*).
Then, having washed the vessel as before, one should place it while reciting at the end of the root mantra:
*amukadevatāviśeṣārghapātraṃ sthāpayāmi namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the vessel with the mantra: *aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāyārthapradadvādaśakalātmane amukadevatāviśeṣārghapātrāya namaḥ*, one should worship the twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun, beginning with Tapinī, according to the procedure prescribed for the installation of the conch (*śaṅkha*). Then, having recited the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order at the end of the root mantra, one should fill the special offering (*viśeṣārgha*) with water from the pitcher. However, those following the left-hand path (*vāmamārgin*) should fill the special offering with substances such as the *svayambhū* flower produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, or with whatever substance is prescribed as the specific cause for that deity in their own ritual manual.
Then:

"Obeisance to the lunar disc consisting of the sixteen digits that bestow all desires, for the sake of the nectar-offering (argha) to the specific deity [Name]—thus worshiping, one should worship each of the sixteen digits of the moon, beginning with Amṛtā, according to the sequence prescribed for the installation of the conch.

Then, having drawn a yantra consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon within the nectar of the vessel, one should write the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* on the three lines of the triangle, the letters from *ka* to *ta*, and the letters from *tha* to *sa* respectively; and in the center—"

Having written the three seed-syllables *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* and worshipped the triangle with the three root-parts (*mūlakhaṇḍa*), one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) within the hexagon. Then, with the mantra beginning "O Gaṅgā and Yamunā," and using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb, contemplate them as consisting of those waters, and cast into [the vessel] sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and *dūrvā* grass. In the practice of the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*), however, having cast a piece of meat using the *mīna-mudrā*, if the vessel is filled by means of the *kāraṇa* [liquor], one should purify the previously mentioned *kuladravya* (family substance) using the *kumbha-mudrā* and cast it in.
Then, having meditated upon Ānandabhairava accompanied by Ānandabhairavī and having invoked them there with these two mantras:

"H S KṢ M L V R YŪ / Vaṣaṭ to Ānandabhairava" and "S H KṢ M L V R YĪ / Vauṣaṭ to Sudhādevī," and having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should utter the three-syllabled *Vālā* mantra.
Born from the essence of the cosmic egg, it is the source of all essences without exception.
O you who bring forth the essence of nectar, filling the great vessel;
O supreme self of nectar, who bestows the bliss of unbroken, singular flavor! 5-11
O you whose form is Akula, place the mantra of spontaneous vibration within me—
within that which abides as Akula, whose nature is nectar, and whose body is the knowledge of spiritual attainment.
Place immortality within this substance of moist form;
and having achieved a state of singular identity with that form, [reside] as one whose very nature is that [substance]. (5.13)
"Having become the form of supreme nectar, cause the consciousness to flash forth within me.
Having consecrated the five jewels with these mantras, one should worship them as follows:

*Glū*, obeisance to Gaganaratna; *Slū*, obeisance to Svargaratna; *Plū*, obeisance to Pātālaratna; *Mlū*, obeisance to Martyaratna; *Nlū*, obeisance to Nāgaratna—thus one should worship [these] in the center and in the four directions starting from the front.

(p. 339) Then, having invoked the heart-deity and the other deities there with the root mantra, having displayed the mudrās of invocation and so forth, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the six limbs, having protected [them] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having veiled [them] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).

Having thus rendered [the water] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, and having worshipped with the root mantra using perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer three handfuls of flowers. Then, having covered the *arghya* with the *matsyamudrā*—using the right hand if one follows the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇamārgī*), or the left hand if one follows the left-hand path (*vāmamārgī*)—one should recite the root mantra eight or ten times. Visualizing the *arghya* as the form of the deity, one should display the *bhūtinī*, *dhenu*, and *yonimudrās*.
This is the procedure for the installation of the special *arghya*.
One should also establish the special *argha* (offering water) for Tārā, Śrīvidyā, and others according to this very same procedure.

Then, having drawn a triangle with the water from the general *argha* to the left of the special *argha*—or, in the case of Vaiṣṇava and other traditions, having merely made a circle—one should perform the placement of the *ācamanīya* vessel as in the case of the general *argha*, and cast substances such as nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola into that water.

Then, having prepared a mandala to its left as before, one should place a vessel for the honey-mixture (madhuparka) filled with honey, curd, and ghee; to its left again, one should place a vessel for sipping water (ācamanīya), filling it with pure water just like the previous sipping-vessel.
Then, having consecrated all the vessels eight times each with the root mantra, one should display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā) and the other mudrās.

Then, having taken a small amount of the nectar from the conch (*śaṅkhāmṛta*) and the special *argha* nectar (*viśeṣārghāmṛta*) with a bundle of *dūrvā* grass or with flowers and so forth, and having poured them into other vessels, one should satisfy Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī on their heads with the *viśeṣārghāmṛta* alone using the two previously mentioned mantras and the *tattvamudrā*. Then, with the nectar from the conch and using the same *tattvamudrā*, one should satisfy the Gurus of the Divine, Siddha, and Human lineages (*divyaugha-siddhaugha-mānavaugha*) as prescribed in their respective *kalpas* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). One should also satisfy one’s own Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru.
It is as follows:
I offer libations to the venerable sandals of the Guru, Śrī-Amukānandanātha; obeisance. Likewise:

I offer libations to the venerable sandals of the Paramaguru; obeisance. I offer libations to the venerable sandals of the Parāparaguru; obeisance. I offer libations to the venerable sandals of the Parameṣṭhiguru; obeisance.
Thus, one should offer libations either three times or once.
In cases such as the Vāmācāra, where the Guru-vessel and other items have been set out separately, one should satisfy the lineage of Gurus using only the substance from the Guru-vessel.
Then, with the water from the special *argha* offering, one should satisfy the root deity in the heart.

Having recited the root mantra, one should satisfy the venerable [Amuka] Devī— along with her limbs (*sāṅgām*), her retinue (*saparivārām*), her weapons (*sāyudhām*), and her vehicle (*savāhanām*)— by saying "I satisfy [her], *namaḥ*," either three times or once. Then, having sprinkled oneself, the worship mandala, and the materials for worship with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using both the root mantra and the weapon mantra (*astramantra*), one should display the *dhenumudrā*.

Then, having worshipped the deities of the *pīṭha* in their respective locations within one’s own body with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the previously mentioned sequence of *pīṭha*-nyāsa; having visualized the *maṇi-pīṭha* in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus and meditated upon the deity there; having visualized oneself as the form of the deity and worshipped the deity with the root mantra using the four services of perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps; having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) once each on the head, the heart, the *mūlādhāra*, the feet, and all the limbs; having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times or as many times as possible; having offered that recitation (*japa*) to the deity; having poured the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel onto the ground; having refilled the vessel with other water; one should worship the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
"Oṃ, salutation to the Sarvatobhadra Maṇḍala.

Then, having filled its pericarp with *śāli* rice, one should place a heap of rice upon it, spread *darbha* grass over that, and set down the *kūrca* (bundle of grass) as prescribed along with unbroken grains; then one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*).
For instance, in the northern direction of the maṇḍala—

Having worshipped with the words: "Salutation to the venerable Gurus; salutation to the venerable Parama-gurus; salutation to the venerable Parāpara-gurus; salutation to the venerable Parameṣṭhi-gurus," one should worship in the southern direction with the words:
"Salutation to Mahāgaṇapati.
Then, through meditative visualization, [one should worship] beneath the mandala—
Oṃ, salutation to the seven netherworlds beginning with Atala.
Oṃ, salutation to Maṇḍūka;
oṃ, salutation to Kālāgnirudra.
In ascending order:
Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti;
Oṃ, salutation to Mūlaprakṛti.
Oṃ, obeisance to Kūrma; Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta;
Oṃ, obeisance to Varāha.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Earth;
Oṃ, obeisance to the Ocean of Nectar;
Oṃ, obeisance to the Island of Jewels.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to the jeweled pavilion (maṇimaṇḍapa)," one should worship in the four directions and the center of the mandala with "Oṃ, obeisance to the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa). By means of visualization, beneath those [trees], one should worship with "Oṃ, obeisance to the jeweled altar (maṇivedikā)," and above that—
p. 341) Oṃ, homage to the Jewel Lion Throne—at the four corners beginning with the southeast:
Oṃ, homage to Dharma;
Oṃ, homage to Jñāna.
Oṃ, homage to dispassion; Oṃ, homage to sovereignty;
[these are placed] in the cardinal directions in order starting from the east.
Oṃ, homage to non-dharma; Oṃ, homage to ignorance;
Oṃ, homage to lack of dispassion.
Oṃ, salutation to Anaiśvarya;
in the center, in the upward sequence:
Oṃ, salutation to Ānandakanda.
Oṃ, salutation to Savinnālā;
Oṃ, salutation to the lotus whose essence is all reality (sarvatattva);
Oṃ, salutation to the petals consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Oṃ, homage to the filaments consisting of the transformations;
Oṃ, homage to the pericarp enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters;
A, homage to the solar disc whose essence consists of twelve digits.
Oṃ, homage to the lunar mandala, whose essence consists of sixteen digits, Ma; homage to the fire mandala, whose essence consists of ten digits, Sa;
homage to sattva.
ra: salutation to Rajas; ta: salutation to Tamas;
ā: salutation to Ātman.
a/ Homage to the inner self; pa/ Homage to the supreme self;
hrī/ Homage to the self of knowledge.

Having thus worshipped, one should worship the respective *pīṭha-śaktis* mentioned in the specific ritual manual (*kalpa*) upon the filaments and in the center of the lotus, proceeding in order from the east and so forth.
Then, having recited the *pīṭha-mantra*, one should worship in the center with: "Obeisance to the yoga-pīṭha of the deity [Name]."
Then, having recited the root mantra—"I fashion the form of the deity [Name] of the seat; *namaḥ*"—one should deposit scents, flowers, and so forth into the center of the seat. (p.
342) Then, in that mandala, one should worship the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, with scents, flowers, and so forth, individually.
Then, having taken the jar fashioned from gold or other materials as described,

and having sprinkled it with pure water while reciting "phaṭ," and having smeared it with sandalwood paste while reciting "huṃ," one should wrap it all around with a triple-stranded thread while uttering the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), fumigate it with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, place the nine gems inside its belly, and set upon it a *kūrca* of grass joined with *dūrvā*, sandalwood, and unbroken rice.
Uttering the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should place the pitcher (*kumbha*) upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

Then, having worshipped the twelve digits (*kalā*) of the Sun—beginning with *Tapinī*—in the pitcher, proceeding clockwise from the east, and having meditated on the unity of the pitcher, the pedestal, and the *yāga*, one should recite the letters of the *mātṛkā* in reverse order. At the end of that, uttering the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should fill the pitcher with the intention that it is the deity itself, using either a decoction of the fifty medicinal herbs, a decoction of milky trees, a decoction made from the bark of the *palāśa* tree, or water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) well-scented with perfumes and flowers.

Then, having worshipped the sixteen digits (*kalās*) of the Moon—beginning with *Amṛtā* and so forth—in the water of the jar, proceeding clockwise starting from the east; and having filled the interior of a conch shell with a decoction of medicinal herbs, or with water from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) well-scented with perfumes and flowers; and having visualized the eight perfumes (*gandhāṣṭaka*) within that water; one should invoke the ten digits of Fire beginning with *Dhūmrārcis* therein, [reciting]:

*Ā*, *Hrīḥ*, *Kroḥ*, *Ya*, *Ra*, *La*, *Va*, *Śa*, *Ṣa*, *Sa*, *Ha*, *La*, *Kṣaḥ*, *Haṃsaḥ So’haṃ*; "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the ten digits of Fire beginning with *Dhūmrārcis* are established here, here. Likewise: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is established here, here. Likewise.
Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) with "All the sense organs," and so forth,

and having worshipped [the deity] with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) beginning with "Salutation to fragrance (*gandha*) from the ten kalās of fire, namely Dhūmrārcis and the rest," according to the sequence prescribed for the installation of the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpana*).

Having worshipped each [deity] individually with scents, flowers, and so forth—beginning with "Obeisance to Dhūmrārcis" (ya) and so on—in this very manner, one should invoke and worship the twelve digits (*kalās*) of the Sun, beginning with *Tapinī*, and the sixteen digits of the Moon, beginning with *Amṛtā*, and thus worship the fifty digits. For example: having invoked the ten digits beginning with *Sṛṣṭi* by means of the Vedic mantra: "Ha Oṃ Saḥ! He who dwells in purity, the Vasu who dwells in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest who dwells at the altar, the guest who dwells in the remote dwelling, he who dwells among men, he who dwells in the best, he who dwells in truth, he who dwells in the sky; born of the waters, born of the cows, born of truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth. Thus one should invoke them.

p. 343) Oṃ, obeisance to the ten kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi—having thus worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), one should worship each [kalā] individually with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as follows: Ka/ obeisance to Sṛṣṭi.
kha/ Homage to Ṛddhi. ga/ Homage to Smṛti. gha/ Homage to Medhā.
Ṅa: Homage to Kānti (Beauty). Ca: Homage to Lakṣmī (Fortune). Cha: Homage to Dhṛti (Fortitude).
Ja/ Salutation to Sthirā. Jha/ Salutation to Sthiti.
Ña/ Salutation to Siddhi.
Having thus worshipped with the mantra:

"Oṃ, Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic power; like a terrifying beast that wanders and dwells in the mountains, in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide," one should invoke the ten digits beginning with Old Age (*jarā*). Then, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) and other rites, one should worship them individually with the five offerings, saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the ten digits beginning with Old Age."
For example: Ṭa / Homage to Jarā (Old Age). Ṭha / Homage to Pālinī (The Protectress).
Ḍa/ Homage to Kṣānti. Ḍha/ Homage to Īśvarī.
Ṇa/ Homage to Rati.
ta/ Homage to Kāmikā. tha/ Homage to Varadā. da/ Homage to Hlādinī.
Having worshipped with "Dha! Salutation to Prīti" and "Na! Salutation to Dīrghā"—

Having invoked the ten kalās beginning with Tīkṣṇā by means of the mantra: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may he release us from death as the cucumber from its stem, [but not] from immortality"—(p.
344)—one should worship them with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the ten kalās beginning with Tīkṣṇā," and then worship each one individually as follows:
Pa/ Homage to Tīkṣṇā. Pha/ Homage to Raudrī.
Ba/ Homage to Bhavā.
Bha / Salutation to Nidrā (Sleep). Ma / Salutation to Tandrā (Drowsiness). Ya / Salutation to Kṣudhā (Hunger).
Ra: Salutation to Krodhinī. La: Salutation to Kriyā. Va: Salutation to Utkāriṇī.

Having worshipped with "Śa / Salutation to Mṛtyu," one should invoke and worship the four digits beginning with Yellow (Pītā) as before, using either the mantra "Oṃ tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ divīva cakṣurātatam" or the Gāyatrī mantra.
For example:
Ṣa/ Homage to Pītā (the Yellow One).
Sa/ Homage to Dāruṇā (the Terrible One).
Ha! Salutation to Asitā.
Kṣa! Salutation to Anantā.
Having thus worshipped—
Oṃ! The wise, praising and ever-watchful, kindle that [fire] which is Viṣṇu’s supreme station.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. || 5-14 ||
May Prajāpati sprinkle [you]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow an embryo. (5-15)

"May the two divine Aśvins, garlanded with lotuses, place the embryo within you"—with this mantra, having invoked the sixteen vowels as kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other rites, and worshipped them with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should worship each individually. As follows: p. 345) [The mantras for the sixteen kalās: 1. oṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ | 2. oṃ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ | 3. oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ | 4. oṃ śāntyai namaḥ | 5. oṃ śāntyatītāyai namaḥ | 6. oṃ raktavarṇāyai namaḥ | 7. oṃ pītavarṇāyai namaḥ | 8. oṃ śvetavarṇāyai namaḥ | 9. oṃ kṛṣṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 10. oṃ dhūmravarṇāyai namaḥ | 11. oṃ nīlavarṇāyai namaḥ | 12. oṃ kapilavarṇāyai namaḥ | 13. oṃ haritavarṇāyai namaḥ | 14. oṃ aruṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 15. oṃ śyāmavarṇāyai namaḥ | 16. oṃ śuklavarṇāyai namaḥ | [The mantras for the sixteen vowels: 1. oṃ aṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ | 2. oṃ āṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ | 3. oṃ iṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ | 4. oṃ īṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ | 5. oṃ uṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ | 6. oṃ ṛṃ raktavarṇāyai namaḥ | 7. oṃ ṝṃ pītavarṇāyai namaḥ | 8. oṃ ḷṃ śvetavarṇāyai namaḥ | 9. oṃ ḹṃ kṛṣṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 10. oṃ eṃ dhūmravarṇāyai namaḥ | 11. oṃ aiṃ nīlavarṇāyai namaḥ | 12. oṃ oṃ kapilavarṇāyai namaḥ | 13. oṃ auṃ haritavarṇāyai namaḥ | 14. oṃ aṃ aruṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 15. oṃ aḥ śyāmavarṇāyai namaḥ | 16. oṃ kaṃ śuklavarṇāyai namaḥ | [The mantras for the sixteen consonant groups (mātṛkās): 1. oṃ kaṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ | 2. oṃ khaṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ | 3. oṃ gaṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ | 4. oṃ ghaṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ | 5. oṃ ṅaṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ | 6. oṃ caṃ raktavarṇāyai namaḥ | 7. oṃ chaṃ pītavarṇāyai namaḥ | 8. oṃ jaṃ śvetavarṇāyai namaḥ | 9. oṃ jhaṃ kṛṣṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 10. oṃ ñaṃ dhūmravarṇāyai namaḥ | 11. oṃ ṭaṃ nīlavarṇāyai namaḥ | 12. oṃ ṭhaṃ kapilavarṇāyai namaḥ | 13. oṃ ḍaṃ haritavarṇāyai namaḥ | 14. oṃ ḍhaṃ aruṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 15. oṃ ṇaṃ śyāmavarṇāyai namaḥ | 16. oṃ taṃ śuklavarṇāyai namaḥ | [The mantras for the remaining letters: 17. oṃ thaṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ | 18. oṃ daṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ | 19. oṃ dhaṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ | 20. oṃ naṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ | 21. oṃ paṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ | 22. oṃ phaṃ raktavarṇāyai namaḥ | 23. oṃ baṃ pītavarṇāyai namaḥ | 24. oṃ bhaṃ śvetavarṇāyai namaḥ | 25. oṃ maṃ kṛṣṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 26. oṃ yaṃ dhūmravarṇāyai namaḥ | 27. oṃ raṃ nīlavarṇāyai namaḥ | 28. oṃ laṃ kapilavarṇāyai namaḥ | 29. oṃ vaṃ haritavarṇāyai namaḥ | 30. oṃ śaṃ aruṇavarṇāyai namaḥ | 31. oṃ ṣaṃ śyāmavarṇāyai namaḥ | 32. oṃ saṃ śuklavarṇāyai namaḥ | 33. oṃ haṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ | 34. oṃ l̥ṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ | 35. oṃ kṣaṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ | [The mantras for the sixteen vowels again: 36. oṃ aṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ | 37. oṃ āṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai namaḥ | 38. oṃ iṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ | 39. oṃ īṃ śāntikalāyai namaḥ | 40. oṃ uṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ | 41. oṃ ṛṃ raktavarṇāyai namaḥ | 42. oṃ ṝṃ pītavarṇāyai namaḥ | 43. oṃ ḷṃ śvetavarṇāyai nama
a/ Homage to Nivṛtti. ā/ Homage to Pratiṣṭhā. i/ Homage to Vidyā.
Ī: Homage to Śānti. U: Homage to Indhikā.
Ū: Homage to Dīpikā.
Ṛ / Homage to Recikā. Ṝ / Homage to Mocikā. Ḷ / Homage to Parā.
Ḷ / Homage to Sūkṣmā.
E / Homage to Sūkṣmāmṛtā. Ai / Homage to Jñānāmṛtā.
Oṃ! Salutation to Āpyāyinī.
Auṃ! Salutation to Vyāpinī.
Aḥ! Salutation to Vyomarūpā.
"Aḥ! Salutation to Anantā.
Having thus worshipped, one should pour that water, which consists of the [sixteen] kalās and is contained within the conch, into the pitcher.

Then, having covered the mouth of the pitcher with sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, *cūta*, and other trees, entwined with *indravallī* and conceived as the Kalpavṛkṣa (wish-fulfilling tree), one should place upon that mouth of the pitcher a cup containing fruit and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), conceived as the fruit of the Kalpavṛkṣa.

Then, having wrapped the pitcher with a pair of linen garments and having prepared eight-petaled maṇḍalas near the doors in the four directions starting from the east beneath the altar, one should place heaps of *śāli* rice upon them and set full pitchers on top. Having invoked Dhruva, Dhara, Vāgīśa, and Vighneśa into those [pitchers] in order from the east, one should worship them with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). In that same manner, having set up pitchers in the corners starting from the southeast, one should invoke and worship Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and Maṅgalā in them.

Furthermore, having installed other jars in the eight directions starting from the east and having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) such as Indra and the others within them, one should also worship the eight elephants of the directions— namely Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Uñjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka— in front of them.
Then, one should perform the worship of the primary deity in the principal pitcher (*pradhānakalaśa*).
Therein, first reciting the root mantra:
"I fashion the form of the deity [Name], obeisance," one should fashion the form with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and then perform the invocation (*āvāhana*).
For example—having placed a flower within the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and meditated upon the deity, one should recite the root mantra either three times or once, saying:

"O Blessed One, O Goddess [Name], come here, come here! Having thus spoken, one should bring the deity from the heart-lotus through the path of the *suṣumṇā* into the handful of flowers; then, having recited the root mantra, one should establish the deity in the image using the *āvāhana* (invocation) mudrā.
Then, with the *saṃsthāpana* (stabilization) mudrā, at the end of the root mantra—
Having said, "O such-and-such deity, stay here, stay," [he recites]:
"O Lord of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, together with all your retinues. (5-16)
"Remain firm as long as I worship you.
Having thus prayed, and having again recited the root mantra while performing the *sannidhāpana* (invocation) mudrā, one performs the invocation with the words:
"O Goddess [Name], be present here, be present here! Then, having performed the invocation, one recites the root mantra as before.

"O [Name] Devatā, be firmly bound here, be firmly bound"—having thus displayed the *sannirodhana-mudrā* (binding mudrā), and having brought her face-to-face with the *saṃmukhīkaraṇa-mudrā* (face-to-face mudrā) by reciting the root mantra at its end:
"O [Name] Devatā, be made face-to-face, be made face-to-face"; then, having again uttered the root mantra—

"O [Name] Deity, be veiled, be veiled"—having thus veiled [the deity] with the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) mudrā, one should assign the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) to the heart and other limbs of the deity. Then, having recited the root mantra:
"O [Name] Deity, be made whole (*sakalīkṛtā*), be made whole," one should perform the rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). As follows:

with the root mantra, the *dīpinī* mantra, and the letters of the alphabet from *a* to *kṣa*, one should sprinkle [the deity] three times each on the head of the deity with the water of the *arghya* offering using the *dhenu* mudrā, with the thought that a rain of nectar is falling. This very process is called the purification of the deity.
And the Dīpinī mantra is:
*ai* vada 2 vāgvādini *ai* *klī* klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru 2 *klī* *sau* mokṣaṃ kuru 2 *ho* *shau*.
Then, having recited the root mantra, [one should seal] with the dhenumudrā alone.

"O [Name] Deity, become nectarified, become nectarified"—having thus rendered [the deity] into nectar and formed the *mahāmudrā*, one should recite the root mantra with the intention of raining down supreme nectar upon the head of the deity, saying: "O [Name] Deity, become supremely perfected.
In cases of incapacity or in all other instances, one should recite the root mantra everywhere.

"Be invoked! Be established! Be present! Be restrained! Be made manifest! Be veiled! Be made complete! Be made nectar! Be made supreme!"—thus one should display the mudrās for invocation and the rest.
Thereafter, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti).

Of this *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣis*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters (*chandāṃsi*); the deity is the Power of Vital Breath (*prāṇaśakti*); *āḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *hrīḥ* is the power (*śakti*); *kroḥ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consecration of the vital breath of such-and-such a deity.
*Oṃ*, salutation to the seers Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—on the head. *Oṃ*, salutation to the meters *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—on the mouth.
Salutation to the deity Prāṇaśakti—at the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable ĀḤ—at the secret place; salutation to the power HrīḤ—at the feet.
*Kro* / *Kīlakāya namaḥ*—at the navel.
*Amukadevatā-prāṇapratiṣṭhāyāṃ viniyogaḥ*—thus for the pervasive application over all limbs.
*Oṃ Ā Hrī Kro A Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ākāśavāyutejojalapṛthivyātmane Ā* / *Aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*.

Oṃ ā hrīḥ kroḥ i ca cha ja jha ña, to the self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, ī, svāhā to the two index fingers (tarjanī). Oṃ ā hrīḥ kroḥ u ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, to the self of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, ū, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers (madhyamā). Oṃ ā hrīḥ kroḥ e ta tha da dha na, to the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, ai, hūṃ to the two ring fingers (anāmikā).
Oṃ ā/ hrī/ kro/ o/ pa/ pha/ ba/ bha/ ma/ to the self of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure, au/ to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ.
(p. 348) Oṃ ā/ hrī/ kro/ a/ ya/ ra/ la/ va/ śa/ ṣa/ sa/ ha/ la/ kṣa/ to the self of mind, intellect, and ego, aḥ/ to the palms and backs of the hands, phaṭ.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs, beginning with the heart—
Oṃ, *namaḥ*—from the navel downwards;
Hrīḥ, *namaḥ*—from the throat downwards;

Kroḥ, *namaḥ*—having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) from below the head, [one should place the mantras] on the petals of the heart-lotus starting from the east and so forth, and in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence—namely, *namaḥ* to *la*, *namaḥ* to *ra*, *namaḥ* to *ha*, *namaḥ* to *ṣa*, *namaḥ* to *va*, *namaḥ* to *ya*, *namaḥ* to *sa*, *namaḥ* to *śa*, and *namaḥ* to *kṣa*—one should meditate.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[One should meditate on her] seated upon a lotus as red as the sun rising over the ocean of blood...
I bow to the goddess who is red in hue, three-eyed, and holding in her lotus-like hands a noose, a goad, a shield, a sugar-cane bow, arrows, a trident, and a skull-cup.

Having meditated thus, one should touch the heart of the deity with flowers and other offerings using the *mṛgamudrā* (deer-gesture) and perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths).
The mantra for this is as follows:
*oṃ ā hrīḥ kro ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha saḥ sohaṃ; at the end of the root mantra: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the deity named [so-and-so] are established here, here."*
Thus,
O living being, here and there;
thus.
"May all the senses—speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath—come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!

Having recited the *praṇava* or the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) three times, and having performed the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), upon the form of the deity, one should display the mudrās prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and offer the articles of worship (*upacāra*).
(p. 349) Therein, first of all—
"O God, this beautiful seat has been prepared by me for you. || 5-18 ||
"Please be seated here while I perform the worship," having said this and recited the root mantra—
"Obeisance to this seat for such-and-such deity"— one should offer the seat on the left side of the deity.

Then, having meditated upon the deity—along with their limbs (*aṅga*), retinue (*āvaraṇa*), and weapons (*āyudha*)—who has arrived for the purpose of worship, one should announce their welcome with the appropriate mudrā at the end of the root mantra, saying: "O [Name] Devatā, welcome! Then: "This [offering], accompanied by *śyāmāka*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*... (5.19)
"O Lord of Gods, accept this water for washing the feet (pādya), prepared with waters from sacred fords.

Having spoken thus, at the end of the root mantra, saying "To the deity [Name], obeisance to the water for the feet," one should offer the pādya to the two feet using the water contained in the pādya vessel.
With perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds. || 5-20 ||

Having said, "May this *arghya*, combined with *dūrvā* grass, be accepted," and having recited the root mantra, one should offer the *arghya* upon the hands and the head, saying: "To such-and-such deity, *arghyaṃ svāhā*.
[The water] should be well-scented with jasmine, cloves, *kakkola*, camphor, and so forth.
Saying, "O Lord of the gods, accept this water for sipping (ācamanīya)," one should,
at the end of the root mantra,
offer the water for sipping from that vessel into [the deity's] mouth with the formula: "To such-and-such deity, this ācamanīya, svadhā."
Clarified butter, honey, and curd have been prepared for your sake. || 5-21 ||
"O Lord of the Gods, accept this madhuparka placed in the bronze vessel"— having recited this and uttered the root mantra—

[one should say] "To such-and-such deity, madhuparka, svadhā," and offer the madhuparka into the mouth. Then, having again offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) from the vessel containing the water for sipping, in the same manner as the previous sipping, [one should say]:
"O Lord, accept this fragrant unguent prepared with sesame oil; be gracious unto me. Having recited the root mantra at the end of this verse, one offers the unguent with the formula:
"To such-and-such deity, obeisance to this unguent combined with fragrant oil. Thus, having presented the unguent—

Having recited: "I bathe you with this *pañcāmṛta*, which consists of cow's milk, curd, clarified butter, sugar, and honey," and having uttered the root mantra, one should bathe the deity [named] *Amuka* with the *pañcāmṛta*, saying either individually or all at once: "I bathe [the deity] *Amuka*; obeisance (*namaḥ*)."
Water that has not been touched by others and the like, which is naturally situated and very cool. || 5-22 ||

Having said, "Please accept this for the purpose of bathing, combined with fragrant substances," one should perform the bath with water from a conch shell at the end of the root mantra, saying either:

"Obeisance to the bathing of such-and-such deity" (*amukadevatāyai snānaṃ namaḥ*), or "I bathe such-and-such deity; obeisance" (*amukadevatāṃ snāpayāmi namaḥ*). However, in the Śaiva tradition, because of the prohibition against using water from a conch shell, the bathing is performed with water from an *argha* vessel alone. Then, at the end of the root mantra—
"Amukadevatāyai punarācamanīyaṃ svadhā"—
or "vaḥ"— thus one should offer the water for sipping (punarācamanīya) with the water contained in that vessel.
However, in the absence of those respective vessels, one should offer the water for washing the feet (pādya) and so forth using water from a conch or similar vessel.
Then—these two [fibers] are extremely fine and soft, produced from the cocoon of a silkworm. || 5-23 ||
Having recited, "O Lord of the gods of gods, please put on these two fine garments," and having uttered the root mantra:

"I offer this garment to [Name] Devatā; obeisance," one should present a pair of linen or similar garments. Then, at the end of the root mantra, having presented the sacred thread with: "The sacrificial thread to [Name] Devatā; obeisance."

"O Lord, accept this divine and delightful golden ornament, adorned with pearls and gems; grant me your favor. Having recited this at the end of the root mantra—*amukadevatāyai svarṇādighaṭitāny ābharaṇāni nivedayāmi* (I offer ornaments fashioned from gold and other materials to such-and-such deity)—one should present them.
Having thus offered the ornaments—
along with musk, camphor, gorocana, and other substances— (verse 5.24).

"Take this fragrant sandalwood produced from the Malaya mountains"—having recited this, and having uttered the root mantra, he should offer the fragrance with the words: "Obeisance to [Name] Devatā, the fragrance. Having thus presented the fragrance—
"O Lord of the World, accept these various kinds of water-born and land-growing flowers, fragrant and beautiful"— having said this,
