at the end of the root mantra—

"Vauṣaṭ to such-and-such deity"—with these words, or simply with "Namaḥ," one should offer the flowers. If the deity is female, however, one should recite "Devī" and so forth in place of "Deva" and so forth.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship as follows: having uttered the root mantra—

"I worship the Śrīpādukā; obeisance"—having thus worshipped three times with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should worship the deity in its respective locations using the letters of the *mātṛkā* encased within the root mantra. Then, having obtained permission for the worship of the retinue (*parivāra*), one should perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
As follows:
"Those whose rays are white as snow, crystal, dark, blue, black, and ruddy... (5.25).
The principal female forms, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, are situated in order in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center. (5.26)

Having thus meditated upon the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*), one should worship the limb-deities in sequence in the corners of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the directions starting from Agni.
Then, having worshipped the three lineages of gurus (*gurvoghatraya*) in the northwest, in front, and in the northeast, [one worships] from the northwest up to the northeast with:
*Oṃ śrīgurubhyo namaḥ*.
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious supreme gurus. Oṃ, salutations to the glorious intermediate gurus. Oṃ, salutations to the glorious ultimate gurus.
Thus one should worship the lineages of gurus.
Regarding the subject of Tripurā and others, however, one should worship in this manner: "Oṃ Ai Hrī Śrī, salutation to the gurus; salutation to the sandals of the gurus."
Then, having worshipped the retinue deities mentioned in one's own ritual manual, one should worship the ten world-protectors, Indra and the others, in the directions starting from the east.
For example:
*laṃ*, obeisance to Indra.
Ra: Homage to Agni. Ma: Homage to Yama. Kṣa: Homage to Nairṛta.
Va: Salutation to Varuṇa. Ya: Salutation to Vāyu.
Sa: Salutation to Kuvera.
Haḥ! Salutation to Īśāna.
Ā! Salutation to Brahmā.
A! Salutation to Ananta.
Having thus worshipped, one should worship the ten weapons, beginning with the vajra.
For example: *vaṃ* | *namaḥ vajrāya*.
Śa: Homage to Śakti. Da: Homage to Daṇḍa. Kha: Homage to Khaḍga.
Pa: Homage to the noose (pāśa). A: Homage to the goad (aṅkuśa). Ga: Homage to the mace (gadā).
Śa: Homage to the trident (śūla); Pa:
Homage to the lotus (padma) — above;
Ca: Homage to the wheel (cakra) — below.

Having thus worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should again recite the root mantra and worship three times or once, saying: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the venerable [Name] Deity—along with [her] limbs (*sāṅgāyai*), along with [her] vehicle (*savāhanāyai*), along with [her] ornaments (*sālaṅkārāyai*), along with [her] weapons (*sāyudhāyai*), and along with [her] retinue (*saparivārāyai*)—*namaḥ*. Then, having recited the root mantra, one should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) three times with the *tattvamudrā*, saying: "I offer libations to the venerable [Name] Deity—*namaḥ*."
Then, having placed incense into the fire of the incense burner and sprinkled it with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) while saying "Namo. Having consecrated it with the root mantra and rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*,
one should worship the cymbal and bell with the mantra "Oṃ jayadhvanimantramātaḥ svāhā" or with the *astra-mantra*, while sounding them with the left hand.
"Born from the essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, this incense is to be smelled by all the gods; please accept it. Having recited this, at the end of the root mantra—

"Amukadevatāyai dhūpaṃ nivedayāmi"—having thus offered incense with a low voice, one should place it to the left side or in front of the deity. Then, having lit a lamp in a lamp-vessel and consecrated it as one did the incense, while ringing the bell, [one recites]:
"The great lamp, well-illuminating, which dispels darkness everywhere. (5.27)

Having recited, "May this lamp, a light both external and internal, be accepted," and at the end of the root mantra, having offered the lamp with the words, "I offer this lamp to [Name] Devatā," one should raise it as high as the deity's eyes, wave it around, and then place the lamp to the right if it contains ghee, or to the left if it contains oil; likewise, if the wick is white, it should be placed on the right, and if the wick is red, it should be placed on the left. There is no fixed rule regarding its placement in front.

Then, having sprinkled the ground with ordinary *argha* water before the deity and drawn a square mandala, one should place upon it a food-offering vessel (*naivedya-pātra*) made of gold or other materials and provided with a stand. Having prepared the food offering in that vessel according to the prescribed rules or as far as possible, one should sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra*, protect it with the *cakra-mudrā*, purify it with the wind seed-syllable *yaḥ*, and burn it away with the fire seed-syllable *raḥ*. Then, touching it with the tips of the fingers of the right hand—

Reciting the seed-syllable of Varuṇa (*vaṃ*), he should transform [the offering] into nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*. Having consecrated it eight times with both hands using the root mantra and displayed the *dhenumudrā*, he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, saying "Namaḥ. Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers to the deity with the root mantra, he presents the food offering:
"This fourfold food offering, endowed with the six tastes, is for you."
"Accepted with devotion as it has been placed before you, grant us satisfaction. (5.28)
"Accept this divine, well-prepared *paramānna* (rice pudding) placed in a golden vessel,

endowed with five or six flavors, for the sake of my spiritual accomplishment. Having recited this, he should touch the vessel of the food offering (*naivedya*) with both hands and utter the root mantra.
Saying, "I offer this to such-and-such deity, as much as is available; obeisance, svāhā," one should present the food offering (naivedya) while holding water with the right hand.
Then, [one should place it] in the right hand of the deity—

Having offered water with the mantra: *oṃ amṛtopastaraṇam asi svāhā*, and having displayed the *grāsamudrā* (the "mouthful" gesture) resembling a full-blown blue lotus with the left hand, one should offer with the right hand using the aforementioned gestures:
*oṃ prāṇāya svāhā*, *oṃ apānāya svāhā*.
Oṃ, svāhā to Udāna; Oṃ, svāhā to Vyāna; Oṃ, svāhā to Samāna.
Having thus offered the five oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*), and having placed water in another vessel and rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, [he recites]:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, the boon that brings satisfaction to all. (5.29)

"Accept this supreme water—unoffered to others, pure, in its natural state, very cool, and filled with supreme bliss. Having spoken thus, he places the water vessel on the left side of the deity, offers a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), performs the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the weapon mantra (*astramantra*), and draws a curtain around the deity.

Then, uttering "Obeisance to the nectar-like food offering (*amṛtātmaka-naivedya*)," he displays the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), meditates upon the deity as partaking of the meal, and recites the root mantra one hundred and eight times or ten times.
"Oṃ amṛtāpidhānam asi svāhā"—with this, one should offer water.

Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south and established the fire according to the method to be described, one should invoke the deity into that fire, worship them with water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, as well as with perfumes and flowers, and perform the Vaiśvadeva oblation with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
In that rite, having first offered oblations with the Vyāhṛtis accompanied by the Praṇava, one should give twenty-five oblations with the root mantra (mūlamantra).

Having again offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and worshipped the deity with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should merge [the deity] into the form on the pedestal (*pīṭhamūrti*) and dismiss the fire.

Then, with the remaining milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one should offer the sacrificial gift (*bali*) to the attendants (*pārṣada*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, this *bali* is offered with salutation to the attendants of the deity [Name]," accompanied by scents, flowers, and consecrated rice (*akṣata*).

Then, having lifted the curtain, the deity partakes of the *naivedya* as desired. Having honored the offering, the vessel for the *naivedya* should be placed in the southwest (*nairṛti*) direction. Having purified the place where the *naivedya* was kept with cow dung and water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should take a small portion of the remains of the deity's food and cast it toward the northeast (*aiśānī*) direction, saying: "Oṃ, salutation to the consumer of the floral offerings (*nirmālya*). Then, having washed both hands and taken betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should place it before [the deity].
Combined with cardamom, cloves, khadira powder, betel nut, and other such ingredients.
"O Lord of the gods, accept this betel; be gracious to me. Having recited this, at the end of the *mūlamantra*, he should offer it with:
"I present this betel to [Name] Devatā, svāhā. Having thus offered it, he should worship [the deity] three times with the *mūlamantra* using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Then, having displayed a mirror and offered the parasol, fly-whisks, and so forth, one should—provided there is the capacity—offer a *bali* of black gram (*māṣa*) cooked rice and other items to the deity using the mantra prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*). Then, in the southeast and other directions, or alternatively in the east, south, north, and west, one should offer the *bali* to Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and the Yoginīs in their respective order.
As for the procedure therein:
having prepared the mandalas and established the vessels for the *bali* offerings—
Having worshipped the bali offering with the mantra beginning with "gaṃ / Gaṇeśāya balimūrtaye namaḥ," [one should offer] "gāṃ / Gaṇeśāya namaḥ" and "vāṃ / Vaṭukāya namaḥ."
Having worshipped them with scents, flowers, and other offerings using the mantras: "Kṣā! Salutation to Kṣetrapāla" and "Yā! Salutation to the Yoginīs."

*gā gī gū gaṇapataye vara-varada sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya baliṃ gṛhṇa 2 svāhā—eṣa balir gaṇapataye namaḥ*. Having thus offered the *bali* to Gaṇeśa: *ehy ehi devīputra vaṭukanātha kapilajaṭābhāra-bhāsura trinetra jvālāmukha sarva-vighnān nāśaya sarvopacāra-sahitaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa 2 svāhā—eṣa balir vaṭukāya namaḥ*. Having thus offered the *bali* to Vaṭuka:

*kṣāṃ kṣī kṣū kṣai kṣau kṣaḥ* — *kṣetrapālāya dhūpadīpādisahitaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa 2 svāhā*. "This offering (*bali*) is for Kṣetrapāla; obeisance! Having thus given the offering to Kṣetrapāla—*yā yoginībhyo namaḥ*. (p.
356) Whether above the Egg of Brahmā (*brahmāṇḍa*), in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, or in the partless realm (*niṣkala*).
Whether in the netherworld or in fire, in water or in wind, wherever they may abide;

or having taken their stations in the sacred fields, seats, and secondary seats, may the Goddesses—who are worshipped by heroic lords and are pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings—always protect us with auspicious rites and oblations. (5.31)
With the words, "This is the offering for the Yoginīs; homage! one should present the offering to the Yoginīs.
However, in the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions, there is only the offering to the Bhūtas.
Then, one should present the offering to the Bhūtas.
For example:

having prepared a mandala in the northeast, and having placed there a common offering bowl (*sādhāra-valipātra*) provided with food, side dishes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), water, and so forth, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting: *Oṃ sarvebhyo bhūtebhyo namaḥ* (Oṃ, homage to all spirits).
Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce abodes; those Yoginīs of terrible form, and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas.
"May those who move on the earth, those who move in the sky, and those who dwell in the intermediate space—all of them, becoming joyful in mind, accept this offering. (5.33)
Having recited this, and having offered a stream of water from that vessel with the left hand, one should offer it with the right hand, saying: "Oṃ, this food-oblation is for all beings; namaḥ.
Then, taking a handful of flowers, one should pray.
May all the beings who dwell here upon the earth, having received this offering presented according to the ritual rules, attain satisfaction and depart.
May they forgive these [faults] here; let there be homage to them. || 5-34 ||
Having thus prayed, offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and bowed, one should dismiss [the deities] with the *nārāca-mudrā*, saying: "May all beings dwell in happiness.
Then, one should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times.
"You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Lord, Master of the World, may success be mine through your grace.

Having thus offered the recitation, having praised [the deity] according to one's ability, and having prostrated, one should rise from the seat, circumambulate three times, and perform a full prostration with the eight limbs.
Then, having placed the *vardhanī*— filled with water, wrapped in cloth, and containing gold— upon the heap of previously gathered scattered offerings (*vikira*) situated in the northeast;

and having meditated upon the Weapon Deity (*astradevatā*) as standing on a lion, holding a sword and a shield, of terrible form, and facing west, and having invoked her into that vessel with the mantra "Phaṭ, obeisance to the Weapon Deity," and having worshipped her with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using the mobile seat (*calāsana*) itself, one should take up that *karkarī*.

Visualizing all the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with "By the command of such-and-such a deity, protect the sacrificial ground of Indra, such-and-such a deity," one should release a stream of water from the nozzle, circumambulate the interior of the pavilion,
recite the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) "Phaṭ," and install [the deities] in their respective places. Then,
having assumed a steady posture and worshipped them as before with offerings such as perfumes and so forth, one should prostrate.
Then the preceptor should perform the consecration of the fire according to the rules in his own sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) situated between the east and the northeast.

Therein, first having gone to the location of the pit and sat upon his seat, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the three principles (tattva), and having taken three blades of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and water, he should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
It is as follows:

Having proclaimed the place and time, beginning with "Oṃ, today," and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I, [Name] Devaśarman of [Name] Gotra, shall perform the rite of *homa*, which is an ancillary part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the mantra of [Name] Deva of [Name] Gotra, performed by [Name] Śarman"—and having offered water for the guest-offering (*argha*) to the Sun with the previously mentioned mantra and established the general *argha*, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), as follows: [The eighteen rites are: 1. Inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), 2. Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), 3. Smearing (*ullekhana*), 4. Drawing lines (*rekhākaraṇa*), 5. Sprinkling again (*abhyukṣaṇa*), 6. Placing the fire-sticks (*darbhatṛṇanyāsa*), 7. Purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*), 8. Strengthening (*balidāna*), 9. Protection (*rakṣaṇa*), 10. Covering (*avaguṇṭhana*), 11. Consecration (*abhiṣeka*), 12. Invoking the fire (*agnisamudbhava*), 13. Establishing the fire (*agnisthāpana*), 14. Offering the guest-offering (*arghadāna*), 15. Circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), 16. Worship (*pūjana*), 17. Offering the oblation (*āhutidāna*), and 18. Releasing the fire (*visarjana*). Thus it is said: 1. Inspection: One should gaze at the pit while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 2. Sprinkling: One should sprinkle the pit with water from the *argha* vessel while reciting the *Taraṇi* mantra. 3. Smearing: One should smear the pit with cow-dung while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 4. Drawing Lines: One should draw three lines in the east, north, and west directions while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 5. Sprinkling Again: One should sprinkle the pit with water from the *argha* vessel while reciting the *Taraṇi* mantra. 6. Placing the Fire-sticks: One should place darbha grass on the pit while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 7. Purification: One should purify the pit with the *pavitra* blades while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 8. Strengthening: One should offer a small oblation (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 9. Protection: One should surround the pit with a protective circle (*rakṣācakra*) while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 10. Covering: One should cover the pit with a cloth while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 11. Consecration: One should consecrate the pit with the *argha* water while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 12. Invoking the Fire: One should invoke the fire into the pit while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 13. Establishing the Fire: One should establish the fire in its seat while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 14. Offering the Guest-offering: One should offer the *argha* to the fire while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 15. Circumambulation: One should circumambulate the pit clockwise while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 16. Worship: One should worship the fire with the prescribed offerings while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 17. Offering the Oblation: One should offer the first oblation (*āhutidāna*) while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. 18. Releasing the Fire: One should release the fire to depart while reciting the *Tryambaka* mantra. Thus, having performed these eighteen purificatory rites, one proceeds with the main ritual.
While reciting the root mantra, one should gaze at the fire-pit; this is the rite of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*). With the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*, one performs the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
With that same mantra, one strikes [the pit] three times with *darbha* grass.
"Huḥ"—with this armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*), one sprinkles [the site].
"Phaṭ"—with this weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*), one digs to the depth of a finger's breadth.
With that same mantra, using the thumb and ring finger, one extracts the earth.
p. 358) [The ritual procedure is as follows: Filling again with earth using the heart-mantra *namaḥ*;
leveling with the weapon-mantra;
sprinkling with water while reciting *huḥ*.
*Phaṭ*—this is the act of pounding.
That is the firming [of the material] by means of wood and so forth, or even with the hand alone.
Then—
With the mantra "huḥ," one should sweep away the earth from the *kuṇḍa* using a handful of *kuśa* grass; this is *mārjana* (cleansing).
With that same mantra, one should smear it with cow dung; this is *lepana* (smearing).
Standing there, with that same mantra, one should contemplate the digits (*kalās*) of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni in the center of the *kuṇḍa*; this is the conceptualization of the forms of the *kalās*.

Reciting the armor mantra (*kavacamantra*) "Huḥ," one should encircle the girdle of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍamekhalā*) three times with three threads; this is the "making of the triple-thread" (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*). One should worship the pit with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the [Name] Pit"; this is the "worship" (*arcana*). Following the worship of the pit—
One should worship with: "Oṃ, obeisance to [Name] Kuṇḍanābhī; Oṃ, obeisance to the girdles of [Name] Kuṇḍa.
One should contemplate the pit as being as firm as a vajra by means of the weapon-mantra (astramantra); this is the "vajrification" (vajrīkaraṇa).

Having placed *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing east in the center of the pit, having placed *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing north upon that, having laid a seat (*viṣṭara*) on top, and having offered flowers upon that, one should worship it with the heart-mantra, saying "Oṃ namas. This is the preparation of the crossroads (*catuṣpathīkaraṇa*).
Having consecrated unbroken-tipped *kuśa* blades with the weapon-mantra, while reciting the armor-mantra, one should strew them around the girdles; this is the clearing of the ground (*akṣapāṭana*).
Thus, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
However, one who is unable to perform the eighteen purificatory rites should perform only the four previously mentioned rites, beginning with *vīkṣaṇa*.
On the Left Path (*vāmamārga*), however, one should perform only these four purificatory rites.

Then, in the middle of the *kuṇḍa*, while uttering "Namaḥ," one should draw three lines with the root of a *darbha* blade or the base of the *sruva* ladle: three lines pointing eastward and three lines pointing northward.
Regarding the sequence of drawing them: the eastward-pointing lines begin from the south and terminate in the north; the northward-pointing lines begin from the west and terminate in the east.
Alternatively, it is stated in the *Śāradā* that one should draw a hexagon with a triangle in its center and surrounded by a circle;
in the *Merutantra*, it is said that one should draw six lines and such a hexagon;
and in some places, it is also stated that one should write the *lajjābīja* and the *praṇava* in the middle of the triangle.
Then—
on the lines pointing eastward and on the upward-pointing lines:
*oṃ mukundāya namaḥ* | *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ* |
Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ, obeisance to Vaivasvata.
Oṃ, obeisance to Purandara. Oṃ, obeisance to Indra.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, following this very sequence of writing.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should worship with the words: "Obeisance to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of such-and-such deity.
However, in the case of Śrīvidyā:
One should worship in this very sequence: *ai hrī śrī ai klī sauḥ mukundāya namaḥ*.
Then, while uttering the *praṇava* (Oṃ), having sprinkled [the area] with the water from the general *argha* vessel, one should worship the deities of the *yogapīṭha*.
It is as follows—in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, according to the sequence prescribed for the placement of the jar (*ghaṭasthāpana*).

Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti)" and ending with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Jewel-Lion Throne (Ratnasiṃhāsana)," one should worship Dharma and the others in the corners starting from the southeast, and worship Adharma and the others in the directions starting from the east.
Then, having visualized an eight-petaled lotus—
Having worshipped from "Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta" and so forth,
up to "obeisance to the Self of Knowledge," one should worship [the deities] upon the filaments starting from the east.
Oṃ, homage to Jayā. Oṃ, homage to Vijayā.
Oṃ, homage to Ajitā.
Oṃ, homage to Aparājitā. Oṃ, homage to Nityā. Oṃ, homage to Vilāsinī.
Oṃ, salutation to Dogdhrī.
Oṃ, salutation to Aghorā.
In the center—
One should worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*) with: *oṃ maṅgalāyai namaḥ*.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however: *oṃ vibhūtyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ, salutation to Unnati. Oṃ, salutation to Kānti. Oṃ, salutation to Sṛṣṭi.
Oṃ, homage to Kīrti. Oṃ, homage to Sannati. Oṃ, homage to Puṣṭi.
Oṃ, obeisance to Utkṛṣṭī; Oṃ, obeisance to Ṛddhī. Thus one should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis).
Then, one should worship the pedestal with the pedestal mantra: *Hrīṃ! Namaḥ to the essence of the yoga-pīṭha of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara*;
or one may worship it with the mantra: *Hrīṃ! Namaḥ to the lotus-seat of all powers (sarvaśakti-kamalāsana)*.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however, one should worship with: "Obeisance to the nature of the yoga-pīṭha of Śrī Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Then—
Vāgīśvarī, resembling a blue lotus, having just bathed after her menses.
Having meditated [on her] as joined with Vāgīśvara... and,
in the case of Śrīvidyā,
having meditated on Kāmeśvarī in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), full of desire and united with the season (ṛtu)— having thus meditated—
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however:

having meditated thus— “There, Lakṣmī is in her menses and united with the Lord Nārāyaṇa through the rite of sexual union”— one should invoke [the deity] there, display the mudrās such as the *āvāhana* (invocation) and others, and proceed.
Hrīṃ! Salutation to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara.
In the Śrīvidyā tradition, however:
Klīṃ! Salutation to Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however, one should worship with the fivefold offerings using the mantra: "Obeisance to Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇau. (p.
361) Likewise, in the Saura tradition as well—
Alternatively, in the Śaiva, Śākta, and other traditions—
one should meditate upon Śiva as intoxicated with desire and Bhuvaneśvarī in her menses,
and worship them with the mantra: *hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhuvaneśvarī and Śiva*.
Then, having placed fire— produced from a sun-crystal, from a fire-drill, or from the house of a Vedic scholar— into any one of vessels such as a golden bowl and covering it with another vessel,
he brings it forward; having established the fire to his right with the weapon mantra *phaṭ*,
and having covered it with the armor mantra *huṃ*, he takes the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) from it.
*Huḥ phaṭ*—with these syllables, one should cast [the remainder] toward the southwest (*nairṛtya*).

Then, having visualized the remaining fire as a portion of the deity and established it in front with the root mantra, one should consecrate it with the four rites beginning with *vīkṣaṇa* according to the sequence prescribed for the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). One should then contemplate the unification of the terrestrial fire with the two fires—the digestive fire (*audarya*) and the divine fire (*vainda*). The divine fire is the fire situated between the eyebrows.
Then—
"Ra! I invoke the consciousness of the fire.

Or, having joined the consciousness of the fire with the mantra "Hu! Ra! Salutation to your consciousness," one should consecrate it one hundred and eight times or ten times with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), transform it into nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and protect it with "Phaṭ!"
Having veiled [the fire] with "Huṃ," one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.

Having honored it with "Raḥ, obeisance to the form of Fire," one should rotate it three times clockwise above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), then, with knees touching the ground and preceded by the utterance of the Praṇava, one should cast it into the womb of the Goddess with the thought that it is the seed of Śiva.

It should be understood that while this is done with the thought of it being the seed of Śiva in the Śaiva-Śākta traditions, in the Vaiṣṇava traditions and others, it is done with the thought of it being the seed of Viṣṇu and other deities.

Then—having offered water for sipping with the mantra: *Hrīṃ! Obeisance to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara for the water for sipping*—and having meditated upon the deity in the form of fire held within the womb of the Goddess, one should offer a darbha-bracelet for the protection of the fetus.
One should kindle the fire with the mantra "citpiṅgala hana 2 daha 2 paca 2 sarvājñā jñāpaya svāhā" while performing the Jvālinī mudrā.
(In the Rudrayāmala, however— )
*p. 362) *Hrīḥ hrīḥ jvala 2 prajvala 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—with this mantra, the kindling of the fire is taught.
Then, with palms joined in reverence:
*Oṃ, I pay homage to Agni, the blazing one, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations.* (5-36)
One should worship the fire with the mantra: "Golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions.

Then, having silently offered into the fire a sacrificial fuel-stick (*samidh*) one span long, soaked in clarified butter at both its base and tip, one should perform the salutation to Gaṇeśa and others, the binding of the quarters (*digbandhana*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the placement of the *mātṛkā* (*mātṛkānyāsa*), and the placement of the root-mantra (*mūlanyāsa*) according to the sequence prescribed in the section on worship. Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the tongues of fire (*vahni-jihvā-nyāsa*) upon one's own body;
therein follows the placement of the *sāttvika* tongues.
For example: *sprū* / *hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*—on the linga;
*ṣprū* / *gaganāyai namaḥ*—on the anus.
ŚPRŪ / Homage to Raktā—on the head.
VPRŪ / Homage to Kṛṣṇā—on the face.
LPRŪ / Homage to Suprabhā—on the nose.
*rprū* / Salutation to Bahurūpā—on the eyes. *yprū* / Salutation to Atiriktā—on all the limbs.
These are the Sāttvika tongues for Sāttvika rites.
But in rites for desired results (*kāmya*) and so forth,
the tongues of the *rājasa* type— namely, Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, Bhadralohitā, Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā— should be placed [upon the tongue].
In rites of a cruel nature (*krūrakarman*):

Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālī—these are the tongues belonging to Tamas that should be deposited. The seed-syllables (bījas), however, are exactly as previously stated.

Then, having first placed those very same seed-syllables in those very locations, one should also deposit in sequence the deities who preside over the seven tongues: the immortals (amartyas), the ancestors (pitṛs), the gandharvas, the yakṣas, the nāgas, the piśācas, and the rākṣasas.
"Sprū / Homage to the Immortal," and so forth.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other components,
as follows:

For the mantra of Agni: Bṛgu is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Agni is the deity (devatā), *ra* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *svāhā* is the power (śakti), and its application (viniyoga) is in the sacrifice to Agni.
*Oṃ*, salutation to the seer Bṛgu—on the head;
salutation to the Gāyatrī meter—on the face.
Salutation to Agni, the deity—on the heart.
Salutation to the seed-syllable *raḥ*—on the secret place.
Salutation to the power *svāhā*—on the feet.
The application [of mantras] for the fire-sacrifice (*agniyajana*)—
thus, with palms joined in reverence (*baddhāñjali*).
Then follows the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).

Oṃ sahasrārciṣe, salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ svastipūrṇāya, salutation to the two index fingers, svāhā. Oṃ uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers. Oṃ dhūmavyāpine, huṃ to the two ring fingers. Oṃ saptajihvāya, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers. Oṃ dhanurdharāya, phaṭ to the palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the eightfold placement (nyāsa) beginning with the heart. Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the forms (mūrttinyāsa).
Namely: Oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ—on the crown of the head;
Oṃ agnaye saptajihvāya namaḥ—on the right side.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Havyavāhana—on the right side;
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Aśvodaraja—on the right hip;
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Vaiśvānara—at the *liṅga*.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni of youthful splendor—on the left shoulder.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni whose face is the universe—on the left side.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni whose face is the gods—on the left arm.
Thus ends the placement of the forms (*mūrttinyāsa*).
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*).

It is as follows: having performed the placement in the aforementioned locations from the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) up to the circle of fire (*vahnimaṇḍala*), [one should place them] on the filaments of the heart-lotus, starting from the eastern one.
Oṃ, obeisance to Pītā; Oṃ, obeisance to Śvetā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Aruṇā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Dhūmrā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Tīvrā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Sphuliṅginī; Oṃ, obeisance to Rucirā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī—in the center.

Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the nine powers of Fire upon the seat (*pīṭha*), and having performed the placement of the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*) right there with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Yoga-seat of Fire," one should meditate upon Fire.
The meditation is as follows:

One should meditate on the Lord who holds a wish-granting jewel, a spear, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness aloft with his long arms; who has the luster of barley, is adorned with golden ornaments, stands upon a lotus, and possesses three eyes.
One should meditate on the Fire-god with his head bound by matted locks— this is the meditation described in the *Śāradā-tantra*.
The meditation described in the *Rudrayāmala* is as follows:
Resembling the bandhūka flower, with the luster of well-refined gold, seated upon a lotus for the sake of the patron, and adorned with two faces. (5.37)
The god consisting of the seven meters, stationed above the celestial chariot,
with three necks and three lotus-feet, who destroys the offerings to gods and ancestors.
It is adorned by the four horns of the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ;
it consists of the Pañcarātra, Pāśupata, Kāpila, and Mahāmata systems.
The Buddhist [tradition] is this altar, possessing six tawny eyes;
the Vedic meaning is the four ears, having the sound consisting of the Śrauta scriptures.
His head was radiant with the tips of his matted locks bound with pale-red flowers;
he was adorned with golden ornaments and embellished with golden earrings.
Seated in the svastika posture in the center of a red lotus,
with his third lotus-foot resting against his back.
Resounding with a great sound and shining with his own splendor, he held a spear, a thunderbolt, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in his four right arms. (5.43)
Holding a *tomara* spear, a palm-leaf fan, and a golden vessel of ghee in his three left arms, he was clothed in red garments.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Atiraktā, Bahuraktā, and Jihvikā are situated on the face of Dakṣa.
These knowers of tastes are eternally situated upon your two beautiful faces;
with these seven tongues, your split-open mouth is endowed.
Having meditated thus and visualized oneself as being of the nature of the deity Fire (Vahni-devatā), one should worship oneself with mental offerings.

Then, with the mantra "Obeisance to the Fire who is my own form," one should fully worship oneself even with external offerings such as fragrance and so forth—excluding the food offering—with the general *argha* water, sprinkle the girdles (*mekhalā*), and perform the strewing (*paristaraṇa*) with the tips of *darbha* grass that have empty interiors.
This is the strewing.
In a pit with one girdle (*mekhalā*), one should perform [the rite] below the girdle; in a pit with two girdles, above the second girdle; and in a pit with three girdles, upon the middle girdle.
And the procedure for that is as follows:

one should spread the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*) by covering the root ends with the tip ends and the tip ends with the root ends, using *darbha* blades whose tips point eastward on the south and north sides, and whose tips point northward on the east and west sides.

Then, having abandoned the eastern direction and having placed enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made from trees such as the *palāśa*, each one cubit in length and accompanied by a supporting stick (*saviṣṭara*), in the southern, northern, and western directions, he should worship them in a clockwise direction with:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra."
Then, on the girdles: *oṃ vāmāyai namaḥ* | *oṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ* |
"Oṃ, obeisance to Raudrī;
Oṃ, obeisance to Ambikā"— having thus worshipped them in clockwise order starting from the east—

Having offered the seat with the mantra: *Raḥ / Vahnaye āsanaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*, one should visualize within the center of the *kuṇḍa* an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three squares and four gates. Then, having performed worship according to the previously described sequence for the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), starting from the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) up to the Fire-Mandala, or alternatively from the Tortoise (*maṇḍūka*) up to the Knowledge-Self (*jñānātman*), one should worship the nine previously mentioned powers at the base of the petals and in the center of the lotus of the fire’s seat, using the mantra:
*Raḥ / Vahnyoḥ yogapīṭhātmane namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the pedestal with the mantra "Obeisance to the one seated upon the lotus of all powers," and having envisioned the form [of the deity] at the end of the root mantra with "I fashion the form of Fire; obeisance," and having again meditated upon the Fire, [one should say]:
"Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, come hither! O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā! O Blessed Agni, come hither, come hither!"
"Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, come hither! O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā!"—with this, one should perform the invocation.
Furthermore, the recitation of the root mantra at the beginning and the end is established by the previously cited authorities.
Then:

Having displayed the mudrās for invocation and so forth in the sequence beginning with "Be invoked! Be established! and so on, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths).
As follows:
Oṃ Ā Hnī Kro Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Ha Saḥ So’haṃ Ra. The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of Vahni are present here, here.
Thus the soul is situated here and there;
thus—
"May all the senses—speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath—come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!

Having thus performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths), one offers [the following] in the proper sequence: "Oṃ Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, come here! O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites; svāhā!"—then offering water for the feet (*pādya*), respectful oblation (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), food, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, sacrificial food (*naivedya*), and betel leaf with the formula "This is the water for the feet for Vahni; obeisance. Thus one presents these offerings.

p. 367) *Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*—*I worship the Śrī-pādukā, obeisance*. Having thus worshipped three times with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇārcana*). It is as follows:
one should worship the seven tongues, Hiraṇyā and the rest, in the six corners and in the center, in the order beginning with Īśāna.
For example: *sprū* | Homage to Hiraṇyā! *ṣprū* | Homage to Gaganā!
ŚPRŪ / Homage to Raktā.
VPRŪ / Homage to Kṛṣṇā.
LPRŪ / Homage to Suprabhā.
rprū/ Homage to Bahurūpā. yprū/ Homage to Atiriktā.
Now, in the Vaiṣṇava [tradition]—

The seven tongues— Prabhā, Dīpti, Prakāśā, Marīci, Tāpinī, Karālā, and Lelihānā— are to be worshipped. Thereafter, one should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) upon the filaments (keśaras),
as follows:
Oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ—[in the] southeast.
Oṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā—[in the] northeast.
Oṃ uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ—[in the] southwest.
Oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya hūṃ—[in the] northwest.
Oṃ saptajihvāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ—in the center.
However, in the Vaiṣṇava and other systems, it should be understood that [the mantra for] the eyes is "netrābhyām."
Having worshipped in the four directions with "Oṃ dhanurdharāyāstrāya phaṭ," [one should worship] on the petals starting from the east.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Jātavedas. Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Saptajihva.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Havyavāhana.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni, born from the womb of the horse.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Vaiśvānara.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni, the splendor of Kumāra.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni, whose face is the universe.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni, whose face is the gods.

(p. 368) Having thus worshipped the eight forms, one should worship Indra and the other deities in order starting from the east upon the *darbha* grass situated on the girdle, and outside of that, the *vajra* and the other [emblems].

"Oṃ Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the deity] here; O Lohitākṣa, accomplish all rites, svāhā! I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Vahni, who is with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his weapons (*sāyudha*), his vehicle (*savāhana*), his ornaments (*sālaṅkāra*), and his retinue (*saparivāra*), [to whom] I bow. Having thus worshipped, one should arrange the vessels as follows:

having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward on one's left side, and having washed pairs of vessels—namely the *sruk*, *sruva*, *prokṣaṇī*, *praṇītā*, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (*carusthālī*), and so forth—with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one should place them there with their openings facing downward.

Although it is stated that the *prokṣaṇī* vessel used for worship should be placed to one's right, nevertheless, that vessel used for the *homa* must be placed only on the left, like the *praṇītā* and other vessels; this is because the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles alone are prescribed for the right, according to the author of the *Śrīvidyāpaddhati*. Even the *sruk* and *sruva* should first be set out on the left and then placed on the right after their consecration (*saṃskāra*). Then, having turned those vessels face-up with a *pavitra* [strainer], washed them again, and sprinkled them with the water from the general *argha* vessel—
Uttering the heart-mantra "Namaḥ," he fills the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with pure water, and having worshipped the three images (*vimbatraya*) in sequence within the waters of the *ādhāra* vessel—

With the mantra beginning "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva," and using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb; protect them with the *astra-mantra*, veil them with the *kavaca-mantra*, and having cast in perfume, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and purifiers (*pavitra*), place them upon the grass-bundle (*kūrca*). Having consecrated them eight times with the *praṇava* and displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should likewise fill the *praṇītā* vessel with pure water and cast in perfume, flowers, unbroken rice, and purifiers.

Then, having poured a little water from the *praṇītā* vessel into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should sprinkle the sacrificial materials (*yāgadravya*) with that water while reciting the *hṛdayamantra* and the *mūlamantra*.
This concludes the placement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*).
Having performed the purification of the materials, one should choose a *brahmā* priest.
For example:
Having seated the Brahman—who has been initiated into the mantra of that deity—on a seat of *kuśa* grass to the south of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [the officiant says]:

"Oṃ, today... [etc. ...I, [Name], of the [Name] lineage, [Name] Devaśarman, choose you, sir, the Brahman of the [Name] lineage, [Name] Devaśarman, for this rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*) which is a constituent part of the initiation rite (*dīkṣākarma*) into the [Name] mantra dedicated to the deity [Name]."
"I have performed [the rite]"—this is the response.
Having said this, one should worship with perfumes and so forth, as well as garments, ornaments, and the like, using the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahman."
Then one should consecrate the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as follows:

having grasped the *sruk* and *sruva* with both hands with their openings facing upward, turn them downward; heat them three times in the fire; holding them with the left hand, take *darbha* grass with the right hand and purify the tips, bases, and middles of the two ladles with those *darbha* blades.
The sequence of purification is as follows:
the tip with the tip, the root with the root, and the middle with the middle.
Then, having sprinkled them with the water from the general *argha* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels, and having heated them again over the fire, one should cast the *darbha* grasses into the fire.
Then, having spread *kuśa* grass to his right, he should place those two upon it.
Thereafter, he should consecrate the clarified butter (*ājya*).

This is as follows: taking the vessel for the clarified butter and sprinkling it with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, he should place the clarified butter into it and gaze upon it with the root mantra.

Having sprinkled [the site] with "Astrāya Phaṭ," having struck it with *darbha* grass using that same mantra, one should perform the sprinkling with the water of the *argha* offering while reciting "Huṃ. Having thus performed these four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should remove the embers from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and place them in the northwest corner; upon those embers—
One should place the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) with the mantra "Namaḥ. This is the heating (*tāpana*).

Then, having ignited a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter, one should throw the remaining burnt residue into the fire with the mantra "Namaḥ. This is the purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).
Again, while reciting the mantra "Huṃ," one should offer clarified butter by waving a pair of blazing *darbha* blades and cast them into the fire. This is the illumination (*abhidyotana*).
Then, taking a handful of blazing *kuśa* grass—
Reciting the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*, one should display [the gesture] and cast [the embers] into the fire; this is the "illumination" (*udyotana*).

Then, having brought the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) from those embers and placed it facing oneself, one should cast those embers back into the fire, sweep the place where the embers were, and touch water.
Thereafter, holding two separate strainers (*pavitra*) about a span in length between the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands with the palms facing upward—
Reciting the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*, one should leap forward facing the fire. (p.

370) Then, having placed the *pavitra* in another spot, one should again take two *darbha* blades in that same manner and, reciting the mantra *namaḥ*, sprinkle the clarified butter toward oneself with that pair of *darbha* blades; then one should cast both this pair of *darbhas* and the previously established *pavitra* into the fire. Thus, both leaping (*utplavana*) and sprinkling (*saṃplavana*) are indeed acts of immersion (*plāvana*).

Then, having placed a pair of darbha blades, one span in length and tied together with a knot, into the middle of the clarified butter in the vessel for the ghee, one should perform the oblation after meditating as follows: visualizing the right side of the ghee as the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) and the left side as the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), and contemplating Iḍā in the left, Piṅgalā in the right, and Suṣumṇā in the middle.
For example, while reciting the mantra "Namas," one should take ghee from the right side using the *sruva* ladle.

"Oṃ agnaye svāhā, agnaye idaṃ namaḥ"—with this, one should offer oblation into the right eye of the fire. One should pour the remaining drops of clarified butter (*saṃpāta*) right there on the southern side. Again, saying "namaḥ," one should take ghee from the left side.
"Oṃ somāya svāhā, [this] is for Soma, obeisance"—with these words, one should offer oblation into the left eye.
One should place the remaining ghee (saṃpātājya) right there on the left side.
Again, having taken ghee from the middle portion in this same manner—

"Oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā; agnīṣomābhyām idaṃ namaḥ. Having thus offered oblations into the fire at the forehead and the eyes, one should pour the remaining clarified butter (*saṃpāta-ājya*) into the central part as before. However, in the case of Vaiṣṇava and other such rites, one should not perform the oblation at the forehead and the eyes. Even in that regard, O Lord, one should indeed perform it for the homa intended for the worship of the feet of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, [reciting]: "To the Imperishable Supreme Self, Acyuta, who shines with three eyes..."
Since it has been stated, "I bow to Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the God of gods, Vṛṣākapi," and because even there—
in the context of meditating on the two eyes with the description, "as if burning the three worlds with his two blazing fire-eyes"— the offering to the eyes (netrāhuti) is not to be performed.
Furthermore:
Saying "namaḥ," and taking clarified butter from the southern portion, one should offer it into the mouth of the fire, saying: "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā; this is *namaḥ* to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
(p. 371) (In the *Śāradā*,
however,) it is stated that one should offer with "svāhā," and then cast the remains of the oblation with "hā."
In that case as well,
it appears that one should offer [the portion] with "Svā" and then prepare the remains of the oblation with "Hā."
Then, one should offer five oblations with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, both individually and collectively.
That is to say: having offered *oṃ svāhā*, *bhūḥ svāhā*, *bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *svaḥ svāhā*, and *oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ svāhā*—thus having sacrificed—

Having offered three oblations with the fire-mantra: *oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*, one should perform the sixteen sacraments (*saṃskāra*) for the fire, beginning with the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*).
For example: *oṃ agner garbhādhānaṃ saṃpādayāmi svāhā*—with this, one should offer eight oblations.
The same applies in the subsequent cases as well:
"Oṃ, I perform the *puṃsavana* for Agni, svāhā!"—thus;
"Oṃ, I perform the *sīmantonnayana* for Agni, svāhā!"; "Oṃ, I perform the *jātakarma* for Agni, svāhā!"—having thus offered the oblations for the birth-rite (*jātakarma*).
"Oṃ, I perform the cutting of Agni’s navel, phaṭ svāhā"— with this, one should offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) soaked in clarified butter at both the base and the tip [of the fire].
Then, having offered one oblation with "Oṃ, I purify the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) of Vahni, svāhā," one should [proceed] by means of the name of one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

Having given the name, "O Fire, you are [Name]," and having contemplated the identity (*aikya*) of the fire and the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should offer eight oblations as before with: "Oṃ, I perform the naming of the fire; svāhā.
Alternatively, one may give the name in this way: "O Agni, you are named Śiva; O Agni, you are named Varada; O Agni, you are named Viśvarūpa."
In the Śrīvidyā tradition, however, one should give the name: "O Agni, you are named Kāmāgni.
Then—
Oṃ, Agni, I perform the rite of departure; svāhā!
Likewise:
Oṃ, [I perform] Agni’s first feeding of solid food.
Oṃ, the tonsure ceremony for Agni;
Oṃ, the initiation ceremony for Agni;
Oṃ, the Mahānāmnī vow for Agni.
Oṃ, the great vow of Agni.
Oṃ, the secret vow of Agni.
Oṃ, the cow-gift vow of Agni.
*Oṃ, the re-entry of Agni.

Oṃ, I accomplish the marriage of Agni; svāhā!*—having thus offered eight oblations for each [verse], one should take a fuel-stick (*samidh*) soaked in clarified butter from both the root and the tip and offer it three times with: *Oṃ hrīḥ, to Vāgīśa and Vāgīśvarī, svāhā*.

Then, having worshipped the two Lords of Speech, the parents of Agni, with the five-fold offerings as before, and having prostrated, one should dissolve them into one's own heart. Then, one should offer a single oblation to each of the seven tongues of the fire using their respective mantras,
as follows:
Sprū! Svāhā to Hiraṇyā! Ṣprū! Svāhā to Gaganā!
Śprū! Svāhā to Raktā!
vprū / To Kṛṣṇā, svāhā!
lprū / To Suprabhā, svāhā!
rprū / To Bahurūpā, svāhā!
One should offer oblations with the mantra of the seven tongues: *yprū* / *atiriktāyai svāhā*.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*).
Namely: (p. 373) Oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā—one should offer oblations in this sequence.
Oṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā.
Oṃ, to the one who has arisen, to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ! Oṃ, to the smoke-pervading one, to the armor, hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ, to the seven-tongued one, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ svāhā!
In the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions, however,
it should be understood as "from the two eyes.
Oṃ dhanurdharāyāstrāya phaṭ svāhā.
Then one should offer oblations with the form-mantras of Agni,
as follows: Oṃ agnaye jātavedase svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni of the seven tongues!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni the bearer of oblations!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni born from the belly of a horse!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Vaiśvānara!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Kaumāratejas! Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Viśvamukha!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni, the mouth of the gods! Having thus offered the oblation:
Oṃ, svāhā to Indra!
Oṃ, svāhā to Agni!
Oṃ, svāhā to Yama! Oṃ, svāhā to Varuṇa!
Oṃ, svāhā to Nairṛti! Oṃ, svāhā to Vāyu!
Oṃ, svāhā to Kubera!
Oṃ, svāhā to Īśāna. Oṃ, svāhā to Brahmā. Oṃ, svāhā to Ananta.
Oṃ vajrāya svāhā | Oṃ śaktaye svāhā | Oṃ daṇḍāya svāhā |
Oṃ, svāhā to the sword! Oṃ, svāhā to the noose! Oṃ, svāhā to the goad!
Oṃ, svāhā to the mace!
Oṃ, svāhā to the trident! Oṃ, svāhā to the lotus!

"Oṃ cakrāya svāhā. Having thus offered [the oblation], one should take clarified butter four times with the *sruva* ladle, place it in the *sruc* offering-spoon, cover it with the *sruva*, place flowers and other offerings on the tip of its horn, and then rise.

"Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā vauṣaṭ"— with this mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should offer oblations into the fire. Then, one should offer ten oblations with the Mahāgaṇapati mantra divided into ten parts, as follows:
Oṃ svāhā | Oṃ śrīḥ svāhā | Oṃ śrīḥ hrīḥ svāhā |
Oṃ śrī hrī klī svāhā | Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau svāhā | Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau ga svāhā |
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau ga gaṇapataye svāhā | Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau ga gaṇapataye vara-varada svāhā | Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau ga gaṇapataye vara-varada sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā |
Having offered oblations with the mantra: *oṃ śrī hrī klī glau ga gaṇapataye vara varada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*,
one should again offer oblations four times with that same entire mantra.
Thus concludes the general procedure for the fire-offering (*agnimukha*).

Thereafter, one should perform the cooking of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*). As follows: the preceptor, facing eastward, takes a vessel made of copper or similar material and washes it with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*. Having placed cow’s milk in that vessel according to the quantity of rice required, he places the vessel upon the fire along with its supporting stand. Then, having consecrated fifteen *śāli* rice grains (or more) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), he casts them into that vessel. He then takes a lid for the vessel and washes it with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*.
Reciting the armor-mantra (*kavacamantra*)—*huṃ*—he should cover the mouth of the cooking vessel with that [other] vessel and, while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), cook the *caru*.
Then, taking clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* ladle, he should sprinkle it over the cooked *caru* while reciting the root-mantra.
Then—
p. 375) Having brought down that vessel with the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*)—*huḥ*—he should place it upon a mandala strewn with *kuśa* grass consecrated by the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*).
Then, having divided the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into three parts, he should set aside one portion in another vessel and offer it to the deity;
he should reserve the second portion for the fire-oblation (*homa*) to be described later, and the third portion for his own consumption.

Then, having worshipped in the fire everything from the *ādhāraśakti* up to the *pīṭhamantra* of the deity, one should invoke the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) therein, worship them with the ritual offerings (*upacāras*), and also worship the deities of the surrounding retinue (*āvaraṇadevatās*).
Then, with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) of the deity to be worshipped, ending with *svāhā*, one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) into the mouth of the fire.
This very act is called the "unification of the mouths" (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) of the fire and the chosen deity.
Then, having contemplated the identity (*aikya*) of the self, the fire, and the deity, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra alone;
this is called the "junction of the channels" (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).

Then, having offered one oblation each to the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-devatās*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should transfer the fire in sequence into the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) located in the east and other directions, which have been consecrated by the officiating priests (*ṛtviks*) according to the prescribed method.

Then all the officiating priests (ṛtvij), having worshipped their respective chosen deities (iṣṭadevatā) along with their retinues in the fires of their own sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) with the ritual services (upacāra), and having offered twenty-five oblations of clarified butter (ājya) with the root mantra (mūlamantra), should offer one oblation each to the deities of the retinue.

Then the Guru, having divided the second portion of the previously mentioned sacrificial rice (caru) into nine parts and taking one part for himself, should give one part to each of the officiating priests.

Then, having placed clarified butter into that sacrificial porridge (*caru*), the preceptor and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) shall each offer twenty-five oblations into their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) using the porridge mixed with butter.

Then, having offered one oblation each to the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*), and having offered ten oblations each with clarified butter using the root mantra, they should bow down to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) who is in the form of the fire.

Thereafter, the preceptor, having divided the third part of the porridge into two portions and placed them on leaves of the *palāśa* or *pippala* tree, shall take one portion himself and give the other portion to the disciple.

Then the teacher and the disciple, reciting the heart-mantra "Namaḥ," should eat either three morsels or eight morsels without touching them with their teeth; having done so, they should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with water purified by the mantra.

Then the teacher, having performed the ritual rinsing himself, should consecrate the disciple who has rinsed his mouth by means of the root-mantra (sakalīkṛtya), and give him a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha) possessing the previously described characteristics and consecrated with the heart-mantra.
Then the disciple, having cleansed his teeth with that tooth-stick and rinsed them with water, should discard the tooth-stick and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
At this very moment, some perform the aforementioned examination of the tooth-stick.
Then, having performed the evening twilight worship (sāyaṃ-sandhyopāsana), the guru [should proceed] with the root mantra or another mantra prescribed for his own specific ritual tradition.

p. 376) Having tied the topknot of the disciple, he should lie down together with the disciple upon a bed of *kuśa* grass on an inner altar to the south of the deity outside the pavilion, with his head facing east.
At the time of lying down, the disciple should pray for an auspicious dream by means of the *Svapnamānava* mantra.
The *Svapnamānava* mantra is as follows:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull!
Proclaim to me, while I am asleep, that which is eternally desired and undesired—
or rather: *Oṃ hili 2 śūlapāṇaye svāhā* || 5-48 ||
Homage to the victorious three-eyed one, to the tawny-hued great-souled one; homage to the left-handed one, to the one of universal form, to the lord of dreams. 5-49.
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dreams regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall bring about the accomplishment of every undertaking. (5.50)
In the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa], however:
"Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the source of all worlds, the sovereign lord;
salutation to the universe, whose form is the universe, the lord of dreams. (5.51)

Or else, having recited: "O Lord, you who are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, moving within as the sustainer of the universe— reveal to me in a dream the path of good and evil," one should touch the ground with both knees, bow to Viṣṇu, and, being composed and restrained in speech, lie down while contemplating one's own desired object.
Then, having seen the dream, one should rise, perform ritual purification (*ācamana*), hold flowers, bow to the Guru, and report the dream to the Guru.

Thereupon, the Guru, having determined whether the dream is auspicious or inauspicious—if the dream is auspicious, one should know that the deity is pleased; if the dream is inauspicious, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*). As for the pacification of an evil dream:
With the mantra: *phaṭ duḥsvapnadoṣān jahi 2 phaṭ svāhā*;

or with the lion-mantra: *oṃ vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāyudhāya mahāsiṃhāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā*; or with the gāyatrī of that deity; one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with a hundred fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood.

(p. 377) Therein, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: *Oṃ*, beginning with "on this day," etc.—I, [name], of such-and-such lineage, [name] Devaśarman, desiring the pacification of bad dreams, shall offer one hundred oblations of *pālāśa* wood fuel sticks smeared with ghee and sesame seeds through the mediation of my preceptor.
This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).

Then, on the day of initiation, the preceptor and all others, having risen in the morning and completed their daily obligatory rites—such as the morning duties, bathing, and the *saṃdhyā*—shall enter the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*). Having bowed to the deity, they shall each offer one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight, oblations into their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) using sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, or other substances prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for that specific deity, reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) ending with "svāhā."

Then, at the conclusion of the *homa*, the Guru should rise, go outside the pavilion, and, having made the disciple bathe and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), lead him into the pavilion through the southern door and bring him to his own sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Then, beholding the disciple with divine vision, he should draw forth the disciple's consciousness from his heart through the channel of the vital breath (*vahannāḍī*) by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*; having united it with his own consciousness in his own heart via the path of his own channel, he should perform the purification of the paths (*adhvaśodhana*).
It is as follows—at the feet of the disciple:

Having meditated upon the five *kalās* known as *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, *śānti*, and *śāntyatītā*, and having touched his feet with the *kūrca* [mantra], one should offer eight oblations of sesame seeds mixed with ghee, reciting: "Oṃ, I purify the path of the *kalās*, svāhā.
Then, having visualized the path of the *kalās* as dissolved into the path of the *tattvas*, [one should touch] the region of the disciple's genitals—

The thirty-six Śaiva principles (tattvas) consist of: Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, Māyā, Vidya, Kalā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Buddhi, Ahaṅkāra, Manas, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and sound, touch, form, taste, smell; as well as ether, air, fire, water, and earth. These constitute the thirty-six categories of the Lord of Ganas.

The thirty-two Vaiṣṇava principles (*tattva*) are: the individual soul (*jīva*), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether (*ākāśa*), air (*vāyu*), fire (*tejas*), water (*jala*), earth (*pṛthivī*), eye (*cakṣus*), ear (*śrotra*), tongue (*jihvā*), nose (*ghrāṇa*), skin (*tvac*), speech (*vāk*), hand (*pāṇi*), foot (*pāda*), anus (*pāyu*), generative organ (*upastha*), and those known as the Sun, Moon, Fire, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.

The twenty-four Saura principles (*tattva*) are: ether (*ākāśa*), air (*vāyu*), fire (*tejas*), water (*jala*), earth (*pṛthivī*), sound (*śabda*), touch (*sparśa*), form (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*mahattattva*), eye (*cakṣus*), ear (*śrotra*), tongue (*jihvā*), nose (*ghrāṇa*), skin (*tvac*), speech (*vāk*), hand (*pāṇi*), foot (*pāda*), anus (*pāyu*), generative organ (*upastha*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Having contemplated the ten *prakṛti-tattvas*— namely, the five *kalās* called Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatītā, along with Bindu, Kala, Nāda, Śakti, and Sadāśiva— and the ten *śākta-tattvas*— namely, Ātma, Vidyā, Śiva, Śivavidyā, Ātmā, Ātmavidyā, Śiva, Sarva, and Śivasarva—
as well as the *traipura-tattvas*— namely, Ātma, Vidyā, Śiva, Śivavidyā, Ātma, and Sarva— one should touch the perineum of the disciple with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle].

"Oṃ, I purify the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), svāhā"— with this, one should offer eight oblations. Then, having visualized the path of the principles as dissolved into the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), one should touch the disciple's navel while contemplating, in sequence, the fourteen worlds known as Pātāla, Rasātala, Mahātala, Talātala, Sutala, Vitala, Talātala, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satya.
"Oṃ, I purify the path of the worlds, svāhā"—with this, one should offer eight oblations.

Then, having visualized the path of the worlds as dissolved into the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan), and having contemplated the letters from *a* to *kṣa* within the disciple's heart, one should touch the heart and offer eight oblations with: "Oṃ, I purify the path of the phonemes, svāhā."

Then, having visualized the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) as dissolved into the path of words (*padādhvan*), one should contemplate the mantra-syllables on the disciple’s forehead, touch his forehead, and offer eight oblations with the mantra: *oṃ padādhvānaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*.
Then, having visualized the path of words as dissolved into the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), one should contemplate the complete mantra upon the disciple’s head, touch his head, and—

"Oṃ, I purify the path of mantra, svāhā"—having offered eight oblations in this manner as before, one should contemplate that the path of mantra has dissolved into the Supreme Śiva residing in the *brahmarandhra*.

Having thus performed the purification of the sixfold paths within the body of the disciple through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), one should then contemplate, by means of the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), that from the Supreme Śiva the path of mantra arises; from the path of mantra, the path of words (*padādhvan*); from the path of words, the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*); from the path of phonemes, the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*); from the path of worlds, the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*); and from the path of principles, the path of energies (*kalādhvan*) has arisen.
Regarding this, some say that one should generate the paths (*adhvan*) in sequence by means of oblations with the mantra: *oṃ paramaśivāt mantrādhvānam utpādayāmi svāhā*.

Then, gazing at the disciple with divine vision, one should unite the consciousness residing within oneself with that [consciousness] in the disciple's heart, via one's own central channel (*vahannāḍī*) and through the path of his own central channel.

Then, having offered ten oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and having given one oblation each to the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*), one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

The procedure for this is as follows: filling the *sruc* ladle with the ghee remaining from the *homa*, placing flowers, sesame seeds, barley, fruits, and so forth [into it], covering the *sruc* with the *sruva* spoon held face down, and placing a flower on its tip; then, leaving a space of four finger-breadths from the base of the *mūla* [mantra], holding the *sruc* and *sruva* with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, joining their bases together, and standing up, one should offer three final oblations with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, preceded by the right foot.
In the Śākta tradition, the Vāmamārga, and so forth, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* preceded by the left foot. In the Vāmamārga, this is done with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
According to the Vedic procedure, however, it is performed with the mantra "mūrddhānaṃ divaḥ."

The specific distinction is that one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra beginning "pūrṇādarvi," and then offer the final oblation with the mantras of the "offering to Brahman" (*brahmārpaṇa*). The mantra is as follows:

Whatever has been thought, spoken, or done by me through mind, speech, or action—with the hands, feet, belly, and genitals—under the influence of the vital breath, intellect, body, and sense-objects, during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; may all that be an offering unto Brahman, Svāhā!

Having thus offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *Brāhmārpaṇa* mantra, one should worship the chosen deity residing in the fire with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), prostrate, perform the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*), and then, having dismissed [the deity] from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of the withdrawal gesture (*saṃhāramudrā*), unite it with the water-pot (*kalaśa*). Then, having dismissed the guardians of the quarters such as Indra—beginning with Dhruva—who were stationed in the directions starting from the east, as well as the deities of the consecrated sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) situated outside, and having brought them into the principal water-pot, one should contemplate the identity of those deities with the chosen deity. Finally, for the purpose of dismissing the fire, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).
p. 380) Namely: Oṃ bhūr agnaye pṛthivyai ca mahate svāhā!
Oṃ bhuvo vāyave antarikṣāya ca dive ca mahate svāhā!
"Oṃ, svāhā to Svar-Āditya, to the Moon, to the Directions, and to the Constellations!
Oṃ Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, svāhā to the Moon, to the Constellations, to the Directions, and to the Great One!

Having offered thus, and having offered one oblation each to the tongues, limbs, and forms of Agni according to the previously mentioned method, as well as to the World-Guardians with their respective weapon-mantras, he should sprinkle the fire within the enclosures with milk or water, and worship it with the fivefold offerings using that mantra.
May there be well-being: faith, fame, wisdom, learning, intellect, prosperity, and strength.
O bearer of oblations, grant me long life, splendor, and health.
O Agni, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!
Even when another rite has arrived, grant your presence with respect.
Having thus prayed—"O Lord Agni, you have been worshipped; forgive me"—and having prostrated before the fire, he should dismiss it with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.

Then, having bid farewell to Brahmā, he should fill a copper vessel weighing thirty-two *palas* with rice, place gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon it, and give it to the Brāhmaṇa who serves as the representative of Brahmā.

The formula for the gift is as follows: *Oṃ, today... [etc.]—for the sake of the consecration of this homa rite which constitutes a limb of the present initiation ritual, I give this full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), dedicated to Prajāpati, and this gold, dedicated to Agni, to you, the Brahmin named Amukaśarman of the Amuka-gotra.* Thus he should give the full vessel.

Thereafter, the preceptor should silently cast the surrounding kuśa grass and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire. However, the distinction is that in the case of the daily homa, one should not burn them.

Then, reciting the eye-mantra "Vauṣaṭ," having bound the disciple's eyes with a new white cloth, filled his joined palms with flowers, and taken hold of his hand, [the teacher] removes the curtain, leads the disciple into the presence of the deity, and while himself reciting the root mantra, casts a handful of flowers upon the seat for the deity.
Then the disciple, whose eye-bandage has been removed by the Guru—

"Salutation to that glorious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge. Having recited this and prostrated at the feet of the Guru, one should prostrate with the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) before the Deity.

Then the Guru, having seated the disciple upon a bed of *darbha* grass, dissolves that body composed of the five elements through the process of elemental purification (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and then generates it again by way of creation. Having performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) prescribed for his own specific tradition upon that body, he seats the disciple upon a pedestal made of *śrīparṇī* wood or similar materials, situated on a square altar (*vedikā*) within a pavilion constructed to the northeast for the purpose of consecration; this altar measures two cubits in length and eight finger-breadths in height. The Guru himself proceeds to the station of the deity, worships the deity with offerings such as water for the feet (*pādya*), and after offering three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, performs the dedication of the worship (*ārādhanārpaṇa*).
For example: having recited the root mantra— "Whether good or bad, whatever action has been performed by me. (5.54)

"O Lord of the gods of gods, accept all this as the supreme worship. Having spoken thus, one should pour the *argha* water onto the right hand of the deity if it is male, or onto the left hand if it is female.
Then, having prostrated before the deity and taken handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should ask for forgiveness as follows:
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is given with mere devotion, and whatever food offering is presented—please accept that out of compassion. (5.55)
I do not know how to invoke you, nor do I know how to dismiss you;
I do not even know how to perform worship. You alone are my refuge, O Supreme Lord.
"By deed, by mind, and by speech, there is no other refuge for me than you;
you are the Supreme Lord, the witness of the inner movements of all beings. Having spoken thus, she should cast a handful of flowers and prostrate.
Then, she should pray for a boon on behalf of the disciple.
Namely:
O Goddess, abode of compassion, refuge of all presences! (5.57)
O Mother, who are a refuge and full of affection, show compassion toward this child,
O Sovereign of the Gods, who is bound by the fetters beginning with those of the individual soul (āṇava).
O Goddess, source of compassion, show mercy to this wretched man; let him be endowed with enjoyments both of this world and the next. (5-59)
"Let all my devotion be offered to him who is the refuge of the partless (niṣkala)"—
thus [it is said]. But in the case of the deity Puraśvara, the reading "O Lord of Devas, refuge of compassion," and so forth, should be understood.

Having thus offered prayers, one should contemplate that all the deities of the enclosure have dissolved into the limbs of the principal deity. Then, having meditated upon the deity in the form of light, one should say: "O Blessed One, [Name] Devatā, you have been worshipped; please forgive me. Having said this, one should dismiss her with the *saṃhāramudrā* and establish her within one’s own heart via the path of the *vahannāḍī*. Then, having prepared a mandala in the northeastern direction, one should worship the *nirmālyavāsī* (the deity who dwells in the remains of the offering) as prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for that particular deity.

"By the command of the Deity, I give to you, who consume the remains of offerings, the food to be licked, sucked, and drunk, as well as the floral garlands and ointments that have been offered. Having thus given the *nirmālya*, one should dismiss the deity residing in the *nirmālya* by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.

Then, having placed a small portion of the *nirmālya* on one's own head with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should lift the water-pot (*kumbha*), go near the disciple, and place the sprouts from the mouth of the pot upon the disciple's head. While reciting the letters of the *Mātṛkā* and the root mantra, accompanied by the sounds of the five musical instruments and the benedictions of the Brahmins, one should consecrate the disciple with the water from the pot.
Then, having lifted the *vardhanī* vessel, he should sprinkle [the disciple] with that water.

Then, having caused the disciple to sip the remaining water and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), he should contemplate him as being of the nature of the deity.
Thereafter, the disciple, having risen and put on two washed garments, and having sipped water, should sit upon a seat in the presence of the Guru, facing either east or north, by the Guru's command.

Then the Guru, having visualized the deity as having been transferred from himself into the disciple's body and having contemplated their identity, should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then bestow the mantra.
As follows:
making the declaration, "I give this mantra of such-and-such a deity," the Guru should pour water into the hand of the disciple.
"Grant [it] preceded by favor"—thus the disciple should say.

Then the Guru, having placed his hand upon the head of the disciple and having recited the mantra to be given one hundred and eight times, should cause the disciple to hear the mantra three times in the right ear. (p.

383) However, for women and Śūdras, he should recite the mantra in the left ear. The bestowal of the mantra preceded by the offering of water pertains exclusively to Brāhmaṇas; for others, however, he should give the mantra without that [water-offering].
Then the Guru, having visualized the luminous Vidyā entering the body of the disciple from himself, should say: "May this mantra grant equal fruits for both of us.
The disciple, likewise, should visualize that same Vidyā entering his own heart from the mouth of the Guru.
Salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru.
To you, who possess the form of all the gods and consist of all mantras, [I say:
by your grace, I have been liberated from the terrible and great noose of death.
"O Lord, by your grace I have achieved my purpose in every respect. Having praised him thus, he should remain prostrate like a staff at the feet of the Guru.
Then the Guru says:
"Arise, child; you are liberated. Be one who perfectly observes the rules of conduct."
