"May fame, glory, beauty, intelligence, longevity, strength, and health always be yours"—having said this, he should raise the disciple up. Then, the disciple, contemplating the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra, should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times in the presence of the Guru by the Guru’s command. The Guru, moreover, after the transmission of the mantra, should himself recite the mantra one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, the disciple, abandoning any stinginess regarding wealth, should give the Guru a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of his entire property, half of that, or a quarter of that.
Taking *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water, [one should say]:

"Oṃ, today, etc.—I, of such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such, for the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the undertaking of this initiation (*grahaṇa*) of the mantra of such-and-such deity, offer this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you, the venerable Guru, of such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such.

In this manner, one should give cows, land, gold, clothing, ornaments, and so forth, to the Brahmin acting as the representative of Brahmā (*brahmapratinidhi*) and to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Then one should present the pavilion, together with the materials for worship, to the Guru.

After that, having fed the Brahmins and given them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having received their blessings, one should give the food offering (*naivedya*) presented to the deity to the devotees of the deity, and then the Guru and the disciple should eat. On the day of initiation, fasting by both the Guru and the disciple is prohibited.

Then, the disciple, having stayed at the Guru’s residence for three days and having performed the worship of the deity on the fourth day, should bow to the Guru, take his permission, and go to his own home.

Thus ends the complete procedure for the initiation involving ritual action (*kriyāvatī-dīkṣā*). In the event of inability to perform this, the abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣepa-dīkṣā*) should be performed. That has been described [in the Nibandha]:
"At an auspicious moment, having placed a nine-jar diagram (*navakumbha*) upon a *sarvatobhadra* mandala... (5.62).
It should be accompanied by water, honored with fragrant flowers, and provided with a cloth;
it should also be joined with all medicinal herbs, the five precious gems, and the five types of sprouts.
Then, having performed the worship of the deity, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations.
Regarding "all medicinal herbs," another tantra states:
*jaṭāmāṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, and the two types of rajanī* (5–64).
Śaṭī, campaka, and musta are remembered as the group of all medicinal herbs (sarvoṣadhigaṇa).
Rajanīdvaya refers to haridrā and dāruharidrā. Pṛśniparṇī, pippalī, sahadevī, and ghṛtakumārī [are also included].
The nine gems (navaratna) have been mentioned previously.
Regarding "the five sprouts" (as stated by Vasiṣṭha): the jackfruit, the mango, as well as the holy fig, the banyan, and the bakula. || 5-65 ||
The five sprouts (*pañcapallava*) have been thus described by the sages who know the tantras.
In another tantra, it is stated: "The *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, and *āmra* are the five sprouts."
(In the Nibandha:
One should cause the well-adorned disciple to sit upon the altar near the fire. 5-66.
One should perform the sprinkling with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel consecrated by mantras, and likewise with the water from the *kumbha* jar;
then, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the root mantra recited one hundred and eight times.

One hundred and eight, or one hundred and eight plus one; then, while accomplishing the mantra and placing his hand upon the head, [the teacher says] "May there be peace," and should offer unbroken grains (akṣata). Then the disciple should worship the guru. (5.68)
Thus concludes the procedure for the abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣepadīkṣā*).
Now, the initiation consisting of phonemes (*varṇamayīdīkṣā*) [from the *Merutantra*]:
"Now, listen to the initiation consisting of phonemes, which bestows knowledge."
And it has been declared that the phonemes have the nature of both the male (puṃs) and primordial matter (prakṛti). || 5-69 ||
And such a nature of the body has indeed been declared by the teachers;
therefore, the best of teachers should deposit the phonemes (varṇas) upon the body of the disciple. (5.70)
The preeminent teacher, by his own power and through the command of the deity-nature, should withdraw the phonemes situated in their respective locations in the reverse order. (5.71)
Then the disciple becomes one whose self is the deity, with his true nature fully absorbed;
thereafter, he should unite the consciousness of the disciple with the Supreme Self.
Having drawn those [deities] from there, one should place them within the body of the disciple;
and within that [body], one should again place that consciousness according to the sequence of vision (dṛṣṭikrama). || 5.73 ||
The disciple shall become one with the deity, Śiva, whose nature is eternal bliss;
this initiation, consisting of the ocean of the gift of knowledge, is said to bestow all perfections.
Thus ends the procedure for initiation consisting of the phonemes (*varṇamayī dīkṣā*).
Now, regarding the initiation consisting of the energies (*kalāvatī dīkṣā*), it is in that same [text]:
"Now I shall describe the initiation of the energies (*kalādīkṣā*), which bestows the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*."
In the Veda, initiation is considered to consist of five kalās; in the Dakṣa [Tantra], it is held to consist of eight or three kalās.
The fifty-second *kalā* on the left belongs to the Guru who has perfected the mantra;
it should be received quickly as it brings about accomplishment (*siddhi*), whereas in the opposite case, the result is the reverse.
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are said to belong to the elements;
the wise one should pierce them in succession into the body of the disciple, which is composed of the elements. (5.77)
The *nivṛtti* kalā is established from the feet up to the knees;
from the knees up to the navel, the kalā called *pratiṣṭhā* is situated. (5.79)
The portion known as Vidyā is situated from the navel up to the throat;
the portion known as Śānti is situated from the throat up to the forehead. (5.80)
The wise one should pierce from another location, starting from the forehead up to the head, according to the sequence of withdrawal, [piercing] the Kalā known as Śāntyatītā.
In this manner, initiation (dīkṣā) consisting of five kalās is prescribed by one's own command in its proper place;
O deities, listen now to the method of initiation consisting of thirty-eight kalās.

Wherein the twelve letters beginning with *ka* are situated in forward order (*krama*), and wherein those beginning with *bha* are in reverse order (*viloma*), there, in those two places, are the *kalās*. (5.83)
The sixteen digits (kalās) of the Sun are to be meditated upon in the sixteen [vowels], and likewise those of the Moon;
in the place beginning with the letter 'ya', the ten digits of Fire are to be meditated upon.
Then follows the withdrawal from the qualities (guṇas), the parts (kalās), and the locations of the phonemes (varṇasthāna);
thereafter, one should generate the disciple once again—this is the procedure for the initiation into the parts (kalādīkṣā).
Thus ends the initiation of Kalāvatī.
Now, regarding the initiation consisting of piercing (vedhamayī dīkṣā), it is said in that same [text]:
"I shall describe the initiation consisting of piercing, having obtained which a person abandons [the body]."
At that very moment, one who is liberated while living transcends saṃsāra. || 5-86 ||
One should also meditate upon the four-petalled lotus in the disciple's mūlādhāra;
in its center is a triangle, and in the middle of that is the kuṇḍalinī.
The Goddess, who consists of three revolutions, whose form is like a mass of lightning,
who is identical with Mahādeva, and whose body is manifestly composed of pure knowledge alone.
The goddess, subtler than the subtlest, who pierces the six wheels, divine, proceeding by way of the *suṣumṇā* toward the abode of Śiva. (5.89)
One should gather the letters beginning with *sa* from the *tala* [of the alphabet] into the position of the lotus;
then, one should place them upon a six-petaled lotus, with pairs of letters beginning with *la* on each petal. (5.90)
Having properly joined the Guru at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should pierce [the path];
one should bring those phonemes into Viṣṇu, and that Viṣṇu into the navel-lotus.
One should oneself pierce the petals of the directions joined with the phonemes beginning with *pha* and *ṭa*;
one should join those phonemes in Rudra, and that Rudra in the heart-lotus.
One should oneself pierce the Lord within the lotus of the first letter, which is beautiful;
one should then extract those letters from this [lotus] and likewise place them in the lotus of the throat.
Having carefully joined the vowels within a lotus consisting of sixteen petals,
and then having joined them to Sadāśiva, one should join them to the lotus in the middle of his eyebrows.
Having pierced the two petals joined with *ha* and *kṣa*, the teacher should lead the self together with the Power (Śakti) up to the level of Paraśiva.
Then, by the power of the teacher’s command, the disciple burns away ignorance on the earth;
having attained higher knowledge (vijñāna), he falls [to the ground] and thereafter becomes omniscient.
Sadāśiva himself shall become [the disciple]; this is the truth, there is no doubt. This auspicious initiation, consisting of piercing (vedha), is said to bestow knowledge. || 5.97 ||
Thus concludes the initiation consisting of piercing (*vedhamayī dīkṣā*).

Now follows the initiation of the five abodes (*pañcāyatanī dīkṣā*). In that rite, having placed the principal jar in the center and having placed four jars in the four corners, one should invoke and worship the five deities.

Alternatively, having placed only a single jar, one should worship the deities according to the sequence to be described hereafter. This is because of the statement in the *Prapañcasāra*: "In this manner, [initiation is performed] by means of the prescribed procedure with either a single jar or with many jars."
The sequence for the installation of the deities therein is stated in the *Jñānamālā*:
"When one worships Śaṅkara in the center, one should worship Śrīpati in the northeast, Haṃsa in the southeast, and the son of Pārvatī in the southwest. (5.98)
And Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, should always be worshipped in the northwest;
however, when Govinda is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast. (5.99)
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should worship Gaṇanātha in the southeast, Tapanas in the southwest, and Ambikā in the northwest. || 5-100 ||
When [the worshipper faces] the thousand-rayed [Sun] in the center, one should worship the Lord of Pārvatī in the northeast,
the One-tusked [Gaṇeśa] in the southeast, and Acyuta in the southwest.
One should worship Divi in the northwest, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
but when Bhavānī is in the center, one should worship Mādhava in the northeast.
The preceptor should worship Pārvatīnātha in the southeast, Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest, and Pradyotana in the northwest. (5.103)
When one should worship Heramba in the center, Acyuta in the northeast, Pañcavaktra in the southeast, and Jagadambikā in the southwest. (5.104)
The practitioner, free from sloth, should indeed worship the Sun in the northwest;
for deities who have been removed from their proper places bestow sorrow, suffering, and fear. (5.105)
The king and the practitioner situated within that mandala will perish. || 5-105ef ||

In another tantra: When Śambhu has gone to the center, Hari, Naha, Hara, Bhū, and Devī are established; when Harī is in the center, Śaṅkara and Bhāsī; when Āgasutā is in the center, Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Ajā, and Ambikā are established.

In the case of a female [child], Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Ravaya, Lambodara, Aja, Īśvara, and Aryena are declared from the portion of Śaṅkara; however, if these are transposed [to other positions], they cause loss. (5.106)
In the *Merutantra*:
[The letters] ī, śa, e, ja, ne, śa, ja, śi, vā, ha, ra, vī, śe, śa, ja, na, sā, [are assigned];
for Svā, vī, śe, śa, ja, jo, mā; and for the Goddess, vi, śi, ga, bhā, sva, rā. (5.107)
(p. 389) Gaṇeśa, Aja (Brahmā), Īśa (Śiva), and Bhā (Sūrya), along with the Goddesses, are to be worshipped starting from the northeast corner.
As for the sequence of worship, it is stated in another Tantra:
"Having offered a handful of flowers to the Principal Deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should take place. (5.108)
If Gaṇeśa alone is the primary deity, then it should follow the sequence of the Sun. Thus it is said.
And this:
"He who performs the ritual on a single seat without separate worship for each [deity] incurs the curse of the deity by abandoning limb after limb. (5.109)

Thus, because the words of Kalāvatī prohibit separate worship on a support other than the yantra, the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the invocation of the ancillary deities (*aṅgadevatā*) concern [only] installed yantras and the like, according to the statement of Sanatkumāra: "The worship of the pedestal, the invocation of the ancillary deities," and so forth. Regarding the time for the worship of the ancillary deities, the author of the *Tantrasāra* maintains that it occurs after the worship of the pedestal. However, in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others is stated to take place even before the worship of the pedestal: "At this very occasion, one who desires the five-shrine system (*pañcāyatana*) should worship Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Īśāna with ritual offerings (*upacāra*)."

In reality, however, statements such as "the worship of the seat is the sacrifice to the ancillary deities" apply to the system of a single pitcher (*ekakalaśa*). But in the system of five pitchers (*pañcakalaśa*), one should install five pitchers within five *sarvatobhadra* mandalas according to the stated sequence and worship the five deities separately; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, the absence of the *pañcāyatana-dīkṣā* (five-shrine initiation) in the case of Śyāmā and others has been stated in the *Cāmuṇḍā-tantra*:
"In the case of Śyāmā, [the deities are] Bhairavī and Tārā; but in the case of Bhairava, [they are] Chinnamastā. (5.110)
Likewise, for Mañjughoṣa and Raudra, the five-limbed [initiation] is not accepted by the wise.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for initiation into the Five Āyatanas (from the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*).
Initiation is manifold: that of the individual soul (āṇavī), that of energy (śākteyī), and again that of Śambhu (śāmbhavī). || 5-111 ||
"Only as one," so it is recited by the wise who are experts in the scriptures;
having stated that the individual (āṇavī) [impurity] is manifold, its divisions are now being explained. (5.112)
The consecration is of eight kinds: that based on tradition (smārtī), that mental (mānasikī), that pertaining to yoga (yaugī), as well as that visual (cākṣuṣī) and tactile (spārśanī);
furthermore, it is verbal (vācikī), mantra-based (mantrikī), sacrificial (hotrī), scriptural (śāstrī), and [finally] the consecration itself (abhiṣecikī). (5.113)
Now, regarding the *smārta* initiation, it is performed in that very same manner:

having remembered the Guru who is situated in another land, one should gradually sever the three bonds of the disciple and, by means of the procedure for dissolution and enjoyment, [unite him] with the supreme Śiva. (5.114)
"This initiation, consisting of the correct conjunction [of mantras], is proclaimed as the Smārta initiation.
Thus ends the Smārta initiation.
Now, regarding the Mānasa initiation, it is stated in that same [text]:
Having perceived with his mind that the pure one was seated in his presence, [he spoke].
"That which liberates from the three impurities by means of [spiritual] methods is the mental [initiation].
Thus ends the mental initiation (*mānasī-dīkṣā*).
Now, regarding the yoga-initiation (*yoga-dīkṣā*), it is in that same [text]:
Then, according to the sequence taught in Yoga, the yogin enters the body of the disciple.
Having grasped his own self by means of one's own self, that which consists of such union is called the initiation of yoga (*yogadīkṣā*), which destroys the three impurities.
Thus concludes the initiation of yoga (*yogadīkṣā*).
Now follows the initiation of vision (*dṛgdīkṣā*) according to the *Merutantra*:
"Having closed one's eyes and meditated upon the deity within the Supreme Self..."
The Guru should gaze [at him] with eyes filled with the bliss of seeing that. || 5.118 ||
With a serene mind, one should subsequently instruct the disciple;
this "initiation by sight" bestows fruit, serving as the means for the disciple's accomplishment. (5.119)
In the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*:
"Having ascertained 'I am Śiva,' one should gaze with a vision moistened by compassion;
that is the visual initiation (*cākṣuṣī dīkṣā*), which destroys all sins. (5.120)
Thus ends the initiation through sight.
Now, the initiation through touch is described in that same [text]:
"The Guru, having himself become Paraśiva, with a mind free from doubt..."
With the hand of Śiva, he should touch the head of the disciple while reciting the mantra. (5.121)
That is declared to be the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*), which effects the manifestation of Śiva.
Regarding "with the hand of Śiva":
one should fashion a mandala with perfumes upon one's own right hand. (5.122)
"One should worship the God according to the prescribed rite; thus there shall be the 'Hand of Śiva'"—this means in the manner described by Somaśambhu.
In the Merutantra:
The Guru should meditate upon his own Guru in the form of Śiva within his own hand, while reciting the root mantra, the six limbs, and the mantras of the Mātṛkās and so forth. (5.123)
Having placed his right hand upon the head of the disciple out of compassion, he should thereafter bestow the instruction; this aforementioned initiation through touch grants supreme accomplishment.
Thus ends the initiation through touch (*sparśadīkṣā*). Now follows the verbal initiation (*vācikī dīkṣā*) [from the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*]:
Having visualized his own mouth as the mouth of the Guru, the Guru, with reverence, [should proceed].
Through the application of the Guru’s oral instructions, the divine mantras and so forth [are bestowed] upon the disciple.
Together with the placement of mudrās and so forth, one should offer this; for this indeed is the vocal [worship].
In the *Merutantra*: "The Guru should cause the mind to rest upon Sadāśiva, whose nature is consciousness."
One should meditate on all the mantras born from that [deity], oneself being of the same nature as them. || 5-126 ||
"By the grace of the Guru, I have become the absolute Sadāśiva.
Meditating thus, one should sit down; this is declared to be the initiation of speech (vāgdīkṣā).
Thus concludes the oral initiation (*vācikī dīkṣā*).

Now follows the initiation of the mantra (*mantrī dīkṣā*): "The supreme initiation is likewise that in which the body is joined with the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*). (From the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*)
Having oneself become the embodiment of the mantra, one should respectfully recite the mantra according to the ritual sequence.
(392) "One should bestow it upon the disciple; that is the Mantra-initiation (māntrī-dīkṣā), which destroys impurity. Thus concludes the Mantra-initiation.
Now follows the Hotṛ-initiation (hotrī-dīkṣā) in that same [text]:
Having placed the fire in either a sacrificial pit or upon a consecrated mound according to the prescribed rule, || 5-129 ||
Precisely by means of the sequence of absorption and enjoyment, one proceeds step by step through each stage:
the mantra, the phoneme, the kalā, the principle (tattva), the word, and the world-sphere.
"One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the sake of purification; this is declared to be the Hotrī initiation.

By the phrase "in the sequence of dissolution and enjoyment" is meant: by the sequence of the piercing initiation (vedhadīkṣā), in the form of the withdrawal of the deities of the phonemes established in the *mūlādhāra*. This is the Hotrī initiation.
Thus concludes the scriptural initiation (*śāstrī dīkṣā*).
Now, regarding the scriptural initiation (śāstrī-dīkṣā), it is said in that very same [text]: "To a disciple of Yoga who is devoted and intent upon service and worship... (5.131).
"Accompanied by the three Vedas and the bestowal of the scriptures, it is called the scriptural initiation (śāstrī dīkṣā).
Thus ends the scriptural initiation.
Now follows the consecratory initiation (abhiṣecikī dīkṣā) in that same [text].
Having respectfully worshipped both Śiva and the consort of Śiva in the water-pot (kumbha), [verse 5-132].
"From the consecration with the auspicious jar (śivakumbha), that initiation shall be the Abhiṣecikī.
Thus ends the Abhiṣecikī initiation.
Now follows the Śāmbhavī initiation (from the Merutantra).
Merely by the sight of a cow, by speaking [to her], or even by touching her, [one attains merit]. || 5.133 ||
Knowledge arises immediately; that is remembered as the Śāmbhavī initiation.
Thus ends the Śāmbhavī initiation.
Now, the initiation by oral instruction (*upadeśa-dīkṣā*) [according to the Viśvasāra]:
If someone is unable even for that, having worshipped a lotus together with grains of rice, || 5.134 ||
Having sprinkled one's own hand eight times with that water while reciting the root mantra, one should place it upon the ear and recite it eight times; this is the procedure for the oral instruction.

p. 393) Regarding the phrase "therein": it means in the previously mentioned abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣepadīkṣā*). "The lotus" refers to the conch. "Placing the hand on the head": the meaning is that one should place the hand upon the head.
Now, regarding another type of initiation, the instructional initiation (*upadeśadīkṣā*), in that same [text]:
"The great initiation (*mahādīkṣā*), likewise the initiation, and thereafter the instruction (*upadeśa*)."
And in every age, instruction must be given; [this is especially so] in the Kali age.

During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva—the mere recitation of the mantra is called "instruction" (upadeśa). (5.137)

(Merutantra) Having examined [the disciple] according to the rules for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, the Guru should subsequently impart the mantra; otherwise, it will be fruitless. (5.138)
He who gives by unjust means, and he who accepts by unjust means—for both the giver and the receiver, there shall be a curse upon their lineage. (5.139)
If both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, give or receive instruction without having examined one another, they shall both attain the state of a piśāca. (5.140)
But he who receives or gives instruction that is contrary to the scriptures—both of them shall experience twenty-one terrible hells. (5.141)
But that person of deluded intellect who gives instruction without performing the consecration—his mantras perish like rice seeds sown in sand. (5.142)
The knowledge of mantras never remains in one who is unworthy;
therefore, it should be spoken only after examination, otherwise it will be fruitless. (5.143)
The knowledge that is imparted to a true disciple who possesses supreme devotion attains the state of direct realization, just as clarified butter is obtained from cow's milk. (5.144)
If one should initiate an unworthy person out of desire for wealth, fear, greed, or the like, he incurs the curse of the deity, and what has been performed becomes corrupted. (5.145)
Thus concludes the procedure for the initiation of instruction (*upadeśadīkṣā*).
Now follows the procedure for the sequential initiation (*kramadīkṣā*). [This is supported by] the words of the *Śaktiśaṅgamakulārṇava* and other texts cited in the *Tantracintāmaṇi*:
"Sundarī, Tāriṇī, and Kālī are those who enter into the sequential initiation."
O Maheśānī, when the Krama is complete, Śumbha shall become [the Krama] through the sequence.
O Goddess, [the sequence consists of] Candra, Agni, Pakṣa, the one called Ṣoḍhā, Parā, Nirvāṇa, and Tatparā; then the six Śāmbhava [mantras], and also the piercing of the wheels (cakrasaṃbheda).
The knowledge of one's own wheel and body, and the entry into another's body—through this knowledge wisdom arises; this has been declared by me to you as initiation.
O Maheśvarī, hear this which has been declared beginning with *ha* and *ka*:
first is Candrāgnirasarājñī, then Mahārājñī, O Śivā;
then Mahākāmakalā Kālī, and then Guhyakālī, O Śivā.
Guhyakālī is said to be twofold, according to the sequence: with parts (sakalā) and without parts (niṣkalā).
The ten-faced one is said to be the complete [form], or else the cause of emanation;
she is also proclaimed to be threefold: fierce, gentle, and extremely cruel. (5.151)
Niṣkalā, Guhyasaṃśāntī, and Kālī are proclaimed as distinct [forms];
this Kevalā is indeed called Medhā, whose nature is imperial sovereignty.
Candrāgni, Vedapañcārṇā, and likewise Nīlā in sequence; then Haṃsatārā, Mahānīlā, and at the end, Cīnasambhavī. (5.153)

Meditation (medhā) may be solitary; however, when it consists of the two types of activity—supernatural power (ṛddhi) and accomplishment (siddhi)—or all three, it is proclaimed as the initiation (dīkṣā) for divine sovereignty.
She is the form of the gods, the divine form, the form of mantra, the Great Supreme. (p.
395) She is the form of all, the foremost of all, through the wisdom of the great empire. 5-155.
The multiplicity of divisions has been described precisely according to the sequence of supernatural powers and accomplishments (*ṛddhisiddhi*).
In the ritual procedure of Chinnamastā, initiation is known by the names *Vidyā* and *Rājya*. (5.156)
Candravahnirasāraktā and Śyāmā are likewise the sixteenth;
the seventeenth is Parāṣoḍhā, and she who follows that would be Parā. (5.157)
Dīpinī, Mālinī, and Kullā bestow, in sequence, the kingdom of knowledge and so forth;
O Maheśānī, Vagalā is established in the supreme sovereignty. (5.158)
The heart-mantra ending in Śiva, which is deficient by one syllable [compared to] Candra, Veda, Sūkṣma, and Meru;
likewise the hundred-syllabled heart-mantra, the five weapons, and the Kullukā. || 5-159 ||
Through the sequential application of the Gāyatrī, one who upholds the Sāmrājya and Parameṣṭhin [stages], being joined with this pentad, maintains the consciousness of universal sovereignty. (5.160)
The initiation into the glorious, divine universal sovereignty (sarvasāmrājya) is the most supreme of all;
even greater than that, O Mistress of the Gods, there is no other initiation within the sphere of the universe.
There are ten divisions of knowledge born from the divisions of great knowledge,
as well as divisions of the knowledge of accomplishments and likewise great mantras.
O Goddess of the Gods, its constituent mantras are Śāvara, Deśaśāvara, Kālaśāvaraka, and likewise Siddhiśāvara. (5.163)

O Śivā, in the Kali age, the mantras of the threefold vision (darśana) that arise from the sequence of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) exist according to the order of *ka* and so forth, as well as *ha* and so forth.
Likewise, O Goddess of the gods, whatever collection of mantras there may be— including those of the Āyatanas— all authority over them shall reside in this rite of initiation.
One who is joined with this initiation is Śrī Kālikā herself;
by means of the sequence of eight watches, she assumes the form of the ten Vidyās. (5.166)

The Vidyā named Kāmakalā, along with its divisions, the presiding deities of the ritual applications (vṛtti), the limb-mantras, and likewise others pertaining to his weapons, are always [to be recited]. (5.167)
O Maheśānī, the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā) is fivefold according to the divisions of the Vidyās;
O Śivā, its constituent mantras are the Gāyatrī and the five Kullukas.
O Supreme Goddess, that which is declared as the most secret of secrets in the ritual procedures of any other Vidyā applies likewise to Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, and Tārā. (5-169)
O Goddess, that lowest of practitioners who recites [the mantra] without the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā) shall become impoverished, most terrible, devoid of fortune, and censured. (5.170)
Alternatively, one who is excessively volatile may undergo agitation of the mantras;
however, one who is joined with the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā) certainly becomes a king. || 5-171 ||
Endowed with great majesty, possessed of all perfections, victorious, disciplined, virtuous, accomplished, the bestower of accomplishment, and auspicious. || 5.172 ||
With a joyful soul, all-knowing, cognizant of the three periods of time, a seer, happy, the lord of ten million siddhis, heroic, beautiful, and a deluder of desire. (5.173)
The self of bliss, the supreme self, transcending all conquered qualities,
he is the manifest Lord of the Kings of Kings, equal to Mahākāla in the Kali age.
For one who knows and worships this, there is never poverty or wretchedness, [provided] there is no lack of a guru, no abandonment of the lineage, and no separation from the oral tradition. (5.175)
Poverty shall first prevail; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Wherever there is a house of the wish-fulfilling gem, there is a palace of jewels. (5.176)
A house that is the abode of all sovereignty, with stairways composed of the nine gems;
where there is a grove of *kalpavṛkṣa* trees as well as a grove of *parijāta* trees. (5.177) p. 397)
But for the touchstone, where indeed could there be poverty?
Therefore, for one who lacks the proper sequence, there is poverty at every step. (5.178)
Having approached a Guru who is endowed with the [proper] lineage, the wise person should request the lineage-transmission;
otherwise, through ignorance regarding the Guru, one may fall into poverty. (5.179)
Or he may have a short lifespan, O Goddess; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Regarding the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣāpaddhati*), the words from the *Vāḍavānalīya* state:
"The lords of the cows, the [planets], and the [lords of the] quarters are described in sequence within the directions. (5-180)

When [initiations] are bestowed by a teacher who knows the sequence according to the prescribed rule, that is called "initiation by sequence" (kramadīkṣā); a reversal of the sequence does not grant success.
"Where there is the procedure for Kramadīkṣā, there is Pūrṇābhiṣeka.
Thus ends the method of Kramadīkṣā.
Now follows the procedure for the initiation of Pūrṇābhiṣeka (from the *Merutantra*), after which the previously mentioned varieties of initiation have been described.
Having thus bestowed the initiation, the Guru should perform the final consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana).
Without which initiation, the practitioner does not attain full enlightenment, nor the status of a teacher, nor the desired higher rebirth. (5.183)

Therefore, having instructed his beloved disciple, the Guru should consecrate him; for without the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), even Śiva remains a mere bound soul (*paśu*). (As stated in the *Śaktisaṅgama*, *Kulārṇava*, and other texts. 5-184.
Without the full initiation, the deity does not become propitious;
he who recites the mantra of Kālī or Tārā without the full initiation [reaps no fruit]. (5.185)
I shall take away his ritual action; the man becomes deranged, O Pārvatī, without the full consecration and the duty toward the Guru. (5.187)
Neither recitation, nor likewise fire-offering, nor worship ever reaches completion [in that way];
(p. 398) especially for the Kaulikas, the Pūrṇā consecration is indispensable.
If a Kaulika dies while deprived of the Pūrṇā consecration, [he suffers]. (5-188)
"One attains the state of a piśāca until the dissolution of all beings"—thus from the *Kulārṇava*.
Likewise:
"O Goddess of the gods, the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) is prescribed for the ritual of the ten vidyās."
The times for the full initiation have been stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"When there is a reversal of the planets, during an eclipse at one's birth asterism, or when two [planets] [are eclipsed]. (5.189)
When the *kuhū* (new moon) occurs during the affliction of an enemy, one should perform a full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*);
by the power of that, faults shall never touch him. (5.190)
In the *Śaktisaṅgama* and other such works,
it is stated that the initiation of full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā*) should take place during an eclipse of the moon or sun;
however, the initiation of full consecration must indeed be performed on other auspicious occasions as well.
"Out of reverence during the seven hymns, at the auspicious times, or at other [times]," according to the statement in the *Tantrarāja*.
He states the procedure: "The Guru, remaining in the previously mentioned maṇḍapa, intent on meditation... (5.191).
On the following day, one should perform the planting of the sprouts and the sacrifice to the site (vāstuyāga),
having carefully constructed the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rules with due reverence.

Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should then respectfully honor and worship the venerable teacher's family; on the altar, one should likewise with devotion worship the chosen deity and the triad of teachers.
The Gurus and the Śaktis are to be worshipped with garments and ornaments;
likewise, O Śivā, the lineage of the Divine Current (divyaugha) and the lineage of the Siddhas (siddhaugha).
O Maheśānī, having fashioned a vast and exceedingly beautiful wheel within the pavilion for the multitude of men and the fourfold assembly of one's own gurus, (as stated in the *Merutantra*), 5-195.
One should place a jar filled with a khārī measure of water in the center of the mandala;
other jars there should be provided with cloth and gold. (5.196)

Various [deities] should be established upon the petals; there, one should invoke the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), worshiping them with the deities of the limbs (aṅga) and the surrounding retinue (āvaraṇa) in the center and at the ends [of the petals].
In another tantra:
"The primary jar should be placed in the center, and then, according to the sequence of worship, all the jars for the obstructions should be placed all around. (5.198)
(In the *Tantrarāja*):
Having fashioned a vast wheel and sixteen [circles] corresponding to their respective origins, and having constructed triangles therein, one should place a jar in the center. (5.199)
[One should prepare] vessels made of gold, silver, copper, glass, or even clay,
filled with a khārī-measure of water boiled with medicinal herbs that do not lose their potency.
Having placed nine gems and various kinds of grain,
as well as gold and copper, one should wrap them with two pieces of cloth.
With red sandalwood, mango, jackfruit, and leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, bound with the *śatakratu* creeper and provided with *mātuluṅga* fruits. || 5.202 ||
Having prepared other pitchers, one should place them individually within others;
they are said to be in sequence in the numbers of five, thirty-six, and one thousand and five hundred.
Regarding the phrase "a khārī of water": the definition of a *khārī* is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Two *palas* make a *prasṛti*; a *kuḍava* is considered to be double that.
Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and an *āḍhaka* is four times those [four *prasthas*]. (5.204)
Four guṇas make one droṇa; two of those are known as a kumbha.
Eight of those kumbhas make a khārī... [and so forth].
(In the *Tantrarāja*):
Having placed water and the other [elements] within the central wheels, and having smelled and worshipped them, || 5-205 ||
Having recited the mantras dedicated to Kālātman on the preceding day,
one should rise early on the morning of one's birth-star (janmarkṣa) and worship them at the conclusion of one's daily obligatory rites.

Afterward, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) on all sides; having worshipped with various offerings according to the *Triśaktiratna*, one should offer oblations a thousand times into the sacrificial ladle (*śruc*). (5-207)
The Guru should consecrate the disciple and personally bestow a name upon him,
amidst the sounding of horns, kahalas, conchs, and other instruments, accompanied by song and dance. (Tantrarāja 5.208)
The Guru himself should perform the consecration together with the joyful throngs of Yoginīs, who are each of the nature of a deity, supported [by him], and well-honored. (5.209)
(The *Merutantra* states: "The preceptor should touch the central jar and recite [the mantras];
then, with that water, [he should sprinkle] the four Vedas along with their ancillaries. (5.210)
"The Guru should consecrate the disciple"—this is the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣecana*).
Alternatively, according to the *Tantrarāja*, one should place eight jars there, as in the case of the *khaṇḍavati* [consecration]. (5.211)
Having invoked the powers (śaktis) into them and worshipped them, one should perform the consecration;
or, having prepared a single water-pot on the birthday, one should perform the consecration.
Likewise: "The nature of water is proclaimed to consist of the moon, the sun, and fire;
therefore, ablution shall serve for the pacification of all suffering and affliction. (5.213)
In another tantra: "O Pārvatī, one who is skilled in the ritual of consecration should diligently perform the two types of bathing as prescribed, preceded by the act of anointing. (5.214)
With the application of the five sprouts, as well as *dūrvā* grass and *bilva* fruits, one should respectfully sprinkle the disciple with Vedic and Tantric mantras. (5.215)
O Great Goddess, this alone is remembered as the sequence of the complete initiation (pūrṇadīkṣākrama);
O Maheśānī, everything else falls within the scope of the chapter on initiation.

Regarding the phrase "the two ablutions": one is that which has been described as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) such as the *kriyāvatī* and others, and the other is in the form of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).
As it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"Then, having obtained the twofold consecration by his command..."
One should perform acts of grace and so forth for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it will not come to pass.
Having fashioned a wheel and placed a jar within its central yoni,
having filled it with decoctions of the [sacred] syllables, and having performed the consecration, one should recite the mantra.

For one who is devoted to the traditional conduct passed down through lineage and is endowed with devotion, one should perform the second consecration for the sake of the self-perfection of the Goddess. (5.219)
(From the *Merutantra*):
Since all tantras have come from the gods, and likewise men [have received them] from the tantras, therefore the disciple is the sole vessel for all mantras. (5.220)
He may bear the name of an Ācārya, yet the Guru may give him another name;
he who receives initiation from such a person shall indeed possess spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
He becomes capable in the bestowal of all mantras;
all the gods are under his control, and he follows the path of the Vedas, which is characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
This very same procedure should be followed on that path known as the Southern;
however, there is a distinction in that case: the wise man should fetch waters from sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
From the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī; from the great ocean, the Sindhu, Godāvarī, Revā, Kāverī, and Pṛthūdaka. (5.224)
From Puṣkara come the waters of the Mahendrī, the Sarayū, the Carmanvatī,
the great river Vedikā, the Kṣiprā, and the Vetravatī.
Having placed [the water] from Kurukṣetra, the Gaṇḍakī, the Pūrṇā, and Lake Mānasa into a jar, one should recite mantras even those belonging to various Tantras.
Once he has been consecrated with those waters, those *mantras* of his become perfected;
having thus applied them for the purpose of ritual practice, [they are used] for the purpose of giving... so it is said.
(In the *Niruttaratantra*):
"The Vaiṣṇava, the Gāṇapatya, and the Saura, O Kuleśvarī. (5.227)
One who is devoted to Śakti and an ornament of the Kula should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Likewise:
"O Goddess, one should perform the consecration preceded by the preliminary rite of propitiation (adhivāsa). (5.228)
Then, having performed the rite of *vṛddhi-śakti*, one should worship the powers of Śiva (*śiva-śakti*).
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with ornaments of gold and other decorations, [one should proceed]. (5.229)
Then, according to the rite of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the selection of the preceptors.
Likewise: "Having worshipped Śiva and Śakti, one should establish the excellent vessel. (5.230)
Neither too short nor too long, fashioned from gold, silver, or other materials,
one should place it upon the yantra or within a triangle for the special arghya offering.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), one should strike it with the syllable of speech (VĀGBHAVA).
Having examined the jar with Śakti, one should fill it with water using Māyā.
With this mantra, the preceptor should there invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas), all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as the oceans and lakes. (5.233)
May the meritorious lakes and springs located in heaven, the netherworld, and upon the earth, and all holy pilgrimage sites, bring their presence into this jar. (5.235)
One should present the sprout with the *śrī*-seed mantra recited;
the bestowing of fruit occurs with the *kūrca* mantra, and stabilization with the *strī*-seed mantra. (5.236)

The wise practitioner should apply vermilion with the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ), flowers with the word for the departed (Preta), and offer dūrvā grass with both the root-mantra and the syllable Om (Praṇava).
One should perform the striking with a blade of darbha grass using the mantra "huḥ phaṭ svāhā";
having meditated upon the celestial seat, one should invoke [the deity] there and worship it. (5.238)
O beautiful one, by this very procedure in all rites,
one should especially establish the water-pot with a devotee of the Goddess.
The wise one should perform the great worship endowed with the sixteen services;
thereafter, he should likewise perform the great worship of the gurus and the śaktis.
After that, there is the sequential worship of the practitioners,
having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) to the young maidens, especially those born of the Kula lineage.
Then, O Goddess, one should perform the consecration according to the path of the Guru, following the procedure taught in the Svatantra, together with the utterances of the mantra. (5.242)
The preceptor, acting as the mantra-master, should move the jar with this mantra:
"Oṃ! Arise, O Brahma-jar, you who bestow all accomplishments when served! (5.243)
You, who are filled with the waters of all sacred fords, fulfill my heart’s desire;
thereafter follow Īśāna, Indra, Smara, Kṣoṇī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
With this mantra, one should shake the jar with the sounds of musical instruments.
Likewise:

for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śakti is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of accomplishing all attainments and intentions.
Oṃ! Rājarājeśvarīśakti, Bhairavī, Kālabhairavī, the goddess Śmaśānabhairavī, and Tripurānandabhairavī. (5.246)
Tripurā, Tripurādevī, as well as Tripurasundarī; Tripureśī, Mahādevī, and likewise Tripuramālikā.
The goddess Nityā, the goddess Nityarūpā, likewise Vajraprastāriṇī, the goddess Sarvacakreśvarī, and likewise Nīlasarasvatī. (5-248)
The goddess who bestows all accomplishments, served by the Siddhas and Gandharvas, is the great goddess Ugratārā as well as Dakṣiṇakālikā. (5-249)
May these [goddesses] consecrate you with water purified by mantras:
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Mahādaṃṣṭrā, Śubhadaṃṣṭrā, and Kapālinī.
Bhīmanetrā, Viśālākṣī, Maṅgalā, Vijayā, and Jayā—may these sprinkle you with water purified by mantras. (5.251)
Maṅgalā, Nandinī, Bhadrā, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Yaśasvinī, Puṣṭi, Medhā, Śivā, Sādhvī, Yaśaḥśobhā, Jayā, and Dhṛti. (5.252)
May Śrīnandā, Sunandā, Nandinī, and Ānandapūjitā consecrate you with water purified by mantras. (5.253)
Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Bhadrā, Smṛti, Śānti, Kṣamā, Dhṛti, Siddhi, Paramā, Puṣṭi, Śrī, Ṛddhi, and likewise Rati. (5.254)
Dīptā, Kānti, Yaśas, Lakṣmī, Īśvarī, and Buddhi;
Śakti, Māyāvatī, Brāhmī, Jayantī, and Aparājitā. (5.255)
Ajitā, Mānavī, Śvetā, Diti, and Aditi as well; Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Mohinī, and likewise Kṣobhiṇī. || 5-256 ||
Kamalā, Vimalā, Gaurī, Lāvaṇyāmbudhisundarī, Durgā, Kriyā, Arundhatī, Ghaṇṭākarṇā, and Kapālinī. (5.257)
Carcikā is to be known as another [form], likewise worshipped by the gods;
and there are Vaivasvatī, Kaumārī, and the supreme Māheśvarī. (5.258)
Vaiṣṇavī, Mahālakṣmī, Kārtikī, Kauśikī,
Śivadūtī, and Cāmuṇḍā, who is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
"May these [deities] protect you—" and so forth.
Indra, Vahni, Yama, Nairṛta, and likewise Varuṇa. (5.260)
Pavana, Dhanada, Īśāna, Brahmā, Ananta, and the lords of the directions—these [protect] you...
[and so forth]. (5.261)
May the year, the two solstices, the months, the fortnights, the days,
and the lunar dates consecrate [him] with water purified by mantras.
May the planets—the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—constantly consecrate you. (5.263)
The lunar mansion, the karana, the yoga, and thereafter the attainment of immortality;
likewise, the burnt [planets], the evils, the auspicious [days], the yogas, the days of the week, and the moments. (5.264)
May Vāravelā, Kālavelā, Daṇḍā, Ṛkṣā, and the others likewise constantly consecrate [him] with water purified by mantras. (5.265)
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Kapālī, the one named Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are the eight Bhairavas. (5.266)
"p. 406) These [mantras]—*ete tvā*—[and so forth]. Furthermore, there are the Drāviṇī-putrikās as well as the Ḍākinī-putrikās. (5.267)
There are other Śākinī-daughters and further Kākinī-daughters;
moreover, there are Śākinī-daughters and likewise Hākinī-daughters. (5.268)
Then the daughter of Rākiṇī, then the daughter of Devaputrī, then likewise the daughter of the Mothers, and then the daughters of the Urdhvamukhīs. || 5.269 ||
"The sons of Adhomukhī and the supreme sons of Jvālāmukhī—these [protect] you... Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (5-270)
"These [are the elements]—you [are the knower of these]—[the rest of the verse follows]: the Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and the sixteen transformations. (5.271)

The self, the supreme self, the self of knowledge, the self of meditation, the selves belonging to the Supreme Self, and those which are the gross and subtle selves of the individual self—these are the supreme ones. (5.272)

"These [syllables]—[omitted]—are as follows: the seed-syllable of the Vedas (huṃ), the seed-syllable of women (strī), its abode (hrīṃ), the seed-syllable of Śakti (hrīṃ), the seed-syllable of Ramā (śrīṃ), the seed-syllable of Māyā (hrīṃ), and the moon (amṛta). (5.273)
The wish-fulfilling gem, the great seed-syllable, the Nārasiṃha which is the savior, Mārtaṇḍabhairava, the Durga-seed, and the supreme male-female [seed-syllable]. (5.274)

May the Gāṇapatya, the Vārāha, and the Kālībīja mantras, which remove all fear, consecrate you—[may they consecrate you]... [thus]. May the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī [consecrate you]. (5.275)
The Ātreyī, the Bhāratī, as well as the Sarayū and the Gaṇḍakī;
the Karatoyā, the Candrabhāgā, the Śvetagaṅgā, and the Kauśikī. (5.276)
"Bhogavatī in Pātāla, and likewise Mandākinī in Svarga—these [are yours]... Bhairavī, Bhīmarūpā, Śoṇa, and Sumukha. (5.277)
And Sindhu, as well as the meritorious Hrada, and likewise Pātālasambhava—these [protect] you... [as above].
And whatever sacred fords there may be, whether more meritorious or less meritorious.
"May those [protect] you... and so forth.
The continents, such as Jambūdvīpa and others; the oceans, such as the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇoda) and others; the serpent named Ananta; and the snakes, such as Takṣaka and others. (5.279)
"May these [mantras]—
tāra, vahnijāyā, vaṣaṭ, kūrcam,
and thereafter vauṣaṭ and phaṭ— always consecrate you. (5.279)
May the pretas, kuṣmāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and dānavas perish;
may the piśācas, guhyakas, and bhūtas be struck down by this consecration.
May misfortune, Kālakarṇī, and very great sins be destroyed by this consecration, struck down by the seed-syllable of Tārā.
May diseases, sorrows, poverty, weakness, and mental disturbances perish, struck by the sprinkling of the water of consecration and by the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja). 5-282.
May their lack of public affection, their renunciation, misfortune, and ill-repute perish, struck down by the very god of love through this consecration. (5.283)
May the decline of splendor, the decline of power, and likewise the decline of intellect perish,
struck by the empowerment through the seed-syllable of power.
Poisons and great diseases, ḍākinīs and terrors as well, terrible malevolent spells, cruel planets, and likewise nāgas— (5.285)
May all calamities perish, struck by the consecration with the seed-syllable of Kālī; may all prosperities remain firmly established. (5.286)
"By means of this consecration, may the desires of the Śākta practitioners be fulfilled.
Having thus sprinkled the disciple, one should again perform the worship. (5.287)
The disciple, having performed worship there, should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru; O Pārvatī, this consists of cows, land, gold, silver, and various kinds of jewels.
One should give one's entire possessions, or even half of them, as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru;
[one may worship] Śrīvidyā, Siddhikālī, Tārā, or Mahiṣārdinī. (5.289)
The preceptor himself should bestow [the initiation] upon a disciple endowed with devotion. As stated in another Tantra:
"Having thus performed the consecration with the water from the primary jar... (5.290)
Having recited that respective mantra, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the water from the attendant jars; thereafter, one should bestow the supreme mantra upon him.
Once the full consecration has been performed, the disciple becomes entitled to all mantras; therefore, having consecrated him, one should bestow the mantra. (5.292)
Even if Manu has been previously instructed by means of a limited rite, he should later perform the full consecration for the sake of all-encompassing authority. (5.293)
Great mantras and secret mantras will grant accomplishment without a doubt.

On the Vāmamārga path, however, the principal flask must be filled with the causal substance (*hetudravya*), while the other flasks are to be filled with water alone. As it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"In the center, the flask of sacred waters (*tīrthaghaṭa*) should be placed; the remaining ones are considered flasks of water. (5.294)
Whichever gods have been invoked by the Guru into the jar, they all, assuming the form of mantras, establish their presence within his mouth. (5.295)
His speech will succeed by itself; one must never cause his head to bow.
For him whose head is made to bow, death is certain; of this there is no doubt. (5.296)
When such a perfected one (siddha) becomes the guru on the left-hand path, and the disciple is free from ego and always devoted to the deity; || 5.297 ||
He whose mind is not elsewhere for the sake of the deity, nor whose mind is set on worldly enjoyment—he alone shall be perfected in the Vāmā; any other is a vessel for hell. (5.298)
The specific rule regarding the Kaula path is stated in that very [text]:
"With a conch or a jar filled with wine, containing living fish and complete with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)... (5.299).
Then one should perform the consecration with sprouts from the family tree;
this is proclaimed here as the "Full Consecration" (pūrṇābhiṣeka) in the path of the Kula.
And the family trees: the mango (*sahakāra*), the *karṇikāra*, the *kesara*, the *tilaka*, as well as the *kadamba*, the *sindhuvāra*, the *kaṅkola*, and the one called *campaka*. (5.301)
"The śleṣmātaka, kuravaka, nimba, caladala,
yajñāṅga, jaṭila, and bilva— these are considered family trees," as stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
In another tantra: "The guru should consecrate the disciple and himself bestow a name upon him. (5.302)
Having first applied the name beginning with "Ānandanātha" and consisting of either two or four syllables, the Guru should then address him as "You are [Name]," using the word *amuka*. (5.303)
Just as a woman, leaving her father’s lineage, takes refuge in the lineage of her husband, so too does the Kaula, through the instruction on power (*śakti*), enter another lineage. (5.304)
Now it is said, O Maheśānī: the supreme lineage of the Kaulas, which is difficult to find in all the tantras, is proclaimed as that of Śambhu. (5.305)
On the paths of the Kaula-Avadhūta, one should not go on pilgrimages;
nor should one undertake wandering to sacred sites, renunciation, or the observance of vows. (5.306)
One should avoid fasting and shaving the head in every respect;
since the head has been consecrated by the full empowerment (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), there is no shaving there. (5.307)
The *Merutantra* speaks of the greatness of the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*):
"Just as iron, when pierced by the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), attains the state of gold, so too the self, when pierced by initiation, certainly attains the state of Śiva. (5.308)
Likewise: "The Śūdra-hood of the Śūdra has departed; the Brahmin-hood of the Brahmin has departed.
In one who is perfected by the purificatory rite of initiation, no distinction of caste exists. (5.309)
Having performed the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), even if one dies anywhere at all, one shall become the very form of the Goddess; that deity shall attain blessedness.
In another tantra: "Whatever untruth may occur for one who is endowed with the full initiation, his ritual action becomes fruitful and the deity is well-pleased. (5.311)
O Śivā, one who is indeed endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) should bestow the mantras and recite them;
at that very moment he attains accomplishment—there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
O Goddess of the Gods, even without a guru, he who has received initiation may recite [the mantra];
having mastered it along with its divisions, he is then worthy of bestowing success.
O Great Goddess, even if he be a Cāṇḍāla, if he is endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), he becomes a Brahman-sage; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (5.314)

p. 411) O Pārvatī, even if he be the best of sages, one who is devoid of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is declared to be the lowest of Brāhmaṇas; whereas one who has received the consecration is the most excellent of the twice-born. || 5-315 ||
O Goddess of the gods, in whatever land one who has received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) resides,
that land attains blessedness for ten million yojanas in every direction.
There is neither disease nor death, nor fear of enemies anywhere;
Śiva is declared to be of perfect form, he is indeed Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt. (5.317)
What is the body, and whose is the body? To whom belong pleasure and pain?
Who is born, and who dies, O Goddess? Everything has the nature of Brahman. (5.318)
O Goddess, at whatever time there may be forgetfulness of the excellent mantra, at that very moment death is said to occur; for [true] death is not merely the cessation of breath. (5.319)
"For those endowed with the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), there is indeed authority in all respects.
Thus concludes the procedure for the initiation of the full initiation.
Now, the method for practitioners (*mantriṇaḥ*) to receive another mantra in the absence of a Guru [is described] in the *Merutantra*:
Now, listen to the initiation for tantric mantras without a guru. (5.320)
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, when endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars,
one should go into the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti and worship him.
Having performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), one should place [the leaf] either in front of it or above it;
having written the mantra on a palm leaf, one should worship the deity of the mantra.
Having meditated upon the mantra as being the deity and the guru, one should clearly recite it one hundred and eight times; this is called the "receiving of the mantra."
This reality has been fully declared; it is to be guarded like a secret from a mother regarding her paramour.
Greed and other such faults reside in the guru; therefore, the mind recoils from him. (5.324)
Therefore, having made the teacher of the scripture [one's own guru], the mantra is derived from Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

In this *Puraścaryārṇava*, composed by the Lord Gorakṣācala— who possesses a multitude of wonderful and purifying words and is graced by a stream of wondrous nectar through his diverse compositions— this fifth [chapter], which contains excellent and highly esteemed classifications, is now complete.
The lofty wave has passed away, shining with a mass of pearls made manifest by sound reasoning.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Varieties of Initiation Preceded by the Application of the Kriyāvatī Initiation," in the *Puraścaryāṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāpasiṃha Sāhi.
Now the procedure for *puraścaraṇa* is described.
Regarding that, the meaning of the term *puraścaraṇa* is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"For the sake of attaining mastery over mantras, beginning with those of the Vedas and ending with those of the *Śāvara*, [the *puraścaraṇa* is performed]."
It is called *puraścaraṇa* because it must be performed beforehand. || 6-1 ||
(Also in the Merutantra:
"Mantra is said to be the means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
that which is practiced beforehand for the sake of its accomplishment is proclaimed as [the preliminary]. (6-2)
The rite known as *puraścaraṇa* must necessarily be performed at the beginning and end of the Veda,
as well as with respect to the mantra and the yantra.
By this, the purpose of *puraścaraṇa* is also stated.
(In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*):
"The practice of the root mantra is called *puraścaraṇa*. (6.3)
(In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*):
For one who is devoid of the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), the accomplishment of the mantra does not arise.
At the outset, one should perform the preliminary service according to the rules and in accordance with the prescribed method. (6.4)
(Also in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

Having received the command of the Guru, a person whose inner organ is purified should then perform the preparatory rite (*puraskriyā*) with the desire for the complete accomplishment of the mantra. (6.5)
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of performing any action,
so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Therefore, at the outset, the wise person should perform it himself, or have a guru perform it;
or, in the absence of a guru, he should have a brahmin who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings perform it.
One should employ this affectionate treatise, which is endowed with various virtues, like a friend, or like a virtuous woman accompanied by her sons. (6.8)

The nature of *puraścaraṇa* has been described [in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*]: "O Great Goddess, the five limbs are: recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the propitiation of Brahmins, O Īśvarī. (6–9)
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is said to consist of one-tenth of each preceding [number of recitations].
(From the *Kulamūlāvatāra*):
"If one desires one's own welfare in this world of existence, which abounds in suffering... (6.10).
"By means of the worship of the five limbs alone, the reciter of the mantra shall proceed happily. (In the *Muṇḍamālā*):
One should first recite the mantra as many times as the number of recitations prescribed for it. (6-11)
Then, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth of that number;
and it is taught that the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with one-tenth of that as well.
Then one should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) specifically as a tenth part of that;
and the feeding of Brahmins is prescribed as a tenth part of even that.
Likewise, one should provide a meal for virgins and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru;
thus, by the grace of the guru, one has performed the rite of puraścaraṇa.
The practitioner indeed attains the perfection of mantras and the ultimate reality. (From the *Merutantra*):
Recitation, fire-oblation, libation, purification, and the feeding of Brahmins—6-15.
In that regard, some say that it consists of the form of five-limbed action;
however, there are also those with four limbs, three limbs, two limbs, and even those with a single limb.
Mantras reside within the Vedas as well as in the Śabara-mantra;
some mantras consist of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), [the fruit arising] from the recitation (japa) of those limbs. (6-17)
Through the *aghamarṣaṇa*, the offering of water (*argha*) to the Sun, drinking that water, prostrations, and the worship of the deity—by these five, the [daily rite] becomes ten-limbed. (6.18)

Through the worship of the messenger (dūtī), likewise through the rite of tonsure (caulīkarma), the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjana), the union of the vulva and the phallus (bhagaliṅgasamāyoga), the recitation of mantras (japa), and the offering of oblations (balidāna). || 6-19 ||
And by the offering of the great *vali*, they become eleven-limbed;
for the Kaulikas they are sixteen-limbed, while for the Vāmikas they are reduced by two.
Due to the service of Amaryaśmari, there are eighteen limbs for the Aghorīs;
in the Vaiṣvavasenī [tradition],
this great sacrifice consisting of five limbs is known as *puraścaraṇa*.
Other sacrifices performed by the thousands for the sake of human goals do not equal even a sixteenth part of this sacrifice of the five fires.
Especially in the Kali Yuga, the sacrifice of recitation (*japayāga*) is praised. (In the *Merutantra*):
When ten thousand years of the Kali age have passed, the stone of Viṣṇu shall abandon the earth. (6.23)
Half of that [is] the water of the Ganges, and half of that is the stone of the deity;
when the terrible Kali age has arrived, which is intermingled with left-handed practices (vāmācāra).

In a world crowded with barbarians who lack discrimination between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, pervaded by people overcome by desire, anger, and other passions, and utterly defeated by women; (6.25)

Where is the disciple, where is the guru, where is the mantra, and where are the ascetic practices and spiritual accomplishments? In the Kali age, the recitation [of mantras] alone is most excellent, as is the worship of the Śālagrāma.
(Yāmale):
O Great Goddess, japa accompanied by its ancillaries is proclaimed as *puraścaryā*.
When that has been performed, the mantra attains perfection; not otherwise. (6.27)
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
Without which there would be no success even in hundreds of years,
by performing which the practitioner obtains his desired fruit— (6.28).
(416) For a mantra that is perfected through preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) indeed bestows its fruit;
therefore, one who knows the mantra and desires accomplishment should perform the preliminary rite (*puraskriyā*). (6.29)
For one who has correctly mastered even a single mantra, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished anywhere;
what need is there to speak of a man who possesses many mantras? He is Śiva himself.
Of what use are fire sacrifices, of what use are recitations, and of what use are the elaborate applications of mantras, if there is no preliminary rite (puraskriyā) for these secret mantras? (6.31)
For the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) of mantras is said to be the primary seed. (In the *Ādiyāmala*):
"But he who performs any ritual action without having completed the preliminary service... (6.32)
That very [mantra] arises for his own destruction; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, having first performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should accomplish the ritual actions.
"Actions" refers to the six types of actions. Likewise:
"Just as there is no cause for the arising of a sprout without the sprinkling of water."
Just as a seed does not produce a sprout, so too is the mantra described [to be ineffective].
For one who is devoid of *puraścaryā* does not achieve success, which is the cause of accomplishment;
therefore, for the sake of that success, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* of the mantra. (6.35)
In that regard, first, concerning the time for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
during the month of Vaiśākha or Mārgaśīrṣa, when the sun is situated in Capricorn, one should begin the *puraścaryā* on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight. (6.36)
In the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa*,

the eminent scholar, relying upon the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), should begin [the rite] after bathing according to the rules at an auspicious moment, under a favorable lunar mansion, and on a propitious lunar day. (6.37)

The bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is the *pūrvapakṣa*. However, in the Śākta tradition and others, both fortnights are indeed auspicious. For there is a statement in the *Yāmala*: "One should begin the *puraścaryā* on the eighth or the fourteenth day of either of the two fortnights, for it must be at the time prescribed for initiation."
(The *Sudhārṇava*) states:
"At whatever time the initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs, at that very time this [should occur]. (6-38)
(In the *Muṇḍamālā*): Having obtained the permission of the guru, especially on an auspicious day, one should begin the *puraścaryā* and complete it according to the prescribed rules. (6.39)
(In the Vaiśampāyanasaṃhitā:

One should begin [the practice] during the bright fortnight when the moon and stars are favorable and on an auspicious day; however, one should not recite [the mantra] while Viṣṇu is asleep, such as at the beginning of Capricorn.
(Also in the *Śrīnṛsiṃhapādārcanapaddhati*): "One should not perform the *puraścaryā* when the Great Hot One is asleep;
for all mantras become bewildered when that Teacher of the World is asleep. (6.41)

"They become deluded" means that because all mantras have Nārāyaṇa as their essence, when He has resorted to the sleep of *yoga-nidrā*, all mantras become bewildered by His *yoga-nidrā*. Thus, the sense is that at the time when the mantras are bewildered, accomplishment (*siddhi*) through preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth does not occur. Nor should it be argued: "Since each specific mantra has the respective deity as its essence, and only those mantras [addressing that deity] possess that essence, how can mantras other than those be said to have that same essence? For, since it is established that the Lord consists of all deities—based on such texts as "Hari consists of all gods"—it is easy to state that those mantras which have the respective deities as their essence also possess that same essence. By this, the view that the prohibition of *puraścaraṇa* during the period of Hari’s sleep applies only to Vaiṣṇava mantras is refuted; for the word "all" (*sakala*) in the statement "all mantras become deluded" indicates that the term "mantra" refers to both Vaiṣṇava and non-Vaiṣṇava mantras alike. Furthermore, just as in the rule "curds should be given to Brāhmaṇas, but not to Kauṇḍinya," the word "Brāhmaṇa" is understood to refer to Brāhmaṇas other than Kauṇḍinya, so too, in the case of the prohibitions regarding prohibited times found in the *puraścaraṇa* section (such as the statements of Vaiśampāyana), the time prescribed in the *dīkṣā* section by authorities like the *Siddhāntaśekhara* is what is captured by the general statement: "In whatever time initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs, in that same time this [practice] should occur. Consequently, even though months such as Śrāvaṇa are prescribed for *dīkṣā*, they are indeed prohibited for *puraścaraṇa*. Only *puraścaraṇa* itself is prohibited during the time of Hari’s sleep; however, the necessity of recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth during that time has been stated.
In that very place:
"Janārdana, while asleep, is to be served by devotees desiring his pleasure through worship, the recitation of hymns, muttering of prayers, and self-restraint. (6.42)
"He who, though asleep, remains awake as the witness of the universe, whose nature is consciousness—
he alone has a fruitful birth by whom he is gratified through devotion."
O Śāmbhavī, [this occurs] even within the domain of power—during the arrival of the clouds, at the end of the rainy season, and during the flowering time. (6.43)
One should propitiate the Mother of the World by day or by night;
on each single day, the Goddess’s satisfaction shall endure for a year.
"Among these times, he by whom Ambikā has not been propitiated shall become a practitioner who is impoverished, seized by fear, and short-lived"—
so say some Śāktas.
The three [seasons] are the cool season, the spring, and the autumn. || 6-45 ||
The excellent seasons are for the preliminary rite of the Goddess.

Based on such statements from the *Yāmala*, because the performance of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the mantra of the Goddess is prescribed during the autumn season—which falls within the period of Viṣṇu’s sleep—some practitioners assume a restriction in the statement of Vaiśampāyana, "One should not recite [the mantra] while Viṣṇu is asleep," etc., interpreting it as referring to mantras other than those of the Goddess. Consequently, they perform the *puraścaraṇa* even during the time of Hari’s sleep. In this context, the term "autumn season" refers specifically to the time of the Durgā festival occurring within that autumn. Even though the performance of the *puraścaraṇa* for Śakti-mantras is prescribed during autumn by the aforementioned Tantric texts and by statements such as those in the *Kālīkalpa* and *Muṇḍamālā* to be cited later—specifying the period from the fourth to the seventh day and so forth—there is no evidence that it must be performed throughout the entire duration of the period during which Viṣṇu is asleep. Otherwise, since the *puraścaraṇa* of Vaiṣṇava mantras is also prescribed for Kārttika and other months falling within the period of Hari’s sleep by statements such as "In the month of Ūrja, Tapas, or Rādha, during the bright fortnight of the Vaiṣṇava [month]" (from the *Candrapīṭha*), and by the *Merutantra* passage in the *Matsya-purāṇa* section on *puraścaraṇa* stating "in Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and likewise... the statement of Vaiśampāyana would become entirely irrelevant. The authors of the *Puraścaraṇa-paddhati* maintain that if, due to the infinite number of Tantras and Upatantras, one were to find a single statement prescribing the *puraścaraṇa* of Śakti-mantras even during the Cāturmāsya (the four-month period of Viṣṇu’s sleep), then the assumption of such a restriction would not be faulty. Otherwise, it is indeed faulty. Thus say the authors of the manuals on *puraścaraṇa*.

But the easterners (Prāñcas) say: although [the performance of] all mantras is prohibited during eclipses and the like that fall within the forbidden months, it is only the general *puraścaraṇa* that is prohibited during the period when Hari is asleep; however, this prohibition does not apply to the specific *puraścaraṇa*.

In reality, however, since the performance of *puraścaraṇa* for Śākta and other mantras is prescribed during the festival of Durgā and similar occasions; for Vaiṣṇava and other mantras during the month of Kārttika and so forth; for Gaṇeśa and other mantras during the month of Bhādrapada and so forth; and for the performance of *puraścaraṇa* for any mantra whatsoever at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and because even specific *puraścaraṇas* not otherwise mentioned are practiced only during times that are not prohibited, one must certainly perform the *puraścaraṇa* of whichever deity’s mantra is prescribed by specific injunctions for a particular period within the prohibited times. However, regarding a time that is prohibited by a general rule but prescribed by a specific rule, the mere *puraścaraṇa* of no mantra should be performed; yet, in the month of Kārttika, the *puraścaraṇa* of any mantra whatsoever may be performed. (Kārttika, p. 419)

"One should perform the *puraścaraṇa* for all mantras during the month of Kārttika"—according to this statement from the *Sādhanasamuccaya*, there is no restriction regarding time or other factors in the *puraścaraṇa* performed according to the sequence of the Mahācīna and other methods to be described hereafter.
As it is said in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"Every time is auspicious; no time is inauspicious anywhere. (6.46)

Likewise: "In this [practice], there is no restriction regarding direction or place, nor indeed any restriction regarding posture and so forth; there is no restriction regarding time for the recitation, nor even for the worship and other such acts. (6.48)
"Here, in the practice of the Great Mantra (mahāmantra), the observance of one's own will has been stated.

In this context, the term "Great Mantra" (*mahāmantra*) is indicative of mantras in general. Otherwise, there would be the consequence that the observance of rules would apply even during the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for a secondary mantra (*upamantra*) according to the Mahācīna-krama; therefore, even here, the word "time" (*kāla*) refers to the specific times included within the "Great Night" (*mahārātra*), and not to prescribed or prohibited months, days, and so forth.
And thus:
"One should recite starting from the morning until midday"—
thus it is stated in the *Pāśavakalpa*.
"When the first watch has passed, until the end of the third watch" (6.49).

"It should be recited only during the night, and one should not recite it when the night has ended"—this is the rule regarding time stated in the *Vīrakalpa*, and its meaning is that such a rule applies here according to the Great Cīna tradition (*mahācīnakrama*).
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the dead of night;
one may worship the Goddess at all times, even while unwashed or after having eaten.
Because it has been stated right there:
"Otherwise, how could it be said:
'For heroes, the time for recitation is praised as being at all times'?"
Thus, the statement from the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* is to be reconciled:
"On the eighth or the fourteenth day of both fortnights. (6.51)
"One should indeed begin the *puraścaryā* at the very time prescribed for initiation," and so forth.

However, there is no contradiction with such statements from the *Yāmala* and other sources concerning the *puraścaraṇa* of the *Vīras*, because—according to the reasoning already stated—the word "time" (*kāla*) refers to the aforementioned [specific] time, and the word "*vīra*" refers to the *Kaulika*. Furthermore, in his own ritual manual (*kalpa*), the *Dīkṣāmañjarī* will state that [the specific time] is the time for the *puraścaraṇa*. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

(p. 420) Likewise, even in the *puraścaraṇa* according to the *Mahānīlakrama*, there is no restriction regarding the aforementioned time, since those same scriptural statements are found to apply there as well.
On this point, some say: "There is no restriction of time for the recitation when accomplishing the Great Mantra. (6.52)
Based on such statements from the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*, they say that there is no restriction regarding time for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Great Mantra. According to their view:
"There is indeed no restriction of place or time, nor any restriction regarding what may be eaten and so forth."
There is no requirement for rules of purification and the like in the accomplishment of the Great Mantra. (6.53)

Thus, according to his words: "The rites of purification and so forth, enjoined by the Smṛti scriptures—such as those proclaimed as 'one [application] on the penis and five on the anus' and so on—are not to be performed. (6.54)
This is also because of the statements of the *Svacchandabhairava* and other scriptures.

Since there would otherwise be a lack of general rules regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Great Mantra, it is said: "In that [practice], numerous rules must be diligently observed."
Through performing what is not prescribed, there will be a loss of accomplishment; of this there is no doubt.
In short, the contradiction with the words of Mahākāla found in this section on the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for the Great Vidyās, beginning with [the verse] "ityādi," is quite evident.
Now, regarding the locations (*yoginītantra*):
first, the determination of the site for performing the preliminary rites is stated.
A field of merit, the bank of a river, a cave, or a mountain peak.
A sacred ford, the confluence of rivers, a purifying forest, secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, and the slope of a mountain. (6.57)
A grove of Tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of a bull, the roots of an Aśvattha or Āmalakī tree, a cow-shed, and the midst of water. (6.58)
A temple is the shore of the ocean, one's own home;
likewise, one should know that [the merit] is a hundredfold at home and becomes a hundred-thousandfold in a cow-pen. (6.59)

(421) A crore-fold merit is obtained in a temple, and infinite merit in the presence of Śiva, provided it is free from the fear and anxiety caused by barbarians, wicked people, hunters, and wild beasts. (6-60)
In a secluded grove, free from censure and filled with devotion;
in a favorable location, in a righteous land that is well-supplied with food and free from calamity.
One should dwell in a delightful place inhabited by devotees, which is dear to ascetics, in the presence of gurus, and likewise in a location where the mind is one-pointed. (6.62)
Resorting to any one of these places, one should begin the recitation (*japa*). (From the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*):
Fields, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), houses, gardens, temples, rivers, and lakes. (6.63)
A hut and a secluded place—these locations grant the accomplishment of mantras. (6.63ef)
(In the *Prapañcasāra*):
Or else, on the shore of the ocean, or on a mountain peak,
or on the banks of rivers flowing to the sea.
A wise man should recite [the mantra] in solitude, either in his own home or in the temple of Viṣṇu.
In a secluded place, pure and free from the fear and agitation caused by barbarians, wicked beasts, or predatory animals, one should practice while endowed with devotion and free from anxiety. (6.65)
One should dwell in a beautiful land, in a righteous kingdom that is well-supplied with food and free from calamity,
in a delightful place inhabited by a community of devotees, and never under the patronage of another.
