The different locations for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) according to the distinction of deities have been stated [in the *Merutantra*].
Now I shall describe the places for recitation (*japa*), both those that are natural and those that are artificial, which are kept secret in all the tantras for each respective deity. (6.67)
The field of Mahāgaṇapati is Māyūra on the bank of the Narmadā;
it is Mahāśmāna, Māyūra, and Gaṇeśa, which bestows the perfection of mantras.
Prabhāsa, Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, Bhṛguparvata, the banks of the Yamunā, Kāśī, and the Sun-god—these grant success. (6.69)
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī,
Badarikāśrama, Gayā, the banks of the Gaṇḍakī, and Dvārakā bestow the perfection of Viṣṇu.
Kedāra, Tryambaka, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantī, and the forests;
the banks of the Gaṅgā, Vaidyanātha, and Rāmeśa, who bestows the perfection of Śiva. (6.71)
Jvālāmukhī, Prayāga, Kāminī, and the place of Mālikā,
as well as the bank of the Sarasvatī, bring about the accomplishment of the Śakti-mantra.
Tīra, Kamaleśvarī, Mekhalā, and Yakṣaparvata, as well as Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, bestow the siddhis of minor deities. (6.73)
Kāmarūpa, Nepāla, Hiṅgulā, Vindhyavāsinī, Jālandhara, and Pūrṇagiri grant accomplishment through the left path. (6-74)
The banks of lotus ponds, plantations of plantains, sugarcane, and Arka trees,
and villages filled with coral— these are exceedingly dear to Gaṇeśa.
Lotus ponds, riverbanks, forests, karavīra groves, fields of wheat and dūrvā grass, and the stone of Śilābhānumat—these are dear to him. (6.76)
In the vicinity of tulasī, aśvattha, dhātrī, sugarcane, śālagrāma stones, and so forth;
in a cow-pen; in a village where a Vedic scholar and his wife reside; or in the presence of one who delights in the Vedas—[these are places for worship].
At a linga facing west, in a temple of Śiva excluding that of Nandin,
at a place pleasing to Śiva, near a banyan tree, at a confluence, in a forest, or by a lake— 6-78.
In a forest of plantains, mangoes, *cambelī*, *sevantī*, and *varbarī* trees, on the banks of the five famous rivers, Śakti finds delight in solitude. (6.79)
(423) In places crowded with ponds, *arā*, *nimba*, *kola*, *śākhoṭa*, and *madhūka* trees, as well as in anthills and dried-up rivers, the minor deities rejoice. (6.80)

In the father’s house, in the cremation ground, at the triple-pathway and the crossroads, in an empty dwelling, and on ground infested with jackals, those who follow the left-hand path find satisfaction. (6.81)
In the house, in the cow-pen, as well as in a garden, in a forest, on a mountain peak, by a river, at its confluence, or in a temple—the Vedic [rite] is superior. (6.82)
In whatever region there is neither the killing of a cow nor the slaying of a Brahmin,
and where Śūdras do not cause [the Vedas] to be heard, there indeed is Vedic perfection.
Barbarians, heretics, rogues, kings, ministers, and the like, as well as young women, do not dwell there; success is then not far off. (6.84)
Now, regarding prohibited places, it is said in that same [text]:
"One should not dwell in dilapidated temples, gardens, houses, or at the foot of trees; nor on riverbanks or mountain peaks, nor in earth-cavities and the like. (6.85)
The state of decay extends as far as the trees. However, the prohibition regarding riverbanks refers specifically to those banks that have collapsed into the ocean. (In the *Yāmala*):
Kings, ministers, royal officials, and influential people.
The knower of reality should not dwell on the path by which they travel.
Having reflected thus, the wise one should perform the ritual acquisition of the ground (*bhūmiparigraha*).
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), the rule concerning food and so forth is [stated] in the *Yāmala*:
Vegetables, roots, fruits, edible grains, sacrificial offerings, or even barley meal.
Alternatively, one may subsist on milk alone for the purpose of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Those fit for sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) have been declared in the *Smṛti*:
winter rice, white unboiled grain, mung beans, sesame seeds, and barley. (6.88)
Pulses such as *kalāya*, *kaṅgu*, and *nīvāra*; *vāstuka*, *hilamocikā*, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *kālaśāka*, radish, and other *kemuka* varieties. (6.89)
Rock salt, sea salt, cow's curd, clarified butter,
milk from which the cream has not been removed, and the fruits of the jackfruit, mango, and myrobalan.
Long pepper, cumin, orange, tamarind, plantain, lavalī, and dhātrī fruits, along with jaggery and sugarcane products. (6.91)
Sages declare that sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*) is that which has not been cooked with oil. (In the *Merutantra*:
One who eats excellent tubers, fruits, and roots; one who eats the alms of the virtuous; [is] a consumer of sacrificial food. (6.92)
"One who observes the milk-vow shall be the best among them—" [and so forth].
In that very same [text]: "The milk of cows is said to be the best; that of Surabhis is middling; that of buffaloes is the lowest; and any other [milk] is forbidden for those observing a vow. (6.93)
(Kulārṇava) "He whose body is nourished by another's food and drink performs an accumulation of merit;
half of the fruit belongs to the giver of food, and half to the doer—of this there is no doubt. (6.94)
Therefore, O Śāmbhavī, at all times and in all rites, a wise person should avoid the food of others with every effort, especially during the period of *puraścaraṇa*.
The tongue is burned by the food of others, the hands are burned by accepting gifts, and the mind is burned by the wives of others; O fair-faced one, how then can there be spiritual success? (6.96)
The phrase "another's food" refers to food obtained from others outside the context of alms; however, there is no fault in the case of alms, as it is prescribed [as permissible].
Thus it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"For those who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, and virtuous..."
For those born into noble families and of high birth, their sustenance is the eating of alms. || 6.97 ||
Rice, roots, fruits, milk, curd, alms-food, and roasted flour—these seven kinds of food obtained through begging are to be consumed by those established in their vows. (6.98)
(From the Agastyasaṃhitā:
Curd, milk, cow’s ghee, sugarcane products excluding jaggery,
black sesame seeds, mung beans, and tubers excluding the kemuka— 6-99.
(In the Paddhati:
And bulbs such as the white lotus root, kaseruka, and others;
the curd, milk, and ghee of cows; and rock salt.
Mudga beans, barley, black sesame seeds, peas, priyaṅgu grains, and sixty-day rice. || 6-100 ||
Kadamba, jambu, panasa, mango, nimba, nāraṅga, dhātrī, kadalī fruits,
kapittha, iṣṭī, and soft pomegranates.
And these are the foods to be served at the welcoming ceremony. || 6-101 ||

*Miṣṭī* is a specific type of fruit distinguished by its sweet taste; *mṛdu* is the grape (*mṛdvikā*). The others are well known. Even those things distinct from these that are not prohibited—such as barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), coconut, and so forth—are indeed edible. Now, the prohibited items: alkaline salt from the earth, as well as *aḍhakī*.
Black gram, lentils, chickpeas, and kodrava; oil, white [grains], mung beans, sour gruel, honey, jaggery, molasses, meat, and so forth. (6.102)
Kūṣmāṇḍa, vṛntāka, palāṇḍu, alābu, chatrāka, nāla, laśuna,
karīra, paṭola, tāmbūla, vibhītaka, and so forth.
And that which has produced an internal change in flavor. || 6-103 ||
The wise declare that these should be rejected: food that is stale, as well as that which is burnt.

*Paṭola* is well known as *paḍavara*. *Alābu* is the fruit of the *tumbī* gourd. *Karīra* is the sprout of bamboo. *Andha* refers to food. Other prohibited items such as *gṛñjara*, *karañja*, and so forth, must also be avoided. *Gṛñjara* is well known in the language of the Middle Country as *gājara* (radish).
Now, regarding the seats (*āsana*) (in the *Merutantra*):
"The seat is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*). (6.104)
It should be joined with a kuśa-grass mat and a deerskin, four finger-breadths in height,
square, two cubits in length, beautiful, soft, and stainless.

This comfortable seat (sukhāsana) constantly brings about the accomplishment of recitation (japa). Now, for the sake of attaining knowledge, the desired seats will be described: the deer-skin (mṛgājina). 6-106.
Tiger skin leads to all accomplishments; sheepskin destroys disease; silk is said to be nourishing; and that made of cane increases prosperity.
On a white woolen blanket, there is the accomplishment of Dharma; on a red one, the accomplishments of wealth;
on a yellow one, the fulfillment of desire; and for others, the black woolen blanket bestows liberation.
However, for the sake of liberation from suffering, the blue color is not auspicious.
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
For malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the black color; for rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*), the red color. (6.109)
In rites for pacification, white [garment] is prescribed; a variegated one is for all rites.
For the rite of immobilization, there should be elephant hide, and likewise buffalo hide for the rite of killing.
Likewise, the skin of a hyena is for eradication; that of a rhinoceros for the rite of subjugation;
the skin of a jackal is prescribed for causing dissension; and the hide of a cow is used for the rite of pacification.
Now, regarding the prohibited [seats] (in the *Merutantra*):
One should avoid what is prohibited; one should not sit upon a prohibited seat unless no other is available.
Now the prohibited seats will be described: there would be grief if one sits on a seat made of wood. (6.112)
(427) On a bamboo seat one becomes poor; on a cloth seat there is destruction of one's position;
likewise, on a stone seat there is expulsion, and on an earthen seat one suffers from fever. (6.113)
If one sits on the bare ground, there will be pain; if on a leaf, there will be confusion of mind;
if on a grass seat, there will be pain; and sitting on a brick seat is forbidden.

The agitation of the mind that occurs for a householder upon wearing the skin of the black antelope would lead to the attainment of perfection for a student, a forest-dweller, a renunciant, or one who has completed his Vedic studies. (6.115)
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):

A householder who has not been initiated should never enter upon the [practice] with a black antelope skin; however, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a celibate student, and one who has completed his Vedic studies may do so. (6.116)
Richly furnished with kusa grass, deerskin, and cloth, it should be square on all sides,
measuring one or two cubits [in length], and four finger-breadths in height.
Then, one should enter there undisturbed, following the sequence beginning with the *svastika*;
namely, the fourfold group consisting of the *svastika*, *bhadraka*, *vīra*, and *kūrma*.
One should recite [the mantra] that is praised; the mention of others occurs only incidentally.
I shall now describe their characteristics according to the order of their enumeration. (6.119)
Having placed both soles of the feet properly between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this is declared to be the Svastika posture.
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineal seam;
having firmly bound the feet on either side with the hands, [the body] should be made perfectly motionless. (6.121)
This is the auspicious posture (bhadrāsana), which destroys all diseases;
it is performed by standing with one foot placed upon one thigh. (6.123)
p. 428) Likewise, the *vīrāsana* is illustrated in the case of the other [posture] and for the thief (*cora*).
However, in another tantra it is said:
"The *vīrāsana* is illustrated as having the right foot placed upon the left thigh."
Having restrained the anus with the two ankles in reverse order, one should remain composed.
This is the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana), which is the tortoise with the body turned face-up;
as well as the cow-face (gomukha), the cock (kukkuṭa), the fish (mātsya), and the bow-backward-stretch (dhanuḥpaścimatānaka).
Those who know yoga recognize the peacock, the quail, the perfected, the lotus, the lion, the corpse-seat, the svastika, the lotus-seat, and the hero. (6.126)
Seated in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana) and clasping the neck with both arms, one lies flat on the back like a tortoise; this is the uttānakūrma posture.
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right; thus it is "cow-mouthed" (gomukha), just like the mouth of a cow.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs,
and having established them on the ground, one attains the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana), which resides in the void.
Placing the right foot upon the root of the left thigh, and grasping it with the right arm wrapped around the outside of the knee,
one should remain standing with the body turned.
That is the seat proclaimed by the illustrious Matsyanātha. (6.130)
Grasping the two big toes with both hands up to the ears, one should perform the drawing of the bow; this is declared to be the Dhanurāsana (bow posture).
Extending his two legs on the ground like staffs and grasping both feet with his two arms,
he placed the region of his forehead upon his knees.
Firmly pressing the earth with the palms of both hands, one should place the elbows of the two arms at the sides of the navel. (6.133)
With the head and feet raised high, standing like a staff in the air—
this is the peacock posture (mayūrāsana), which is supreme for removing all diseases.
Placing one's head upon the ground and likewise the elbows on the hands, one should keep the feet like a staff; this is declared to be the Naraka posture (Narakāsana).
Having placed the left ankle above the penis,
and then having placed the other ankle upon that, this is known as the *muktāsana* (liberated posture).
Some call this Siddhāsana; others know it as Vajrāsana. Some speak of it as Muktāsana, while others call it Guptāsana. (6.137)
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh,
holding them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method,
placing the two big toes at the heart, and resting the chin [on the chest], one should gaze at the tip of the nose.
This lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys disease for those who practice self-restraint, is thus described. (6.138)
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on the sides of the perineum;
the left ankle on the right side, and the right ankle on the left side. (6.139)
Having placed both hands upon the knees and fully extended the fingers,
with the mouth closed, one should gaze at the tip of the nose, being well-composed.
This lion-throne (siṃhāsana) should always be honored by yogins;
lying on the ground like a corpse with the face upturned is the corpse-posture (śavāsana).
The corpse posture (śavāsana) removes suffering and is a means for the mind to find rest.
(In the *Yāmala*):
Having placed the feet successively upon the thighs with the toes pointing backward toward the knees... (6.142)
One should place the two hands [in this manner]; it is declared as the unsurpassed Vajrāsana posture. (6.142ef)
(In the Gorakṣaśataka:
Having firmly joined the soles of the feet at the root of the perineum, one should place one foot upon the penis; then, having kept the body perfectly balanced and motionless, [one should practice].
Remaining steady with the senses restrained, gazing at the space between the eyebrows with a fixed vision—this is called Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation. (6.143)
Likewise: "There are as many seats as there are living beings; Maheśvara alone knows all their distinctions. (6.144)
Now, the varieties of rosaries (*mālābheda*) [according to the *Merutantra*]: Now I shall explain the rosary; it is of two kinds, fixed (*sthira*) and mobile (*cala*).
The fixed [rosary] is for those of steady mind, while the mobile is for those of restless intellect. (6.145)

In the *Yāmala*, the rosary is said to be of three kinds: the first is the *varṇamālikā* (rosary of letters), the second is called the *caramālikā* (rosary of movements), and the third is the *karamālikā* (rosary of the hands). (6.146)
(From the Merutantra:

By means of the garland of letters fashioned from the syllables of the Mātṛkā, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, marked with the *bindu*, and arranged in both direct and reverse order. (6.147)
The individual mantras for each pair of syllables, when recited, bestow all accomplishments.
Furthermore, even the Āryās and others—what more need be said? This is called the "Stable Garland. (6.148)
(Also in the *Triśaktiratna*):
"Alternatively, the wise one should perform recitation with a rosary consisting of the *mātṛkās*.
Having uttered each individual phoneme, he should recite it as being interspersed by that [next] phoneme. (6.149)

The wise practitioner alone should bring together that which ends in *la* and that which ends in *ṇa*; indeed, the practitioner must never overstep the syllable *kṣa*, which is the form of Mount Meru. (6.150)
(From the *Muṇḍamālā*):
"A garland that is deficient in the central peak (*meru*), or one that bypasses the central peak, would be impure in this context; such a garland would be fruitless. (6.151)
That which is variegated, possessing the luster of twenty threads, and situated within the Brahma-nāḍī—by it [the body] is strung together;
it should be meditated upon as the bestower of the fruits of all desires. (6.152)
In the case of one hundred and eight recitations, one should first utter the neuter [syllable];
the four phonemes ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are declared to be neuter. (6.153)
Or else, there is a group of eight classes according to the sequence of the divisions of desired objects;
namely, the eight groups are: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa. (6.155)

One view is that when the recitation of one hundred and eight [mantras] is to be performed, one should first utter the four neuter vowels (*klība*) and, at the conclusion of the reverse order, likewise recite those four in reverse. Another view is that one should utter fifty letters through both direct and reverse orders, and then utter the remaining letters of the eight groups (*varga*). The distinction therein is that the letter *kṣa* is to be uttered only once as the "Meru," and after that, the mantra is not to be recited again. An alternative method is stated in the *Sādhanasamuccaya*:
"Through the union with the Śrī Māyā, Kāma, and Vāg [mantras], and through the union with the letters of the Mātṛkā..."
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, both in the direct and reverse orders.
In another tantra:
"O Goddess, three [offerings] are proclaimed for the Guru, and three for Gaṇapa;
in cases of deficiency or excess, one should apply two [offerings] to the Śiṣa and the Iṣṭa. (6.157)
Now the moving rosary (*carā-mālā*) is described in the *Merutantra*: for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), it consists of [rosaries] numbering according to the lunar days;
for the sake of liberation, one should always recite with twenty-five [beads], and for contentment, likewise. (6.158)

With thirty [beads] there is an increase of Dharma; with fifty-four, one's desires are fulfilled; with a hundred, there is happiness; likewise, with eight hundred, there is the attainment of all fruits and perfections.
Rudrākṣa beads are considered to grant all accomplishments and bestow wealth;
a conch shell brings about the attainment of what has been lost, and crystal is held to provide enjoyment. (6-160)
Those made of Putrajīva grant sons; those of lotus-seeds increase nourishment;
those originating from coral bring about subjugation; and those made of pearls are considered to bestow liberation.
Those made of kuśa grass destroy evil; those made of gold grant all desires; those made of tāra (silver) increase one's wishes; and with those made of indrākṣa, the goal is attained. (6.162)
Haridrā is for the purpose of subjugating women; dārvī brings about the subjugation of men;
lākṣā removes fever; and [the offering of] a sword's blood brings satisfaction to the ancestors. (6.163)
A rosary made of *arka* wood is to be used for eradication; one made of *śrīphala* for the attainment of knowledge;
one of ivory for all purposes; and one made of copper is considered suitable for enchantment. (6.164)
An iron needle is prescribed for killing; one made from white lotus for the sake of wealth;
one arising from sandalwood for neutralizing poison; and one made from white wood for performing pacification rites.
For the accomplishment of Yakṣiṇīs and others, [an image] produced from the seeds of red sandalwood is used;
for the sake of satisfaction, one made from Padmaka wood is used; and with those made from Devadāru wood, there is great splendor.
Tāmasa action is accomplished by means of [substances] produced from black wood;
for the paralyzing of spirits, [those] born of the neem tree are used, and for the paralyzing of people, those that are smooth. (6.167)

With *mahānimba*, *ḍākinī*, and *bhūnimba*, there is the immobilization (*stambhana*) of diseases; from the *indravṛkṣa* tree comes the immobilization of wounds, or the neutralization of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), using the bone of a monkey.
By means of a bear-bone, one attains success in the forest; his deities are [subdued] by a tiger-bone.
By means of a human bone, the rākṣasas are brought under control; by means of horse-bones, heroes are brought under control. (6.170)
With the bone of a donkey, one attains minor accomplishments; with the bones of an elephant, one gains honor.
A rosary made of clay or baked gems bestows the siddhis of Śabara.
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
[One may perform the rite] with rudrākṣas, conch shells, lotus seeds, putrajīvaka berries, and pearls;
with crystals, precious gems, gold, silver, and coral. (6.172)
With all the previously mentioned *kuśa* grasses, with the joints [of reeds], with the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*),
and even with the teeth of donkeys, horses, and humans for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
A garland of *tulasī* is recommended for the worship of Viṣṇu; for Gaṇeśvara, one made of elephant tusks;
and for the recitation (*japa*) of Tripurā, beads of *indrākṣa* and red sandalwood are prescribed.
In the Mantra of Nīlasarasvatī, it should be known that [the rosary] is made of large conch shells.
(Also in the *Triśaktiratna*:
"Recited with a secret rosary, Tāriṇī shall become the bestower of siddhi. (6.175)
Therefore, one who desires accomplishment should fashion a rosary from that [material]:
a rosary made of great conch shells, constructed from fifty beads. (6.176)
The *Rahasyamālā* has been fully proclaimed; it must be guarded with great effort.
That which resides between the ears and the eyes is celebrated as the Great Conch (*mahāśaṅkha*). (6.177)
But in the absence of those, according to the *Yāmala*, one should take the head of any suitable limb— such as that of a man, an elephant, a horse, or a camel— cut off in the chaos of battle. (6.178)
The practitioner should indeed have a circular rosary made for the Mahāvidyās;
in its absence, a crystal rosary shall serve, bestowing all prosperity.
In the *Vīratantra*, it is said:
"Kālikā, when recited with the secret rosary, bestows all accomplishments;
[the rosary] made of great conch shells and bones is prescribed in the ritual of Tāriṇī-Kālikā. (6.180)

In its absence, it may be made of crystal or likewise of lotus seeds; according to the Tantra: "O Goddess, a rosary made of self-originated [seeds] is used for Bhairavī and in the ritual of Kālikā. (6.181)
(434) O Goddess, in the ritual of Chinnamastā, a rosary made of large conch shells and bones is prescribed;
for Bālā and Bhuvaneśvarī, one made of crystal is proclaimed. 6.182.
A garland of *guñjā* beads is for *Mātaṅgī*; one made of donkey teeth is for *Dhūmrā*; *haridrā* is for *Vagalā*; and *kamalākṣa* beads are for the ritual of *Ramā*.
Likewise:
"With [beads] made of crystal in the Eastern Tradition; with those born from Rudra’s eyes [ruby] in the Southern;
with coral and pearls, O Goddess, in the deity of the Western Tradition. (6.184)
The rosary of the goddesses of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) is made of great conch shells and bones;
in the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya) it is self-arisen, and in the Netherworld (Pātāla) it originates from jewels.
A rosary made of coral with the Sūrya mantra, pearls for the Śakti-mantra,
as well as one made of Rudrākṣa and crystal, consists of both Śiva and Śakti.
Know that a rosary joined with Rudrākṣa beads and gold is identical in nature to Śiva;
in all Tantras, Rudrākṣas are not used for Śakti-mantras during the day.
(A Yāmala text: A rosary fashioned from rudrākṣa beads accomplishes all desires;
one made from conch-shell beads bestows wealth and fame. (6.188)
With lotus seeds, it bestows the fortune of nourishment and likewise destroys enemies;
born from the Putrañjīva tree, it grants sons, cattle, prosperity, grain, and abundance. (6.189)
A garland fashioned from pearls bestows abundant good fortune, prosperity,
the direct realization of mantras, and the accomplishments (siddhis) of pacification and enrichment.
Likewise, even a crystal rosary bestows liberation; a ruby rosary grants eloquence, and similarly, one of emerald brings abundant wealth. (6.191)
A golden or silver garland bestows all desires; one made of coral brings mastery over speech and the acquisition of abundant wealth.
(435) A rosary fashioned from all these materials, beginning with *kauśī* and ending with *kuśa*, which destroys evil, shall lead men to liberation. (6.193)
One should constantly perform the recitation of the garland of letters along with the joints;
when placed with a steady mind, it grants all desires. (6.194)
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), a rosary made of horse teeth is prescribed, along with horse-tail hair;
likewise, one made of donkey teeth turned downwards, together with threads from human sinews.
A garland fashioned from knotted [bones] is considered to destroy enemies;
a rosary for recitation should be made from the lower teeth of a *preta*. (6.196)
In the rite of hatred, [the mantra] should be strung with hairs from the body of the victim;
this is declared as one method for counting the finger-recitations (aṅgulījapa). || 6.197 ||

With *putrañjīva* seeds multiplied tenfold, one hundred is reached; with *śaṅkha* shells, one thousand; and with coral, gems, and precious stones, it is traditionally held that ten thousand is attained.
That same [number] with crystal and so forth is declared; with pearls, it is said to be a *lakṣa*;
with lotus seeds, it would be ten *lakṣas*; and with silver [beads], it is called a *koṭi*.
That same [number of] repetitions performed with golden beads is said to be twofold; with all [precious materials], it is considered a hundredfold.
With knots of *kuśa* grass and *rudrākṣa* seeds, the fruit is multiplied infinitely.
Even with rosaries made of white lotus seeds, the fruit shall be immeasurable; indeed, the same result is obtained even with a rosary produced from the letters of the Mātṛkā.
In the *Merutantra*:
"A Brahmin should recite [the mantra] with knots of *kuśa* grass; a Kṣatriya, with gold and gems; a Vaiśya, with *putrañjīva* seeds; indeed, everyone may recite with lotus seeds. (6-202)
One should not place anything between the rudrākṣa and the indrākṣa;
by placing something in between while performing the recitation, one destroys both desire and liberation. (6.203)
(p. 436) Regarding the greatness of the rudrākṣa, preceded by a description of its various types, it is said in that very same [text]:
"The best is like the fruit of the dhātrī tree; the middling is similar to the jujube (badara); the inferior is like a chickpea (caṇaka); anything smaller than that brings misfortune. (6-204)

White, red, golden-hued, and black in color—these correspond respectively to the twice-born classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Among these, the white [beads] are most excellent for the purpose of making a rosary for recitation.
In the absence of twice-born men, however, even those of their own respective castes may be accepted;
for in the Kali age, O Brahmins, learning that conforms to one's own duty is as difficult to find as [learned] Brahmins who follow their own dharma.
A Rudrākṣa that is too large, too small, cracked, fragile, light, split, previously worn by another, or decayed does not bestow auspiciousness. (6.207)
Likewise, they should be made with one face, two faces, four faces, five faces, or six faces; they may be combined with one another, but one should avoid [mixing] them otherwise.
Śiva is its single face; for one reciting it, the rosary removes sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and likewise bestows desired things such as sovereignty. (6.209)
This two-faced one named Umāśaṅkara removes sins such as the killing of cows and bestows happiness upon the householder stage of life.
The three-faced [deity] is of the nature of fire and destroys sins such as the killing of women;
through its retention and even through its recitation, dharma, artha, and kāma are accomplished. (6.211)
One becomes four-faced Brahmā, the destroyer of the sin of foeticide and other such evils;
all branches of knowledge flash forth, and mastery over speech is also attained. (6.212)
Śiva with five faces is known to be the manifest remover of all sins;
through the recitation of that [mantra], success is swiftly attained for those of the Śaiva, Gāṇeśa, and Śākta traditions. (6.213)
Kārttikeya, who has six faces and removes the sin of broken vows—by wearing him on the right arm according to the prescribed rite, one attains victory in battle. (6.214)
Then, by the recitation of that [mantra] of the great naga named Ananta, who has seven faces, infinite accomplishments are attained and no fear of snake venom arises. (6.215)
The eight-faced Gaṇeśa is the remover of all obstacles;
by the recitation of his mantra, all enemies such as desire, anger, and the like are destroyed. (6.216)
Bhairava shall have nine faces; the deities who abide on the Left Path are pleased by mere recitation, while Oghahā resides upon the left arm.
By reciting [the mantra of] Janārdana ten times,
Piśācas, Grahas, Vetālas, Brahma-rākṣasas, and serpents perish through its retention.
By wearing this, one becomes Rudra himself, manifest with eleven faces;
and through its recitation, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice.

The Sun-god has twelve faces; by reciting [the mantra] and likewise practicing its retention, one becomes radiant and majestic, and shall partake in the fruit of a horse-sacrifice to the earth (gomedha).
The thirteen-faced [Liṅga] is remembered as being the manifest embodiment of the Viśvedevas;
when worn during the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, it bestows upon the ancestors an inexhaustible state.
Recited fourteen times, it then becomes infinite;
one is honored by gods and men and attains an imperishable state. (6.222)
Likewise:
"Those Vedic deities who nourish the gods are themselves [mere] sacrificial animals;
those in the Kaula tradition who cause them to fall—Yama himself is their punisher. (6.223)
For the sake of their protection, there is nothing else on earth superior to the rudrākṣa;
rudrākṣas bestow the accomplishment of mantras for all the gods.
If even a dog dies with a rudrākṣa resting upon its neck, it attains the state of Rudra; how much more so for humans and others? (6.225)
Whether one is impure from eating leftovers, engaged in forbidden acts, or burdened by all manner of sins, a man is liberated from all evils by wearing rudrākṣa beads. (6.226)
Even one devoid of devotion who wears a rosary of rudrākṣas around the neck, though he be a constant performer of sinful deeds, is honored in the world of Rudra. (6.227)
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing rudrākṣa beads, he does not obtain the fruit thereof. (6.228)
The method for wearing rudrākṣas is described in that very same [text]:
"A garland for the head consists of twenty-six [beads], while the necklace for the neck consists of thirty-two;
sixteen are prescribed for the elbows, and thirty-two for the two wrists. (6.229)
An upper garment (upavīta) consisting of one hundred and eight [threads] is prescribed;
half of that for the chest-garland, and one [thread] is said to be for the topknot (śikhā).
The sequence of concentration (dhāraṇā) for the two ears is also said to be sixfold in number.
One should not perform it with fewer than that number; however, having more does not cause any fault.
In another tantra: Ten rudrākṣas at the region of the neck, twenty-two on the head,
six on each ear, and twelve on each of the two hands.
He who places one digit of the moon on each of his two arms, one for each of his two eyes, and eighteen upon his chest—he himself is Nīlakaṇṭha. (6.232)
One who thus wears rudrākṣas shall become Śiva at the end of the body;
he acquires abundant merit and is born fortunate in this world. (6.233)
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a Śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation.
And whatever Vedic rite a Brahmin may constantly perform while wearing Rudrākṣa beads, that rite shall become fruitful. (6.235)
By wearing Rudrākṣa beads on the neck, the head, the hands, the ears, and as a sacred thread, a human being becomes Rudra himself. (6.236)
Even while eating meat, drinking liquor, or associating with those of mortal birth, one whose soul is instantly purified by wearing a rudrākṣa on the head. (6.237)
The distinction regarding the time for stringing the rosary according to the specific deity is stated in that very same work:
"On the fourth lunar day, one should string the rosary with the mantras of Gaṇanātha;
at midday on a Sunday, the seventh lunar day, with the mantras of Ravi (the Sun) or Vāta (the Wind). (6.238)
On the twelfth day, the Vaiṣṇava rosary should be strung with the mantra of Viṣṇu;
on the thirteenth day, at the twilight, the Śiva rosary should be strung with his mantras.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day, O son of the Earth,
the Śaktis should also be worshipped at night after eating, according to the prescribed rule.
The distinctions regarding the threads are stated in that very same [text]:
"A garland for the pleasure of the Goddess should be strung with silk thread;
a Vaiṣṇava garland may likewise be made of cotton or even of *vadma* fibers. (6.241)
The thread of Śiva should be made from wool or from bark, together with that produced from [ordinary] thread;
for almost all the gods, hear now the procedure for the production of the thread. (6.242)
The Sūtra, fashioned from the meritorious fibers of the lord of birds, free from knots,
and consisting of three strands, should be carefully washed and then taken up after having been tripled.
(Regarding Umāmaheśvara:
A woman who has living sons, who is beautiful and devoted to her husband—by her, a garland that brings good fortune should be woven with thread spun by her own hands. (6.244)
In another tantra: [It may be made] with thread spun by a maiden, even from base metals or gold. (p. 440) "Base metal" (durvarṇa).
The method of stringing the rosary and its consecration (*mālāgrathanaprakāra* and *tatsaṃskāra*) [as described] in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*:
"Now, therefore, I shall explain the stringing of rosaries as taught in the Tantras. (6.245)
Having first observed the practice of eating only one meal a day, the practitioner himself should string [the beads]. (6.245ef)

By the statement "one should not wear sandalwood paste that has been ground by oneself," the wearing of it is prohibited because of its proximity to [the prohibition against] wearing a garland made by oneself.
In this context, "sraj" refers to a garland of flowers and not a rosary of beads.

Having performed his daily rites and being purified, the knower of mantras should diligently bring the eyes from among the aforementioned trees, according to his desire and as they are available. (6.247)
They should be uniform in shape, neither too thick nor too thin, free from defects such as insects, not bleached, and indeed new. (6.248)
Having washed those [vessels] individually with the five products of the cow, the specific rule regarding the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"The cow dung should be from a white cow that has the color of gold-infused milk. (6.249)
The cow's urine should be from a copper-colored cow, and the curd from a blue-colored one;
the ghee, however, must be from a black-colored cow; the same applies to the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
In some regions, cows of various colors are easily found;
there, one should collect the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to their respective colors.
There is a fault in the loss of color; therefore, one should avoid that which lacks the proper measure.
One should provide cow urine twice the amount of cow dung, and ghee four times the amount.
Milk is declared to be eightfold [in quantity], and likewise curd for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having taken the cow’s urine with the Gāyatrī mantra and the cow dung with the mantra "Gandhadvārā," [one should proceed].
With the mantra "āpyāyasva," one offers milk; with "dadhi krāvṇa," curd;
with "tejo 'si śukram," clarified butter (ājya); and with "devasya tvā," water with *kuśa* grass. (6.254)
One should wash [it] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth... thus.
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
Having fashioned a lotus shape with nine fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, one should place there the beads, which have been washed with scented water, upon a thread. (6.255)
Having placed the Tāra, the Śakti, and the Mātṛkās upon the thread and likewise upon the beads, one should worship them and offer oblations of clarified butter according to one's capacity.
The wise one should take each individual bead and join it to the thread;
joining mouth to mouth, he should likewise join tail to tail.
It should be made resembling a cow's tail, or auspiciously shaped like a serpent; one [point] of the same nature as that, having a single eye, should be placed at the front as the Meru.
(In the Merutantra: "There, one Meru should be given which is the thickest among all;
the first [Meru] is thick, and from that, each subsequent one is smaller and smaller. (6-259)
One should fashion it in the shape of a serpent at each Brahma-knot, or alternatively, without knots, provided with strong cords. (6.260)
Then, by winding it three times with the middle [finger], and half a turn from the end, the knot formed turning clockwise is called the Brahma-knot. (6.261)
From mutual friction alone, the loss of the recitation (japa) will certainly occur.
Knots should be made in the middle; one should not insert pearls or other such items here.
(puraścaraṇacandrikāyām) One should fashion a *brahmagranthi* within each individual bead;
having thus prepared the rosary for recitation, one should then perform the consecration. (6.263)
One should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and pure water while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra:
"Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. (6.264)
"Obeisance to Bhava, the source of existence; in every birth, in non-birth, and in becoming, protect me! Obeisance to Bhavodbhava.
With sandalwood, agallochum, and other fragrances, one should rub [the image] while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra. (6.265)
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva.
Oṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭha. Oṃ, salutation to Śreṣṭha.
Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra. Oṃ, obeisance to Kāla.
Oṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇa.
Oṃ, homage to the subduer of strength.
Oṃ, homage to the tamer of all beings.
Oṃ, homage to the self of the mind.
One should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra: *Oṃ aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyo ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyo namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyaḥ*.
One should then smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
"Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us.
One should consecrate each [item] one hundred times with this very fifth mantra.
Oṃ, Īśāna, lord of all sciences, lord of all beings, sovereign of Brahman, sovereign of the Veda; may there be for me the blessing of Brahman, ever auspicious!
With this fifth mantra, one should consecrate Mount Meru.
Having thus purified the rosary, the wise practitioner should then establish its vital breaths (prāṇas). || 6.266 ||

In the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*, one who knows the reality of mantras should consecrate [the materials] with the root mantra, both in forward and reverse order; likewise, one should consecrate them with the letters of the Mātṛkā. (6.267)
Having worshipped the chosen deity in due order according to the rule,
one should first perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and then recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
And one should perform oblations with a tenth part [of the total] of whatever is dear to whichever deity;
then, according to the Yoginītantra, one should perform the rite of homa for the sake of attaining identity with the deity. (6.269)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the remaining drops of clarified butter into the vessel.
If one is unable to perform the rite of homa, one should perform twice as much recitation (japa).
O Mālā, you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments upon all worlds;
by that truth, O Mother, grant me success—homage be to you!
Having spoken thus and performed worship, the householder should then carefully conceal [the rosary].
(In the *Yāmala*, however:
"O garland, O garland, O great garland, you who are the very nature of all principles! (6.272)
"The fourfold group of goals has been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me.
Having performed the preliminary rites beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should worship with red flowers—thus it is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Having done this, the wise one should perform the recitation upon the rosary using the Mātṛkā.
From the various phonemes of the Mātṛkā, all tantras were born;
therefore, the recitation of all mantras should be performed with this garland.
Having worshipped the guru, one should receive [the rosary] from his hand for the sake of all accomplishments;
however, some Tantrika, while reciting the Gāyatrī, strings the rosary himself. (6.275)
For such a method of binding [the thread] has not been described anywhere in the scriptures of mantra;
one who is impure should not touch it, nor should one allow it to slip from the hand.
(p. 444) (In the *Merutantra*:
One should recite with that very rosary by which it was made for a particular mantra;
from reciting another mantra, a curse upon the deity arises. (6-277)
One should employ a firm thread so that it does not break during the recitation;
if the thread wears out, one should knot a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times.
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):

If [the rosary] falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Likewise, upon touching anything forbidden, one should wash it and then proceed as prescribed.
(Merutantra) One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor should one shake it or fumigate it.
One should not touch it with the left hand, nor should one allow it to fall from the hand. (6-280)
When moving the beads, the thumb should not touch any other bead;
at the time of recitation, the wise practitioner should always avoid crossing over the *meru* bead.
At the time of turning [the manuscript], one must not cause any clashing; for when there is a rattling sound or when it is swaying, the mind becomes agitated. (6.282)
If it moves, there is enmity; if it breaks, the arising of disease;
if it falls from the hand, a great obstacle; and if the thread snaps, it brings about destruction. (6.283)
(Kriyāsaṃgraha) "But when the string of the rosary is cut, one should perform the consecration again;
one should recite [the mantra] either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times. (6-284)
(From the Śaivāgama:
When the garland has been thoroughly purified and strung as before, one should, with undistracted mind, recite the mantra over it once it has been consecrated. (6.285)
Elsewhere it is also said:
"If the garland should break by itself, one should perform the penance;
one should perform a thousand recitations and fire-oblations of Gajāntaka. (p. 445)

Having performed the stringing once more, preceded by the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*), then the rosary shall bestow accomplishment; otherwise, it is not so—this is the word of Śaṅkara.
If [the image] is burnt by fire, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; if it is lost or broken, two hundred thousand times;
if it has been stolen by thieves, six thousand times; but if it has fallen, one should recite it one hundred times.
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
One should move the rosary located on the thumb from the tip of the middle finger;
one must not touch it with the index finger—this is the method of counting that bestows liberation. (6.289)
The wise practitioner should recite while experiencing joy during both enjoyment and liberation;
however, for the highest rite, one should recite using the thumb and the ring finger.
For the rites of inciting hatred and eradication, one should perform recitation with the index finger and thumb joined;
for the rite of killing, one should perform recitation with the little finger and thumb joined.
At other times, having worshipped this garland, one should keep it concealed;
the wise person should reveal the guru, but never the mantra.
One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru.
[For otherwise] bhūtas, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas [would seize them]. (6.293)
Since [the mantras] carry [the practitioner away] when recited openly, therefore the wise person should recite them in secret.
Now, regarding the consecration of the rosary for women and Śūdras (*Merutantra* 6.294):
"The consecration of the rosary is now described for the sake of Śūdras or for the sake of women."
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā with devotion,
one should then consecrate that rosary with the seed-syllable *hsauḥ*.
One should place it in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three days, reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, on the fourth day, having extracted it, one should wash it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Having tied it together with the heart-mantra, one should place it upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
Then, having lifted that garland from there, one should place it in a golden vessel.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water,
[one should anoint him] with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and other [scents].
Then the practitioner should perform the consecration with the mantra;
having worshipped the nine planets, he should also worship the guardians of the directions. (6.299)

In this regard also, the masters of the tradition maintain that one should consecrate the rosary with the letters of the *mātṛkā* and the root mantra, and then perform the worship of the chosen deity within it, preceded by the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, as described before.
Likewise: "Then, one should offer oblations (*homa*) with sesame seeds mixed with ghee according to one's capacity."
One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, equal in weight to the number of gems.
One should feed Brahmins who are reciters of that mantra or those learned in the Vedas;
in the absence of a golden vessel, a leaf of the Aśvattha tree may be used.
The consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*) is said to bestow success (*siddhi*) in the practice of recitation (*japa*).

Now, regarding the consecration of the rosary for those following the Left Path (*vāmamārgin*), as well as for the Kaulikas and Vāmins, [it is performed] with rosaries made of bone and so forth; thus it is stated in that very [text]. (6.302)
For the sake of accomplishment, I shall explain the consecration that is hidden in all tantras:
one should first worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and unguents. (6.303)
Highly delighted, he should count the rosary and drink honey purified by mantras.
A rosary made of fifty beads should be fashioned and inserted into the womb of a woman in her menses.
Having set aside one night, he should then wash [the object] with appropriate causes;
he should consecrate it with pure waters, with the root mantra, and with the juices of vijayā.
Having washed it, one should afterwards fumigate it and thread it with desired cords;
for one's own desired recitation, the cord should be blue, and black for the rite of killing.
For subduing it is green; for paralyzing, smoke-colored; for hostility, the color of a palm tree (dark brown).
For pacifying and nourishing it is white; for hatred it is red, and for eradication it should be [the same]. (6.307)
For subjugation (*vaśya*), yellow decoction is used, while for causing distraction (*vikṣepa*), it is considered appropriate;
thereafter, one should perform the wheel-worship (*cakrapūjā*) one thousand and eight times.
And with meat, liquor, and betel, the practitioner [should worship] with the root mantra;
thereafter, he should cause an offering (bali) of buffaloes and other animals to be presented according to the rule.
One should also feed the Śaktis and the practitioners, numbering as many as the jewels [in the rosary].
One must not give a rosary consecrated in this manner to an uninitiated person (paśu).
Now, regarding the *karamālā* (the rosary of the hand) in the *Bālātantra*:
the index finger, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger—these three fingers [from the index to the ring finger] have three joints each, while the middle finger has only one joint. (6.311)
One should conceive of the two joints of the middle finger as Mount Meru.
As stated in another tantra: "Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger, and proceeding in order through the little finger... (6.312)
The hand-garland (karamālā) is proclaimed to extend as far as the base of the index finger.
Sanatkumāra also says: "Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger, and starting from the little finger... (6.313).
One should recite over the ten joints starting from the base of the ring finger up to the root of the index finger,
and likewise starting from the base of the little finger up to the end.
One should perform the recitation (*saṃjapet*) over the eight joints, ending at the middle finger and the index finger (*tarjanī*).

This subsequent verse refers to the performance of eight recitations after the completion of one hundred recitations when performing a total of one hundred and eight recitations. Furthermore, this rule pertains to the Vaiṣṇava tradition; however, in the case of the Śākta tradition:
Starting from the base of the ring finger, however, in a clockwise sequence.
One should recite [the mantra] over the eight joints up to the base of the middle finger;
making the middle joint of the ring finger the *meru*, one must not cross it. (6.316)
If a person recites [the mantra] there, at the tip of the index finger and likewise at the middle finger, four things of his will perish: life, knowledge, fame, and wealth. (6.317)
Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntasāra*. In that very same work:
"Starting from the base of the ring finger, however, in a clockwise sequence..."
One should recite [the mantra] over the nine joints, extending as far as the base of the index finger.
And this [practice] culminates in twelve repetitions of one hundred and eight recitations.
Regarding the Śrīvidyā, however, [it is stated in the Yāmala]:
"The two [tips] of both the ring finger and the middle finger [are placed] at the root and the tip."
And three joints of the little finger and the index finger, O Maheśvarī.
"O Goddess, the ring finger and the middle finger shall form the Meru; these two are auspicious.
One should recite [the mantra] for Tripurasundarī in a clockwise sequence"—thus the specific instruction has been stated.
(Merutantra) One should never separate the fingers at any time during the recitation of mantras. (6-320)
Through the separation of the fingers, the recitation flows out through the gaps;
one must not skip any count, nor should one contract the palm.
One should not show the hand; otherwise, the Rākṣasas seize the fruit [of the recitation].
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
Whatever is recited on the tips of the fingers, and whatever is recited while crossing over the *meru* [the ring finger], [is fruitless]. 6-322.
Whatever is recited during the junctions of the lunar phases shall all become fruitless for one who, out of negligence, recites while transgressing the rules of counting. (6.323)
Since Rākṣasas seize [the merit] from that which is not counted, the wise person should certainly count it.
(In the Rudrayāmala:
Not with unbroken rice grains, nor with the joints of the hand, nor with grains of corn, nor even with flowers. (6.324)
One should not perform the counting of recitations using sandalwood, clay, lac, black pigment, vermilion, cow dung, or dried cow manure. (6.325)
Having stirred [the mixture] and made it into a pill, one should perform the prescribed number of recitations (*japa*).
As stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"In that regard, while performing finger-recitation (*aṅgulijapa*), one should recite using all the fingers including the thumb. (6.326)
Any rite performed without the thumb shall be fruitless.
(From the *Muṇḍamālā*):
One should always perform the recitation with the hand, but never that which is for the sake of specific desires. (6.327)
One may perform even optional rites with the hand if a rosary is not available.
Now begins the section on mudrās.
Regarding that, the meaning of the term *mudrā* is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
They bring joy to the gods and cause their minds to melt with delight.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Family, they are known as *mudrās* and should be displayed. (Also in the *Merutantra*:
"Joy (*muda*) arises for the self through the two doors of the body by means of [attaining] its own nature and [its] acquisition. (6.329)

Those mudrās which, by effortless application, are considered to be powers (śaktis), they bring joy [from the influence of] planets and the like, and they cause the flood of sins to melt away. (6.330)
Because they cause delight (*modana*) and melting (*drāvaṇa*), they are therefore proclaimed as *mudrās*. (In the *Yāmala*:
"Because of the delighting of all the gods and the melting away of the succession of sins... [6.331]
Therefore, this mudrā is proclaimed as the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites. Now I shall explain the mudrās that are concealed in all tantras.
One should worship with those [mudrās] which, when performed, cause the deities of the mantra to rejoice, during the time of recitation, meditation, and in rites for specific desires.
In bathing, invocation, the installation in the conch, protection,
the offering of food, and likewise elsewhere as revealed in their respective ritual manuals (kalpas).
The mudrās should be displayed in their proper places, characterized by their respective defining marks;
these nine mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), are considered common to all. (6.335)
Likewise, one should employ the six-limbed mudrās in all mantras;
nineteen mudrās of Viṣṇu have been taught by the wise. (6.336)
The conch, discus, mace, lotus, flute, śrīvatsa, kaustubha, the forest garland, as well as the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and that called the bilva fruit. || 6.337 ||
Likewise, the mudrā called Garuḍa increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu;
as do the Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Hayagrīvī, and the Dhanus [mudrās]. (6.338)
Then the Bāṇamudrā, the Paraśumudrā, and likewise the Jaganmohanikā;
the supreme Kāmamudrā is proclaimed—these are the ten mudrās of Śiva.

The [emblems] known as the Liṅga, the Yoni, and the Trident; the Rosary, the Mace, the Terrible One, and the Deer; the Khaṭvāṅga, the one called the Skull, and the Hand-drum (Ḍamaru) which delights Śiva. (6.340)
The seven mudrās of the Lord of the Gaṇas, including that of Sūrya, are known as Padma, Danta, Pāśa, Aṅkuśa, Vighna, Paraśu, and Laḍḍuka. (6.341)
In the worship of Vighnapa, the mudrās are to be known as those called *bījapūra*;
[the remaining attributes are] the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, the fear-dispelling gesture, the sword, the discus, the bow, and the arrow. (6.342)
The Mauśalī, Mudrikā, and Daurgī mudrās bring favor to Śakti;
the Lakṣmīmudrā is for worship, while [the Vāgvādinīmudrā] is for the propitiation of Vāgvādinī.
The rosary, as well as the lute, the gesture of exposition, the book, and the seal;
these are to be known as the mudrās called the Seven Tongues for the worship of Fire.
The Matsya-mudrā, the one called Kūrma, the Lelihā, the one named Muṇḍa, and the one known as Mahāyoni—these bestow the abundance of all siddhis. (6.345)
In the worship of Śakti, the Mahāyoni is used; in the worship of Śyāmā and others, the Muṇḍamudrikā; while the Matsya, Kūrma, and Lelehā seals are considered common to all.
p. 451) These ten mudrās are to be known for the worship of Tripurā: Saṃkṣobha, Drāvaṇa, Ākarṣa, Vaśya, Unmāda, Mahāṅkuśa, [Khecarī, Bīja, Vajra, and Yonimudrā]. (6.347)
Khecarī is proclaimed as Bījayoni and Trikhaṇḍā;
Kumbhamudrā is for the consecration, and likewise Padmamudrā is for the seat.
Kālakarṇī should be employed in rites for pacifying obstacles;
and Gālinī should be employed in the rite of purifying water.
In the worship of Śrī Gopāla, one should display the flute; in that of Nṛhari, the lioness (Nārasiṃhikā);
and in the worship of Varāha, one should show the boar-face (Vārāhāsya).
In the worship of Rāma, the mudrās of the bow and arrow are used; likewise, in the worship of Paraśurāma, the mudrā of the axe is to be known as that which is called "the Deluder of the World."

One should employ the mudrā called Kumbha in meditation on the one named Vāsudeva, in protection, and in every kind of petition; indeed, one should employ the one called Prārthanā for making petitions.
And their characteristics are stated according to the order of their enumeration. (6.252ef)
The mudrās for invocation and so forth, as well as the mudrās for the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, have been described previously; others are now stated here.
In that very same [text]:
"The fingers of the hand are straight, with the thumbs [extended]."

The mudrā for the heart and the head consists of fists with the thumbs tucked underneath; for the crest-lock, it is the fingers of both hands joined together, and for the armor, it is the fingers of the two hands [spread out]. (6.353)
The *nārācamuṣṭi* (arrow-fist) is the sound produced by the thumbs and index fingers raised from the pair of held arms;
these are described as the mudrās distributed in all directions.
In this [mudrā], the two eyes are formed by the index fingers and the middle fingers.
Therein, there shall be three eyes; the six-limbed mudrās have been described exactly as they are.
Now, the characteristics of the Vaiṣṇava mudrās are being told.
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist, || 6.355 ||
Then, having turned the fist palm upwards, one should extend the thumb;
likewise, the fingers of the left hand are joined together and fully extended.
This mudrā, known as the *śaṅkha*, is formed by joining the right thumb [with the left].
Having brought the two hands face-to-face, they are joined together and well extended. (6.357)
The little fingers and thumbs joined together—this is the mudrā known as the wheel (cakrasaṃjñakā).
Having placed the two hands facing each other, the fingers are then interlaced.
Furthermore, when the two middle fingers are joined together and well extended,
this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā*, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other,
with the fingers slightly bent and the thumbs pressed against the palms, this is the Padma-mudrā (Lotus Gesture).
The thumb of the left hand is placed upon the lip;
the little finger [of the left hand] is joined with the right thumb, while the little finger [of the right hand] is well extended. (6.361)
When the index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved, this becomes the flute mudrā; it is well-guarded and is the beloved of Hari.
One should join the middle and ring fingers of the two hands which are touching each other,
holding them with the thumbs positioned at the base of the little fingers.
One should form the two index fingers; this mudrā is named Śrīvatsa.
The little finger of the right hand is joined to the back of the ring finger. (6.364)
Having bound [the left hand] with the other little finger and likewise with the right index finger, one should bind the left ring finger at the base of the right thumb. (6.365)
Having joined the left thumb and middle finger together, the other four fingers straightened and with their tips touching one another— this is the mudrā known as the Kaustubha.
If one touches from the throat down to the feet with both hands using the index finger and thumb,
this mudrā is called Vanamālikā.
One should place the index finger and thumb, joined as a spear-point, at the heart in front;
then one should place the lotus-hand of the left hand on the left knee and upon the head.
This Jñānamudrā shall be the beloved consort of Rāmacandra.
Having raised the left thumb and bound its tip with the thumb of the other hand,
and having pressed those [other fingers] as well with the fingers of the left hand,
the one of pure intellect, firmly binding [the hands], should place them at the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra.
This ring, known as the *vilvā*, is clearly described here as the *goyanī* by those who know the ritual procedures.
Having turned the two hands away from each other and joined the little fingers together,
the index fingers are likewise joined to one another, as are the thumbs.
One should move the two middle fingers like two wings;
this is called the Garuḍa-mudrā, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu.
Placing his hands between his knees with the chin and lips evenly covered,
and with his hands touching the ground, he trembled again and again.
One should open the mouth wide and flick the tongue;
this is the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which increases his delight. (6.374)
Then, having pressed the two little fingers with the two thumbs of both hands, while all the other fingers are turned downwards— this is considered the mudrā of Nṛhari.
Placing the left hand above the right with the palm facing upward, the wise one should bend it downward;
this is declared to be the mudrā known as Vārāhī. (6.376)
With the right hand facing upward and the left hand facing downward,
with the tips of the fingers joined together, this is the mudrā known as Vārāhī.
Having placed the fingers of the right hand with their palms facing downward upon the palm of the left hand, one should raise the middle finger among them and bend it downward.
The mudrā dear to Hayagrīva imitates his form:
one should join the tip of the middle finger of the left hand with the tip of the index finger. (6.379)
One should press the ring finger and the little finger with its thumb;
this, shown upon the left shoulder, is declared to be the bow mudrā.
The arrow-seal consists of the index finger extended while held within the right fist;
or else, as it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Dear One, make the hand like a bow held in the hand. (6.381)
This is declared to be the bow mudrā, situated in the left hand;
it is the kalpadruma bow mudrā, which increases fame and renown.
Just as an arrow already held in the hand, so too should you form the hand, O beloved;
this is declared to be the "Arrow Mudrā," which cuts down the host of enemies.
Having joined the palms of the two hands together obliquely, one should make the fingers closely pressed and extended; this is the mudrā known as the axe (paraśu).
The two fists with the thumbs pointing upward constitute the Trailokyamohinī mudrā;
likewise, having joined the two hands together with the fingers extended, [one forms the next]. (6.385)
With the two index fingers on the backs of the middle fingers and the two thumbs resting upon the middle fingers—
this is declared to be the Kāma-mudrā, which brings delight to all the gods.
Now, the characteristics of those dear to Mahādeva are described:
one should raise the right big toe and bind it with the left big toe. (6.387)
One should bind [the fingers] with the left fingers and the right fingers;
this is declared to be the *liṅgamudrā*, which brings about the presence of Śiva. (6.388)
Having joined the two little fingers together, [place] the two index fingers upon the two ring fingers; beneath the two long middle fingers, which are joined upward with the ring fingers. (6.389)
Placing the tips of both thumbs [over the palms], this is declared to be the *yonimudrā*.
Having bound the little finger with the thumb, the three remaining fingers are held closely together.
One should extend [the fingers]; this is proclaimed as the mudrā called the Trident (triśūla).
Having tied the tips of the thumb and the index finger together like a finger-ring (aṅgulitra), [this is the trident mudrā]. (6.391)
One should extend the rosary; this is proclaimed as the *mudrā*.
With the right hand positioned below, it is extended; this is the *avarāmudrā*.
The left hand is raised with both fingers extended;
one should join the ring finger and the thumb together, placing them at the tip of the middle finger.
When the fingers are joined and resting [against one another], this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā*.
The five fingers of the right hand, however, are joined and raised upward. (6.394)
The Khaṭvāṅga mudrā is renowned and considered exceedingly dear to Śiva;
it is formed by placing the left hand like a vessel upon the left side of the body. (6.395)
Having placed [the hands] as if raised, one should form the mudrā; this is considered the Kāpālikī.
Having formed a loose fist with the middle fingers slightly raised— || 6.396 ||
Raising the right hand upward, one should move it to the region of the ear;
this is called the ḍamaru-mudrā, which destroys all obstacles.
Next, the characteristics of the Gaṇeśa mudrās are described as follows: the middle finger is turned upward with its face facing up, straight, and held in a clenched fist. (6.398)
The *dantamudrā* has been fully described by those learned in all the scriptures:
[it is formed] by the index finger of the left fist touching the index finger of the right fist. (6-399)
Having joined the tips of the two thumbs, one should place them at the tips of one's own index fingers;
this is the mudrā called Pāśa, as proclaimed by the wise.
Having made the middle finger straight and joining the index finger at its middle joint, one should bend it slightly; this mudrā is known as the goad (aṅkuśa).
The fist formed by the index, middle, ring, little, and thumb fingers, with the palm facing downward and the middle finger extended, is the *vighna-mudrā*. (6.402)
The *parśu* mudrā has been described, as has the well-known *laḍḍu* mudrā;
the mudrā called *bījapūra* has been omitted because it is already well known. (6-403)
Now, the characteristics of the Śākta mudrās are described:
the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the boon-granting gesture (vara), the gesture of fearlessness (abhīti), the bow (dhanus), and the arrow (bāṇa) are proclaimed.
Having bound the little and ring fingers with one's own right thumb, the extended fingers joined together form the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā). (6.405)
Likewise, having placed the left hand sideways and extended it, one should make the fingers curved; this is declared to be the *carma-mudrā*.
Having formed a fist with both hands, placing the right hand over the left,
one should perform this mace-mudrā (*muśala-mudrā*), which destroys all obstacles.
Having placed it upon the head and joined them together, this is declared to be the Durgā-mudrā;
likewise, having formed the Cakra-mudrā and extended the two middle fingers.
Having likewise brought the two little fingers together, one should place the two thumbs at their tips;
this is indeed the supreme Lakṣmī-mudrā, which bestows all prosperity.
Placing the hands like those of a lute-player, one should move the head; this is declared to be the Vīṇāmudrā, which brings favor to Sarasvatī. (6.410)
Having formed the left fist facing oneself, this is the book mudrā;
the tips of the right thumb and index finger are joined, while the other fingers of the hand are extended. (6.411)
This gesture of explanation, with the hands extended, joined, and palms facing upward, is considered exceedingly dear to Śrī Rāma’s Sarasvatī. (6.412)
Having placed the two hands with fingers extended at the wrist-joints,
one should extend the pair of little fingers and thumbs joined together.
This mudrā, known as Saptajihvā, is indeed dear to Vaiśvānara;
in it, the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are interlocked with one another.
The index, middle, and ring fingers joined together and not bent—this is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā; it is moved over the top of the conch.
Having placed the right thumb upon the left thumb with both hands, one should form a fist that leaves some space; this is the *kumbha-mudrā*.
With the thumbs raised in both fists, one should place them at the tips of the index fingers;
this is indeed the "all-protecting" mudrā, declared to be the Kumbha mudrā.
With the fingers extended, the two hands joined together and facing each other, one should place them at one's own heart; this is the mudrā known as Prārthanā (the Request).
The añjali and añjalimudrā is that which is designated as vāsudeva;
it is formed by making the two thumbs raised while the two fists are joined together. (6.419)
One should bring those two very same hands face-to-face; that mudrā is Kālakarṇikā.
It consists of a tight right fist with the index finger placed upon the nose. (6.420)
The *mudrā* known as *vismaya* causes one to be overcome with wonder;
it consists of the right fist with the thumb raised upward, and is called the *nāda-mudrā*. (6.421)
By joining the index finger and the thumb, there is the *bindu-mudrā* at the front.
With the left hand facing downwards, the right hand is turned upwards. (6.422)
Having cast [the fingers] and having interlaced the fingers with the fingers, one should rotate them;
this shall be the *saṃhāramudrā*, prescribed for the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*).
One should touch the palm of the left hand to the back of the right hand and properly move the two thumbs; this is the mudrā known as Matsyarūpiṇī.

With the index finger of the left hand, one should grasp the little finger of the right; with the index finger of that same right hand, one should grasp the little finger of the [other] right hand. (6-425)

the right thumb should be raised, and the middle and other fingers of the left [hand] [should be joined]. (6.426)
One should join the fingers on the back of the right hand;
likewise, with the middle and ring fingers of the left hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.
One should turn the right hand face downwards and make the right palm level with the back of a tortoise on all sides.
This is declared to be the *kūrmamudrā* for the practice of meditating upon the deity:
having formed a fist with the left hand, with the thumbs placed between [the fingers], [and] on the back and chest. (6.429)
Having likewise carefully grasped the tip of the right middle finger, one should then join the tips of the middle and index fingers to the tip of the thumb. (6.430)
The practitioner should join the right hand into the left fist;

One should hold the index, middle, and ring fingers level and facing downward;

This mudrā is named Lelihā, proclaimed for the placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*); it is formed by placing the little fingers in sequence between the index, ring, and middle fingers. (6.433)
One should join the two hands and place the deity at the base of the little fingers;
having cast [the tips] onto the ends of the fingers, it is proclaimed as the Great Yoni (Mahāyoni).
The mudrās taught in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* are revealed here.
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain the mudrās that grant the accomplishment of all aims. (6.435)
By means of these [mudrās], when they are performed, the presence of the Triple City (Tripura) is established.
Having rotated the two hands, one should cause the two thumbs to touch and be made equal.

O Supreme Goddess, when the middle fingers of this very same mudrā are kept straight, it becomes the Sarvavidrāviṇī. (6.440)
O Supreme Goddess, with the middle and index fingers, and the little and ring fingers made equal, one forms two mudrās in the shape of hooks with the middle fingers. (6.441)
One should place the thumb upon the little finger and the ring finger;
this is the supreme *ākarṣaṇī* mudrā, which attracts the three worlds. (6.442)

Having formed the hands into the hollowed-cup shape (*puṭākāra*), with the two index fingers curved like hooks, one should rotate them in sequence so that the two middle fingers are positioned below them.
O Goddess, in that same sequence, the little finger, the ring finger, and the others should all be joined closely together at the tips of the thumbs. (6.444)

Speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste, atheists, or those who have consumed leftovers. 6-486.
