having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and so forth, one should offer the *bali* to the deities of the directions. (6.547)
One should write the word *asitāṅgabhairava-brahmī* ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*;
then "accept the offering" (*valiṃ gṛhṇa*) repeated twice, ending with *svāhā*—this is the mantra for the offering to the quarters. (6.548)
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra— these are the eight Bhairavas.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, followed by Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī;
likewise Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and immediately after that Cāmuṇḍā.
Mahālakṣmī is proclaimed [to be worshipped] according to the sequence beginning with her own seed-syllable;
having worshipped her with incense and lamps, one should subsequently insert the ritual stake (kīla).
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (Om), [one should utter] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha;
then, having uttered the word "to Indrāṇī," [one should utter] the word "O Cāmuṇḍā."
After the word "vicce," one should nail down this field;
after that, one should write the words "rakṣa rakṣa" followed by "kālike."
This mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), should be placed in order starting from the east;
having uttered the root mantra, one should then utter the word "Āgneyī."
The word "to Yāmyā" [is placed] after, and again the mantra for Nairṛtyā;
then "to Vāruṇī," "to Vāyavī," and likewise "to Kauverī, Īśānī, and Bhairavī. (6.555)
Having first uttered the mantra, O Dear One, one should again address the Goddess;
one should offer the bali in due order and present the bali in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable Hṛllekhā; thereafter, the word "Vaṭukāya" and "Āpaduddhāraṇāya. (6.557)
Having uttered the two *kuru*s, one should extract *māyā* and *tāra*;
this mantra, joined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), should offer the oblation (*bali*) to Vaṭuka.
Having offered the bali-oblation in the southeast, [one should worship] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha;
then, having extracted the seed-syllable of Vārāhī, one should again [worship] the end of the five seed-syllables.
To Gaṇapati, the word *pada* follows, and likewise *varavarada*;
one should then say *sarvajana*, and further say *vaśamānaya me*. (6.560)
One should first place the wife of Vahni (the letter *ra*); then the great mantra of Gaṇanātha (*gaṃ*).
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Vārāhī (*mlau*), one should likewise extract the Raudra syllable (*ha*) tripled, and then Nārāyaṇa (*na*). (6.561)
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Sūkṣmeśa, one should extract the seed-syllable of Amareśa;
then [the syllable] ending in Ṅ for Kṣetrapāla, followed by the pair "valiṃ gṛhṇa."
The mantra of Kṣetrapāla is proclaimed as being joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-syllable).
Having written the seed-syllable of Vāyu three times, one likewise [employs] Ananta and Mādhava.
Likewise, having extracted the syllable *vaṇa* and *tulākṣī*,
the mantra joined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*) is the offering for the Yoginīs in the northwest.

The fierce Śakāra. Threefold means three times. Nārāyaṇa is the letter Ā; Sūkṣmeśa is the letter I; Amareśa is the letter U. The seed-syllable of Vāyu is the letter Ya; Ananta is the letter Ā; Mādhava is the letter I; Vartulākṣī is the letter U. The letter Kṣa is mounted upon Kāla (the letter Ma); at its end is the syllable of fire (Ra).
One should extract [this] from all beings for those who have committed the state of all obstacles. (6–565)

Having extracted *varma* (huṃ) and *phaṭ* from [the preceding mantras], followed by the two words "gṛhṇa" (accept), ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā)—this is declared to be the bestower of success; one should offer the *bali* to all beings. (6.566)
*Kāla* is the letter *ma*; *mā* is the vowel *ī*; the syllable of fire (*analākṣara*) is the letter *ra*. Thus, [the seed-syllable] is *kṣmrī*.
Rice, milk-rice, milk, fish, and likewise meat; sweetmeats, stuffed cakes, and fried cakes, as well as the three kinds of liquor. (6.567)

"Delicate cooked rice and other prepared foods, clarified butter, honey with sugar—these one should offer everywhere according to the rules; one should perform the ritual dismissal (utsarga) with milk."
(From the *Yāmala*):
He who would resort to a sacred field (*kṣetra*) without the worship of the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*)— 6.568.
He is afflicted by great obstacles; therefore, one should worship the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).

Herein lies the specific rule: whichever Kṣetrapāla’s name begins with the same initial letter as the name of the field, that very Kṣetrapāla is to be worshipped in that field. The Kṣetrapālas are mentioned in another Tantra:
Ajara, Apakumbha, and likewise Iḍārambha. (6.569)
Indramūrti, Ulkāsya, Ūṣmāda, Ṛṣusūdana, Ṛmukta, Ḷptakāya, Ḷpāda, and Ekadaṃṣṭraka. || 6-570 ||
Airāvata, Odyāmbu, Oṣadhīśa, Antavāhaka, Astaka, Arthavāha, Kamala, and Kharānana. || 6-571 ||
Gomukha, Ghaṇṭāla, Ṅaṇama, Candradhāraka, Chaṭāṭopa, the one named Jaṭāla, Jhaṅkāra, and Ñamaṭeśvara. || 6-572 ||
Furthermore, there is Ṭaṅkapāṇi, as well as Aṣṭāṇḍabandha, Ḍāmara, Ḍheḍhakarṇa, Ṇavīkānta, and Thāvira, whose tongue is a lute-string (Tantrījihva). || 6.573 ||
Dantura, Dhanada, Nāgakarṇa, Pracaṇḍaka, Phetkāra, Vīrasiddhi, Bhrukuṭi, and Meghabhāsura.
Yugānta, Raurava, Lamboṣṭha, Vasantaka, Śukamuṇḍa, Ṣaḍālāsya, Sumana, and likewise Hūnaka. (6.575)
And Kṣapāntaka, as well as the fifty Kṣetrapālas residing in the [fifty] castes;
the specific varieties of Kṣetrapālas in Ekaliṅga and other places have been described right there.
Furthermore, the remaining Kṣetrapālas are likewise devoid of caste. (6.576)
Huṃkāra resides at Ekaliṅga, Bhayāvaha in the cremation ground,
Ghora in the Mahālakṣmī forest, and Jvālāmukha during the forest festival.
Or else, Viḍālavadana should dwell in a forest of solitary trees;
Ghaṇṭārava in a cave-dwelling; and Jarāmara in a cluster of lotuses.
At the confluence he is Bhūridhāraugha; likewise on the mountain he is Māruta;
at Nirjara he is Śravaṇa; in Vahni he is Nidhāna; and at Maṇibhadra he is Maṇibhadraka.
One should know Dhanādhyakṣa in the field of juices, Kroṣṭaka in the sacrificial enclosures,
Śambara in the forest, and likewise Makara in the garden.
Having protected the world, the sixty-four great vidyās remain established;
one should always offer oblations and worship in their respective fields at all times. (6.581)
Now, the tortoise diagram (kūrmacakra): La, Kṣa,
Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṅa.
ca cha ja jha ña śa ṣa sa ha aṃ aṃ iṃ iṃ.

(Yāmala) Having taken recourse to the center of the field, one should contemplate the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*).
He who performs the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) without knowing the tortoise-diagram— (6.582).
There is no fruit for one who recites that [mantra]; it leads to all manner of misfortune.
(From the *Merutantra*) A great obstacle arises for one who does not understand the *kūrmacakra*. (6-583)
(In the *Sārasaṃgraha*):

That [system] exists in the world in four ways; its varieties are described accordingly: first is the supreme (*para*), then the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*), and likewise that which pertains to regions (*deśagata*). (6.584)
It is established as fourfold: [the village-goer] and the house-goer;
(in the *Tantrarāja*) the consonants are in the village-tortoise, and likewise the vowels are in the house-tortoise. (6.585)
In the village-tortoise, those two [divisions] exist; in the foreign tortoise, those two do not.
(From the *Gautamīya*):
A person should divide a country, a village, or even a house into nine parts. (6-586)
One should place the letters from *ka* to *ma* from east to west;
likewise, one should place the eight letters beginning with *ya* and *ra* in the [remaining] squares.
One should place two *ī*’s below and in the middle, and the vowels starting from the east (and proceeding clockwise).
Afterwards, the letters from *śa* to *sa* are for the directions; [the placement] proceeds from the first letter of the name. (6.588)
The face, the two sides, the two hands, the two flanks, the two feet here and there, the single tail, and then the middle and the back— thus it possesses six limbs.
In the *Merutantra*: "The tortoise is of four kinds, distinguished by [the layout of] foreign lands, villages, and houses.
One should construct two circles divided into nine squares. (6-590)

The seven groups beginning with the *ka*-group should be written in the directions starting from the east; the two *lakṣaka* syllables should be written in the northeast. In the center, within the circular cell, one should write two by two. (6.591)
The seed-syllable of Śrī should be written in the central square to the east of the vowels;
thus, the other tortoise is always produced facing eastward.
In whichever direction the first letter of the name of the place of instruction is situated, in that direction shall be the mouth of the village tortoise. (6.593)
Two faces are to be known: one from the vowels and likewise one from the consonants.
The face of the House-Tortoise should have its opening toward the northern door.
The two hands at the sides of the face, the two flanks, the two feet here and there, the single tail, and the back in the middle—thus he possesses six limbs. (6.595)
(Yāmala):
Having taken recourse to the location of the lamp, the rite performed brings auspicious results.
Having divided the ground into a square, one should draw a grid of nine compartments. (6.596)
One should write the seven groups [of consonants] in order in the compartments starting from the east;
thereafter, one should write the vowels of Lakṣmī and Īśa in pairs.
In whichever direction, starting from the east, the first syllable of the name of the field is situated,
one should know that to be its face, with the two hands positioned on either side.
The abdomen consists of both sides of the belly and the two feet; the remainder is declared to be the tail.
By this sequence, the practitioner should also divide that which stands in the middle.
Situated in the mouth, it attains success; situated in the hand, it shortens one's life;
situated in the belly, it remains indifferent; situated at the feet, one shall experience suffering.
If situated in the tail, the practitioner is afflicted by imprisonment, eradication, and the like.
Gautama says: If [the mark] is in the mouth, there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; if on the two hands, there are minor accomplishments. (6.601)
In the belly there is constant fruitlessness; in the feet, no accomplishments at all. In the tail, death is certain; on the back, all goals are accomplished. (6-602)
Therefore, having thoroughly understood that, one should perform all rites for victory and so forth. || 6.602ef ||
Regarding the house-tortoise (*gṛhakūrma*), the method for determining the name of the house is found in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*):
when the width is multiplied by the length and divided [by nine], that remainder shall be the first [sign] among the *dhvaja* and so forth.
The banner, smoke, lion, dog, jackal, donkey, elephant, and crow—these are declared to be the eight inheritors in their respective order. (6.603)
There is also another method:
having combined the width and the length [of the site], divide it again into three parts;
if the first syllable of the mantra corresponds to one of these [parts], it belongs to the house of the mantra-practitioner.
"What is the use then of visiting holy pilgrimage sites or wandering through sacred fields?"— this is the sense of the remainder [of the verse] in the *Merutantra*.
The first syllable alone is the mantra for accomplishing the field.
If it should exist, that mantra will certainly bestow the fruit of all accomplishments,
provided that the syllable of the mantra is friendly and belongs to the name of the "Illuminator" (Gautamīya). (6.606)
And by means of the name of the practitioner, what is there that the mantra-reciter does not accomplish?
For the lords of the fields possess all-pervading forms in the nature of the fifty letters. (6.607)
Therefore, that field, being endowed with qualities, leads to accomplishment and not otherwise;
if it is devoid of qualities, even if one faces it directly, one will not attain accomplishment through it.
Therefore, having carefully examined the circle and the friend who bestows all accomplishments,
[one should consider] in which country the lord of the island possesses the qualities of both name and mantra.
One should go there with effort, for it is considered difficult to find even with one's seat.
(In the *Kālikodbhava*) where the names of the place and the practitioner are found to be in harmony— 6.610.6.
Having understood this from the science of phonetics (*akṣaśāstra*), one should abandon each respective position.
It is stated in another tantra regarding friendliness and enmity:
"The state of being an enemy between the non-dual [vowels] and the letter *ga* is declared to be mutual. (6.611)
By means of the letter *ca*, [the *m*] of the two *ṛ*s becomes [the *k*]; by means of the letter *ya*, [the *p*] of the two *ḷ*s becomes [the *kh*].
And by means of the letter *ya*, [the *m*] of the two *ḷ*s becomes [the *ph*]. (6.612)
The letter *o* is [substituted] by *ṣa*; *ṣa* by the pair *au*;
*ja* by *ḍha*; and *ū* by *kha*. (6.613)
The letter *u* is [merged] with *ta*, the letter *pha* with *dha*, the letter *ma* with *ra*, and the letter *ya* with *sa*. (6.614)
There is enmity between these classes and others, while there is a state of friendship; where enmity exists between the names of the place and the practitioner, [there is conflict]. (6-615)
Having learned that from the science of dice, the practitioner should diligently avoid it,
lest he become an enemy of Garga, like the great city of Adṛhāsa.
Auḍḍiyāna is the wheel of Ṣaṇmukha and Ṛjubhaṭṭa; Jayantī is the enemy of Ḍhaṅkaṇa, and Khadhāra belongs to Ūjhaka. (6.617)
Ukadeva’s [city] is named Tārā, Phaja’s is named Dhūma,
Bhadra’s is Ramyaka, and Yajñaśarman’s is Somanagara.
Having thus understood the positions of the enemies in due order, the wise man should abandon them. (In the *Merutantra*):
In the case of a "great enemy" there is loss of life; in the case of "enmity," there is loss of wealth. (6.619)
Now, a certain reduction in pleasure due to enmity is being described:
[the syllables] *aga*, *ama*, *jhaṣa*, *jahā*, *mukha*, *jatha*, *dava*, and *uta*. (6-620)
*Phadha*, *bharau*, and *yasau* are proclaimed as the *mahārī*;
likewise, *ṛcchau*, *odvayaṣau*, *jaṭau*, *ūṣau*, *vadhau*, and *ḍhalau*. (6.621)
In the fifth group, however, there is enmity; that occurs somewhat in the *ka* and *ṭa* groups, as well as in the *ca*, *pa*, *ta*, *ḍha*, and *ḍha-śa* groups. (6.622)
When there is a desire for a single group, double one's own group; add the square of the position, and divide by eight—this is called *āya*. (6-623)

The place-value is doubled and its own square is reduced by eight; the difference between these two results for each place-value should be calculated, and that which remains as the remainder [is the result]. (6.624)
"As long as it remains [in that position], it bestows wealth; the practitioner does not bestow wealth [otherwise].
However, there is enmity in the fifth"—thus it is said.
This is also stated in the Jyotiḥśāstra:
The groups of consonants beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa* belong respectively to the lord of birds (*khaga*), the cat, the lion, and the dog.
There are eight [notes] for snakes, mice, elephants, and sheep, which are their own fifth and their enemies. 6-626ef.
The method for determining the vowels within one's own group and so forth, including their doubling and other operations, is also stated in that very same place:
"The elephants (8), arrows (5), seasons (6), yugas (4), horses (7), earth (1), and qualities (3), increased by two, are the directions starting from Indra (the East) in sequence."
The house of the householder is measured by the directions starting from Abhijit; that is the ten-fold period (daśā) of the house, divided by nine. || 6-627 ||
In another tantra: "Once his enmity has been ascertained, one should purify [the mantra] beginning from its second syllable.
Having thus prepared the house of the locus, the practitioner of mantra should offer an oblation there. (6.628)
In the *Gautamīya-tantra*,
it is said: "One should draw the Lord of the Island in the center, worship him, and meditate upon him."
One should worship the lords of the fields there within the nine squares starting from the east.
Amṛta is declared in the first [case], and likewise Vṛṣabha in the second;
Śailarāja would be in the third, and Vāsuki is remembered in the fourth. (6.630)
The one who accomplishes the purpose is proclaimed in the fifth; the one who accomplishes power is declared in the sixth.
Padmayoni shall be in the seventh, and Mahāśaṅkha is remembered in the eighth.
In the ninth [section], the group of shadow-umbrellas is proclaimed by the leaders of the ministers (in the *Merutantra*):
Amṛta, Vṛṣabha, Śailarāja, and Vāsuki. (6-632)
One who possesses strength should worship Padmayoni, Mahāśaṅkha, and also the one called Chāyā in the middle of the sacrificial wood and other materials used for the purpose of ritual efficacy.
Having constructed a small hut on the back of a tortoise, the householder should perform his recitation (*japa*). (In the *Yāmala*:
"And in the great seats (*mahāpīṭha*) of Śakti, such as Kāmarūpa and others... [6.634]
If one should perform the *puraścaryā*, then one need not contemplate the tortoise (*kūrma*).
The sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) such as Kāmarūpa and others have been mentioned [in the *Yoginīhṛdaya* and other texts]:
"Kāmarūpa, Kāśī, Nepāla, and Pauṇḍravardhana... (6.635).
Kāśmīra, Kānyakubja, Pūrṇaśaila, as well as Arbuda;
Amrātakeśvara, Ekāmra, Trisrotas, and Kāmakoṭaka.
Kailāsa, Bhṛgunagara, Kedāra, Candrapūraka,
Śrīpīṭha, Oṃkārapīṭha, Jālandhara, and Mālava.
Kulāntaka, Devīkoṭa, Gokarṇa, Māruteśvara,
Adṛhāsa, Viraja, Rājagṛha, and Mahāpatha.
Kolāgiri, Melāpura, Kāleśvara, Jayantikā, Ujjayinī, Vicitra, Kṣīraka, and Hastināpura. (6.639)
Uḍḍīśa, the one called Prayāga, Ṣaṣṭhī, Māyā, Jaleśvara, Malaya, Śrīśaila, and Meru, the best of mountains.
Māhendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura;
Mahālakṣmī, Uḍḍiyāna, and thereafter Chāyāchatra.
These seats (pīṭhas) have been fully described as having the form of the Mātṛkā.
In another tantra, concerning Dākṣāyaṇī, it says:
"From the womb, the heart, the anus, the left eye, and then the left ear. (6.642)
Likewise, from the right ear, from the nose, from the left breast,
from the right cheek, from the nails, and then from the vicinity of the anus.
From the navel, from the fingers, from the teeth, from the right hand, from the left cheek, from the head, and also from the right breast. (6.644)
From the shoulder, from the right armpit, and likewise from the left armpit and the belly;
then above that, from Balimadhya, Talabali, and then Atha.
Then [he should touch] the garment, the buttocks, the hips, the right thigh,
the left thigh, the right knee, and the left knee.
Then, from the right shank and the left shank, from the right ankle and the left ankle,
from the right eye and the left eye, and from the right heel and the left heel.
From the blood, from the bile, as well as from the fat, the tongue, and the marrow,
and also from the right big toe of the sandal, and from the left, [arises] the splendor.
From the shadow of the tip of a reed, from a shadow, and from a mass of hair— in this sequence—
[the drops] falling upon their respective locations are indeed bestowers of all accomplishments.
And the fifty-one sacred seats (pīṭhas), beginning with Kāmarūpa and so forth, were born in the form of the phonemes from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*. (6.650)
From the bones and hair of his various limbs and from the collection of his ornaments,
countless secondary seats (upapīṭhas) manifested everywhere.
In the *Merutantra*:
"At Kurukṣetra, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, at Mahākāla, and at Kāśī—one should not contemplate the seat of the Tortoise. (6.652)
On a mountain (according to the Gautama tradition), on the bank of a river, in a sacred forest, or on a riverbank—
if one performs the *puraścaraṇa* there, one need not worry about a tortoise. (6.653)
In the *Yāmala*:

"One should not contemplate the *kūrmacakra* at a watchtower (*aṭṭāṭṭaka*), at a seat of power (*śaktipīṭha*), at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or again in sacred fields (*kṣetra*); nor in a forest, on a mountain, or in any other holy place. (6.654)
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*): That which is called the "Tortoise Diagram" (*kūrmacakra*) is declared to be the means for accomplishing the success of mantras.
Having taken recourse to its mouth, one should construct a small hut equal in size to a wind-shelter.
It should be square, four cubits in size, with a well-raised platform one cubit high,
and adorned with moon-canopies, banners, and other such archways.
One should construct a secluded, plastered, and well-surrounded [shrine],
and then, on an auspicious day, one should observe a single meal.
Having bathed in the morning and being self-restrained, one should first recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sin. (6.658)

Having bathed according to the rules at an auspicious moment, lunar mansion, and lunar day, one should recite the *gāyatrī* of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) and diligently gratify the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other offerings. (Merutantra 6.659)
Having satisfied one's own guru with land, wealth, clothing, ornaments, and so forth, one should commence the *puraścaryā* preceded by his permission. (6.660)
(In the Siddhāntasāra:
Having performed everything from the morning duties up to the end of the worship, one should then begin the recitation.
(In the Yāmala:)
But he who, without performing his morning duties, should worship the Goddess with devotion—
His worship is indeed fruitless, like a ritual performed without purity.
Therefore, at the outset, he should perform the morning rites. As it is said in the *Siddhāntasāra*:
"At the hour of Brahmā, the wise man, having abandoned sleep and being undisturbed... (6.662).
Having risen from the bed, one should remember the venerable Guru situated upon a white lotus on the crown of the head;
during the final watch of the night, one should also remember one's chosen deity. (Merutantra, 6.663)
Having risen, one should place the left foot on the ground with the right side [of the body].
Then, having gone outside the house, one should perform the necessary bodily functions with care.
Having discarded the night-garment and put on two [fresh] garments,
and having sipped water so as to be pure of body—
thus [it is said] in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Having performed the necessary duties, the wise practitioner, seated upon an auspicious seat,
should assume the bound lotus posture (*baddha-padmāsana*) with his body, head, and neck held straight. (Yāmala 6.665)
(Merutantra) Thereafter, one should contemplate a thousand-petaled lotus upon one's own head;
there, one should remember the venerable Guru in his own form, with the luster of camphor. (6.666)
Extremely serene, adorned with shimmering ornaments and white sandalwood paste,
with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons, fearlessness, and knowledge, as well as holding a book.
He is joined [in union], clad in white garments, peaceful, and adorned with white flowers;
he is embraced by his Śakti, who is red in color and rests upon his left lap. (6.668)
She is embraced by [his] left [arm], which holds a playful lotus and wears red garments and ornaments along with a garland of red sandalwood, while [he embraces her] with his right [hand].
One should meditate upon the yogin who is inward-turned, peaceful, and of the nature of Śiva—
resembling pure crystal and dispelling the darkness of ignorance. (From the Kālānalatantra, 6.670)
Resembling pure moonlight, adorned with two silken garments,
anointed with fragrant unguents, peaceful, and with his two hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Joined with the Śakti on his left thigh, adorned with red garments,
he holds his own beautiful body with his right hand by means of his Śakti.
He is beautifully adorned by a red [goddess] holding a blue lotus in her left hand,
and his two lotus-eyes are radiant with supreme bliss.
(From the Merutantra:
Having been consecrated by the stream of nectar heard from the pair of his lotus feet, the disciple should contemplate his own body in this way. (6.674)

One should worship with external substances such as perfumes and flowers, or with mental offerings, using his names that are established by convention and which proclaim the greatness of the Guru. (6.675)
Having prostrated thus with the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu), one should contemplate their dissolution into one's own heart.
As stated in another tantra: "And having received his command, one should remember one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā). (6.676)
She exists in the form of Kuṇḍalinī from the base [of the spine] up to the aperture of Brahmā,
blazing with the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes, and more slender than a single strand of a lotus fiber.
Together with the form of three coils, having the shape of a sleeping serpent;
(in the *Śyāmāpaddhati*):
having the form of a sleeping serpent, residing in the *mūlādhāra*. (6-678)
Having raised her up by way of the suṣumṇā path, [the practitioner], having brought her who is the very form of the Supreme Goddess to the end of the aperture of Brahmā, should unite her with Śambhu.
Then, having contemplated her state of aesthetic resonance (*sāmarasya*), the wise one should cause a shower of nectar to fall and restore her to her former position. || 6.680 ||
(From the Merutantra:
Then, from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*,
there arises within the *suṣumṇā* a column of light resembling a thousand suns.
Having meditated upon that root mantra as being of the nature of that [deity] and enveloped in splendor,
and having contemplated one's own body as such, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and other attributes of the mantra using the root mantra;
then, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should contemplate the deity within the heart.
Having worshipped with mental offerings, one should mutter the mantra;
then, according to one's ability, one should offer that recitation to the deity.
Having praised and bowed to the deity, one should entreat him with these verses for his command.
O primordial God Śrī Śaṅkara, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, having arisen at dawn by the very command of your feet for the sake of your beloved—
I shall continue to follow the journey of saṃsāra.
O Śaṅkara, O God of gods, as I continue upon the journey of saṃsāra by your command,
may rivalry, contempt, strife, and negligence—
O Protector, may fears not overcome me.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods—[as stated] above—now follows the procedure for the *ajapā* [mantra]. As it is said in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*:
"I shall describe the worship of that which is called the *haṃsa*, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners."
By the mere knowledge of which, one becomes omniscient on earth.
The individual soul always recites this mantra consisting of the Goddess Haṃsā;
by the mere remembrance of it, a man becomes liberated while living. (6.689)
The seer is declared to be Haṃsa, and the deity is Parahaṃsa;
the meter is the unmanifest Gāyatrī, and the application bestows accomplishment. (6.690)
(In the Surendrasaṃhitā:
"The seer is Haṃsa, the metre is said to be Gāyatrī preceded by the Unmanifest, and the deity is the Supreme Beginning; Haṃsa is said to be the seed-syllable. (6-691)
"Aḥ" is the Śakti, "Kīlaka" is "So'ham," and "Praṇava" is indeed the Tattva; thus is the Udātta accent proclaimed as the mantra of this [mantra]. (6.692)
This application is for the sake of liberation; thus a man should always perform it. (In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*):
"O Goddess, [one should assign] the heart to the self of the Sun, and likewise the head to the self of the Moon. (6.693)

In the stainless [crown], one should place the crest-light (śikhājyotis) which is without appearance; likewise, in the supreme [space], having placed the unmanifest (avyakta) in the two eyes, one should worship Ananta with the weapon-mantra "phaṭ".
Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the others.
(In the *Surendrasaṃhitā*:
"The individual soul (*jīva*) always recites the mantra consisting of the *haṃsa*, which is the Goddess herself. (6.695)
With the sound *ha* one goes out; with the sound *sa*, one enters again.
Merely by awakening to this, a person becomes liberated while living.
By the power of *prāṇāyāma*, one indeed becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*);
[this occurs after] twenty-one thousand and six hundred [repetitions]. (6.697)
One should recite daily the supreme mantra consisting of the bliss of Brahman as the individual soul;
its birth is the commencement of the recitation, and its death is the offering of it. (6.698)
Even without formal recitation, it is always considered as constant recitation;
when such recitation has been understood, one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the other deities. (6.699)
In the Yogaśāstra:
The Gāyatrī, which sustains the vital breaths, has arisen from Kuṇḍalinī;
she is the science of breath, the great science—he who knows her is a knower of yoga. (6-700)
With the syllable *ha* it goes out; with the syllable *sa*, it enters again.
The individual soul (*jīva*) constantly recites this mantra: "Haṃsa, haṃsa. (6-702)
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times—endowed with this number—the individual soul constantly recites the mantra day and night. (6-703)
The Ajapā Gāyatrī bestows liberation upon yogis;
by the mere intention of it, one is released from all sins. (6-704)
A science like this has never existed nor will it ever exist; a recitation like this has never existed nor will it ever exist; a knowledge like this has never existed nor will it ever exist.
The meditation on the Haṃsa has been described [in the Bālāpaddhati]:
the pair of Agni and Soma, the two Garuḍas, the Praṇava, radiant with the Bindu and the three-eyed one, the shining face of Ugra, the pair of Śiva’s feet, and the Kālānala situated at the sides.

One should always meditate upon the Swan, whose splendor resembles ten million rising suns, who pervades the universe, and who consists of eternal bliss, within the nest of the cottage of the heart-lotus. (6–706)
In that very place [it is said]:
"Gaṇeśvara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Jīva, and likewise the Guru—these six, having attained the state of the Haṃsa, reside in the Mūlādhāra and the other centers. (6.707)

"Attaining the state of the *haṃsa*" means having attained the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is non-different from the *haṃsa* seated in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus. This contemplation on the identity with the *haṃsa* is stated in that very [text]:

The *haṃsa* is Gaṇeśa, the *haṃsa* is indeed Brahmā; the *haṃsa* is Hari, and Śambhu consists of the *haṃsa*. The *haṃsa* is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), the *haṃsa* is the Guru; I am the *haṃsa*, the Self whose nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
In the state of the *haṃsa*, these six faces have been described as their locations (*Yogasāra*):
"Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis, this is declared to be the *mūlādhāra*, yellow in color and having four petals. (6.708)
The Mūlādhāra is a triangle situated between the anus and the genitals, beautifully adorned with the four colors beginning with the color of water. (6-709)
Likewise: That very seat (pīṭha) called Kāmarūpa, which bestows the fruit of desire, is the wheel (cakra) named Svādhiṣṭhāna at the base of the liṅga, possessing six spokes. 6-710.
The ten-spoked maṇipūraka-cakra, located in the region of the navel, is endowed with six syllables beginning with the color of the rising sun.
Adorned with the ten colors, such as blue light and others, the great wheel has twelve spokes; it is called the Heart and the Unstruck (Ahanāda).
Endowed with the first syllable of Krodhīśa and possessing a luster like that of an indragopa insect,
this is that sacred seat (pīṭha) called Pūrṇagiri, O fair-faced one.
In the region of the throat is the wheel called Viśuddha, which has sixteen spokes;
it is smoke-colored and joined with the sixteen vowels beginning with Śrīkaṭhā.
O Goddess of the Immortals, the seat named Jālandhara is situated here;
the Command (ājñā) is between the eyebrows, a two-petaled lotus with filaments.
Endowed with the last two syllables and possessing a luster like the autumnal moon, the great pīṭha named Udyāna is established above. (6-716)
The great thousand-petaled lotus is established below the visarga;
it faces downward, is endowed with all phonemes, and has reddish filaments. (6.717)
This very wheel is called Kailāśa, wherein the moon, ever-risen, three-peaked, and raining nectar, resides. (6.718)
Likewise:
"O Goddess of gods, in the Sahasrāra, however, is the supreme Śiva in the form of the Haṃsa.
O Goddess of gods, these are the locations in which Śakti is manifested. (6–719)
The meditation on Gaṇeśa and others at the Mūlādhāra and other centers has been described in the *Bālārcanapaddhati*:

"Upon the perfectly formed lotus of the Ādhāra, which possesses six petals marked with the letters *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *la*, [one should meditate upon] the youthful one with a reddish body, elephant-faced, and three-eyed."

One should meditate upon the primordial form, whose hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and who holds a beautiful noose and goad raised in his hands, appearing most charming.
Regarding the meditation on Brahman in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], it is as follows:
in the beautifully described lotus fashioned by the syllables known as ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, and saṃ, there is the presence of the lotuses.
One should meditate upon the Source of the Universe, whose form is stainless, holding the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, as well as a water-pot and a rosary of beads.
The meditation on Viṣṇu in the Maṇipūra-cakra is as follows:

Hari, who possesses the luster of the sun, the primordial Person, the unborn Nārāyaṇa, consisting of pure consciousness, is seated upon a lotus whose petals are fashioned from the consonants beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha*.

One should meditate upon the Enchanter of the World, who holds a mace, a discus, a conch, and a lotus in his hands, wears yellow garments, possesses the Kaustubha jewel, is marked with the Śrīvatsa, and resembles a sapphire.
The meditation on Śiva in the *anāhatacakra* is as follows: (p.

492) Upon a lotus whose petals are fashioned from the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṣṭha*, [one should meditate on] the beloved of Pārvatī, who resembles ten million full moons and is radiant with his matted locks (*kaparda*).

One should meditate on him as peaceful, bestowing fearlessness upon the deer-marked ṭaṅka, radiant with ornaments such as serpents, wearing a neck-ornament, armlets, a necklace, and earrings, and clad in a garment of skin. (6–723)
The meditation on the individual soul (jīvātman) in the Viśuddha-cakra is as follows:

It is seated within the limbs of the Form, yet devoid of limbs; it is peaceful, radiant with splendor, pervading all that is moving and unmoving, consisting of qualities, and in essence composed of Being and Consciousness.
One should directly contemplate the supreme soul—the manifest and unmanifest, formless, singular, and stainless light resembling a lamp—within the sixteen-petaled variegated lotus. || 6-724 ||
The meditation on the Guru in the *ājñācakra* is as follows:
In the divine lotus of two beautiful petals formed by the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, the cause of the world,
which transcends the universe and dwells within many bodies, is the *Svacchanda* [Lord], who acts according to his own will.

According to one's respective capacity, one should meditate upon the supreme deity, the excellent Guru, whose body is that of his own teacher, who consists solely of pure consciousness and being, and whose form is the perceptible, imperishable syllable.
The meditation on the Supreme Self within the thousand-petaled lotus is as follows:
[one should meditate upon] the primordial deity, all-pervading, stainless, eternal, supreme, and partless,
within the eternally blossomed thousand-petaled lotus adorned with jewels and the letters of the alphabet.

Having remembered the Self as consisting of the vibration of the supreme consciousness-existence—eternal bliss, infinite, and full—and having entered into the cavity [of the heart] by one's own will from all sides, [one remains there]. (6-726)
Their powers (*śakti*) are also mentioned in that very same place:
"The power of Gaṇeśa is Siddhi; Sarasvatī is that of Brahmā;
Lakṣmī is that of Nārāyaṇa; and Pārvatī is that of the wielder of the Pināka bow. (6.727)
Ignorance belongs to the individual soul, while knowledge—both higher and lower—belongs to the Guru;
and wisdom, which is the essence of the seed of liberation, belongs to the Supreme Self as His power.
Having meditated in that very way upon one's own self as being of the nature of the chosen goddess,
one should offer the recitation of the *ajapā* in its proper sequence and according to the prescribed number. (6.729)
Six hundred [obeisances] to Gaṇeśa, six thousand to Brahmā,
six thousand to Viṣṇu, and six thousand to Pitāmaha.
One should duly offer one thousand [oblations] to oneself, one thousand to the guru, and one thousand to the Supreme Self (parātman). || 6-731 ||
"According to the rule" means having worshipped with mental offerings:
"I offer to Gaṇeśa, who is accompanied by the power of accomplishment (Siddhiśakti), the recitation of the Ajapā mantra six hundred times; obeisance!
Likewise."
I offer this Ajapā-japa, numbering six thousand, to Brahmā accompanied by the power Sarasvatī; salutations!
Likewise:
I offer this Ajapā-japa, numbering six thousand, to Viṣṇu accompanied by the power Lakṣmī; salutations!
Thus:
"I offer this Ajapa-japa, numbering six thousand, to Maheśvara accompanied by the Śakti Pārvatī; salutations!
Thus—

I offer salutations; I present this Ajapa-japa, numbering one thousand, to the individual soul (jīvātman) accompanied by the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti). Likewise: I offer salutations; I present this Ajapa-japa, numbering one thousand, to the Guru accompanied by the supreme and intermediate power of knowledge (parāpara-jñāna-śakti).
p. 494) Thus:

"To the Supreme Self, who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, who is as cool as ten million moons, and who is accompanied by the power of Vidyā, I offer this Ajapā-japa performed a thousand times; salutations!
This is the meaning of "one should offer [the japa] in this manner."
Regarding Tārā, however, one should employ two white [mantras] in the *ājñā* [cakra], which has the luster of lightning;
and in the *paramātman*, the supreme power (*parāśakti*), one should offer a thousand [oblations]. (6–732)
One should meditate upon the Guru, whose nature is blue, within a thousand-petaled lotus shining with the luster of camphor; one should then offer [the mantra] a thousand times.
Thus the distinction has been stated. Likewise:
"Then, having praised, bowed, and made the formal resolve according to the rule..."
And having received his command, one should perform the necessary rites.

"Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)," means: "Beginning from today's sunrise until tomorrow's sunrise, I shall perform the recitation of the *Ajapā-Gāyatrī*, numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred times in the form of inhalations and exhalations.
This is the meaning of "having made the formal resolve."
Having requested boons in the *Merutantra*, one should place the foot accompanied by the breath [of the mantra]:
"O Goddess girdled by the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges! (6.735).
"O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch upon your feet.
Now, the rule for purification is stated in that very same place:
"Then one should go outside the house toward the southern or the south-western direction. (6-736)
At every step he should discharge his weapon; he should go far from his own dwelling, and having passed a distance of one arrow-length, he should look back toward the village. (6.737)
One should recite this at a clean place free from insects, water, and the like:
"May the sages, gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas arise! (6.738)
"Let this place be abandoned on all sides for my discharge of feces and urine.
Having thus dismissed the deities with clods of earth and grass while reciting this mantra, [one should proceed].
One should effect the removal of impurity there by wrapping oneself with a cloth; having performed purification with water, one should not look at the sky or the directions. (6-740)
One application of clay should be made on the penis, seven on the anus, ten likewise on the left hand, seven on both hands together, and three also on the two feet.
During the voiding of urine, one should apply five applications of clay to the left hand and the penis;
three to each of the two hands; and one to the two feet—or one may perform it in this manner.
After voiding excrement, one should perform twelve mouthfuls of gargling, which removes odors and stains and is supremely effective at dispelling mental fatigue.
Upon voiding urine, one should perform the *ācamana* rite four times; thereafter, three times. Now, the procedure for cleaning the teeth is described in that same [text]:
[A tooth-stick] produced from the *arka*, *nyagrodha*, *khadira*, *karambha*, *kakubha*, or similar trees... (6.744)
Having a thickness equal to the tip of the little finger, straight, and twelve finger-breadths long;
having uttered "Klīṃ" for Kāmadeva, the beloved of all people. (6-745)
This mantra, ending with "namas," is for cleansing the teeth;
having rinsed the tooth-stick, one should discard it in a clean place to the east. (6-746)
One should constantly wash the mouth with the root mantra for the sake of attaining accomplishment.
As stated in another tantra:
"For the sake of the mantra, one should remember its meaning; having gone to a sacred ford, one should perform the ritual bath. (6.747)
p. 496) Now, the procedure for bathing (*snānavidhi*). It is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"Now, bathing is described for the sake of accomplishing the rites of worship and fire-offerings (*pūjā-homa*).
One should take earth from a pure place with a ritual stake (*śaṅku*) consecrated by the recitation of the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). (6–748)
Having taken [the water] with the Astra-mantra and sprinkled it, one should go to the water-source.
In another Tantra:
"Then, having taken darbha grass, sesame seeds, and cow dung, one should proceed. (6-749)
Silver should be worn on the ring finger, and gold should be worn on the middle finger;
this alone is declared to be *kuśa*, not the *darbha* grasses that grow in the forest.
(Rudrayāmala) Three types of *darbha* grass are specified: those made of gold, silver, and *kuśa*.
Among these, two are prescribed for the Śākta [tradition], while three are considered appropriate for others. (6–751)
Gold and silver are indeed prescribed for rites such as recitation (japa) and worship;
they are said to perform the functions of kuśa grass, yet wild kuśa grasses are not [considered] true kuśas.
First, one should wash the edge of the water with the water of the weapon-mantra (*astravāri*).
Then, having divided the clay into three parts, one should take one portion from them. (6–753)
Having placed cow-dung, darbha grass, and consecrated sesame seeds [on the ground],
one should perform the ritual bath (snāna) using both earth and cow-dung.
Then, having performed the cleansing bath with water drawn from outside,
one should likewise perform the Vedic bath and its ancillary libation (tarpaṇa).
Then, following the procedure for the tantric bath, one should take earth with the Astra-mantra and consecrate it, as well as grass and other materials, with the Astra-mantra.
Having removed [the water] with the *śikhā* mantra, one should consecrate it three times with the root mantra;
having smeared [it] from the head down to the feet, one should bow to the water.
I bow down to those waters, the support of Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor, the soul of all beings; for they have arisen from him and possess his very form. (6.759)
Having bound the mudrā that brings [the deity] face-to-face and having restrained the vital breath (prāṇa),
one should submerge oneself and then rise silently, standing in water reaching up to the navel.
Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the Tantric bath, preceded by the mention of the month and other details,
one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should fashion a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in front,
within a square measuring one cubit, prepared in that water.
O Ravi, the sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays;
by that truth, O Lord of Gods, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.
Having thus prayed to the Sun, and piercing the solar orb with the syllable *krom* and the goad mudrā,
one should invoke the sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*) from there into this [world].
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters!
Having spoken thus, one should direct the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) into that water;
then, with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should invoke the power of the sacred ford (*tīrthaśakti*) therein.
Having visualized the orb of the sun, one should worship it with its mantra.
Consisting entirely of bliss, destroying all sins, radiant as the moon, and three-eyed, she holds in her two upper hands a noose and a goad on the left,
and within [the other two] a golden vessel filled with nectar, a rosary of pearls, and the gesture of granting boons.
I worship the Śrītīrthaśakti, accompanied by the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the two rivers, and others.
The mantra of the power of the *tīrtha* is stated in another Tantra:
"The vowels [A, Ā, I, Ī, U, Ū] mounted upon the fire [R], adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and conjoined with the six long vowels, constitute the state that consists of all-bliss. (6-769)
"O Tīrthaśakti, awaken! Come, come, O wife of Vahni!
This is declared to be the twenty-one-syllable great mantra of Tīrthaśakti. (6.770)
(Merutantra) One should consecrate that water eight times with the Gāṅga mantra: *Tāra* (Oṃ), *namo bhagavati ambe ambike*. (6-771)
"O Ambālikā, O Mahāmālinī, come, come, O Blessed One!
At the basin of all holy fords (tīrtha), one should utter the seed-syllable of Māyāśrī. (6-772)
"O Gaṅgā seated upon the matted locks of Śiva!
O Mother Gaṅgā!"—this is declared to be the Gaṅgā-vidyā consisting of fifty-three syllables.
Having stirred it with Bhuvaneśī and rendered it nectarine with the *sudhā* syllable,
the knower of mantras should then envelop it with the *kavaca* mantra and protect it with the *astra* mantra.
Having invoked the deity there along with the limbs and the retinue by means of the root mantra, one should meditate upon [the deity] in the water as emerging from between its two feet.
Having meditated and recollecting the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should bathe three times in the water while reciting the root mantra;
thereafter, recollecting the deity in the heart, one should sprinkle oneself with the water using the *kumbha* mudrā.
With three verses, [the text describes] the root-mantra, the savior, preceded by seed-syllables,
for Prajāpati who repeatedly desires to emit the entire universe as semen.
May the divine Waters, the mothers of all beings, purify me—
those who exist as the root form of misfortune (alakṣmī) dwelling within all creatures.
May the divine waters, by their very touch, cleanse me;
may they purify whatever misfortune is in my hair, at the parting of my hair, or upon my head.
"May darkness be destroyed on your forehead, ears, and eyes; salutations to you.
Then, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times with the *svāhā* mantra and the *ātma-mantra*.

In the *Gandharva-tantra*, the foremost of practitioners, while reciting the root mantra, should pour water upon his head with the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (*kumbha*), and having done so three times, he should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). (6.783)
"By means of the principles of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva...
[as stated]. The *kumbhamudrā* will be described [in the *Merutantra*]:
"Having satiated the threefold deity, one should proceed from the middle of the water to the bank."
Having put on a pair of washed garments and likewise having washed his thighs and hands.
Then one should sip water with clay; thus is the procedure for bathing prescribed.
Now, regarding the procedure for the mantra-bath, it is stated in that very same source:
"The mantra-bath should be performed during cool places and times. (6-785)
In the absence of water, on a difficult path, during an urgent task, when one is unwell, or in old age,
one should wash the feet and perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water drawn up [from a well].
Then, having purified the site and the ten directions as before, one should sit down;
then, having placed the *astra* mantra on the palms of the hands, one should perform the successive ritual depositions (*nyāsa*).
Likewise, one should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* and so forth, as well as the placement of the root mantras in their entirety;
at the conclusion of the placement, one should touch water—this is the excellent "mantra-bath. (6.788)
Whatever fruit belongs to a bath-graduate from bathing at sacred fords such as Prabhāsa and others, that [fruit] is not obtained merely by bathing in water devoid of ritual consecration.
The object of knowledge [attained] from the certain practice of mantra-bathing is ten times greater than that.
Now, regarding the bath of meditation (*dhyāna-snāna*), it is said in that same [text]:
"I shall now describe the bath of meditation, which is superior even to both of the preceding ones. (6–790)
One should meditate upon the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who abides in the heart and whose form is the mantra;
[one should meditate on] the stream of water born from his feet falling upon one's own head.
One should imagine [the breath] entering one's own body through a subtle aperture;
by means of that, one should wash away all this impurity residing within the body. (6.792)
At that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion and resembles crystal;
this supreme bath is considered to be a hundred times more effective than the mantra-bath.

He who is purified in mind is pure in all ritual acts. "The lotus-eyed one" (Puṇḍarīkākṣa) is an elliptical designation; they say that whatever deity one worships, one should meditate upon that deity. Now, regarding the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*), it is described in that very same source:
Now follows the mental bath, performed mentally with the root mantra.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with devotion at the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) seen [therein];
even according to the Śaiva Āgama, preceded by breath control, one should do so mentally with the root mantra. (6-795)

One should perform the mental bath, which is prescribed for all occasions; or else, having created a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) consisting of the nature of Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva. (From the *Merutantra*, verses 6–796).
The purification with the Saṃhitā mantras is declared to be the "bath of Śiva.
All ritual actions preceded by this bath become pure and attain success.
Therefore, one should first perform the bath, or any one of these [rites] according to the capacity of the body.
Now, the procedure for wearing the *tilaka* is described in that very same place:
"Thereafter, one should apply the *tilaka*, either according to one's caste (*jāti*) or according to one's deity (*daivata*). (6–798)
Whatever sacred site yields auspicious fruit, or with earth from there, one should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* out of a spirit of devotion;
for a Brāhmaṇa it shall be the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, while for a Kṣatriya it shall be the *tripuṇḍra*.
The Vaiśya’s [mark] should be a half-moon, while that of Śūdras is circular in shape;
one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with clay and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes.
With saffron and musk, one should apply the remaining cool paste as desired;
for a Vaiṣṇava there should be the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, while for a worshipper of Śiva there should be the *tripuṇḍra*.
One devoted to Gaṇeśa [should wear] a crescent moon; one devoted to the Goddess, a circle;
and one who is intent on Nārāyaṇa, a trident made of sandalwood. (6.802) p. 501)
On his forehead, this venerable one bears that which consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Now, the procedure for wearing the sacred ash (vibhūti) is stated in that very same place:
"If the sacred ash of the giver of prosperity is worn according to the prescribed rite, it shall indeed be prosperity. (6.803)
If held improperly, it reduces a person to ashes;
however, the ash produced from the fire-oblation should be collected in the presence of Śiva.
Or else, one may take the mud arising from the nuptial fire—pure and fragrant—which falls from the sky and is caught in a single drop by a tawny cow; this is most excellent. (6.805)
Neither moist, nor hard, neither foul-smelling nor sticky;
having discarded what is above and below, one should take it if it has fallen [into the water]. (6.806)
Having formed it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire with the root mantra.
Whether it be uncooked or cooked, black or white, it is to be discarded.
Having taken it and stirred it with a cloth, one should cast it into the receptacle for ashes;
one should collect the ashes while the deity has not yet been dismissed.
O Prajāpati, because the fierce ashes are produced when the dismissal (udvāsana) has been performed,
or else the twice-born may prepare the ashes by bringing cow-dung with their left hand.
Having placed [the substance] in the vessel with the left hand, one should burn it away with the Aghora mantra;
having lifted it up with the Puruṣa mantra, one should purify it with the Īśāna mantra.
Having thus consecrated the ashes with the mantra beginning with "agniriti," one should recite over them eleven times with the Yajus formula "tad rudrāya."
With the names preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), ending in the dative case and the word *hṛt* (heart),
and beginning with the syllables of the five colors, [one should place them] on the forehead, the shoulders, the belly, and the heart.
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the head with the five-syllabled mantra;
furthermore, the twice-born and others should wear the sacred ash while reciting these names. (6.813)
Brahmā is to be known on the forehead, Havyavāhana (Agni) in the heart;
Skanda at the navel, Pūṣan in the throat, and Rudra in the right arm.
Āditya is in the middle of the right arm, and Śaśin is at the wrist;
Vāmadeva is on the left arm, and Prabhañjana is in the middle of the left arm.
The Vasus are at the wrist, and Hari is remembered as being in the region of the back;
Śambhu is declared to be in the hump of the neck, and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is remembered as being in the head.
A Śākta, however, should wear ashes mixed with musk and other substances,
applying them with the root mantra and the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva by means of the twice-born.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
having taken [the ash] with the three middle fingers consecrated by the root mantra.
Alternatively, the *tripuṇḍra* may be made with the ring finger, the middle finger, and the thumb.
Now follows the procedure for the *sandhyā* (according to the *Bhairavītantra*):
having sipped water (*ācamana*), the knower of mantras, facing east, should sit down. (6–819)
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the Vedic and Tantric *sandhyā*. (In the *Merutantra*:
Now I shall describe the Tantric *sandhyā*: three sips of water (*ācamana*) with the root mantra;
Having tied the topknot with the root mantra, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the placement of the limbs upon the body, preceded by the placement of the hands,
having rendered the water before one nectar-like by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*.
And having consecrated it with the root mantra seven times thereafter,
[one should do so] with the letters of the Mātṛkā, from 'a' to 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu (anusvāra).
One should sprinkle water three times upon the head with kusha grass and the root mantra for each syllable;
then, the knower of the mantra should meditate on the deity seated within the solar orb.
Having taken water and addressed it with the seed-syllables representing the elemental spirits—namely *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*—one should thus empower the water sevenfold with these. (6.824)
Having recited [the mantra] again seven times with the root-mantra,
one should hold that water in the left hand and [sprinkle it] with the drops flowing from it.
Having sprinkled [the water] with the right hand while reciting the root mantra,
the practitioner of the left-hand path (vāmācārī) should perform the sprinkling by switching the hands.
Having embraced them with that remaining form of radiant energy,
it entered within, purified all internal impurity, and emerged.
Having recollected this through the right nostril,
one should visualize a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) on the left side with the right hand and cast it away with that [hand].
Having washed his hands and sipped water, the knower of mantras should then offer three arghyas with either the root mantra, the Gāyatrī, or the root mantra.
One should offer libations to one's chosen deity seated within the solar disc with water, reciting at the end of the root mantra: "I satisfy [Name]. (6.830)
Having spoken thus, one should perform the threefold libation with the left hands for that reason;
[one should recite] the Gāyatrī of the chosen deity twenty-eight times.
If [the specific mantra] is absent, one who follows the Vedic tradition should recite the Brāhmī;
however, the Tantric practitioner should recite the Śivagāyatrī, which is now described.
Oṃ, may we know that Great Lord; may we meditate upon Him whose speech is purified; may that Śiva impel us. In another tantra:
Oṃ, may we know that Puruṣa; may we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra impel us—thus the Śiva-gāyatrī is declared.
(p. 504) Now, the Gaṇeśa-gāyatrī (from the *Yāmala*):
*oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe vakratuṇḍāya dhīmahi tanno dantī pracodayāt*.
Now, the Sūrya-gāyatrī (from the *Merutantra*).
Oṃ, we know the one with seven horses; we meditate upon the one with a thousand rays; may that Sun inspire us.
This Sūrya-gāyatrī bestows the desired objects upon those who recite it, and it restores the Kṣatriya-splendor of fallen princes. (6–833)
Now, the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī is as follows:
*Oṃ nārāyaṇāya vidmahe vāsudevāya dhīmahi tanno viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt*.
Now, the Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī (from the *Taccaraṇārcanapaddhati*):
Oṃ, let us know Nṛsiṃha; let us meditate upon Him with sharp fangs; may that Lion inspire us.
The Rāma-gāyatrī has been stated previously.
Now, the Gopāla-gāyatrī (from the Merutantra):
Oṃ, may we know Dāmodara; may we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Kṛṣṇa inspire us.
Now, the Sudarśana Gāyatrī is likewise therein:
Oṃ, may we know Sudarśana; may we meditate upon the Great Flame; may that Discus inspire us.
Now, the Gāyatrī of Hayagrīva is as follows:
*Oṃ vāgīśvarāya vidmahe hayagrīvāya dhīmahi tanno haṃsaḥ pracodayāt*.
Now, the Gāyatrī of Śyāmā (from the Kumārītantra):
Having uttered the word *kālikāyai*, immediately thereafter one should say *vidmahe*;
then one should say *dhīmahi* following *śmaśānavāsinī* ending in the feminine nominative suffix *ṅi*. (6.834)
Having uttered "Tanno Ghore Padas," one should then recite "Pravadecca Pracodayāt.
By the mere grace of this [mantra], millions of great sins (mahāpātaka) [are destroyed]. (6.835)
They undergo immediate dissolution for the practitioner; it is not otherwise.
Likewise, even one joined with great sins, if he should mutter [the mantra] ten times... [6.836]
"Truly, truly, O Great Goddess, one becomes liberated at that very moment.
(In the Bhairava-tantra, however:
[The word] *kāma* with the vowel *u*, followed by *parākṣiṇā*, ending in *dānta*, and again *dakṣiṇā* joined with *ṅe*. (6-837)
One should know the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* [hūṃ] and then Cāmuṇḍā joined with the suffix *ṅe*;
then one should say "dhīmahi," and then "tannaḥ kālī pracodayāt. (6-838)
"This Gāyatrī has been proclaimed by me; it is hidden in all the Tantras.
Without it, no vidyās ever attain perfection"—so it is said.
Now, regarding the Nakṣatra-vidyā (in the Kālikārṇava):
Ai! O Blessed One, Ekajaṭā, we know [thee]—and then the word "ca" (and). || 6-839 ||
We meditate upon her with formidable fangs; may that Tārā inspire us.
(From the *Mālinītantra*) O Beloved, we know her as the most fierce one, and we meditate upon Tārā. (6.840)
"Then, at the end of the word *devī*, [one recites] 'and may she inspire our intellects' (*dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*).
Having uttered the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], one should recite: 'We know her who is Ekajaṭā' (*ekajaṭāyai vidmahe*)... (Vīracūḍāmaṇi, 6.841).
Having pronounced "Devīm" and "strī," one should say, "we meditate upon Nīlasarasvatī";
then, having pronounced "Hṛllekhā," one should say "Tāre pracodayāt. (6.842)
In the *Jñānārṇava* [of Tripurasundarī], it is said:
"First, we know the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] for the goddess Tripurā;
immediately after that, having uttered the Kāma-bīja, we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī. (6-843)
p. 506) Having uttered the word *tannaḥ klinne*, one should afterwards say *pracodayāt*.
In that very [context], Bhairavī says:
"One should extract the word *vidmahe* for Tripurā, likewise ending in the feminine suffix *ṅi*. (6-844)
Then, having uttered "Bhairavyai," one should say "dhīmahi";
then, having uttered the word "devī," one should pronounce "pracodayāt. (6.845)
The Gāyatrī known as Traipurā should extract the Vāgbhava syllable first;
[this is stated] in another tantra regarding Bhuvaneśvarī:
"Having uttered the Māyā-bīja, [one says] 'vidmahe' for Bhuvaneśvarī. (6-846)
Having first uttered the word "Ādyāyai," immediately thereafter one should say "dhīmahi";
having then pronounced the word "tanno devī," the word "pracodayāt" should be given next.
Now, within that [section] regarding Chinnamastā:
"We know Vairocanī; we meditate upon Chinnamastā;
may that Goddess impel us"—having spoken these words, they should be joined with the word *pada*. (6.848)

Now, for Dhūmāvatī: Having uttered the seed-syllable "dhūm," one should recite "Dhūmāvatī" [as the first part], and from the word "devī" [one should take] the word "dhīmahi" [as the second part]. (6.849)
The Gāyatrī of Dhūmādevī is: "Tanno Ghore Pracodayāt. Now, for Mātaṅgī:
"Oṃ, we know her who is dear to Śuka; we meditate upon the glorious Kāmeśvarī; may that Śyāmā inspire us."
Now, regarding Vagalāmukhī:
having pronounced the stable *māyā* (the syllable Hrīṃ), [one adds] the word "Vagalā" and then "Mukhī. (6.850)
One should utter the word *vidmahe* followed by the word *duṣṭapadataḥ*, then the word *stambhanī*;
at the end of the word *dhīmahī*, one should say *tanno devī pracodayāt*. (6-851)
Now, the Lakṣmī-gāyatrī:
Having uttered the word "Mahālakṣmī," one should then say "vidmahe"; having spoken the word "mahāśriyai," one should utter the word "dhīmahī. (6-852)
From that [word] "tat," one should give the word "śrī"; from that, "pada"; and then "pracodayāt.
This is the Gaurī-gāyatrī (from the Merutantra):
*oṃ subhagāyai vidmahe kāmamālinyai dhīmahi tanno gaurī pracodayāt*.
Now, I shall explain in sequence the Gāyatrī of Guhyakālī (from the Mahākālasaṃhitā), for the purpose of reciting those respective mantras. (6-853)
That [verse] should be known as having three feet; it is called *trika* and also *tripadikā*.
At the beginning, there are two words ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, while the remainder consists of nouns in their nominal case endings (*suvantaka*). (6.854)
I shall state some further particulars regarding the three sets of three words:
at the very beginning one should indeed say "vidmahe," and likewise in the middle, "dhīmahi. (6.855)
At the end of the word *suvantīya*, one should insert a single word;
before that, [the word] *tataḥ*—thus has the extraction (*uddhāra*) been declared by me. (6.856)
Likewise: from *rāva* comes *kāpālinī-siddhi*, and immediately after that *karālī*;
at the end is *guhyā* for the sixteen-syllable mantra of Bhāratī, ending with *namaḥ*. (6.857)
After Karālinī, from the seed-syllables of the bride (Vadhū) and the garland of skulls (Muṇḍamālinī), the Goddess [arises]; at the very end of all, this Gāyatrī is indeed Cyāvanī.
Phetkāriṇī and Ugracaṇḍā, and after that Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrā;
finally, Caṇḍī, who is worshipped by Hārīta—this [deity] indeed has three feet.
Likewise: first is Aṭṭāṭṭahāsinī, then Ghoradaṃṣṭrā, and finally Ghorā; she who is worshipped by Rāmacandra is remembered as Tripadā. (6.860)
p. 508) Now, the *kāmakalāgāyatrī* is found in that very same [source]:
*oṃ anaṅgākulāyai vidmahe madanāturāyai dhīmahi tannaḥ kāmakalākālī pracodayāt*.
The *durgāgāyatrī* is in another tantra:
Oṃ, may we know Kātyāyanī; may we meditate upon the maiden princess; may Durgā inspire us.
Now, the Kāma-gāyatrī (from the Merutantra): Oṃ, may we know Kāmadeva; may we meditate upon the one with flower-arrows; may Anaṅga inspire us.
Now, the Garuḍa-Gāyatrī is found in that very same place:
I shall declare the Gāyatrī that removes the fear of serpents and grants all desires:
*Oṃ, may we know Suparṇa; may we meditate upon the King of Birds; may that Garuḍa inspire us.*
Now, the Hanumat-gāyatrī according to another Tantra:
*Haṃ / hanumate didmahe, āñjaneyāya dhīmahi, tanno vīraḥ pracodayāt* (from the Merutantra).
The root mantra one hundred and eight times. || 6-861 ||
Having recited [the mantra] and offered it to the deity, and having praised and bowed to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā),
one should place the deity from the solar disc into one's own heart.
Then one should prostrate to the Guru; this is the Tantric Sandhyā.
It should be performed in this manner at the three times of day, for there is no fruit from the omission of the Sandhyā.
If there is an omission due to fate, then one should recite the root mantra a hundred times;
having performed that as an atonement, one should perform the rite as it has come down in the tradition.
(Also in the Śaiva Āgama:

"The omission of the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*) must not be performed by one who has received initiation through this very [tradition]. One who is initiated but devoid of the twilight prayers shall not obtain the fruit of initiation. (6.865)
Alternatively, due to incapacity, the mantra-practitioner may perform the abbreviated twilight ritual;
at evening, morning, and midday, having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, he should recite the mantra. (Gautamīya-tantra 6.866)
"Kṛṣṇa" is an elliptical expression; the meaning is "having meditated upon one's own chosen deity. If the twilight prayer (*saṃdhyā*) has been omitted, one should recite the *gāyatrī* ten times.
Now, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) [as described in the Meru-tantra]:
Having performed the Vedic libation, one should then perform the Tantric one.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root mantra;
then, in front of the triad beginning with the seer (ṛṣi), [one should seal] with the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā).

Having consecrated the water with the recitation [of the mantra] and made it nectar-like, one should meditate there upon the God together with His wheel (cakra), along with His limbs (aṅga) and His retinue (āvaraṇa), and then utter the root mantra.
Having said, "I satiate such-and-such a person," he should perform one hundred and eight,
or half of that, or twenty-eight oblations into the lotus of his mouth.
One should satisfy the Deity with the waters of those sacred fords, perceiving them as nectar;
likewise, one should satisfy the deities of the surrounding retinue one by one.
Having satisfied the deity within one's own heart, one should dismiss the sacred water (*tīrtha*) into the sun.
(From the *Nandikeśvarasaṃhitā*):
"As long as the offering (*argha*) is not given as a presentation to the Sun... (6.872).
One should not worship Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara until one has recollected the god Bhairava, the Lord of Umā known as Mārtaṇḍa, O Sovereign of the Gods. (From the *Māheśvarīya*)
O Goddess, [one should worship] with the root mantra or with the mantra of the Sun;
having extracted the *māyābīja*, one should then utter "so 'ham" in reverse order.
The wise one should offer three arghas with the mantra "mārttaṇḍabhairavaṃ ṅentaṃ prakāśaśaktisaṃyutam eṣa te'rgho'gnijāye. (6.875)
Having gone to my house of worship, as prescribed for the offering of water to the Sun,

and having bowed to the Guru, the lords of the directions, and the birds, I shall go holding a vessel filled with water in my hand, observing silence while remembering my chosen deity in my heart. (6-876)
One should go to a secluded, uninhabited place that is pleasing and free from defects;
one should not look around in other directions until one has indeed reached the dwelling. (6.877)
Having circumambulated the sacrificial enclosure and having washed his feet and hands,
he performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and stood at a distance of one staff’s length from the house of worship.
And standing at the doorway of his house, having mentally bowed to his guru,
he should salute his own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) as well as the guardians of the quarters with his mind.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated, whether on that day or on another day,
one should recite these two mantras for the purpose of removing that sin.
O Deva, this ordinary mind of mine is overcome by evil;
extract that evil from my mind, phaṭ phaṭ! And homage to you! (6-881)
The sun, the moon, Yama, time, and the five great elements—these nine are the witnesses here of one's auspicious and inauspicious actions. (6.882)
Uttering "huḥ phaṭ," one should gaze at both sides with a wrathful look;
when this has been done first for the rite of destroying evil.
Whatever sin may be most formidable, it remains far away;
yet when the occasion for worship has passed, that very sin returns once more to itself.
Whatever slight sin there may be, it goes to destruction;
for one who has abandoned sin through worship, their desired wish shall be fulfilled in an instant.
Then, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with care, he should offer the arghya to the Lord of Day; the procedure for that is described here. (6.886)
Having prepared a mandala on ground smeared with cow dung,
one should then sit upon one's own seat using vermilion.
Facing the east, the knower of mantras, intent on devotion, should bow to his chosen deity after performing three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the Sūrya mantra.
"Hrāḥ hrīḥ saḥ" is said to be the three-syllable mantra of the Sun;
having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Indra and the other deities, one should meditate on the Sun with undistracted mind. (6.889)

Holding two lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons with his lotus-like hands, wearing a ruby crown, possessing a reddish bodily luster, and having three eyes; seated upon a red lotus, he is the unique ocean of all virtues.
I worship Bhānu, the sovereign lord of all the worlds.
One should worship with ritual offerings according to the procedure prescribed in that *kalpa*,
having first drawn a square mandala with water in front [of oneself].
Having placed there a copper vessel with its base intact, filled with water, along with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, darbha grass, dūrvā grass, and mustard seeds; || 6.892 ||
One should also arrange sesame seeds, red flowers, and barley;
while touching that vessel, one should recite the Sūrya mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having consecrated that vessel and risen from his two hands,
the wise practitioner should offer the *argha* with the Sūrya-mantra, extending it from the hands up to the crown of the head.

One should utter *hrāḥ*, *hrīḥ*, *saḥ*, along with the words for the planets (*graha*), zodiac signs (*rāśi*), and lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); and then [the words] "yoga," "karaṇa," "parivṛtta," and "āsana. (6-895)
"O Śrīsūryā, established [here], this is your arghya; svāhā"—this is recorded as the mantra.
This thirty-four-syllable mantra is for the offering of arghya to Sūrya. (6.896)
Then, with one-pointed mind, the best of teachers should recite all the mantras according to his ability;
he should meditate on the sun submerged in that offering water. (6.897)
Having offered praise and prostrated, one should dismiss the Sun from within the maṇḍala;
then, having risen, one should duly commence the worship of the gateway.
The procedure for the worship of the doors has been stated in the *Dīkṣātaraṅga*.
Now follows the procedure for daily worship (*nityapūjāvidhi*) [as described] in the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*.
Now I shall describe the daily worship (nityapūjā) briefly, as it has been taught:
having arrived at the place of worship, one should perform the triple sipping of water (ācamana).

Having sat upon his seat, the practitioner should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with devotion. The resolve is of this form: "For the sake of pleasing such-and-such deity, I shall perform its daily worship."
Likewise,
one should offer the arghya water to the Sun, the witness of all rites.
Having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇapati, one should prostrate to one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā);
then, having first performed the three claps of the hands (tālatraya), one should bind the ten directions.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other preliminary rites, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*);
and likewise, one should perform the deposition of the *mātṛkā* (*mātṛkānyāsa*) as well as the deposition of the root mantra (*mūlanyāsa*).
Having meditated upon the deity within his heart,
the best of those who know mantras should worship himself in the form of the deity with mental offerings.

One who knows the ritual procedure should worship with external offerings, excluding the food offering (naivedya); then, having displayed the mudrās prescribed in the ritual manual, [he should proceed].
Having arranged the *argha* and other offerings, one should purify the ritual substances;
then, having meditated upon the deity as described, one should invoke her with the root mantra.
(From the Merutantra:
One should then perform the installation (*saṃsthāpana*), the invocation (*sannidhāna*), and the confinement (*sannirodha*);
furthermore, the facing (*saṃmukhīkaraṇa*) and the ritual of making [the deity] whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*). (6.906)
Then the veiling (avaguṇṭhana) should be performed, followed by the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa);
one should then perform the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa) in due order with their respective mudrās.
Having displayed the mudrās for summoning and so forth, one should establish the vital breaths; and one should respectfully arrange the ritual offerings as far as possible. (Kriyāsaṃgraha 6.908)
Having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers using the root mantra,
the practitioner of mantras should duly worship the deities of the enclosures as they have been described.
Then one should worship the deity together with their limbs (aṅgas), vehicles (vāhanas), ornaments (alaṅkaraṇas), and seals (mudrās), along with their weapons (āyudhas) and retinue (parivāra).
Then the wise practitioner of mantra should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
he should then devotedly offer that recitation to the deity.
Having praised [the deity] with various hymns, one should prostrate on the ground with the eight limbs.
Then, having requested boons, one should dissolve the deity into one's own heart.

The floral remains (nirmālya) should be worn upon the head, and one who eats the leavings of the deity should eat the food offering (naivedya) after having given it [to others]; this is remembered as the daily worship (nityārcana).

This has merely shown the sequence of the worship (*pūjā*). Whatever is prescribed here as being to be performed should all be consulted in the chapter on initiation (*dīkṣātaraṅga*). Now follows the procedure for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*);
it is stated thus in the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
A mantra is not perfected without being recited; it does not bestow fruit without being offered in sacrifice;
and it does not grant desires without being worshipped; therefore, one should practice this triad.
Through worship one obtains worship; there is no doubt that accomplishment is attained.
Through the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one gains prosperity and finds all accomplishments. (6.915)
(In the Jñānārṇava:
O Supreme Goddess, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the rite of the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
As for the resolve:
"I shall offer this many oblations for the pleasure of such-and-such a deity"—this is the form [of the declaration].
(In the *Nīlatantra*):
"I shall proclaim the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), by which one attains all goals. (6-916)
Having properly performed the ritual service (saparyā), one should offer the oblation (bali) as before;
thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform the recitation (japa) and the libation (tarpaṇa).
A Brahmin should perform the Vaiśvādika offering;
having duly taken up the fire, he should likewise offer salutation to the flesh-eating spirits (kravyādas).
Having recited the root mantra, one should spread the fire upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even on the bare ground, by means of the three Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered oblations three times with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, one then performs the six-limb (*ṣaḍaṅga*) homa;
thereafter, having invoked the Goddess with the root mantra, one offers sixteen oblations.
Having offered oblations, having praised, and having paid homage, one should dismiss [the fire] into the lunar disc.
(In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"But when the fire has been thus withdrawn, the knower of mantras, having invoked the deity... (6.921).
Having performed worship with the root mantra, one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter,
sacrificial food, sesame seeds, or auspicious milk-rice.
One should offer a single oblation for each of the deities of the limbs and the enclosures using rice mixed with sesame seeds, or with flowers alone.
Having dismissed the deity and the fire, one should then proceed to the place of worship.
