This *homa* should be performed either after the offering of the food oblation (*naivedya*) or after the completion of the worship.
As it is stated in the *Māheśvarīya*:
Having offered the food oblation, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
"Or, when the worship is completed, one should perform the fire-oblation according to the rules;
this is remembered as the 'mouth of the fire' for the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites"—
thus it is stated in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*.
As before, the knower of mantras, having invoked the deity into the consecrated fire, [should proceed].

Because it is stated thus in the *Merutantra*, the authors of the *Śrīvidyāpaddhati* maintain that the consecration of the fire (*vahnisaṃskāra*) must indeed be performed here. Others, however, hold that there is no consecration of the fire specifically for the daily homa (*nityahoma*), on the basis of the prohibition in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "The rites such as the establishment of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) do not exist in the daily homa. Some say that since both an injunction and a prohibition are heard, there is an optional choice (*vaikalpika*), just as there is an option between sixteen or twenty-five oblations (*āhuti*).

However, according to the Sudhārṇava, they say that here the consecration of the fire should be performed exactly as prescribed in the Nīlatantra, and no more, because of the prohibition of anything additional due to specific scriptural statements.
Thus ends the rule for the daily homa. [End of] Kumbhasambhava.
Then, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) with devotion.

(From the Merutantra: One should commence the *puraścaryā* on an auspicious day as prescribed for initiation, having first prostrated before the gurus and brahmins and fully worshipped Gaṇeśa. (6.927)
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of an auspicious day), one with *kuśa* grass in hand should say:
"The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, the two twilights, the spirits, Day, and Night."
May Pavana, the Lord of the Quarters, Bhūmi, Ākāśa, the sky-dwellers, and the immortals,
having received the command of Brahmā, grant their presence here.
Having spoken thus and having placed copper, kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains [on the ground],
he, facing north, should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the year and other durations.
One should utter twenty-three [syllables] ending with the word *kāmanā*:
the year, the solstice, the month, the fortnight, and the fivefold limb (*pañcāṅga*). (6.931)

One should declare the positions of the nine planets, the portion of the day, and the momentary [astrological] factors; according to the differences of one's own location, one should state these accordingly, together with the specific desires [of the querent].
In such-and-such an island, in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a country, and in such-and-such a field; [therein] one should utter the lineage and the *pravara*. (6.933)

After his own name and the name of his lineage, a twice-born man [should append] "Śarman" or "Varman"; [others may use] "Gupta" or "Dāsa. Then [he declares]: "I, the seeker of the accomplishment of such-and-such a mantra... (6.934)
"Beginning today, I shall perform this *puraścaryā* consisting of a recitation of this many times within these days, provided there is no obstacle. (6.935)
One should form the resolve "I shall do it" by means of the mind alone;
one should express the desire with speech and accomplish it through action. (6.936)
(In the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*):
"The *praṇava*, *tat sat*, and *adya*, as well as the month, fortnight, and lunar day; then, having uttered 'I, of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so,' followed by the root [mantra]... (6.937).
One who desires success in this mantra should then perform a recitation (japa) of such a number;
from that, an oblation (havana) consisting of a tenth part [of the japa], and then a libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of a tenth part of the oblation.
One-tenth of that is the rite of sprinkling (mārjana), and one-tenth of that is the feeding of Brahmins;
indeed, I shall perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in this manner, facing the northeast.
Having performed worship, one should then perform the recitation (*japa*) for two *praharas* (eight hours), according to the *Nāradapañcarātra*.
(From the *Tantradīpa*)
Having duly constructed a most beautiful pavilion, the wise one—

Having placed the water-pot upon that [pedestal], one should worship it with the waters of sacred fords (tīrtha), after having cast nine gems and again the eight fragrances (gandhāṣṭaka) therein. (6.941)
Having invoked the deity there along with the surrounding retinues, the practitioner of mantra should worship them;
he should recite the mantra before the water-pot until the prescribed number is completed.
Then, when [the time] is complete, the divine Guru, having arrived, shall according to the prescribed rite sprinkle the head of the disciple with the waters from the jar.
Then the disciple should diligently satisfy the Guru with wealth and other offerings;

having established the water-pot according to the sequence prescribed for initiation and having invoked the deity therein, he should worship it according to his capacity and perform recitation (*japa*). This is the meaning.
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*)
These and many other such means for worship are also [to be employed]. || 6.944 ||
There are three types [of means]: superior, middling, and inferior.
One who is healthy and capable should employ only the superior means. (6.945)
One of middling capacity should practice with middling means, and one of inferior capacity with inferior means;
however, if one has fallen into adversity, even if capable, one should practice with inferior means alone.
Through the specific performance of worship, according to place and time, according to one's capacity, according to what is proper, and in a manner not censured by the world. (6.947)
If the practitioner is unable to perform the worship in detail,
he may worship his chosen deity with external offerings such as incense, vajras, and so forth.
Alternatively, having meditated upon the deity and the mantra, one should perform the worship correctly;
or else, one may perform mental worship, or even self-worship.
Alternatively, the wise practitioner should perform only the external worship.
Likewise, due to an inability to perform each preceding rite, one should perform each subsequent one. (6.950)

If one should act otherwise than this, it is taught that there will be an undesirable result, especially regarding images fashioned from the elements or from mechanical devices. (Missing page no. 518 and 519; p. 520) 6-951.
In the hymn of seven verses beginning with "Agniḥ saptim vājam," the Sapti is mentioned;
the sage is said to be [Vasiṣṭha], the metre is Triṣṭubh, and Agni is proclaimed as the deity. || 6.952 ||
One should recite this hymn one hundred times, omitting the word "Agni," and then perform the consecration with pure water using the complete hymns.
One should consecrate [the image] one hundred times; this is known as the "crossing over the fire" (agnyuttāraṇa).
Likewise: first with honey, clarified butter, and milk, and thereafter with coconut water. (6.954)
Then, having consecrated [the wheel] with water boiled with medicinal herbs containing the two syllables,
and having invoked and worshipped it, one should install and worship the wheel at that auspicious moment (lagna).
One should worship the Goddess for three nights, at the three junctions of the day, according to the prescribed ritual, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and libations.
(In the Vāmakeśvaratantra) Bhairavī said:
"O Mahādeva, by your grace I have heard the classification of the cakras."
Now I wish to hear the determination of the ritual for consecration.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O illustrious Goddess, O Kaulinī who creates the universe,
to the determination of all the castes as part of the ritual for the installation of the Yantra.
Having bathed, the mantra-practitioner should form a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and perform the worship of the Guru;
thereafter, he should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), consecrated with the Śiva-mantra.
There, the mantra-practitioner should cast the wheel, thoroughly permeated by the *praṇava*;
then, having lifted that wheel, he should place it upon a golden pedestal.
O Goddess, one hundred and eight [times] for the sake of attaining the state of the deity. (6.961)
Then, having performed the purification of oneself, one should worship the deity with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Having invoked the Great Goddess there, one should perform the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa).
There, one should worship the Goddess with the sixteen services, as well as with the great mudrās and so forth, along with fruits, food offerings, and betel.
One should offer silk thread and the like, along with garments, ornaments, and so forth;
and a mirror, a fly-whisk, and a bell as appropriate, O Maheśvarī. (6.964)
One who is devoted to his own welfare should bestow all of this with diligence;
thereafter, he should recite [the mantra] one thousand times for the sake of accomplishing every desired goal.
Having offered garlands and other gifts, one should prostrate before the Cakrarāja;
having performed one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the remaining clarified butter (saṃpātājya) [into the fire].

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of grain and sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter while reciting the root mantra, the practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual upon the limbs of the yantra.
If one is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should perform twice the number of recitations (japa).
Having brought a single cow adorned with golden horns and other ornaments, [one should give it as a gift].
One should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor; thereafter follows the dismissal of the Goddess.
The mantra of Śiva is the grace.
(From the Siddhāntasaṃgraha)
Having purified it with the five products of the cow and bathed it separately with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), || 6-969 ||
One should bathe [the deity] with eight holy jars while reciting the root mantra;
thereafter, one should consecrate the yantra with the Gāyatrī that is about to be described.
One should likewise recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times over the thread.

Then, the knower of mantras, having invoked the deity and established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) within the Yantrarāja, should recite: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us. (p. 522) Thereafter, having invoked the deity and stabilized the *prāṇas*, the knower of mantras [proceeds].
One should worship the chosen deity with the sixteen types of offerings.
And one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter into the consecrated fire; therein, one should pour in the residual ghee from the offerings.
Afterwards, the practitioner should feed the Brahmins with the thought that they are the deity;
when the yantra has been thus consecrated, the God becomes present within it.

(Merutantra) Having invoked [the deity] and worshipped it, one should establish the wheel at that very moment and worship it with perfumes, flowers, fresh incense, lamps, food offerings, and mirrors. (6.974)
One should worship the Goddess for three nights, at the three junctions of the day as well as at night.
Regarding the specific distinction between the Vāmācāra and Kulācāra, he says: "Those who follow the Vāmācāra should perform the worship endowed with the five 'M' syllables. (6.975)
During the night, the Kaulikas perform the worship of Śakti and the sacrifice to the female messenger (dūtī).
Having done this for three days, they should thereafter engage in the daily ritual sequence.
Thus, in the consecration of a goddess, this is the sequence that brings about her presence;
this is the ritual procedure for women, Śūdras, Vāmiṇas, and Kaulikas.
Likewise:
Those who follow the path of the Veda and animal sacrifice do not commit great sins;
Agni is the most pure in his vows, the Brahmin is pure, and that which is uttered by the Brahmin is pure. (6.978)

And because they are not tainted by those minor sins—which are destroyed by the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyābandana*)—they are therefore remembered as *paśus* (the bound). || 6.979 ||
If a yantra worshipped by a woman on the left-hand path comes within their field of vision,
it causes agitation in those deities, and the practitioner becomes distracted.
He is like the sun to the owls, burning away the vision of the wicked. (6.981)
Just as everything established by Dakṣa is perceived by men at the rising of the sun,
so too is the machine regarded by those of meritorious soul.
The presence of all the deities must necessarily be brought about through mantra;
for mantra is said to be like a seed, while the image and so forth are like the body. (6.983)
Even when the collection of conditions is perfected, there is indeed no fruit without the mantra. Likewise:
"Whether it be ten finger-breadths in measure, or even measured by fifteen finger-breadths... (6.984)
Having worshipped the image of Viṣṇu, householders should worship the Śiva-liṅga equipped with the five threads in their homes.
That [liṅga] bestows enjoyment, liberation, wealth, and health upon householders;
its length is equal to the width of the top of the liṅga. (6.986)
The fivefold equality of the five— the liṅga, the liṅga-shālākī, the water-channel (jalaharī), the pedestal of the liṅga (liṅgapīṭha), and [the base]— is the "five-thread" (pañcasūtrikā).
In that very same [text]:

"He who performs the worship of a yantra separately on a single pedestal without [performing] the worship [of the other deities]—if he worships the yantra with such a [single] tantra, he shall always incur a curse. (6.988)
If one worships another deity after having invoked a different deity,
or performs worship with a different yantra, that deity will bring about a curse.
If the worship of many forms takes place upon a single pedestal, then according to the tantra,
there should be separate sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth for each.

The Tantra is without purpose [in these cases]: when it is broken, cracked, burnt, fallen, devoid of human [care], mutilated, touched by unworthy animals, fallen [from its place], or located on defiled grounds. (6.991)
Furthermore, when [a site] has been worshipped with another mantra, or defiled by the touch of a fallen person—in these ten cases, the gods do not grant their presence. (6.992)
In that very same [text]:
"O Śāmbhavī, for those who do not know the pervasion of the yantra belonging to the Lord whose form is mantra, all worship and other rites performed become fruitless. (6.993)
The meaning of the term *yantra* is stated in that very same place:
"Because it restrains all defects arising from faults such as desire and anger, they call this a *yantra*; when worshipped, the deity is pleased therein. (6.994)
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):

One should draw the excellent yantra with the substances prescribed for each respective ritual manual upon a pedestal made of gold, silver, or copper, or else on birch bark or directly on the ground. (6.995)
If worship is performed without a yantra, the deity does not become pleased.
Regarding the materials for drawing the yantra, it is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"In the path of the Dakṣas, the worship-yantra is [drawn] with those respective eight fragrances. (6–996)
Or one should draw it with saffron, camphor, and yellow pigment;
or if the yantra is to be drawn on the left-hand path, one should draw it with the first flower.
By worshipping there for six months, one shall swiftly attain accomplishment;
in its absence, however, the blood of a buffalo is recommended.
In the absence of that, however, one should take the flower of Aparājitā;
having placed red sandalwood rubbed [with it] upon its upper part.
(In the *Svatantratantra*):
In gold, silver, copper, stone, or the eight metals; the self-arisen flower (*svayambhūkusuma*), the *rocanā* produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, and *agaru*. (6-1000)
By means of this application of fragrances, one should draw the *yonicakra*.
This is the supreme secret of the heroes.
(From the Rudrayāmala:
Thereafter, the yogi should prepare the yantra with saffron and vermilion.
In one made of gold, silver, copper, crystal, or likewise of wood.
The Goddess should be worshipped by the best of men according to the prescribed rite.
(In the *Sārasaṃgraha*):
"Twelve years [are required] for copper, but for crystal and other materials, it may be done at all times. (6.1003)
Among them, the crystal one shall bestow all accomplishments;
gold [bestows them] for as long as one lives, and silver for twenty-two years, O Dear One.
On copper, the duration is twelve years; on birch bark, it is half of that.
And this refers specifically to a yantra consisting of stable lines.
(Also in the Rudrayāmala:)
It is said that [the merit] is a hundred-thousandfold when offered in copper, and it becomes ten-millionfold when offered in silver.
On a golden [yantra] it yields infinite fruit; what more need I tell you regarding those made of jewels and the like, O beloved, or on a yantra fashioned from coral or ruby?
Furthermore, one certainly obtains wealth, sons, a wife, and fame from [images made of] sapphire, cat's-eye, crystal, and likewise emerald. (6.1007)
In the *Gaurīyāmala*, it is said:

"The wheel indeed possesses fourfold varieties, and there are also the *prastāras* [arrangements]; the *bhū-prastāra*, the *kūrma-prastāra*, the *padma-prastāra*, and likewise the *meru-prastāra*. (6.1008)
The arrangement of the earth with horizontal lines has been described by me;
the arrangement of the tortoise-lotus with vertical lines has also been described by me.
(In the *Sautrāmaṇītantra*):
Fortune shall exist where the lines are straight; where the lines are curved, there is poverty.
(*Kulārṇava*, p. 526).
And especially from the original form of the image during worship. || 6.1010 ||
Through the practitioner's faith, the presence of the deity occurs.
(In the *Yāmala*) Having thus fashioned the yantra, one should worship the Goddess therein. (6-1011)
The term "the Goddess" is an elliptical expression; it means "one's own chosen deity.
The method of worship has already been explained in the section on initiation (*dīkṣātaraṅga*) in the *Kulārṇava*.
If the mind is in one place, Śiva in another, and Śakti in another, or if the vital breath (māruta) is elsewhere,
O lady of excellent hips, one does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*, will find no accomplishment even through a hundred million recitations. (6.1013)
And those mantras whose seed-syllables are lost, O Dear One, will not yield fruit;
however, mantras endowed with consciousness are traditionally held to grant all accomplishments.
Mantras devoid of consciousness are said not to bestow fruits at all;
likewise, mantras affected by the two types of impurity (sūtaka) do not bestow fruits.
The meaning of the mantra should be understood from the mouth of the Guru.

The consciousness of the mantra (*mantracaitanya*) will be explained [later]. The *yonimudrā* has been described in the second wave (*taraṅga*). The method for knowing birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and so forth is also in that very place:
"First there is the birth-impurity, and at the end, the death-impurity."
A mantra that is joined with two *sūtaka* [impurities] does not attain success.
The meditation on the Guru-Kuṇḍalinī is proclaimed as the marriage;
the twice-returning [of breath] constitutes the bath, and the union occurs with the Sandhyā.
The offering of *argha* constitutes the embryo; the *gāyatrī* mantra represents the eighth month.
Therein lies the conceptualization of the limbs, beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and ending with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). (6-1018)
The embodied soul becomes [one with] Mātṛkā; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the purification.
O Maheśānī, meditation and recitation are said to be the birth of the child. (6.1019)
O Goddess, that which arises from the utterance of a mantra is called *jātasūtaka*.
O Maheśvarī, [this is taught] for the purpose of pacifying the defect of *jātasūtaka*.
O Śivā, one should recite ten, twenty, or fifty [times], according to one's capacity;
this has been prescribed at the outset—now listen with respect to death.
The knowledge of the limbs (aṅgajñāna) and identity (tādātmya) are taught immediately after that;
O Great Goddess, dismissal (visarjana) is said to be the birth and death of the deceased (mṛtasūtaka).
For the sake of pacifying the impurity caused by death or birth, one should recite [the mantra] ten or twenty times;
by that, its cessation certainly occurs, there is no doubt. (6.1023)

Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, having bestowed the seed-syllable of Brahma upon the mind, one should recite the mantra seven times at the beginning and the end for the sake of liberation from the two types of birth-taint (sūtaka).
The seed-syllable of Brahman is the *praṇava*.
Now, regarding the times of sleep and awakening for mantras (*Pañcarātra*): "At the time of sleep, however, the recitation of a mantra does not bestow fruit."
The time of sleep is the flow through the left [nāḍī], and waking is the flow through the right.
One should know that the time of awakening for both the fire-mantra of Manu and the lunar mantra is the reverse of this [sleeping] state for both of them.
Mantras are to be known as belonging to Agni (the fiery), while Vidyās are proclaimed to belong to Soma (the lunar).
The distinction between Mantra and Vidyā has been stated in the first chapter.
Now, the knowledge of the crest of Mantra is [found] in another Tantra.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme reality, the most excellent among all forms of knowledge.
By the mere knowledge of which the Vidyā quickly becomes propitious:
that power which resides in the root-pit (mūlakuṇḍa) and has the form of a serpent.
This wind of the whirlpool of that delusion is designated as *prāṇa*.
Having abandoned it, she suddenly rose up, warbling with an unmanifest sweetness. (6.1029)
Going out through the aperture of Brahmā and entering the body again,
one should effect the dissolution of the mind there by means of this very process of going and returning.
By that, the crest-mantra (mantraśikhā) is born, which illuminates all mantras;
for just as nothing at all appears in a house filled with darkness, [so it is without this illumination]. (6.1031)
Likewise, mantras devoid of the *śikhā* never attain success;
O Supreme Goddess, the instruction regarding the *śikhā* is concealed everywhere.
Without which there would be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of years;
therefore, one should diligently perform the mental cultivation of the crest-lock (śikhā) of the mantra.
Now, regarding the consciousness of mantra, it is said in that very same place:
"The deity exists in the form of the mantra; the guru exists in the form of the deity;
the self exists in the form of the guru; and the mantra exists in the form of the self. (6.1034)
Thus, O Goddess, I have declared to you the supreme consciousness of mantra;
by the mere knowledge of which, the highest non-dual wisdom is attained. (6.1035)
Now, from the *Yāmala*,
the venerable Goddess said:
"Now, indeed, tell me the origin of the *kullukā*."
What is the nature of the *kullukā*, O Lord? And what is the nature of the bridge (*setu*), O God?
Or what is the Great Bridge (Mahāsetu), and what, moreover, is Nirvāṇa? Or whatever else has been told to me, tell me, O Lord, what that is like. (6.1037)
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess, even this secret is being told to you; listen now.
Without it, O Maheśānī, recitation and other such practices are indeed fruitless. (6.1038)
Kullukā, as well as Setu and likewise Mahāsetu; Nirvāṇa, Kuṇḍalī, Ṣaṣṭi, and Sarvotpatti—listen, O beloved. (6.1039)
Because she is worthy of worship by the family of the Vidyās, she is therefore celebrated as Kullukā;
for, O Śivā, she devours the defects associated with the Vidyās.
Therefore, O Goddess, this [mantra] named Kullukā is hidden in all tantras; by means of it, one reaches the further shore in the ocean of the accomplishment of vidyā. (6.1041)
Therefore, O Maheshani, it is proclaimed as the path of Vidyā;
O Maheshvari, the manifestation of the attainment of Mahāvidyā is the Great Setu.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, he is the great bridge that reveals consciousness within the ocean of great vidyā,
and he assumes the very form of great vidyā itself.
The liberation of the deity is that which is proclaimed as consciousness;
O auspicious lady, liberation is said to be [attained] through the letters of the Vidyā, Speech, and Mātṛkā.
O Supreme Goddess, Nirvāṇa is said to have four quarters;
and O Great Goddess, Nirvāṇa is considered to be of the nature of the Great Brahman.
The fourth has been described, O blessed lady, as it is called Vidyācaraṇa; now listen duly to the fifth, the goddess Kuṇḍalī.
[She is] thinner than a lotus fiber, extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *āvilānta*, having the nature of all the gods, and illuminating all phonemes. (6-1047)
[To] the goddess Mahākuṇḍalinī, the supreme Samalī Kuṇḍalī,
the Śrīdevī said:
"Tell me, in due order, the ritual procedure for the tenfold Kullukā of the Vidyā."
The venerable Śiva said:
The five-syllabled *kullukā* of Kālikā is now fully described;
and the *kūrca* of Kālī and [the mantra] of Dhūmā end with *phaṭ*, O Supreme Goddess. (6.1049)
The sage is declared to be named Aghora; Virāṭ is proclaimed as the meter;
the deity is Kullukā Kālī; and the seed-syllable is considered to be that called Māyā. (6.105)
The power of desire (kāmaśakti), as well as the tuft (kūrca) and the wedge (kīlaka), are proclaimed [as the seed-syllables].
The ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is taught by means of the desire-mantra (kāma) enriched with the six long vowels.
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, just as in the case of Kālikā;
likewise, the Māyā-vadhū, the *kūrca*, and the Tāriṇī-kullukā are intended [to be used]. (6.1052)
Virūpākṣa is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of Tāriṇīkullukā;
the meter (chanda) is declared to be Uṣṇik, and the deity is Nīlatāriṇī. (6-1053)
The seed-syllable of the *kūrca*, likewise *māyā*, *śakti*, and *vadhū* are the *kīlaka*;
with *māyā*, the six limbs [are formed]; all this is Nīlasarasvatī.
(From the *Triśaktiratna*):
"He who recites the mantra of Tāriṇī without having first recited the Kullukā-mantra and without remembering Hari, the Lord of Śrī, shall dissolve into hell. (6-1055)
Having recited the Kullukā-mantra one hundred and eight times, the wise practitioner should thereafter recite the Tāriṇī-mantra; otherwise, he shall not attain success.
Following the recitation of the *Kulasarvasva-nāmasahasra* hymn, there is the statement:
"One should neither utter the name of Hari nor touch a leaf of Tulasī.
However, this injunction should be understood as referring specifically to the *vīra* (heroic) practitioner.
However, the utterance of Hari’s names acquired through the recitation of hymns is not prohibited even during the Virakalpa.
Whatever names of the Enemy of Mura exist here, they [are to be used] by occasion. (6.1057)
For it is stated in that very [text]:
"O Maheśānī, the eight-syllable *kullukā* belongs to *Chinnā*," as found in the *Yāmala*.
And at the end of Vajravairocanīye, one should recite the armor mantra (varma). || 6-1058 ||
Atikāla is declared the Sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be the Metre (chandas);
Ha is the Seed-syllable (bīja), Hu is likewise the Power (śakti), and Rocanī is considered the Pin (kīlaka). (6-1059)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) joined with the syllable *Śiva* and the six long vowels;
all [rites] such as meditation and worship should be performed according to the *Chinnamastā* tradition. (6.106)
O Goddess, the twelve-syllable mantra of Sundarī is proclaimed as the *kullukā*:
the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, the Lajjā, and the word "Tripurā. (6.106)
Having uttered the word "Bhagavatī," one should speak two "ṭha" syllables at its end.
For the Kullukā of Sundarī, the seer is Ānandabhairava.
The Gāyatrī meter is prescribed; the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be Vāgbhava.
O Maheśānī, Lajjā is the power (śakti), and the Kāmabīja is the pin (kīlaka).
The deity is Tripureśī; the six limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the triad and the pair.
One should perform all rites, such as meditation and worship, in the same manner as for Sundarī. (6.1064)
The first seed-syllable of Saṃpatpradā is [placed] in the fire of Śrībhairavī;
Vikarāla is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is proclaimed as the meter (chandas). || 6-1065 ||
The deity is celebrated by the name Bhairavī as Kullukā;
"ha" is the seed-syllable, "sa" is the great power (mahāśakti), and this is considered the peg (kīlaka).
One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllable enriched with the six long vowels;
now listen to the sequence for Mātaṅgī, Vagalā, Lakṣmī, Dhūmā, and Ucchiṣṭā.
And the sage named Bhairava, O Pārvatī, [revealed] as many verses as there were. (6.1068)
And according to the sequence of one's own respective deity, beginning with all the seed-syllables of the deities,
one should perform all activities such as meditation and worship just as one does for one's own tutelary deity.
O Goddess, this Kullukā has been described by me to you in brief.
That base and dull-witted person who recites it without knowing this Kullukā [is lost]. (6.1070)
One quickly meets with death, the loss of accomplishment arises;
the mantras turn away, and the failure of the mantra occurs. (6.1071)
Likewise, all [practices] such as recitation (japa) and so forth are fruitless; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, with every effort, one should recite the Kullukā on the crown of the head.
(Rudrayāmala):
Having meditated upon Kullukā at the crown of the head, one should contemplate Setu in the heart;
one should then uplift Mahāsetu at the Viśuddhi and in the Sahasrāra.
In Maṇipūra, however, is Nirvāṇa, and below it is Mahākuṇḍalinī.
Now, regarding the bridge (according to the *Merutantra*): the Praṇava is proclaimed as the bridge of mantras, just as [the Setubandha] is for the twice-born.
The fourteenth vowel, joined with the moon (the letter *i*) and the anusvāra, [is for others];
or else, as stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"For Brahmins and likewise for Kṣatriyas, the Praṇava is the bridge. (6-1075)
The syllable *phaṭ* is for Vaiśyas, while *māyā* is said to be for Śūdras.
O Goddess of the Gods, he who utters a mantra without first reciting it in his heart [is at fault]. (6.1076)
O Goddess of gods, O Bhuvaneśvarī, he has no authority over any of the mantras, nor over the Great Bridge (Mahāsetu) of Sundarī.
But for others, O fair-faced one, the seed of the bride is the Great Embankment (mahāsetu). (6.1078)
Having first recited the Mahāsetu, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
such a person becomes equal to the Lord of Wealth in riches and comparable to the Lord of Speech in eloquence.
For one who possesses such understanding, he is like Death himself among women and like the God of Love;
for him, every moment is a time for recitation—of this there is no doubt.
Just as water flows downward in an instant when there is no dam,
so too does the mantra of sacrificers flow away in an instant when it is unrestrained. (Merutantra 6.1081)
Therefore, in all mantras, the twice-born and others of the four castes should perform the rite of recitation while maintaining the *setu* on both sides.
Now, regarding Nirvāṇa (from the Rudrayāmala):
Now I shall speak of Nirvāṇa; listen with focused attention, O sinless one!
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then utter the beginning of the Mātṛkā. 6-1083.
Then, O Maheśānī, one should utter the Mūla-mantra, followed by the Vāgbhava-mantra;
then one should utter the entire Mātṛkā, and again the Praṇava.
Thus, O Īśānī, one should recite [the mantra] with the root thus enveloped within the Maṇipūra;
that vulgar person who does not know this [attains] Nirvāṇa.
Even in a hundred million years, success does not arise for him;
therefore, O Maheśvarī, one should practice with every effort that which has been declared. (6.1086)
One should recite the unsurpassed mantra according to the ritual procedure of each respective preceptor;
[one should also consider] the seer, the meter, the deity, the seed-syllable, the power, and the pinning-stake.
O Goddess, one should meditate with effort and then recite the mantra for one's own desired goal and so forth;
if the practitioner of mantra recites the unsurpassed king of mantras in this manner, [the result follows].
Within six months one attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He himself is directly the sovereign lord of the worlds; of this there is no doubt. (6.1089)
He is blessed, he is wise, and he alone knows the reality of the mantra;
he alone, having attained liberation, may dwell upon this earth as he pleases.
By the mere sight of him, enemies flee.
Having done thus, whoever should recite the king of mantras encased within the *praṇava*, their state of nirvāṇa is honored by the world; and likewise, having recited the *kullukas*,
for them the entire world and the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are in the palm of their hand.
Out of affection, these words were spoken in secret concerning [our] successive births throughout many lifetimes.
Now, the mantra for purifying the tongue (from the *Yāmala*):
O Great Goddess, I shall proclaim another supreme method for purifying the tongue, without performing which recitation and worship become fruitless. (6-1093)
O Goddess, he who recites with an impure tongue is a doer of evil;
therefore, one should perform the purification of the tongue with every effort. (6-1094)
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, bearer of the Pināka bow;
O Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, please explain each one separately.
The purification of all vidyās is the auspicious purification of the mouth.
Śrīśiva said:
[One should employ] the Śrī-bīja, the Praṇava, the Lakṣmī-tāra, and likewise the Śrī-praṇava. (6-1096)
One should recite this six-syllable mantra of Sundarī ten times;
now listen, O fair-limbed one, to the supreme purification of the mouth for Bhairavī. (6.1097)
One should first recite this three-syllable mantra ten times. (6-1098)
Listen, O beautiful one, to the supreme purification of Śyāmā’s face:
O Goddess, [recite] her own three seed-syllables, and again the three *praṇavas*.
The three Kāmas, joined with the fire-drop (ra) and the supreme seed-syllable (hrīṃ),
form this nine-syllabled vidyā which effects the purification of the tongue.
Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the unprecedented purification of the mouth of Tārā:
Jīvanī, Bhuvanā, Lajjā, and then Bhuvaneśī, O beloved. (6.1101)
This three-syllabled great vidyā should be known as the showerer of nectar;
O lady of beautiful limbs, hear now the supreme purification of the mouth for Durgā.
Having extracted the twelve vowels and likewise the triad joined with the bindu,
I shall now declare another single [mantra] for the purification of Vagalāmukhī.
O Bhuvaneśānī, praised by the gods, the Vāgbhava is the seed-syllable of speech;
O Goddess, it is the purifier of Mātaṅgī, as is the goad and the Vāgbhava.
This seed-syllable, O Goddess, should be known as the goad consisting of three syllables;
it is the purifier of Lakṣmī, O lotus-faced one, and the seed-syllable of Śrī. (6.1105)
Having extracted the *praṇava* (OM) ending in the dental [na], adorned with the left ear [the letter u],
and having again extracted the *praṇava*, this is to be known as the one considered to consist of three syllables (*tryakṣarī*).
O Maheśānī, for the hair and other such [impurities], the *praṇava* is the purifier; however, for women and Śūdras, purification is performed with the syllable *au*.
By the mere cleansing of the mouth, the tongue becomes nectar-like;
otherwise, the tongue remains perpetually covered with impurities and filth. (6.1108)
The tongue is defiled by eating; the tongue is defiled by false speech;
the tongue is defiled by quarrels—how then can such a tongue recite the mantra? (6.1109)
A common person should never recite that purification mantra without a teacher;
it is mandatory for all followers of Śiva, Śakti, and Viṣṇu alike.
Otherwise, O beautiful lady, if one recites the mantra out of delusion, all of it is in vain, O Goddess, and the accomplishment of the mantra does not arise. (6.111)
If a deity should recite a mantra without having performed the purification of the mouth, he will fall into hell; that shall indeed be so, and not otherwise.
O Goddess, even his downfall [is certain]; how much more so for those who dwell in the mortal world?
(From the *Gautamīya*):
Mantras established in the state of a bound soul (*paśu*) consist merely of the forms of phonemes. (6.1113)
When uttered in their respective sounds, those mantra-syllables attain sovereignty; one should contemplate them as being contained within feces and urine.
In that very Supreme Sky, known as the Supreme Nectar,
he shall reveal the true nature of the Self, even without [the need for] worship, fire-offerings, and so forth.
(Rudrayāmala) "If another person hears one's recitation, that mantra is said to be void;
it is like a serpent abandoned by its seer, meter, and deity. (6.1116)
Now follows the knowledge of the components of mantras.
This has been stated [in the Viśuddheśvara and other texts]:
"Having taken the mantra to the presence of the Guru, one who is devoted to the Guru..."
Having understood, according to reality, the mantra’s ears, mouth, heart, eyes, and vital breaths, || 6.1117 ||
Having diligently understood the *kīlaka*, one should perform the preparatory rites for the mantra;
the *praṇava* is proclaimed as the ear of mantras, and the letter *ra* is proclaimed as their mouth. (6.1118)
The vowels should be known immediately by those who know the mantras as being located in the eyes.
(In the *Bījakośa* of the *Bhūtaḍāmara* and *Yakṣaḍāmara*):
through the knowledge of the ears, mouth, heart, and eyes, liberation from the mantra occurs instantly.
There shall be the accomplishment of all rites; the practitioner himself is directly Śiva and is worthy of worship.

If there is an absence of knowledge regarding the ears and other [senses], then merely by grasping the mantra, there will be poverty, misfortune, falling into hell, and the destruction of one's lineage. (6.1120)

One who is dejected, sharing in extreme suffering, defeated, oppressed by enemies, or grieving—such a practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the cognition of the ears and other senses. (6-1121)

When, through one's own extreme devotion, knowledge arises for the ears and other senses from the Guru, then that mantra-practitioner has accomplished his purpose, is honored by the three worlds, and is irreproachable. (6.1122)
Likewise: Laya, Śrotra, Asṛk, Āsyā, Hṛt, Śūnyā, Senā, Dṛś, and Svarā; however, in the absence of Garjinī, Dhūmra, Bhairavī, and Urabhā, Dṛś is prescribed [in their place]. (6-1123)
The root-syllable is taught as the mouth, and the powers of the vowels as the heart;
[these are to be applied] at the beginning, middle, and end, with each subsequent one taking precedence in the absence of the former.
Likewise: "In the systems of Saura, Gāṇapatya, Daurga, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Bhautika, as well as in the Manu-mantra, the heart and the eye shine forth just as [the sun does]. (6.1125)
This investigation concerns the root-syllable; the root-syllable is said to be the seed.
When the seed is present and endowed with poison, one must apply the investigation to that poison.
Likewise: "By these, the heart, eyes, and mouth of all mantras without exception are to be fully understood; they are concealed in all tantras. (6.1127)
In the seed-syllable, all [faces] have red faces; the root-syllable is the heart, and the vowels are the right and left eyes, Caṇḍī, and Vikalā, bowed in the middle.
In the absence of the seed-syllable (bīja), Manovidyut is the eye and face; Manoharā is the root-syllable and the heart; Daṇḍin is the vital breath (prāṇa), as are the powers of the vowels. (6.1129)
In the [mantras] known as Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha, the seed-syllable (bījākṣara) is located in the eyes, face, vital breath, heart, and ears;
wherever that seed-syllable is, the mantra is there, for everything is indeed that very [seed-syllable].
Where the primary [limb] is seen to be missing along with what precedes and follows it, one should know that to be the eye, and the face is smeared with blood. (6.1131)
With the exception of red, the color of his face is established as the root color;
his eyes are specified as being like lightning, and he is devoid of the fierce (caṇḍi) aspect.
The heart and eyes of this [mantra] are like lightning; it is devoid of heart, mouth, and breath.
A mantra lacking ears causes bodily affliction and creates obstacles. (6.1133)
Likewise: "Having established his form in the heart, with a firm mind and concentrated, he should gaze at the tip of his own nose, not looking around at the directions. (6.1134)
Having withdrawn the mind from the objects of the senses through every means, the practitioner perceives; thus the ear is dissolved, for otherwise one could not hear from that state.

Blood is the letter *ra*; the Void is the letter *ha*; the army is the *visarga*; Garjinī is the letter *i*; Dhūmrabhairavī is the letter *ī*; Poison is the *praṇava* (*oṃ*); Blood is the letter *ra*; Caṇḍī is the *visarga*; Vikalā is the *anusvāra*; Lightning is the letter *a*; Manoharā is *svāhā*; Daṇḍī is the letter *ya*. The seed-syllable of Cintāmaṇi and the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha will be explained further on. Blood-smeared is the letter *ra*.
The relationship of signifier and signified between the deity and the mantra has been stated in another Tantra:
"All mantras are established through the relationship of signifier and signified."
Furthermore, whatever mantra belongs to a deity, that [mantra] is the denoted and the [deity] is the denoter. || 6.1136 ||
Now begins the commencement of the recitation (*japa*). (In the *Merutantra*):
Having bowed to the Guru, Gaṇapati, Durgā, and the Mothers, and having performed their worship...
Having performed this, one should practice three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with one's own root mantra.
Having performed the placement of the ṛṣis and so forth, as well as the placement of the mantra, one should meditate on the deity in the heart, having placed the rosary in the vessel. (6.1138)
(Uttaratantra) At the beginning of recitation and other rites, one should carefully worship the rosary by sprinkling it with water;
having placed it within the mandala, it should be held in the left hand. (6.1139)
The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is prescribed;
having sprinkled it with the water of the *arghya* offering, one should then pray to it—thus it is declared in the *Merutantra*. (6-1140)
Oṃ, O Mālā, O Great Illusion, whose nature is all-pervasive power!
The fourfold aims of human life are entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of my spiritual accomplishments.
Having performed worship, one should then take the garland in the right hand,
first uttering the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati and immediately thereafter [the mantra].
"O Mālā, grant me freedom from obstacles; immediately thereafter, one should take you in the right hand and then meditate upon Śiva in one's mind. (6-1143)

And one should contemplate the Guru upon the crown of the head according to his color and other attributes; one should meditate on the mantra in the middle of the throat as being yellow and golden in hue.
One should contemplate Mahāmāyā in the heart, oneself at the feet of the Guru,
and thereafter the command-wheel (ājñācakra) of the Guru, the mantra, and oneself.
Then, having brought even the Goddess to a state of oneness by way of the *suṣumṇā* path,
one should transcend that single wheel which is the very nature of reality (*tattva*).
Having meditated with effort for a moment upon Mahāmāyā within the six cakras,
one should cause the primary sixteen cakras to descend by means of the root mantra.
The practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows bliss upon the aspirant and resides in the midst of the sixteen [vowels] beginning with 'A', and then commence the rite of recitation.
p. 540) Above the two eyebrows, the cluster of the three channels is said to be located;
that cluster stands at the place of the triple path, being hexagonal and four finger-breadths in extent. (6-1149)
And that which is red is called the wheel of command (ājñācakra) by those who know the yoga of the families;
at the throat, there exists an encircling of three channels for human beings.
The hexagon formed by the Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā is six finger-breadths in extent;
it is called the "six wheels" (ṣaṭcakra), white in color, and situated in the middle of the throat.
The three channels also become one within the heart;
that location is a sixteen-spoked [wheel], measuring seven finger-breadths in extent.

That [practice] involving the sixteen cakras from the beginning has been taught by those who know yoga as being for the sake of the objects of meditation, the mantras, the visualization, and the recitation. (6.1153)
Because it is the primordial heart, it is therefore called the "beginning" (*ādi*).
(In the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*:
[One should worship] the Guru, the deity, the mantra, and likewise one's own self. (6.1154)
One should meditate on [the deity] as having become one within the first sixteen cakras (Merutantra).
Having contemplated thus, one should place the rosary in the central portion of the middle [cakra]. (6-1155)
Without touching the ring finger, one should move the garland with the tip of the thumb;
he who, while reciting the previous mantra, touches another jewel [of the rosary], [commits a fault].
If he holds it with his thumb, that recitation is always fruitless;
having held the rosary near his own heart with his right hand. (6-1157)

Meditating upon the Goddess, one should perform the recitation; one should not touch [the rosary] with the left hand. With a single-pointed mind, a tranquil self, holding the rosary, and being pure—(6.1158).
With his neck slightly bent, composed, free from scratching or blinking,
neither too fast nor too slow, the wise man should recite the mantra in its proper sequence with composure.
(Yāmala)
Excessive speed is the cause of disease; excessive length is the loss of wealth.
One should recite [the mantra] joined with the syllables and the imperishable, like a string of pearls.
(From the *Merutantra*) One who is established in that, whose vital breath is absorbed in that, whose mind is fixed on that, and who is devoted solely to that— 6-1161.
While reflecting upon the meaning of those words, one should mutter the mantra slowly;
when weary from muttering, one should meditate again, and when weary from meditating, one should mutter again.
For one engaged in recitation, meditation, and so forth, the mantra is quickly accomplished. Sanatkumāra said:
Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, one whose consciousness is directed toward the meaning of the mantra [attains success].
One should recite neither too quickly nor too slowly, like a string of pearls.
Japa is the repetition of syllables, performed mentally, in a whisper, or aloud;
it is that which, by means of the intellect, consists of a sequence of syllables composed of phonemes, vowels, and words. (6.1164)

One should utter the meaning while directing the mind [toward it]; that is known as mental recitation (mānasajapa). One should move the tongue and lips slightly while the mind is fixed upon the deity.
That which is suitable to be heard slightly is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa);
that which one should utter the mantra with the voice is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa).

The whispered recitation is proclaimed to be a hundred thousand times more meritorious than the vocal; the mental recitation, however, is praised as being ten million times more meritorious than the whispered.
In another tantra:
"Whoever should recite a hymn with the mind and mutter a mantra with the voice—both are fruitless, like water in a broken vessel. (6.1168)

(Kulārṇava) For those desiring spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*), the mental recitation is prescribed; for those desiring nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the whispered recitation; and the vocal recitation is praised as being [performed] with passion (*māra*). Thus has the recitation been described. (6-1169)
The vocal [practice] is the performer of the six rites; the bodily [practice] accomplishes all siddhis;
the mental [practice] achieves liberation; other than that, there is the performer of minor rites. (6.1170)
By constant recitation, the deity, being praised, becomes pleased.
Through recitation comes success; through recitation comes success; through recitation comes success—it is not far off.
Just as a petty lord becomes satisfied with wealth, so too do minor deities become satisfied by offerings and worship. (6.1172)
Just as a virtuous lord becomes submissive through great qualities,
so too do I, you, and Viṣṇu bestow fruits solely through the power of japa.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, grahas, and terrifying serpents—stricken with fear on all sides—do not approach the one who recites [the mantra]. (6-1174)
Vaiśampāyana said: Whatever recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), or gift (dāna) is performed with dry clothing in water, or with wet clothing on land— all that shall be fruitless.
(Rudrayāmala) Excessive eating, over-exertion, idle chatter, obsession with rules, attachment to people, and wandering in crowds— by these six, the mantra perishes. (6.1176)
O Dear One, endowed with faith, conviction, compassion, devotion, self-restraint, and resolve, and possessed of contentment and qualities such as pure action, one should perform the recitation.
Sanatkumāra said:

Having first performed the recitation (japa) in this manner, one should offer the form of radiant energy (tejas) into the right hand of the deity with kuśa grass, flowers, and water for the arghya offering. (6.1178)
Regarding the scope of one's capacity:

having thus performed the recitation previously, the wise practitioner should offer the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and water mixed with kuśa grass.
Likewise: "One should perform the recitation (japa) day by day neither deficient nor excessive;
if one should do so through negligence, however, one will not obtain the desired fruit. (6.1180)
(From the Merutantra:
At the end of the recitation, having recited one hundred and eight times, one should place [the rosary] upon the head.
As for the mantra of the rosary: "Hrīḥ, obeisance to Siddhi"; thus one should offer a prayer. (6-1189)
O Mālā, you who grant pleasure to all the gods and bestow auspiciousness upon me;
O blessed one, bring me prosperity and increase my fame and valor.
The mantra of the rosary is prescribed for the acts of grasping, placing, and worship;
thereafter, one should pray to one's chosen deity with the five-syllabled mantra.
O you who are protected by the secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Lord of the World, may success be mine through your grace.
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer it into the hand of the deity;
and at the time of midday, one should likewise perform this recitation with the water of the arghya offering.
Thereafter, having bathed as before, the knower of the ritual rules should perform the entire sequence of rites previously described, specifically ending with the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, having performed everything up to the worship and the fire-oblation, he should begin the recitation (*japa*).
O twice-born one, he should continue until its conclusion, and then bathe once again. (6.1195)
Having performed the twilight worship as before, one should again worship the God;
having dismissed [the deity], one should always take food at the rising of the stars. (6.1196)
In the *Yāmala*,
it is said that a person performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite eats sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) at night.
The meaning of the word "night" (*nakta*) is explained in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
The wise declare that a day minus one muhūrta is called "night."
"O lord of men, I consider it night when the stars are visible. Thus [he spoke].

In this context, during the preliminary observance (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Sūrya-mantra, one should take food at a time when the sun has not yet reached its meridian. As it is stated in the *Matsya-purāṇa*: "When the sun stands at a shadow twice the length of one's own body, one should know that as the solar *nakta*; otherwise, eating occurs at night."
(For me,) the meal should be prepared by the twice-born after spreading [the base] and pouring [the clarified butter] over it. (6.1198)
One should purify it with Vedic mantras through rites such as sprinkling; then, having consecrated it again with the root mantra, one should eat while reciting the *hṛdayāṇu* (heart-mantra).
One who is thirsty should drink water consecrated with the root mantra while eating;
one should eat from a *palāśa* leaf, avoiding the middle leaf.
In the absence of that, having eaten from a plantain tree, or a Madhūka, or even a Sarjaka,
one should sleep on a bed purified by the surface of the earth.
On a pure, excellent bed spread with unwashed coverlets,
having consecrated it with the root mantra, he whose anger is conquered and whose senses are subdued— || 6.1202 ||
Meditating upon his chosen deity, he should sleep at night with his head toward the east;
then, having risen at midnight and performed the cleansing of his feet, [he should proceed].
Having sipped water (ācamana), recollected the deity, and quickly performed worship as before,
one should perform recitation (japa) according to one's ability and likewise offer it to the Lord.
Then, having slept, he should report to his guru whatever dream he has seen.
This recitation is prescribed for forest-dwellers and for those practicing celibacy (brahmacārins). (6.1205)
If the completion must be performed with haste due to fear of disturbances such as those arising from the region, this is the time prescribed; and it is also taught for cases of extreme necessity.
Recitation until midday is best; for three *praharas* it is middling;
and for three and a half watches it is inferior—provided the necessary characteristics previously described are present.
Vaiśampāyana said: The number prescribed for the Kṛta age remains as stated; in the Tretā it becomes double;
in the Dvāpara it is declared to be triple; and in the Kali age, the number is fourfold.
In the *Ekavīrākalpa*, it is said:
"For Śūdras who lack meditative cultivation and possess small minds, the recitation is declared to be fourfold for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it shall not be so. (6-1209)
(In the Vārāhītantra:
"The wise have not prescribed a specific number for the recitation and the fire-oblation of these;
for them, the number for both recitation and oblation shall be eight thousand. (6-1210)

(Kriyāsaṃgraha) When the number of recitations is complete, one should perform the fire oblation (*havana*) ten times the amount of the recitation in a fire consecrated according to the rules, using the substances prescribed in the ritual manual.
When clarified butter is prescribed as the sacrificial substance, one should perform the oblation with ghee;
this rule for the performance of the oblation is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.

The consecration of the fire for the purpose of the *homa* and the procedure for the *homa* itself have already been clarified in the section on the rules for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*), and thus they are not elaborated upon here. Now, [regarding this] in the *Kulārṇava*:
Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with water from sacred fords mixed with moonlight;
having invoked the deity into the water, [one should worship] with the parts beginning with the feet, consisting of water.
Having worshipped him together with his retinue according to the rules and with devotion,
one should satisfy each member of the retinue by offering water in a single handful (añjali).
Then, one should satisfy the deity with a tenth part of the oblations (*homa*).
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
Having uttered the root mantra, at its end [one should utter] the name of the deity. (6-1215)
I shall later offer libations with [the names] ending in the accusative case, using "namas" at the end;
this is declared to be the mantra for the libation (tarpaṇa), and one should likewise arrange it for the limbs and other parts.
In the case of the Śakti [as taught in the *Yāmala* and other texts], one should utter the name at the end of the mantra and then say "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*).
One should then satisfy the Supreme Deity with the mantra ending in the "wife of fire" (*vahnijāyā*, i.e., *svāhā*). || 6-1216 ||
Likewise: having uttered the root mantra, at the end of the mantra one should state the name of the deity, say "I satisfy, obeisance," and thus satisfy the Mistress of the Kula. (6.1216)

Thus, there is an option between ending with the *vahnijāyā* (the fire-wife, *svāhā*) or ending with *namaḥ*. Even in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, the *tarpaṇa* mantra ends only with *namaḥ*. As it is said in the *Gautamīya*:
"Having first uttered the mantra, followed by 'Śrī Kṛṣṇa,' and having spoken the word 'tarpayāmi,' a person should offer libation ending with *namaḥ*. (6.1216)

Likewise: "The word 'tarpayāmi' (I satisfy) should be joined at the end of these names [of the deities], and also at the end of those ending in the accusative case; such is considered the mantra for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (6-1217)
Now, regarding the ritual of sprinkling (*mārjana*):
according to the *Nīlatantra*, having recited the mantra ending with "namas," one should utter the name of the deity at its conclusion.
"Afterwards, however, I shall consecrate her, who is in the accusative case, with this [mantra]."
One should sprinkle one's own head with water using the mudrā called *kumbha*.
Vaiśampāyaṇa says:
Reciting the mantra ending in "namaḥ," one should perform [the rite] with a tenth part of the *tarpaṇa* offering. (6-1219)
One should sprinkle one's own head with water using the mudrā called *kumbha*.
As it is stated elsewhere:
"At the end of the mantra, having uttered the name, one says 'I sprinkle,' followed by the word *namaḥ*. (6-1220)
In this context, they recite the root mantra, joining it with the words: "I consecrate such-and-such deity; obeisance. Then follows the feeding of the Brahmins.
(In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*): One should feed Brahmins with a tenth part of the number used for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*).
Having invited the Brahmins and prepared food of six flavors, [one should proceed]. (6-1221)
One should offer the seat of the assembly with the root mantra,
and having meditated upon the chosen deity, one should perform the invocation, as well as [the invocation of] the Brahmins as prescribed.
One should worship the Brahmins, who are the embodiments of one's chosen deity, with water for the feet and other offerings;
then, regarding them as deities, one should feed them various kinds of food endowed with diverse flavors.
In the *Merutantra*:
"By the mere act of propitiating Brahmins, that which is deficient in its parts becomes complete; whatever ritual acts may have been omitted are restored by feeding the twice-born. (6.1224)
Those seeds would be as useless as those sown in saline soil;
afterwards, one should satisfy the teacher with cows, gold, garments, and other such gifts.
For when the guru is satisfied, the mantra becomes fully contented and attains accomplishment for the practitioner.
As stated in another tantra:
"One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru through offerings such as food, clothing, and so forth."
By the mere satisfaction of the guru, all success will certainly be attained. || 6-1226 ||
"Those who know the Tantras have said that all this has its root in the Guru.
(Merutantra) "In this regard, a fivefold procedure is taught which brings the recitation (*japa*) to completion. (6.1227)
The first rite is that one should perform the recitation daily until midday;
then, with a tenth part of that, one should arrange the fire-oblation (homa) using the substances prescribed for the ritual period (kalpa).

Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ritual purification (mārjana), as well as the feeding of Brahmins, one should then perform this [recitation] ten times that amount; this is declared to be the primary method.
This is the second ritual procedure: one should perform one hundred thousand recitations;
having performed the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites for that, one should commence the subsequent hundred thousand.
This is the third ritual procedure: one should perform the complete recitation (*japa*).
In the case of the full oblation (*pūrṇahoma*), one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites first. || 6-1231 ||

But in the fourth case, the ritual procedure is as follows: for those who are poor, the recitation (japa) should be doubled; and in the absence of fire-oblations (homa) and other rites, it should be performed by multiplying [the number] threefold, fourfold, and so on, according to the status of the king and others.
But the fifth method is as follows: whatever is dear to whichever deity, that very thing should be performed doubly for the swift gratification of that divinity.
All goddesses are fond of recitation; on the Left Path they are fond of sacrificial offerings (bali);
in the Siddhānta they are fond of drinking; but in the Kaulika [tradition] they are fond of sexual pleasure.
Mahādeva is fond of the fire-oblation (homa), and the Sun-god (Bhāskara) favors libations and food offerings;
if an expiation (prāyaścitta) is not performed, the twice-born man shall remain impure.
According to the *Yāmala*, members of the Kṣatriya and other castes should perform expiation by means of the fourfold set of penances;
for Brāhmaṇas who are unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites, the recitation (*japa*) shall be doubled. (6-1236)
For the other castes, however, according to the numbers three, four, or five,
there is only the alternative of performing twice as many oblations and so forth; thus says Sanatkumāra.
If any limb should break, the recitation must be performed twice that number of times.
In the absence of a fire sacrifice (homa), recitation (japa) should be performed four times the number of the homa;
for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, it is recorded as six times the number.
For Vaiśyas, this rule applies to women numbering eight;
as for a Śūdra, he should follow the rule of whichever caste he has taken refuge in.

In another tantra it is said: "The recitation prescribed by the wise for the twice-born in the absence of fire-offerings is indeed the same for beautiful-browed women who are devoted to Him, as well as for Śūdras. (6.1240)
(From the Merutantra:

Now I shall explain how the accomplishment of mantra may come about for a poor man; for a Brahmin who is unable to perform the rite of fire-oblation, the recitation [of the mantra] must be doubled. (6-1241)
For the other castes, however, a triple [number of recitations] and so forth is prescribed;
through twice the number of recitations as the oblations, there shall be a complete satisfaction.
It is taught that if the ritual cleansing (mārjana) has not been performed, the recitation (japa) must be double the amount required for the libation (tarpaṇa).
However, I have never heard it stated anywhere that feeding Brahmins serves as a substitute (pratyāmnāya) for this.
In every way, one should feed the Brahmins for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the ritual;
for here there is the scriptural injunction: "Neither women nor Śūdras should perform the oblation preceded by the utterance of mantras."

Regarding women and Śūdras, however, the author of the *Sudhārṇava* maintains that in place of the fire-oblation (*homa*), there is only the recitation (*japa*) as prescribed; even if they possess the capacity [to perform it], the oblation is not permitted.
And so it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"The rule for the performance of the fire-oblation is declared for the three [upper] castes alone. (6.1244)
But a Śūdra, desiring that same fruit, should perform twice as many recitations (*japa*) as the number of oblations (*homa*).
(In the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*:
"For women and Śūdras, the oblation is said to be performed through the agency of a Brāhmaṇa. (6-1245)
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) five times or twice the number of the oblations (*homa*).
(In the *Vārāhītantra*, however:
"Śūdras have the right to perform the ritual of oblation (*homakarma*) according to this tantra. (6-1246)
"Having abandoned the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), 'Namaḥ' is considered [to be used] at the end of 'Svāhā'"—thus it has been stated.
In another tantra:
"If, once the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) has begun, birth-impurity (sūtaka) or the like should occur," [6.1247]
What has been commenced must not be abandoned; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of fault.
Furthermore, [it is stated] in the Smṛti:
"In sacrifices, vows, marriages, funeral rites (śrāddha), fire-oblations (homa), worship, and recitation... (6.1248).
When [the rite] has commenced, there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka); when it has not commenced, there is birth-impurity.
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the formal invitation (varaṇa); in a vow and a recitation, it is the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
In rites such as the *nāndīmukha* ceremony at the beginning of a marriage, the preparation of the sacrificial food (*pāka*) for the *śrāddha*,
and even in the *tantra* tradition, the practice of recitation (*japa*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and the ritual of worship must be performed by men who have received initiation.

For those self-controlled ones, there is no sin, nor any impurity arising from childbirth; likewise, during the period of death-impurity, or even when smoke issues forth [from the mouth], there is no fault.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) and the offering of water (*argha*), preceded by the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*).
(From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*):
Having thus properly performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*), the most excellent of practitioners—
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship and feed the Brahmins;
one should honor one's own guru with many garments and ornaments.
Having gratified the lords of the lamps, the mantras of the practitioners of mantra (mantriṇaḥ) become effective. [This is] the description of the constituent parts of the fire-oblation (homa).
For one who is self-restrained, the mantras grant success through recitation, oblation, and worship. (6-1254)
Even with double the number of recitations, mantras are traditionally held to grant success.
(From the *Rudrayāmala*) Without food and furthermore without the libation to the Goddess... (6-1255)
Even without performing *homa*, one should recite the mantra three times over for the sake of accomplishment;
likewise, according to the *Agastyasaṃhitā* (6.1256), by means of the five-limbed practice (*pañcāṅga-upāsanā*) of a single mantra that has been perfectly mastered.
"O Maheśvarī, by your grace all mantras are accomplished.
In another tantra: "Among practitioners of mantra, one who has mastered the mantra is difficult to find in the three worlds. (6.1257)
O Goddess of gods, there is nothing [that does not face obstacles]; therefore, one should accomplish the mantra.
Also elsewhere:
"The wise have declared that auspicious undertakings are beset by many obstacles. (6-1258)
Therefore, having conquered all obstacles, one should perform the practice of mantra-sādhana;
then, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall fulfill his own heart's desires.
(Merutantra) When a single task has been accomplished, the mantra becomes faltering; by performing the recitation again, it shall once more become capable of accomplishing that one task. (6-1260)

In that very same [text], and in another mantra, it is said: "A guru who is fully accomplished bestows the mantra; through the practice exactly as prescribed, accomplishment arises for that disciple. (6.1261)
If there is compassion, and if the Guru bestows the perfected mantra,
then even without recitation and without worship, the accomplishments (siddhis) reside in the hand of that person.
In the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*:
"The wise know that unwavering devotion toward the guru and the deity, as well as confidence in the mantra and the scripture, is the seed of accomplishment. (6.1263)
(From the *Pratyaṅgirā-kalpa*):
When the mass of fuel that is evil has been consumed by the fire of preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*), fanned by the wind of devotion, the mantras of the practitioners attain success. (6-1264)
Thus concludes the general procedure for the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*).
[This work] is worthy of veneration as a confluence of rivers of excellent compositions, abounding in streams of nectar variegated by the wonderful splendor and the diverse beauty of sacred words.
The sixth wave in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Naradeva has concluded; it is lofty with the luster of a multitude of clearly manifest pearls of sound reasoning. || 6-1265 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The General Procedure for Puraścaraṇa," in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha Sāhi.
The Characteristics of Mantra-Siddhi.

Now, among the various topics to be examined—such as the different types of *puraścaraṇa* and the characteristics of mantra-siddhi—the characteristics of mantra-siddhi are first described according to the maxim of the needle and the frying pan (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*).
As it is said in the *Pañcarātra*:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the accomplishment of mantra;
the effortless fulfillment of one's desires is the supreme characteristic of accomplishment.
Likewise, the removal of deaths, the vision of deities, the accomplishment of difficult feats through ritual applications, and the characteristics of such accomplishment [are described]. (7.2)
Likewise:
"Entering another's body, as well as entering a city, and likewise ascending upwards—such indeed is the movement within the cities of the moving and the unmoving. (7-3)
One should indeed behold the union with the Khecarī, the hearing of its discourses, and so forth;
therefore, one perceives the apertures of the earth as the supreme characteristic.
Upon remembering or glorifying Viṣṇu, there is the shedding of tears of joy,
horripilation, faltering speech, and likewise one-pointedness of mind.
Detachment from sense objects and love for the Supreme Lord, eagerness to hear His stories, and delight in serving His feet. (7.6)
The quality of composing poetry in praise of his virtues without delay, and the sight of the marks of his lotus feet during acts such as worship; (7-7)
There may be a sudden hearing of the unstruck sound (anāhata) even without the practice of yoga; this is a supreme sign. || 7-8 ||
Fame, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, long life, and the supreme subjugation of kings and those who have gone to them. (7.9)
He is pure and a source of wonder everywhere in all the worlds;
by his very sight, he removes disease and likewise removes poison.
The practitioner effortlessly attains fourfold wisdom:
dispassion, the desire for liberation, renunciation, and mastery over all things. (7.11)
The practice of the eightfold yoga, free from the desire for enjoyments;
compassion toward all beings; and the arising of qualities such as omniscience. (7.12)
The attainment of such qualities as these is the characteristic of middling accomplishment;
[furthermore,] renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, and long life. (7.13)
Affection for kings and women, popularity among the people, great sovereignty, wealth, and the abundance of sons and other riches. (7.14)
The inferior accomplishments (siddhis) are said to belong to the first stage of the practitioner;
however, he whose mantra is truly perfected is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt.
(From the *Sādhanasamuccaya*):
For one whose great mantra has been mastered through powerful practice, even those accomplishments difficult for the gods to attain rest in their hands. (7.16)

The accomplishment of moving through the quarters (dikcarī), the accomplishment of moving through the sky (khecarī), the accomplishment of the sandals (pādukāsiddhi), the accomplishment of invisibility (antarddhisiddhi), the accomplishment of the vetāla, and the entering of another's body (kāyapraveśana). || 7-17 ||

The accomplishment of the yakṣiṇī, the accomplishment of Bhairavī, and likewise the accomplishment of the sword; the accomplishment of the command, and the accomplishments of alchemy, the pill, and the collyrium. || 7-18 ||
Attraction and subjugation, melting and likewise deluding;
expulsion, immobilization, causing enmity, and likewise killing. (7-19)
It effects intoxication, desiccation, fainting, and agitation;
it likewise causes the arrest of the movement of planets and the suppression of the force of the wind.

He brings about the immobilization of rivers, great oceans, and pillars, as well as the immobilization of the speech of opponents—whether they be Gandharvas, Uragas, Daityas, Kinnaras, or Rākṣasas. (7.21)
Likewise, there shall be the attraction of maidens from among the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, as well as the instantaneous attraction of kings and deities. (7.22)
It effects the cooling of fire, the neutralization of the venom of serpents, the drying up of even the ocean, and the subjugation of the three worlds. (7.23)
And there is the unfailing nature of his speech, both in cursing and in bestowing grace;
likewise, he possesses the ability to assume any form at will, to move anywhere at will, and to grant all desires.
Aṇimā, mahimā, and likewise garimā, laghimā, as well as īśitva, vaśitva, prākāmya, and prāpti. (7.25)
All such accomplishments (siddhis) arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
What need is there for much speaking here regarding the practitioner who has mastered the mantra? (7.26)
Whatever is desired, all that shall become as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand for one capable of propitiating the mantra during the first three years. (Nāradapañcarātra, 7.27)
O Nārada, many obstacles arise at the conclusion of the rite for one established in the observance;
yet the practitioner does not succumb to agitation, provided he remains so in action and mind.
From the third year onwards, even kings and lords of the earth, though proud and honorable, seek [the hand of the girl] out of consideration for [her father's] wishes. (7.29)
O Lord, grant your grace for the sake of my deliverance;
they behold you blazing with splendor and majesty.
Therefore, O tiger among sages, they are unable to speak harshly;
after the ninth year, the king of mantras becomes effective by itself.
Various wonders consisting of the accomplishment of mantras indeed exist within the heart; they swiftly bestow supreme bliss both internally and externally through direct perception. (7.32)
But the dull-witted Brahmin was for a moment despondent, for a moment filled with great joy,
and for a moment he even heard the sound of drums resounding through the sky.
For a moment he enjoys sweet music accompanied by various songs;
for a moment he smells fragrances produced from camphor and musk.
For a moment he sees himself by means of his own self as if leaping up;
for a moment he gazes at the sky overspread with the rays of the moon and the sun.
And for a moment the twice-born man should listen to the roars of elephants, bulls, and cows;
at another moment he even draws in the tumultuous roar of a rain-cloud.
The yogin always sees the various stars situated in the sky, and he perceives them being held up for a moment by those who possess the mantras.
At one moment he might hear the sound of joyful clamor, or likewise the cries of swans and peacocks;
at another moment he might see the rising of clouds, or night appearing even while it is day.
And at night, he beholds the light of day together with the sun for a moment;
full of strength, he is like the sun in splendor.
He was like the full moon in his radiance, like a bird in his gait,
and endowed with mature tranquility, profound depth, and ease.
By eating very little, one does not become emaciated, yet even with much food one suffers distress;
for there is indeed a reduction in feces and urine, as well as a decrease in sleep. (7.41)
O Sage, the mantra-practitioner engaged in recitation and meditation does not experience fatigue for a fortnight, a month, or longer, even without food and drink. (7.42)
By such signs as these, which cause great wonder, Bauddhāyana says:
"There are three signs of perfection: being a giver, being an enjoyer, and not being a beggar."
(In the Bhairavītantra:
One perceives light everywhere, or the body endowed with radiance. (7.44)
Or rather, one's own body is indeed composed of the deity itself.
(In the *Vakratuṇḍakalpa*):
Serenity of mind, contentment of the heart, moderation in eating, and aversion to sleep;
Furthermore, the perception of vehicles and other such things in dreams are the immediate signs of one who has attained perfection. (7.45)

(Merutantra) Thus, when the mantra has been mastered, even those gods who obstruct the path to liberation become possessed of manifold supernatural powers that cause the exhaustion of their ascetic merit. (7.46)
If one is immersed in minor accomplishments, the powers such as *aṇimā* do not arise;
if one is immersed in the powers such as *aṇimā*, news of liberation is extremely difficult to obtain. (7.47)
(Also in the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa:
Just as one who is immersed in a small pleasure does not attain great happiness, so for one who is immersed in supernatural powers (siddhi), liberation remains far away. (7.48)
Therefore, disregarding all other accomplishments, one should worship the sandals of Nṛhari;
from that, one attains the bliss of the indivisible, single essence, and not otherwise. (7.49)
Even though one becomes the locus of all accomplishments through the power of *puraścaraṇa*, practitioners who desire liberation must not abandon devotion to the Lord. (7.50)
There are many who desire worldly enjoyment, and some who desire liberation;
but rare is he who, free from longing for both enjoyment and liberation, worships Hari. (7.51)
He alone is liberated while living, who, free from desire for yoga, devotes himself to the flawless Nārāyaṇa, whether success has been attained or not. (7.52)
In the Merutantra it is said:
"Little austerity perishes in an instant, and even middling austerity perishes through pride;
