the sign of great [austerity] is said to be its characteristic mark regarding the attainment of siddhi. (7.53)
If a marvel that causes joy—whether occurring in one's presence or before one's eyes—should suddenly arise, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru. (7.54)
One who desires mundane accomplishment should never disclose [the mantra] anywhere; yet some, out of delusion or impatience, reveal the bliss born of the mantra. (7.55)
The supernatural powers that were close to him move far away;
various sufferings and sorrows also manifest themselves. (7.56)
Eating little, sleeping little, constant clarity of mind, and a body endowed with radiance—truthful speech arises from these. (7.57)
Likewise:
"The donor who does not beg, having achieved the fulfillment of his speech and mental desires, is the true enjoyer.
(Prapañcasāra)
Then, as he recites the mantra, these signs indeed arise for him.
A house blessed by a lamp at night becomes free from darkness.
By his splendor, he becomes like the sun; O Lotus-born One, she shall be his constant servant;
diseases perish instantly at his sight; and then, surrounded by wealth and grain, they gather near him.
The gods always offer salutations to him, and serpents do not bite his sons.
Having protected his grandsons, friends, and elders during times of personal calamity, he attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus are the signs of accomplishment.
(From the Phetkāriṇītantra:
By means of a powerful rite that does not conflict with obstacles.
If one does not obtain success, one should perform it again two or three times.
Now, he describes the means for the accomplishment of mantras when they remain unaccomplished even after two or three preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*). (In the *Merutantra*):
"Due to the lack of accomplishment on the part of the guru, by fate, success does not arise in the disciple."
Then one should indeed employ the means which is now being declared as that which must be kept secret.
One should recite the mantra encapsulated by the letters of the Mātṛkā in both forward and reverse order, like [the seed-syllable] Vindu, a hundred times every day.
Then, after one month of performing the fire oblations and other rites, the mantra becomes perfected;
one should also perform the entire daily regimen as prescribed for the preliminary service (puraścaryā).
However, a specific rule regarding Vedic mantras is stated in that very same place:

"In this way, for the accomplishment of a Vedic mantra, the letters of the mountain (seven), the tastes (six), and the digits (nine) should be assigned in order and in reverse order, conjoined with the bindu. (7.64)
The vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* are considered to be of three kinds through the distinctions of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*).
The vowel *ḷ* is of two kinds (short and protracted), and the diphthongs (*ec*) are also considered to be of two kinds. (7.65)
Due to the distinction between long and protracted [vowels], the anusvāra and visarga are likewise [distinguished];
thus, together with the *yamas*, the vowels are said to be twenty-four.

The four letters beginning with *ka*, together with the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *kha*-sound), thus constitute the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) in ten ways; these are remembered as the first fifteen [consonants].
The letter *pa* joined with the *upadhmānīya*—by that [combination], there are six;
thus, the eight beginning with *ya* are proclaimed as the *mātṛkās* in the Yajurveda. (7.68)

In the Rigveda, two hundred thousand [recitations] are prescribed; in the Atharvaveda, one hundred and eight more are traditionally taught. This recitation (japa) should be performed every day for the duration of one month.
Excluding the days of suspension for study (anadhyāya) as well as forty days, one should thus perform all rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) daily, just as previously prescribed.

On that very point, he states another method: "One should encase the mantra of one's family deity with the *bhūtalipi* [alphabet]. One should perform it one hundred times in both direct and reverse order; success will come within a month. (7.71)

Likewise: one should mutter the mantra of the most formidable deity one thousand and eight times during the three periods of the day, and again at midnight with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, including the fifth [type of offering].
If she is worshipped by the Kaulikas and others for six months, she becomes well-pleased.
The Bhūtalipi will be explained hereafter.
Now, the other means (upāyas).
(From the Gandharva Tantra:
If a mantra does not achieve success even when practiced according to the proper rule, [verse 7-73].
Furthermore, it should be recited again; then it shall become effective once more.
And even if the mantra has been performed repeatedly yet still does not become effective, [it should be recited again]. (7.74)
In that case, the seven methods spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed;
[if the result] does not arise due to hatred of Brahman, fault of the guru, or hatred of women, [then these methods are required]. (Merutantra, 7.75)
Due to a curse or because it is unfastened, there may be eight methods for that [mantra]:
inflaming by contact, nourishing, liquefying, awakening, and subjugation. (7.76)
Oppression, nourishment, and emaciation, as well as burning—these are said to be its ritual actions.
Having procured birch bark, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus. (7.77)
With the eight fragrances, or with yellow pigment (rocanā) and sandalwood, one should write the name of the deity and the name of the practitioner, interwoven with the mantra syllables. (7.78)
One should write the name of the practitioner, preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), at the beginning and end until the completion of two [revolutions], and then [place it] upon the eight petals.
Two by two, the vowels should be written, and one should meditate correctly upon that as being of the nature of nectar;
having thoroughly enveloped that with clay, one should properly wrap the Brahmin and the others.
p. 561) Afterwards, one should wrap it with beeswax colored white and so forth, and then place it in a small earthen vessel containing the three sweets. (7.81)
One should place that [substance] in a small vessel within a new jar filled with milk,
having established the fire in the vicinity of that jar.
One should establish [the deity] with the three sweets and perform the fire oblation (homa) with the root mantra;
one should cast eight thousand or more drops of the residue into the ritual jar.
Having completed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should cast that pitcher into a body of water;
and one should gratify one's own guru and other Brahmins with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other offerings.

This is said to be for the purpose of replenishing through the "collision" (saṃpāta); however, if success does not occur, one should then perform the "melting" (drāvaṇa), the method for which is stated here.
Having tied it with a seed-syllable (bīja), one should write the mantra on birch bark using usīra and rocanā,
as well as realgar, camphor, and saffron.
One should place that written [mantra] in the midst of milk, ghee, honey, and water;
through worship, recitation, and burnt offerings, it becomes fluid and yields its fruit.
If, even after being melted, he is not perfected, one should cause him to undergo awakening;
having encapsulated his name with the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, one should recite it.
In this way, one becomes a perfected Buddha; otherwise, if one does not perform the rite of subjugation, [one should employ] kucandana, mahādāru, haridrā, madanī, and śilā.
This mantra, written by these [sages] upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf, shall bring one under control when worn around the neck; otherwise, it will cause great suffering.
One should recite the first syllable with an anudātta accent, the second with an udātta, the third with an anudātta, and the fourth with an udātta. (7.91)
In this manner, the practitioner of the mantra should recite all the words;
while pronouncing the words in an unaccented (anudātta) tone, he should meditate on the deity situated below. (7.92)
One should recite the mantra eight thousand times while standing upright during the utterance of the *udātta* accent;
thereafter, one should write [the mantra] on birch bark with the milk of a cow.
One should step upon that mantra with the left foot and then perform the fire oblation;
when one is thus afflicted, the mantra becomes propitiated after reciting it one hundred and eight times.
If [the deity] is not yet accomplished, then he is said to be one who must be nourished; his ritual is now described.
Having written the mantra enclosed within seed-syllables on birch bark, [one should perform the rite]. (7.95)
One should apply rocanā and kuṅkuma with curd and milk;
this is called nourishment (poṣaṇa), and the drying of the humors (doṣaśoṣaṇa) is now described.
One should write the desired mantra, interspersed with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, using the ashes of a sacrificial fire upon a birch leaf; then, one should wear that on one's neck. (7.97)
This has been called "drying"; now "burning" is being described, performed separately for each mantra, encompassed in the four directions.
One should inscribe [the mantra] with the seed-syllable *ra* and the seed-oil of the *palāśa* tree upon a birch-bark leaf;
that should then be worn around the neck—this is the procedure for burning.
Other methods have been taught [in the *Yāmaleśvara*, *Gandharva*, and other texts]:
"The Praṇava, the Mātṛkā, and the goddess Hṛllekhā—these are the three nectars.
Through the conjunction of these three nectars, even a corrupt mantra attains success. (7–100)
Gold, monkey oil, ground [substances], and consecrated mantra-water—
when these are smeared upon the limbs and the mantra is recited over them, even a dull mantra becomes effective.
(Gautamīya):

When a mantra has become blunted, it becomes instantly propitious when one offers oblations with one's own water mixed with gold, sunflower oil, and flour, having smeared one's limbs with that same mixture. (7.102)
Thus are the means for the accomplishment of mantras: (p.

563) Having placed the *hṛllekhā*, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), and the seed-syllable of Śrī at the beginning and end of the mantra, one should recite the mantra for the sake of accomplishment. (7.103)
Alternatively, having encapsulated the mantra with the *tāra* (the syllable Om), the practitioner should recite it exactly one hundred thousand times; even a wicked mantra will then be accomplished.
Thus are the means.
Now, the varieties of *puraścaraṇa* (according to the *Vāḍavānalīya*):
"Without *puraścaraṇa*, mantras are never successful."
Those mantras are not fit for application; those mantras do not bestow results.

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, those mantras which are devoid of the preliminary practice (puraścaryā), yet for which a greater number of recitations (japa) has been prescribed—[these are ineffective]. (7.106)
If the practitioner is unable to perform the recitation for that many counts,
he should do so on the bank of a river flowing into the ocean, or else in a temple of the deity.
In the month of Māgha, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
with devotion, one should worship the Goddess at the three junctions of the day with various offerings.
Then one should perform the fire-oblation and other ancillary rites according to the prescribed rule;
when this is done, O Great Goddess, the mantra becomes bestower of fruit. (7.109)
Indeed, initiation should be known as fruitless for those who do not perform the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*).
(From the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the [next] eighth day of the dark fortnight... [7-110]
When it has been recited a thousand times, the *puraścaraṇa* is considered complete.
In that very context:
"Having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight during the great festival, while performing austerities... (7.111).
On the eighth and ninth nights, one should perform worship especially;
on the tenth day, one should break the fast with fish, meat, and other such offerings.
One should recite [the mantra] six thousand times daily, being entirely devoted to a spirit of devotion. Likewise:
"Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner. (7.113)
O Maheśānī, beginning from the fourteenth day until the next fourteenth day, the recitation performed during that interval is considered the *puraścaraṇa*.
Indeed, mantras become perfected merely by recitation;
they are especially so through offerings of bali and homa, and particularly through the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
The Yonipīṭha, the Mahāpīṭha, and likewise the other, Kāmarūpa—one of these two should be worshipped as if it were another body of Rudra himself. (7.116)
(Candrapīṭha):
Beginning with Mahālakṣmī up to Mahānavamīśvarī—from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the ninth in the month of Madhu—this is remembered as the Śākta Manu. (7-117)
In the months of Ūrja, Tapas, or Rādha, the bright fortnight belongs to Viṣṇu;
however, in Āiśa (Mārgaśīrṣa) it ends with the eleventh day, while in Phālguna it is traditionally held to end with the fourteenth day (bhūta).
Even for the King of Obstructors (Gaṇeśa) in the month of Bhādrapada, as well as for [the deities of] Māgha and Bhādrapada from their own day,
and for other mantras as well, the previously mentioned Navarātra [observance applies].
The recitation [of mantras] with the Mātṛkā should be performed from morning until midday;
at night, it should be done for the duration of one watch (yāma), while subsisting on water, roots, and fruits.

In the fourth watch of the night, the oblation (homa) should be performed for the garland-mantra at one-tenth [of the total recitation], or at one-twentieth, or even at one-tenth; this is considered the rule for other mantras as well. (7.121)
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should also be as prescribed, and one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth;
in this way, the mantra will certainly become fit for application—of this there is no doubt. (7.122)
(In the *Sādhanasamuccaya*):

Starting from the lunar day (*tithi*) of that deity until the lunar day of that same deity— in the month of Kārttika, during the fortnight other than the dark one— beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
One should indeed mutter the Vaiṣṇava mantra until the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
On the twelfth day, one should perform the rites beginning with the fire-oblation and ending with the communal feast;
by this procedure, the mantras of the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) are perfected.
(From the *Kālikākalpa*):
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described in another manner:
specifically during the autumn season, from the fourth to the ninth lunar day. (7–126)
Having worshipped with devotion, one should then recite the mantra a thousand times alone at night in a solitary place, a dwelling of total darkness.
One should be intent on fasting from the eighth day until the ninth;
such a person shall become a lord of all accomplishments—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
In the autumn season, during the fortnight of the goddess, [one should perform] one thousand or six thousand [recitations]. (In the *Muṇḍamālā*):
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described in another manner.
The great autumnal worship, which is performed annually, is carried out during the autumn season.
In that case, being especially intent on the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa),
one should be devoted to fasting from the eighth day until the ninth.

One should worship with devotion at night and perform six thousand recitations (*japa*). Here, it should be understood that the *japa* begins on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and continues until the ninth day (*navamī*).
(From the Viśvasāra)
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner. || 7-131 ||
Having placed a human skull above that at the place of worship,
and having spread a soft seat, one should worship the Supreme Deity.
What is not accomplished by reciting six thousand [mantras] every day?
(In the Kālītantra:
Or else, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner. (7.133)
On a Tuesday or a Saturday, having procured a human skull,
it should be mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and especially with sandalwood and other such substances.
Having buried it in the ground within a forest, at a depth of half a cubit,
if on that very day and night the practitioner [attains] a thousand [results] there— || 7.135 ||
If one recites the mantra alone, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa).
In that very same [text], it is further stated: "Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described by another method. (7-136)
Having brought the corpse to that door, it should be buried right there;
from that day until the end of the day, one should perform this [rite] one hundred and eight times.
The word "should recite" (*japet*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

He shall become the lord of all siddhis; no deliberation is required here. Regarding the phrase "on that day": it refers to the previously mentioned days of Saturn and Mars. Regarding the phrase "by that very [measure]": the meaning is "by the measure of half a cubit."
In that very same [text]:
"Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner. (7.138)
On the eighth or the fourteenth day of either fortnight, beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise. (7.139)
Having recited [the mantra] that many times, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhīśvara*).
In this regard, rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) must also be performed, because it is heard in the context of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*). As stated in another Tantra:
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner. || 7-140 ||
Having recited [the mantra] from sunrise until the next sunrise, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments.
In this case, the specific rule regarding the lunar day (*tithi*) is not mentioned; this is the distinction from the previous method.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
"Starting precisely at sunset and continuing until sunset [on the following day]. (7.142) p. 567)
Having recited that many times, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhiśvara*).
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described by another method.
O Goddess, beginning from sunrise until sunset, one should recite with devotion; thus one shall become a master of all accomplishments.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
beginning from sunset until sunrise. (7.145)
O Great Goddess, by reciting [the mantra] for that long, one shall become a master of all siddhis;
or else, the purascarana is described in another manner.

O Maheśvarī, during the autumn season, from the fourth to the ninth lunar day, one should perform the *puraścaryā* in the form of fire-offerings (*homa*); thus one shall become a master of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Now I shall describe to you the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consisting of libations (tarpaṇa),
performed with milk, water from a horse's hoof-print, blood, and even marrow.
O Maheśvarī, [this is performed] with honey, fragrant water, and streams of blood,
as well as by the libation of pure water alone.
In this regard, one should understand that there is a distinction in the substances used for libation according to the difference in the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*).
(From the *Sādhanasamuccaya*):
During the great festival, beginning from the first day and ending on the ninth day...
Whether by day or by night, one should perform six thousand recitations.
By worshipping the Goddess according to the prescribed rule, one becomes the master of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
In another Tantra it is said: "Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described in another manner. (7.151)
One should recite six thousand [times] by day and likewise at night;
O Goddess of Gods, by following this sequence, one shall become a master of all siddhis. (7.152)
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner:
one should recite the mantra six thousand times by day and perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the same number at night.
"May one become the lord of all siddhis; hear now another [method], O Pārvatī.
Or else, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner."
Having performed his daily duties during the day, he should spend the night alone in a place of darkness;
by being intent on chanting at night, he shall become a master of all supernatural powers.
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
having performed the recitation while situated within the circle of the Gāna, one becomes the sovereign of the three worlds. (7.156)
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner:
one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times during the day, and at night, while performing worship, one should recite it. (7.157)
One who is devoted to meat and food should recite [the mantra] exactly one thousand times;
he shall become a master of all siddhis and attain the accomplishment of a vetāla.
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner: beginning on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and ending on the ninth (*navamī*).

In a solitary place on a mountain, in a void that is solely a dwelling of darkness, by reciting [the mantra] at sunrise and sunset, one shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 7.160 ||
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
on a mountain, in a forest, or in a deserted place, one who has conquered the senses [should practice] for nine nights. (7.161)
Upon the severed head there should be a skull-cup, and above that,
having lit a lamp, one should be intent on gazing at the light.
O Goddess, for nine nights one should recite the root mantra, intent upon gazing at the lamps, [placing] the supreme seed-syllable of Kaumārī within skull-bowls. (7.163)
By means of a yantra drawn with vermilion, one becomes the master of all siddhis.
(From the Kālītantra) Or else, the puraścaraṇa is described in another manner: 7-164.

At the junction of the eighth lunar day, the practitioner of mantra, having entered the house of creepers consisting of one hundred and eight, should diligently worship them according to the prescribed rite.
Having adopted the ritual procedure previously described, one should perform the worship and other rites;
this Kāmadeva alone should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Having recited [the mantra] at the base of their leaves and taken [them], one should place them upon the head;
through the sight of the worship of the creeper, great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi) shall arise immediately.

On the junction of the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) and at the junction of the eighth and ninth days; the "house of the eight plus one creeper" (*aṣṭottaralatāgṛha*) refers, as the case may be, to the house of the powers (*śakti*) up to the number eight—the temple of Madana. This is the previously mentioned ritual known as the *dūtī-yāga*. Having recited the seed-syllable (*bīja*) upon the leaf-base (the private organ) and having cast it away, one should grasp that very same seed-syllable on the head and apply it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*); this is the meaning. This is intended for the supreme hero (*vīra*). In the same way, it should be understood that for others as well, their adherence to specific paths or their commonality with all [paths] is determined by the particular nature of the ritual action.
Furthermore: "Alternatively, the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described in another manner."
And having written the mantra itself in the family abode of one who has been drawn [to the practice], || 7-168 ||
Having worshipped there, performed the consecration, and offered something to her,
and having muttered the mantra a few times, one should lead [the disciple] forth, intent upon the state of the deity.
Having dismissed her and paid homage, one should sleep oneself, well-restrained;
then, having offered the oblation to the women in the morning, there will be the accomplishment of the mantra—of this there is no doubt.
Regarding this, the Ṭhakkuras maintain that there is only worship here, and not even sexual union.
In that very same [text]:
"Having brought the Guru and established him, one performs the worship of the All-pervading Lord as if he were a deity."
Having gratified the guru himself with garments, ornaments, gold, and other such gifts. (7.171)
Having honored his son, his daughter, and likewise his wife,
and having worshipped them and recited the mantra, one shall himself become a master of supernatural powers (siddhi).
In the Merutantra, another [practice] regarding the mantras of the Vāmamārga is stated as follows:
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. (7-173)
Having meditated upon the deity, one should recite the mantra forty thousand times;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number, and then offer libations and perform the ritual consecration.
(Kalpalatā: These are the words of Dhṛta:
"O Goddess of Gods, having gone to the cremation ground specifically on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth [lunar days], by means of the night-conjunction. (7.175)
O beautiful goddess, having become naked and with disheveled hair,
the practitioner of mantra, intent on the state of the deity, should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
The accomplishment of mantras shall belong to that son of a goddess upon the earth.
(In the *Muṇḍamālā*):
"O Goddess, O Beloved, that which is the supreme secret, more hidden than the hidden... (7.177).
I shall explain this very thing, and it will become manifest;
yet, O Great Goddess, that which is spoken must be kept secret as a mystery. (7.178)
In a beautiful and auspicious house, well-perfumed with camphor and other fragrances, its walls smeared with red pigment and adorned with a garland of red sandalwood; (7.179)
Seated upon a red seat, one should wear red flowers;
always smeared with red sandalwood and clothed in red garments. (7.180)
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times while meditating on the Goddess of the Gods as red in hue;
thereafter, one should offer a blood-oblation and worship her with red flowers. (7.181)
One whose body is as red as vermilion should offer a tenth part of oblations with red flowers known as *vajra*, sprinkled with the three sweets.
Afterwards, one should feed a maiden with red flowers, liquor, and so forth;
by performing it in this way, the practitioner indeed attains his desired accomplishment. (7.183)
He states what follows the *puraścaraṇa*:
"Alternatively, one should prepare a house whitened with lime and the like;
having sat upon a white seat, [one should perform the rite] with a rosary of pure crystal. (7.184)
Anointed with camphor and sandalwood, wearing white garments, and being pure,
one should worship with white flowers while meditating upon the auspicious Goddess of the Suras.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times while beholding the world illuminated;
one should then perform the fire-oblation with auspicious lotus petals using one-tenth of that number.
Likewise, with offerings mixed with sugar and honey and stirred with clarified butter,
[he should offer] white garments, a white garland, and ornaments such as white flowers.
Likewise, one should give a white unguent as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
and similarly, one should give [gifts] to young maidens and feed them with devotion.
The practitioner should afterwards eat himself with [food] accompanied by the three sweets, having first offered it before the Goddess with devotion and a pure disposition. (7.189)
Having performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) in this manner, it becomes supreme for increasing wisdom;
likewise, it increases fame and similarly brings about the subjugation of kingdoms.
In that same way, one should imagine the practitioner as having a serene heart;
or else, one may perform the rite of *puraścaraṇa* in another manner.
One who is devoted to the guru attains the desired accomplishment, having placed vermilion in the center of the maṇḍala within the interior of the temple. (7.192)
There, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus smeared with vermilion powder;
one should paint the petals in yellow, green, white, and blue, respectively.
Having drawn a stainless pericarp with powders of turmeric,
one should worship the chosen deity there in the center, in the form of a full water-pot.
Having placed the five jewels as well as the water of the five nectars,
the best of practitioners should cover the jar with a red cloth.
Having paid homage to the Guru, one should perform ten thousand recitations of the supreme mantra;
one should diligently perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a thousand bilva leaves.
A person should offer oblations upon an eight-petaled lotus diagram smeared with red sandalwood paste, drenched with the three sweets, and sprinkled with goat's blood. (7.196)
In the center, it should be served with milk-rice mixed with jaggery, its head adorned with honey,
and previously worshipped with a garland of red flowers belonging to a goat.
Having released the supreme *vali* offering, one should then gaze toward the directions;
those enemies will flee swiftly at night, driven by fear.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
on a Thursday coinciding with the fourteenth lunar day, one should take an offering from the temple. (7.199)
Having gone to the cremation ground, one should perform the offering of the *bali*;
having constructed the previously described pavilion, one should then present the *bali* at night.
Having first worshipped Bhairava, one should then worship the Goddess;
seated upon a tiger skin with disheveled hair, the wise man should perform the recitation (japa).
O Goddess, the most excellent of heroes, being fearless, [should offer] ten thousand;
then he should present the bali-offering, beginning with wine, situated at the gate of hell.
Having paid homage to Bhairava and the Goddess, [one should offer] blood and liquor, as well as milk-rice, curd, boiled rice, or even rice with jaggery. (7.203)
Having become fearless, one should bow down; then, filled with joy, one should go to the temple.
Freed from great sins, one becomes a partaker of sovereignty. (7.204)
Invincible by hosts of enemies, he shall become a master of explanatory speech;
merely upon being seen, he will captivate the hearts of women like another god of love. (7.205)
Alternatively, in an empty temple, within a circle reddened with vermilion,
one should [worship] a woman on the night of the fourteenth day during the dark fortnight, in the middle of the night.
Having brought a woman endowed with beauty and having adorned her with ornaments,
garments, garlands, and unguents, one should especially worship her.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon her, one should worship Ānandanandinī while consuming fragrant substances, a thousand and one hundred times.
One should offer an oblation of fresh milk mixed with wine and sweet substances;
endowed with devotion, one should present this as a food offering (naivedya) to her.
From that, one shall obtain the supreme power of subjugation over the three worlds,
as well as perfect skill in poetic composition and the ability to perform effective attraction.
When that faultless [state] is attained, O Supreme Goddess, the most excellent practitioner will certainly become one who possesses perfect bliss through this [means]. (7.211)
O Goddess, this is even more secret; it must not be revealed under any circumstances by a practitioner who desires great siddhi, for it is difficult to find on earth. (7.212)
Alternatively, O Goddess of gods, hear the supreme *puraścaraṇa*:
subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) with hair loosened, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times with devotion.
p.574) His speech shall be of every kind, consisting of both prose and verse;
or else, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner. || 7-214 ||
O Goddess, one should have lamps offered at night after the [deity] has been adorned during the day;
one should draw a mandala in the center with sixty-four [lamps] in the four directions. (7.215)
Then, using vermilion and colored powders, one should again draw a sixteen-petaled lotus;
thereafter, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should fashion the pericarp in the center.
Having drawn two triangles, one should place a water-pot there;
furthermore, it should be filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and provided with leaves of dūrvā grass, mango, and other such plants.
Having covered it with a soft cloth, especially one that is red,
and then having performed the binding of the directions, he should remain seated upon a seat of leopard skin.
Having sat down, one should invoke the desired deity and worship her there according to the ritual of the five services; thereafter, one should begin the recitation.
Excluding the first watch and avoiding the fourth,
one should perform the recitation during the two middle watches, preceded by the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and other preliminary rites.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should diligently offer an oblation of a black goat;
thereafter, following the sequence of the recitation, one should perform the fire sacrifice and other rites in the morning.
Having performed the libation and the ritual sprinkling, as well as the feeding of Brahmins,
the practitioners should then worship the young girl and subsequently satisfy her.
Having performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) in this manner, it always brings about great accomplishment;
Bhairavī herself becomes subject to those who perform the *puraścaraṇa*. (7.223)
By the power of a perfected mantra, one may bring the three worlds under control;
furthermore, I shall now explain the supreme preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
Listen, O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, to that which swiftly bestows swift fruit:
beginning from the fourth day of the dark fortnight until the fourth day of the bright fortnight. (7.225)
A woman, being self-restrained, should recite the mantra preceded by the observances;
thereafter, the fire-oblation and other rites should be performed, so that this may become complete.
Then, having meditated upon the Goddess with enthusiasm, one who is well-established should perform the recitation;
thereby the practitioner of the mantra attains his desired success. (7.227)

Alternatively, on the thirteenth lunar day falling on a Tuesday, one who is well-adorned with soft garments and having applied fragrant unguents to the body may joyfully lie upon a bed of flowers. (7.228)
Having adorned and brought into his presence a woman who is unfaithful, he should grasp her with a flower and recite [the mantra] in a secluded chamber. (7.229)
The wise one should recite the mantra with a rosary of coral or a rosary of pearls according to his capacity; thereafter, he should offer an oblation to the Goddess.
Having prepared excellent milk-rice mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sugar, and having fashioned a garland from fragrant flowers and fresh sprouts, [he should offer it]. (7.231)
Having offered that garland to the Goddess and placed it upon her hair,
the best of practitioners should not perform any act of desire.
Having given her ornaments and other gifts, one should present them before the Goddess;
having especially offered them to the Goddess, one should then dismiss her.
Then, the wise one should spend the remainder of the night in vigil;
such a rite as this increases the joy of the Goddess. (7.234)
By performing it thus through the mantra, the practitioner attains accomplishment;
O Goddess of the Gods, this rite is easy to perform, provided it is governed by fortitude.
(576) "What has been told to you is indeed to be well-guarded; it must not be revealed under any circumstances.
O Pārvatī, for the sake of curiosity, I shall tell you something else. (7.236)
The practitioner, having prepared a mandala made of turmeric powder in front of him, shall become beloved by all the world through this ritual. (7.237)
One should place an auspicious plantain tree with four doors and provided with leaves;
having offered rows of lamps upon them with particular skill.
On the eighth day, beginning in the morning, one should recite [the mantra] throughout that day and night;
having offered the bali according to the rules, one should perform the rites from the fire-oblation (homa) at the end to the beginning.
Having observed a fast, one should perform the rites ending with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the morning;
the practitioner of mantra, holding yellow orpiment in his hand, shall attain supreme great accomplishment.
All of this has indeed been told to you, O beautiful lady, for it is to be well-guarded.
(From the Kālītantra) Or else, in a secluded and pleasant place, a man [should practice] on a seat consisting of a bed of bones. (7.241)
Having recited the mantra *ubhayāstam*, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
having diligently placed a corpse upon one's own lap at the root of a *bilva* tree. (7.242)
Having gazed with the Nṛsiṃha-mudrā, a person should recite the Mātṛkā;
having recited it a thousand times there, he shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
(In the Bhairavatantra:
Having performed one thousand and eight [recitations], one should chant it every day; within six months, one becomes endowed with supernatural powers, a poet, and a treasury of knowledge. (7-244)
In another tantra:

"Seated upon a corpse-bed at night in the Great Forest of Ancestors (Mahāpitṛvana), the mantra-practitioner should recite [the mantra] six thousand times; he shall become a master of all accomplishments. (7.245)
(p. 577) These three also pertain to the subject matter of the first vidyā. (In the *Sādhanasamuccaya*:
"On whichever lunar day belongs to whichever deity, on that [day] the most excellent practitioner [should practice]."
Beginning from sunrise until sunset occurs. || 7-246 ||
Starting from sunset until sunrise, one should recite the mantra for that duration; this is declared to be the *puraścaryā*.
The wise should perform the rites, beginning with the fire-oblation and ending with the feeding of Brahmins, as previously described.
(From the Agastyasaṃhitā:
On the ninth day of the month of Caitra, Rāma himself was born as Hari. (7-248)
That lunar day conjoined with the Punarvasu asterism grants all desires;
likewise,
on that most meritorious day, one should act with devotion directed toward Rāma.
Seated in solitude, one should recite [the mantra] until the tenth day;
by that alone the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is accomplished. On the tenth day, one should feed the twice-born brahmins.
One should devotedly offer various kinds of food and drink, as well as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
by that, one’s purpose is accomplished and Rāma immediately becomes pleased. (7.241)
He states the determination of the lunar day (tithi):
"If the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Caitra is joined with the asterism Punarvasu, that very day becomes most meritorious through its conjunction with midday. (7.243)
The ninth [tithi] pierced by the eighth must be avoided by those devoted to Viṣṇu;
indeed, the fast is on the ninth, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the tenth alone.
(Vāḍavānalīya) I shall now describe the supreme *puraścaraṇa* for those who are unable [to perform the full ritual].
Starting from the first lunar day (*tithi*) of the fortnight, it continues until the lunar day of that deity. (7.246)
One should recite [the mantra] for two watches (six hours) using a rosary made of beads;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform worship every day, including the fire-oblation and other rites.
"Regarding 'for whichever mantra the *puraścaraṇa* is desired': the meaning here is that the *puraścaraṇa* consists of the previously mentioned recitation of one hundred thousand times (*lakṣajapa*).
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* performed at the time of an eclipse. As it is said in the *Merutantra*:"
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner. || 7-248 ||
During an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, being pure and having fasted beforehand,
one should stand in water reaching to the navel in a river that flows to the ocean.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the time of touching [the water] until liberation;
having recited it for that duration, one should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and other rites. (7.250)
One should subsequently feed the Brahmins; this [rite] is equal to the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) for the performance of the expiation and for the destruction of transgression. (7-251)

For those [practices] in which no specific number for recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed in the tantras, this preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is the one kept secret in all the tantras. (7.252)
Also in another tantra:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, being pure and having previously fasted, one should stand in water reaching to the navel in a river that flows to the ocean. (7.253)
Alternatively, having bathed in pure water, being composed in a clean place, one should perform the recitation with undistracted mind from the time of contact until liberation. (7.254)
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites in sequence, using a tenth part [of the total].
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a grand worship and feed the Brahmins.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra, one should worship and satisfy the guru;
thereafter, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual applications (prayoga) as set forth in the Kalpa.
(p. 579) (In the Kālītantra:
Or else, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, from the moment of the first contact until its release. || 7-257 ||
Having recited the mantra for as many times as the number [prescribed], one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites for that same number of times.
(From the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*):
Alternatively, there is another method for the procedure of the *puraścaraṇa*. (7-258)
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, having bathed with a restrained mind,
one should recite the mantra with undistracted attention from the moment of contact until its release.
Having seen [the eclipse], bathed, and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the recitation (*japa*) until its release;
likewise, a pure man should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites until the end of the eclipse.
In this way, through recitation, the accomplishment of the mantra certainly occurs; there is no doubt.
"To that extent" means as much recitation as has been performed.
This has also been stated in the *Siddheśvarīmata*:
O Goddess, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, [the period of merit lasts] from the beginning of the eclipse until its release. || 7-261 ||
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites for as many times as the mantra has been recited;
the five-limbed ritual (pañcāṅga) should likewise be performed that many times, for recitation and homa are traditionally considered equal.
The *Siddheśvarīmata* has been proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
(As stated in the *Candrapīṭha*, *Mantradevaprakāśikā*, *Ratnāvalī*, and other texts:
"Having observed three fasts, or otherwise according to one's capacity," (7.263).

The *śrāddha* and other rites are performed with extreme brevity; upon grasping [the water], it is sufficient merely to touch it while standing waist-deep in the water of a river flowing to the ocean. (7.264)
One should perform the recitation (japa) up to its conclusion, followed by the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites consisting of a tenth part of that;
having given the complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one shall attain the perfection of the mantra.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*) as set forth in the ritual manuals (*kalpanā*).
(From the *Tantracintāmaṇi*, citing the words of another tantra:
"Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described in another manner. (7.266)
During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, O Maheśvarī, standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should perform the recitation from the moment of the first swallow until its release.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that, and then again with a tenth part of that—thus three times in succession;
or, by this sequential method, one may perform the recitation (japa) at the place of union.
Standing upon a single big toe until liberation from the final morsel of food, one performs the preliminary rite known as the five-limbed, the eight-limbed, or the ten-limbed [observance]. (7.269)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform this with effort and shall become a master of all siddhis;
or else, the puraścaraṇa is described by another method.
During an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one who is pure and has previously fasted [should perform the rite];
for half a ghaṭikā before the eclipse begins, the eclipse is already present. || 7-271 ||
At that time, one should perform the ritual bath; when [the moon] is eclipsed, one should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
O Pārvatī, there is no impurity arising from birth or death during an eclipse.
One should perform the recitation up to the end of the liberation; when it is correctly known, one should conclude.
One should consider half a ghaṭikā as not yet arrived when the sun is obscured. (7.273)
Then one should perform the conclusion; thus, one whose mantra is perfected will certainly become successful.
If the sacrifice is ruined through negligence, one should feed many Brahmins. (7.274)
If any limb [of the ritual] should be omitted, one must perform the feeding of twice-born men along with its constituent parts;
one should perform the fire-oblation (havana) as a tenth part [of that], and the libation (tarpaṇa) as a tenth part of that.
The cleansing should be performed with a tenth part of that [number], and the consecration with a tenth part;
likewise, the feeding of Brahmins should be a tenth part, and the man shall become like a god. (7.276)
For whichever limb is deficient, the recitation (japa) should be double that number;
for Brahmins and the others, the sequence is remembered as being two, three, three, and fivefold respectively. (7.277) p. 581)

During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind from the moment of contact until its release; during that time, one should perform the fire-oblation and other rites. (From the Vāḍavānalīya) 7.278.
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is said to consist of one-tenth of that [number].
Here, the term "point of contact" (sparśapada) refers to the knowledge of the contact.
That which is the visual perception of Rāhu is called "grasping" (grahaṇa). (7.279)
"One should perform the rites there merely by counting [the beads]," according to the statement of the Smṛti;
and likewise:
No other time is praised for such acts as much as the time of a solar eclipse and so forth.
But he who, out of regard for ancestral rites during an eclipse of the moon or sun, does not perform the preliminary practice (puraścaryā), he is cooked in hell. (7.281)
According to such statements, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) involving the recitation of mantras is mandatory for practitioners.
"At the sight of Rāhu (during an eclipse), a *śrāddha* must certainly be performed even at the cost of one's entire wealth;
he who, out of atheism, does not perform it, sinks like a cow in the mud. (7.282)

The author of the *Sudhārṇava* maintains that the deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the performance of *śrāddha* according to the *Smṛti* refers to those other than the initiated (*dīkṣita*).
This has also been stated by Sanatkumāra:
"He who, having abandoned the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), performs the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*)."
He becomes an offender against the deities and leads seven generations of his ancestors to the netherworld.
Thus some prescribe the *śrāddha* by means of a substitute;
others, however, state:
"In the absence of food, in the absence of twice-born [guests], during travel abroad, or at the birth of a son..."
Indeed, during an eclipse, a Śūdra himself should perform the Hemaśrāddha.
Based on this statement, they perform the *puraścaraṇa* after having performed the *hemaśrāddha*. The *hemaśrāddha* is the gift of gold according to one's capacity, dedicated to the ancestors.

However, the authors of the *Kalpalatā* state that the statement by Sanatkumāra beginning with "having abandoned the sacrifice of recitation" (*japayajñaṃ parityajya*) refers to a solar eclipse occurring at midday during the course of an already commenced *puraścaraṇa*.
In reality, for the followers of the Smṛtis, the Śrāddha is essential, whereas for the Tantrikas, the *puraścaraṇa* is essential;
for it is stated in the *Siddhāntasāra*: "The Tantrika should perform *japa*, while the Smārta should perform the Śrāddha."

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) during an eclipse is as follows: *Oṃ, today [etc.,] when the sun or the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu, I, belonging to the [such-and-such] lineage (*gotra*) and named [such-and-such] Śarmā, desiring the perfection of the mantra of such-and-such deity, shall perform the preparatory rite consisting of recitation (*japa*) from the moment of the eclipse until its release.* Regarding this, some say:
Recitation, fire-oblation, libation, sprinkling, and the feeding of Brahmins. || 7.285 ||
In this world, the five-limbed worship is considered the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
Likewise:
"One who desires success for this mantra should perform as many recitations [as prescribed] from that point. (7.286)
One should perform the fire-oblation (havana) consisting of one-tenth [of the recitation], and the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth of that;
one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) one-tenth [of that], and the feeding of Brahmins one-tenth of that. (7.287)

Based on such statements, it is held that within a single formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the *pañcāṅga-upāsanā* (five-limbed worship) alone constitutes the *puraścaraṇa*. However, in cases such as the *puraścaraṇa* for an eclipse, the term *puraścaraṇa* is used figuratively (*bhākta*). This is because [in those cases], it consists merely of recitation (*japa*) and lacks the five-limbed worship separated by a single resolve. They further state that the injunctions regarding fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth therein are intended to indicate an equivalence to the primary *puraścaraṇa*; however, this view is to be considered with care (*taccintyam*).

In the *Merutantra* and other such texts, even regarding the primary *puraścaraṇa*, it is stated that one should first make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for mere recitation (*japa*). Furthermore, since it is stated in those very same sources that *puraścaraṇa* may have fewer or more ancillary parts (*aṅga*) depending on the distinctions of the Mantra-path and so forth, there is no authoritative evidence that the term *puraścaraṇa* applies exclusively to the worship of the five ancillaries preceded by a formal resolve. Moreover, statements such as "the worship of the five ancillaries is desired in the world as *puraścaraṇa*" refer specifically to the *puraścaraṇa* of those mantras for which the five ancillaries alone constitute the *puraścaraṇa*, and do not apply to the *puraścaraṇa* of mantras in general. The inclusion of the resolve for the recitation along with its ancillaries in a single sentence, however, is for the sake of brevity.

(Sādhanasamuccaye) Having abandoned fear of even minor defects, and having observed Rāhu as determined by the science of astrology, one should perform recitation (*japa*), which bestows the fruit of ten million merits. (7-288) p. 583)
The remedy for the defects mentioned in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra) is also stated in that very same place:
"A wise man, having worshipped with the five services a silver moon and a golden sun, should give them to a Brahmin."
Likewise:
"When the recitation has been resolved upon as lasting from the beginning of a meal until its conclusion... (7.289)
Having understood from the scriptures that they are seized by [planets], one should abandon the recitation for the sake of liberation;
without having seen the sun or the moon [emerge], one should certainly not eat. (7.290)
Likewise:
"One should not eat for three watches prior to a lunar eclipse, nor for four watches prior to a solar eclipse. (7.291)
As for that which is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:

"One should eat in the afternoon, not at midday; if one eats at midday, not during the *saṃgava* [period]; if one should eat during the *saṃgava*, one must not have performed a meal previously. (7.292)
This statement refers to the case of children, the elderly, and the sick.
As stated by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"During a solar eclipse, however, one should not eat for the four watches (yāmas) prior [to the eclipse]."
But during a lunar eclipse, one should observe three watches (yāmas), except for children, the elderly, and the sick.
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the medicinal herbs of the [five] colors. (From the *Merutantra*):
Having received [the transmission] from an unsuitable guru, they take refuge in a place such as water and so forth. (7.293)

Because of the difficulty of the location, it is indeed not possible to perform the preliminary practice (puraścaryā), whether due to the king’s fortune or because one is too delicate, as the case may be. (7.294)
Success shall thus come to pass; I shall now describe the ritual application of colors and medicinal herbs.
That [application] should be understood as sevenfold, granting success through the months corresponding to the colors.
One should fashion auspicious pills from the syllables of the mantra and medicinal wood;
these should be moved according to the sequence of the letters, both in direct and reverse order. (7.296)
The beads should be made such that they range from large to small;
the garland should have the form of two serpents, and with it one should always perform the recitation.
This first type of recitation is known as the "garland" (mālā), consisting of a specific number of beads;
all the beads, being equal, should be strung upon a golden thread.
This second [practice] is that the garland for the neck should always be worn around the neck;
likewise, having strung these upon a thread, one should worship them so that they shine beautifully. (7.299)
This third stage is the progression by way of the path resembling that of the gods;
the fourth is the daily bath with a decoction of medicinal herbs and grains.
The fifth [method] is that one should lick the powder of the *varṇa* herb with cow’s ghee;
one should perform anointing with that powder—this is proclaimed as the sixth.
"One should perform the constant wearing of that ash"—this is the seventh [verse].
The medicinal herbs for the castes have been mentioned previously.
Now follows the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the hero (*vīra*).
In this context, only the night is the [proper] time, not the day; as it is said in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "When the first watch has passed, until the end of the third watch... (7.302).
One should perform the ritual at night, but one must not recite [the mantra] when the night has passed;
being well-restrained, one should always eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) as a single meal.
(In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*):

At the time of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one who has been initiated should worship the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) with garments, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with foods consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (7.304)
Having brought [the vessel] into an empty house and purified it with argha-water,
and having performed the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), one should lead the Śaktis before oneself.
Having brought together the substances and other items required for the worship of the *śakti*, one performs the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of making them nectar) upon those very things.
Likewise: "Having sprinkled all of them with the *argha* water according to the prescribed rule... (p. 585).
One should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), and thereafter the rite of total integration (sakalīkaraṇa).
Herein are the rites such as the consecration with nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) for the powers (*śakti*). He speaks of the powers to be worshipped:
"Now I shall describe the eight maidens, since they bear the form of the Goddess."
The Brāhmaṇī, the Kṣatriyā, the Vaiśyā, and the Śūdrā who is an ornament to her family. || 7-307 ||
The courtesan, the barber’s daughter, the washerwoman, and likewise the female ascetic—all these indeed are noble women endowed with exceptional skill. (7.308)
Beholding the eightfold variety of forms of the maidens, they acted out of indignation and were designated by the names of the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmaṇī.
The forms, such as white and black, their gentleness, qualities, and so forth,
as well as the names of the Śaktis, are to be stated in the hymn that will be spoken. He now describes the method of worship:
Having first offered a seat, he should then say, "Welcome. (7.310)

Then one should offer the water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water; thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with scented flowers and water and perform the consecration of the hair.
Then, having incensed the hair, one should offer the silk garment;
thereafter, during another bath, having spread out a seat, [one offers] a pair of sandals.
Having given [these] and seated her there, having adorned her with various ornaments and decorations, one should offer unguents, perfumes, and garlands. (7.313)
Having invoked each respective power, one should bring them together upon their heads within a beautiful golden vessel in the center of the banquet hall.
When the food to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, eaten, and even consumed has been offered,
then one should present the *māyā*.

Regarding the phrase "tāṃ tām" (that [one] and that [one]): the meaning is that one should invoke and worship that specific Śakti upon the head of whichever [deity] has been designated by that name. And this invocation, though mentioned in the middle [of the ritual], ought to be performed at the very beginning, as it is observed to be so in all cases.
There, [having placed them] on their left ears, one should then perform the hymn of praise:
"O Mother, O Goddess, salutations to you, O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman. (7.316)
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra;
O Goddess Māheśī, granter of boons, whose form is supreme bliss! (7.317)
O Kṛpā, O Kaumāri, O Sovereign of all obstacles, you who delight in the play of Kumāra! || 7.318 ||
O Goddess who assumes the form of Viṣṇu, O you who are borne by the great Garuḍa! (7.319)
Out of compassion...
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting goddess, you who lifted up the earth with your tusk!
O Goddess who assumes the form of Śakra, you who are worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra—out of compassion... [7.321]
Obeisance to you,
O Cāmuṇḍā, who are smeared with blood from garlands of severed heads, O destroyer of obstacles!
Obeisance to you, O Mahālakṣmī, who destroys the affliction and agitation caused by great delusion! (7.323)
O Goddess, who consists of father and mother, yet is beyond father and mother! (7.324)
O Goddess of manifold forms, who are exceedingly vast, let there be salutation to you! (p.
587) He who, being well-restrained, recites this hymn at the commencement of a rite—7-325.
Or, having observed a clever woman, no obstacle arises for him;
however, if they are overcome by shame, then [the obstacle occurs] outside his house during the meal. (7.326)
Having stood, one should recite the hymn of praise until satisfaction arises;

Adorned with garments, ornaments, decorations, and the like, and facing the eastern direction,
the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) should be as follows:

*Oṃ, today [and so forth], I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious [Name] Śarmā, desiring the perfection of such-and-such mantra, shall perform the practice for the accomplishment of the cremation ground.* Such is the form of the resolve.
In the *Vīratantra*, it is stated:
"Sprinkling upon the sacrificial grounds is performed with the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra. (7-611)
Having meditated upon the pair of the Guru’s feet, as well as Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Yoginī, and the Mātṛkās, beginning with the left foot; 7.612.
And those gods who are stationed here, as well as the terrifying rākṣasas, piśācas, siddhas, yakṣas, and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases. || 7-613 ||
May the yoginīs, the mothers, the spirits, and all the women who move through the sky be the bestowers of accomplishment here, and likewise be my protectors. (7.614)
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should offer three handfuls of flowers to the Lord of the Cremation Ground,
Bhairava Kālabhairava.

The knower of mantras should worship Mahākāla with effort in the four directions, starting from the east, with water for the feet and other offerings; thereafter, he should present the bali offering. (7.616)
After that, the seed-syllable of sound (*śabdabīja*), followed by the Lord of the Cremation Ground (*śmaśānādhipati*);
at the end of this, the phrase "accept this offering of meat and food" (*sāmiṣānnaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa*). (7-617)
"Seize, seize the pair that wards off obstacles! Then bring about my success! Having spoken thus, give [it] accompanied by *svāhā*. (7-618)
O Goddess, the first offering (bali) is said to be with the mantra beginning with Tārā;
after Māyā and Bhairava, the word "Bhayānaka" follows. (7.619)
Having first extracted the *bali* offering for the east, one should bring forth the *bali* for the south;
then, after [the offering] to Mahākāla ending with *hūṃ*, one should extract it for the west as before.
In the western direction, one should assign [the mantra] to Kāladeva, beginning with the *praṇava* (OM).
At the end of the word "sound" (*śabda*), and at the end of the word "time" (*kāla*), the word "Bhairava" follows. (7.621)
One should likewise remove [the syllables] in between as before, saying "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (Śmaśānādhipa); then, one should place three excellent coils in the middle of the funeral pyre.
O Kālarātri, O Mahākālī, O Kālikā of terrible sound!
Accept this offering, O Mother, and grant me supreme accomplishment.
Having offered the bali with "HŪḤ! To Kālikā, svāhā!", one should cause it to be given to Bhūtanātha;
at the end of the word [for the deity] and at the end of Bhūtanātha, one should also say "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (śmaśānādhipa).
One should cause the supreme bali offering to be given with a mantra beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ).
At the end of "hūṃ, [name of] all Gaṇanāthas," one should likewise place the word "adhipati" (lord). (7-625)
Having placed it on the head in a cremation ground, one should extract it as before;
O beautiful one, having offered the bali-oblation with the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ) and so forth, [one should purify] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having performed the sprinkling of the bones, one should again place the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
On either birch bark or a banyan leaf, one should place the mantra of the seat there. (7.627)
In another tantra:
Then, having gathered the heap of bones together behind the funeral pyre, [one should worship] again with the mantra: "Oṃ Hrīḥ, obeisance to the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti). (7.628)
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow, one should write the mantra "hasauḥ" on birch bark or a banyan leaf, and then place that [leaf] there once again.

Having placed a seat made of wool cloth and so forth there, one should worship the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) with the mantra "Obeisance to [Her]," and there, one should also worship the one beginning with Hrīṃ.
(In the Vīra-tantra:

Having spread out the seat and having assumed the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*) upon it, one should then, O Goddess of the Gods, cast clods of earth in all directions during the "Heroic Assault" (*vīrārdana*). (7-631)
O Goddess, there are two *kūrca* seeds, followed by a pair of *māyā*s; then [the names] Kālike, Ghoradaṃṣṭre, Pracaṇḍe, and Caṇḍanāyike. (7.632)
Having said "dāraya" (tear asunder) for the Dānavas, then "hana" (slay) twice;
then "chedaya" (cut down) twice for the enemy hero and the great obstacle-maker.
This mantra, ending with *sarvāstrānta* and *dviṭhānta*, is known as the *Vīrādanumanu*.
One should cast a clod of earth consecrated with this mantra in the ten directions. (7.634)
In the midst of that, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles;
yet, O Goddess of gods, if through negligence the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear, [he is overcome]. (7.635)
Protected by all those various friends, he is not overcome.
[He who uses] a wick made from the cotton of the Arka, Indu, Sita, Vādya, and Āla plants...
Having established a lamp there, one should worship the weapon-mantra there;
if that great lamp goes out, one is overcome by obstacles.
And below that, one should bury the Kuladīpikā with the Astra-mantra;
then, according to the specific ritual procedure for each respective Kalpa, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites. (7.638)
Then, having projected either the sixfold [syllables] or the star [mantra], one should worship the deity; this is the ellipsis.
For this very reason, [it is stated] in the *Yāmala* and other texts:
Then, one should worship the deity in front with the fivefold offerings.
After closing one's eyes and meditating upon the deity, one should recite the mantra;
if it consists of a single syllable, one should then recite it a thousand times.
For a mantra of two syllables, the limit is eight thousand; for one of three syllables, it is fifty thousand;
beyond that, the knower of mantras [should practice] one thousand repetitions of the Gajāntaka mantra.
One should perform [the rite] starting from midnight until sunrise;
however, if the fear [of the darkness] is unbearable, one should bind the ears and eyes with a cloth. (7.642)
If nothing is seen until midnight, one should scatter mustard seeds with that same [mantra] while offering the *argha* with the Jayadurgā mantra. || 7-643 ||
Oṃ! You are sesame, having Soma as your deity; you are the essence of the *gosava* sacrifice, the cause of satisfaction.
You are the giver of heaven to the ancestors and the protector of mortals such as myself. (7-644)
"Bringer of peace amidst the obstacles caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*.
Having thus cast sesame seeds there, [one should worship] with four portions, beginning with Śiva.
Then, having gone seven steps, one should return and sit down in that very place;
having thus worshipped there as well, one should mutter the supreme mantra.
Being fearless, one should recite [the mantra] until success is produced.
Any fear should be understood as being like a dream; on the following day, one should perform the remaining rites.
In the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*,
at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to the deity according to the prescribed rule,
having taken a buffalo, a goat, or even a boar. (7.648)
p. 618) One should go home together with one's circle of friends, with a joyful mind.
Thus ends the procedure for preparing the funeral pyre.
Now follows the procedure for the preparation of the corpse.
As it is said in the Bhāvasarvasva of the Bhūtaḍāmara: "That which is hidden in all the tantras. (7-649)
Indeed, this procedure for the accomplishment of the Hero was taught by Śambhu, the God of gods;
by the mere knowledge of which even one of meager fortune attains success. (7.650)
Likewise:

"One who has completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) should practice for heroic accomplishment (vīrasiddhi), being entirely free from attachment to children, wife, wealth, affection, greed, and delusion. (7.651)
"Either I shall accomplish the mantra, or I shall cast off this body. Having made such a vow, one should contemplate the sacrificial offerings (validravya). (7.652)

(In the Vīratantra: Having taken up the previously mentioned offerings and so forth, the practitioner should accomplish the siddhi that is beneficial for himself; he should resort to a place suitable for practice. (7-653)
The wise one should rely upon everything previously mentioned, such as meditation on the Guru;
in the presence of Vīrārdaṇa, there is no delusion of illusion (māyāmoha) upon the ground.
With the mantra beginning "ye cātra... and so forth, one should offer three handfuls of flowers upon the ground;
then, as before, one should present the bali offering to the lords of the cremation grounds.
One should perform the offering of the bali-oblation with the mantra known as Aghora;
or one should arrange for protection with the Sudarśana mantra, or with both.
Again, the pair flashing forth from Māyā, and again the pair flashing forth;
at the end [of the mantra] is "ghoraghoratara," and after that the word for its form (rūpapada).
And within the space between the two *vaṭa* syllables, there is again a pair of *pra-caṭa*;
then a pair of *he*, a pair of *ra*, and after that, a pair of *bandha*. (7.558)
"Strike, strike"—this armor mantra, ending with *phaṭ*, is proclaimed;
this fifty-one-syllable mantra consists of the Aghora weapon. (7.659)
Having extracted the *hālāhala* [syllable], which has the nature of the thousand-spoked [wheel],
the great mantra of Sudarśana is proclaimed, ending with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) [syllables].
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), one should duly perform the network of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*).
With the mantra known as Jayadurgā, one should scatter mustard seeds in all directions.
"Oṃ durge durge rakṣāṇi svāhā"—this is the mantra known as Jayadurgā.
One should also scatter sesame seeds with the mantra "tilo 'si.
[The images of] those pierced by a spear, pierced by a trident, pierced by a sword, or those who have died in water [should be offered]. (7.662)
One who has been pierced by a rope, bitten by a snake, or overcome by outcasts;
one who is young, handsome, brave, radiant, yet lost in battle. (7.663)
One who is devoid of flight, most skilled in facing the enemy in battle,
one who has died by his own will, a two-year-old child, an elderly woman, and likewise a twice-born man.

Having abandoned a corpse that is devoid of food, one dead from leprosy, or one who has been dead for more than seven nights— thus discarding these eight types— one should take any other corpse previously mentioned.
Having taken it with the root mantra, one should bring it to the place of worship;
even if it has been seized by outcasts and the like, it quickly bestows the fruit of accomplishment. (7.666)
One should perform the sprinkling of the corpse with the weapon-mantra beginning with the *praṇava*:
"The *praṇava*, the *kūrca* seed-syllable, obeisance to the dead body, *phaṭ*. (7-667)
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should prostrate while touching [the deity], saying:
"O Vīraparamānanda, O Śivānanda, O Kuleśvara! (7.668)
O Śaṅkara, who has the form of Ānandabhairava and sits upon the lap of the Goddess, I, the Hero, offer you; arise for the worship of Candrikā! (7.669)
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should then cause [the deity] to sleep.
The mantra is said to consist of the syllable *tāra*, the word "sound" (*śabda*), and ending with "namas" directed toward the deceased body. (7-670)
This mantra for inducing sleep has been taught in all tantras;
having fumigated with incense or having smeared it with perfume and the like. (7.671)
O Lord of Gods, if one smeared with blood should eat the Kula-practitioner,
he should go into the presence of a corpse and wear [the remains] around his waist.
If it should cause distress, one should place spittle in its mouth;
having washed it again, one should lead it back to the place of recitation.
Having spread out a bed of *kuśa* grass and placed the corpse upon it there,
[one should offer oblations] with cardamom, cloves, camphor, jasmine, and the heartwood of *khadira* and *ārdraka*.
Having placed betel leaf in his mouth, one should turn the corpse face downwards;
having positioned it thus, one should smear its back with sandalwood paste.
One should visualize [the area] from the base of the arms to the hips as a square;
in its center is a lotus with four doors, endowed with eight petals.
Then one should place a deer-skin covered by a woolen blanket;
and sacrificial wood pieces, measuring twelve finger-breadths, should be placed in the cardinal directions.
"Accept this offering; cause a pair [of attendants] to accept it. Having warded off obstacles, bestow success"—thus is the second [mantra]. (7-678)
With this mantra, one should first offer an oblation containing meat;
having uttered each respective name and so forth, one should present the oblation as before. (7.679)
Then, the most excellent practitioner should offer an oblation (*bali*) together with wine to all the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and to the deities presiding over the corpse.
One should offer the bali to the sixty-four yoginīs and ḍākinīs;
the offering materials should be placed nearby, while the superior practitioner remains at a distance. (7-681)
Having prepared the seat and worshipped it, one should then mount the horse there with the mantra "trapāṃ phaṭ" at the end of one's own mantra.
Having placed *kuśa* grass under the soles of his feet and having wiped away the hair of the corpse,
he tied his topknot firmly, being one who accomplishes his resolve.
Having mounted upon the corpse and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should cast clods of earth in all directions with the Vīrārdana mantra.
Then, O Goddess, having worshipped the deity with extensive offerings,
one should perform the ritual for the nourishment of the deities (devatāpyāyana) according to the rules upon the mouth of the corpse.
Rising and standing facing [the deity], one devoted to devotion should recite:
"O Lord of Gods, may there be glory for me; thereafter, [grant] such-and-such a station for me. (7-686)
"O illustrious one, bestower of success, you whose feet are the sky that supports all beings!"—uttering this root mantra, the practitioner should then [grasp] the two feet of the corpse. (7.687)
One should bind it with silk thread; then it cannot be raised.
Oṃ bhīrubhīma bhayābhāva bhavyalocanabhāvuka! (7-688)
"Save me, O Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the lords of the dead!"—thus one should draw a triangular wheel upon the sole of his foot. (7.689)
At that time, even a corpse would be unable to rise and would become motionless;
then, having sat down again, one should pull out its two arms from the sides. (7-690)
Having spread kuśa grass upon his hands, he should place his feet there;
with his lips closed like a casket, he should remain steady-minded and firm in his senses.
Always meditating on the Goddess within the heart, one should perform the recitation while observing silence;
O Kuleśvarī, one should perform the recitation in a cremation ground for the number of times previously specified.
Alternatively, from the time of commencement until the sun rises—if, up until midnight, nothing at all is perceived while reciting—[then one should continue]. (7-693)
Then, as before,
having performed the offering of water for the feet (*argha*) and other rites according to the rule, one should sit right there and perform the recitation (*japa*) with undistracted mind.
"There is no fear from a moving seat; when fear arises, one should then say:
'O Goddess of gods, whatever you request—be it an elephant or anything else—it must be given. (7-695)
"I shall give you my name on another day; tell it to me.
Having spoken thus in Sanskrit, the fearless one should then recite [the mantra] again.
Therefore, if he speaks sweetly, one should then speak sweetly; at that time, one should speak the truth with refinement and then make a request of the man.
If he does not fulfill the truth or does not grant the boon,
then the wise man, worshipping with a one-pointed mind, should recite the mantra once again.
(Yakṣaḍāmara) When a marvel has occurred, one should not look at it, nor speak of it, nor touch it;
with a single-pointed mind, one should perform the recitation until [the deity] becomes manifest. (7-699)
(In the Vīra-tantra:
"There is no deity here in human form who approaches as a man; therefore, one must diligently discern whether it is a human or those born of divine lineage. (7-700)
Whether it be his mother, or his daughter, or even his maternal aunt,
having arrived and concealed her form through illusion, she creates an obstacle.
Arise, my child; everything that was to be done by you has been accomplished, there is no doubt.
The time of dawn has arrived, and your father is crying out in the house.
Generally, all kings who wield the rod of punishment are [themselves] commanded by someone at some time; what then will he do for you? (7.703)
By such various statements as these, one should not abandon the recitation (*japa*).
There, the hosts of ancestors who reside in distant lands have passed away. (7.704)
Then, kinsmen appearing in divine forms arrive there;
seizing his wife, sons, servants, and others, he is led away by his enemies.
All the sons, brothers, younger siblings, and disciples weep,
[remembering] the touch of their own beloved's body, as well as her garments, ornaments, and so forth.
The wife is seized and led away by the Pālakas; one should abandon fear of them.
If one is not agitated therein, then what indeed cannot be obtained? (7.707)
The goddess assumes the form of a woman, and the man assumes the form of a brahmin;
at the end of three recitations of the words "Receive the boon," he shall indeed obtain the boon.
Whether by a virtuous man or even by one who is not virtuous, if a woman grants her boon,
then what on this earth would not be accomplished for that heroic lord?
A man who is sinless and well-refined within his family,
while a goddess who is unrefined, will undoubtedly be possessed by sin.
Whether in his presence or not, he speaks another word in Sanskrit;
she is that very Goddess, there is no doubt, and he is Bhairava himself.
If it were not thus, then because the body is enveloped by illusion, one would not choose a boon there, nor would one ever proclaim a boon. (7.712)
