If he speaks in refined Sanskrit, he should be addressed in this manner;
otherwise, one should accept the boon without agitation according to the oral instruction of the Kaulika.
Alternatively, one may obtain some intense benefit for oneself;
or a true reputation arises, or even the nectar of immortality is attained. (7.714)
Having deliberated upon everything, one must grasp it; thus has the direction been proclaimed. (p.
624) The forms of the Goddess are manifold; in some places they take the form of humans and so forth. || 7.715 ||
One must certainly fear that [place], for there is no trust whatsoever to be placed in it;
for there dwell Bhairavas and Vaṭukas who are devoted to the Kula scriptures.
Under the pretext of this treatise, those of crooked form shall perform their deeds; having become his son, they shall choose him as a husband, and having become women, they shall delude him. (7.717)

Therefore, a hero devoted to reality should exert effort in the conduct [of practice]. (In the *Būtaḍāmara*) it is said that [the deity] comes and speaks what is desired, or indeed causes a throbbing in the body. (7.718)
By this, the accomplishment of a hero is born; then one should offer the bali-oblation.
Having bowed to the deity and the guru, and having dismissed them, one should again [dissolve them] into the heart.

The wise one should establish [the deity], satisfy [him], and cast the corpse into the water. (In the *Vīra-tantra*) once truth has been established and the boon obtained, he should abandon the recitation and other such practices. (7-720)
Knowing that the fruit has been produced, one should then loosen the tuft;
having washed it and established it, one should loosen the tuft at the foot.
Having cleansed the footprints, one should cast the ritual substances into the water;
then, having placed the corpse in the water or in a pit, one should perform the ritual bath.
Then, having gone to his own home and offered the oblation on another day, he said:
"At night, I am the sacrificer for those gods whose fire [is maintained]. (7.723)
May they accept this offering of food with meat given by me;
and likewise those who, when entreated, [take] horses, men, elephants, and pigs.
Having given [the gifts], one should observe the fast using only items made of flour;
in that regard, it may also consist of barley meal or rice powder. (7.725)

On the following day, having performed the daily rites according to the rules, he should cause [the image] to fall with the Candrahāsa weapon using its respective mantra; thereafter, he should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should feed twenty-five Brahmins there,
or take five at a time until reaching ten in sequence.
Then, having bathed and eaten, one should dwell in an excellent place;
if there is no food to be eaten by Brahmins, then one shall fall into poverty.
If, because of that, one should become destitute, then the Lord becomes enraged;
for three nights or six nights, one should conceal the practice of the Kula.
If one should go to bed [during these times], then disease arises;
by hearing music one becomes deaf, and from seeing a dance one becomes blind. (7.730)
If he speaks a word during the day, then he shall become mute;
for the residence of the deity within the body lasts until the end of fifteen days.
One should never at any time utter censure against cows, Brahmins, or the gods;
rather, being pure, one should touch the gods, cows, Brahmins, and so forth, every single day.
In the morning, after completing his daily obligatory rites, he should drink water from a bilva leaf;
then, when the sixteenth day has arrived, he should bathe at a sacred ford or similar place.

Having recited the root mantra ending with "svāhā," one should utter the words "tarpayāmi namaḥ. In this manner, following these three words, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the deities with water.
Without the satisfaction of the Munis, there can be no satisfaction for the God;
by this procedure, one certainly attains success. (7.735)
Having enjoyed excellent divine pleasures here, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari;
whether it be without passion or with passion, whether fruitless or fruitful. (7.736)
Having performed this very sādhana, one becomes most dear to Śakti.
(p. 626) In the absence of a corpse, the vīrasādhana should be performed in a cremation ground. 7-737.
If one does not worship with those very entities that have been declared for a particular [deity], the practitioner becomes fallen through such a yoga of sequence. (7.738)
One should not teach the nature of reality there, nor should one prescribe worship there;
only by reaching the limits of the cremation ground does purification arise. (7.739)
(From the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*):
Or else, I shall tell you another method of practice:
having thoroughly purified the place of recitation through digging and other efforts. (7.740)
In the center of that, one should offer the bali-oblation and draw a triangular yantra;
and in the middle of that, having placed the great conch, one should arrange the five severed heads.
Upon that, one should perform the anointing and other rites for a very beautiful great preta with unbroken limbs, and bathe it according to the prescribed ritual.
Having caused him to be clothed in a red garment and having applied collyrium to his eyes,
one should place betel and other items in his mouth and apply red sandalwood paste upon his forehead.
One should draw the yantra on the heart, a triangle in the center of a lotus;
then, one should inscribe the worship-yantra on the forehead with a weapon.
The wise practitioner should drive stakes made of *khadira* wood and other such woods into the head, the arms, the hands, the feet, and likewise the hips. (7.745)
One should increase the binding there and bind it with a firm bond;
one should offer the oblation in the six vessels, separately for each stake.
One should not offer as an oblation black gram, meat, fish, milk-rice, the three kinds of liquor, sweetmeats, large cakes, or milk-based foods. (7.747)
Having uttered the seed-syllable of armor (vaṃ), mounted upon the fire of Krodhīśa and endowed with the fourth vowel, and [the word] "Śmaśānakālike," || 7.748 ||
Having written the primordial seed-syllable (*pūrvabīja*), the mantra is said to end with the weapon-syllable (*astrānta*).
Having uttered the seed-syllable of *māyā*, [one says] "and to Śmaśānabhairava" (7.749).
"O deity Mahākāla, be the remover of all obstacles!
Accept the offering!"—thus one should divide [the mantra] into two parts; the thirteenth [syllable] is accompanied by the bindu.
O Rudras who dwell in cremation grounds and delight in offerings of fat and flesh,
ward off all obstacles and accept this oblation properly in two parts.
"Avoid obstacles and grant me an excellent pair;
the mantra ends with *dviṭha*—thus it is said—and *vali* is recited according to the prescribed rule. (7.752)
One should draw Māyā, Lajjā, and by her, Lakṣmī; then Nandinī, [and] the triad of Śata; likewise Nārāyaṇa, Sūkṣma, and Madhusūdana.
After the Yoginīs, [one should worship] the one who dwells in the cremation ground;
and [the mantra] "To Pracaṇḍā, who has a fierce form and carries a skull-cup and a knife. (7.754)

"Accept the offering (valim), seize the pair (gṛhṇāpaya yugam), ward off all obstacles (sarvavighnaṃ nivāraya), grant the boon (varaṃ dehi), say 'padaṃ', ending with 'dviṭha'—this is the offering to the Yoginīs. (7-755)
The fierce [seed-syllable] mounted upon fire, endowed with the fourteen vowels, pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā, and followed by "ṅe" for Kṣetrapāla. (7.756)
One should address the dweller of the cremation ground, who is fond of blood and bones;
having uttered the mantra ending with the *dviṭha* syllable, one should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Vārāhī, and then again the seed-syllable of Pañcāntaka,
one should extract the word "vakratuṇḍāya" and the armor-mantra (varma) as well.

One should utter the words "Accept the offering" (valiṃ gṛhṇa) and "Ward off obstacles" (vighnaṃ nivāraya), as well as "Grant me success" (siddhiṃ prayaccha me); this mantra, ending with the weapon-syllable (astra), is supreme. (7-759)
One whose form is the bliss of wine should perform the bringing down of the foot;
the Great Hero [places] the Śakti upon the heart and likewise upon the corpse. (7.760)
Naked and with disheveled hair, holding a knife and a skull-cup,
one should wash the *kulacakra* with *kuladravya* and worship it.
One should offer the bali-oblation of the five elements with incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth;
one should perform recitation according to one's ability and dedicate the root mantra. (7.762)
If the sash is tied in reverse or sexual intercourse occurs upon a corpse, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times there; one will then become a master of all accomplishments.
When he is indeed terrified and devours [the offering] at that very moment, and when he says, "Give! Give!", then one should offer the goat-sacrifice.
Violence must never be committed without the offering of a sacrificial victim (balidāna).
Through the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), the accomplishment of the mantra (mantrasiddhi) will certainly occur.
(From the *Muṇḍamālā*): Or else, one may perform the *vīrasādhana* in another manner:
having brought the spirits (*pretas*) who have fallen in battle, according to the prescribed ritual. (7.766)
Having established eight [stakes] in the eight directions and the ninth situated in the center,
they were fixed upon firm pegs with rope after rope.
Having sprinkled it with sandalwood and other substances, and having carefully adorned the head of the central [image] with fragrant flowers and the like, || 7-768 ||
One should worship the Goddess on the forehead with radiant offerings;
one should present oblations in the eight directions with black gram, meat, liquor, and corpses.
Then, with milk-rice mixed with honey, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice,
one should perform the recitation fearlessly at the heart of the corpse.
Having sat upon a red seat made of tiger skin,
and having recited the mantra fifty thousand times, one should then offer the bali oblation as before.
Having seen tigers, monkeys, bears, jackals, and those with faces like flaming torches, one should not feel fear; rather, one should contemplate them as mere illusion. (7.772)
Then, having obtained the [necessary] power, he should offer an oblation of a goat or similar animal;
likewise, having become free from mental distress, he should cast the corpse into the water. (7.773)
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born, especially to practitioners,
as well as with great effort to well-dressed women and maidens.
Likewise, clothing and ornaments, as well as the consumption of sweet substances, he himself may enjoy, but he should avoid them for other men. (7.775)
By this, however, the great accomplishment arises, which is difficult to obtain on earth:
sovereignty, prosperity, supreme bliss, and likewise victory over the kingdoms of enemies. (7-776)
Furthermore, his skill in poetry, such as that which enchants and subjugates the world,
and when directed toward him in battle, the army of enemies [is overcome] by the practitioner.
Even one who is bold flees [from it], let alone a petty enemy;
he shall become a vessel for the accomplishment of the various eight siddhis. (7.778)
This which has been spoken by me, O Goddess of gods, must never be disclosed.
This is supremely secret for you, especially in the assembly of the bound (paśu).
This is the supreme secret, the sole life-force of the scripture.
Thus ends the procedure for the *vīrasādhana*.

This highly esteemed confluence of rivers of excellent compositions abounds with the streams of nectar from the diverse and wondrous words of the pure speech of the Blessed One, which possesses marvelous splendor.
In this new *Naradevanirmitapuraścaryārṇava*, the seventh wave—towering with the brilliance of a cluster of clear pearls of sound reasoning—has come to an end. (7.780)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Mantra-Siddhi, the Means, and the Varieties of Puraścaraṇa," in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāpasiṃha Sāh.
Now, the mantras of Gaṇeśa and others, along with their specific preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), are presented.
Among them, first, the mantra of Vighnarāja is stated in the *Merutantra*:
A mantra given by an unaccomplished guru will bring many obstacles;
therefore, one should first practice the mantra of Vighnarāja, and only after that [proceed further].
For one who is free from sin, the supreme mantra shall be accomplished through the power of *puraścaryā*;
therein, according to the divisions of the traditional lineages (*āmnāya*), it is concealed within all the tantras.
I shall now declare the Vighna-mantra consisting of a single seed-syllable, which bestows excellent accomplishment.
In that regard, for the followers of the Vedas, the letter *ga* alone is considered [the mantra] at the outset. (8-3)

The [syllable] *dakṣiṇā* joined with a bindu is for the followers of the Eastern Path (*pūrvamārgin*); that same one joined with two bindus is for the Western Path; and in the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*), it is *gauṃ*. (8-4)
The Pātālāmnāya is proclaimed [to be recited] at the Glau and the Uttara Gomati;
Gaṇapa is its sage, Nivṛt its metre, and Vighna its deity.
"Gaṇaṃ japāya svāhā" is for the heart; "mekadaṃṣṭrāya huṃ phaṭ" is declared as the crest (śikhā); then "acalakarṇine namaḥ" is the armor (varma). || 8-6 ||
And "Salutation to the Elephant-faced One"—this is proclaimed as the weapon-mantra for the eyes;
and "Mahādaśamacāṇḍāya hūṃ phaṭ" is [the mantra] used by those following the Vedic tradition.
The Tantrika should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
Now, the meditation: [He is] clad in red garments, red in color, and anointed with red perfumes and unguents. (8-8)
He was being worshipped with red flowers; he was pot-bellied, bore the moon upon his crest, possessed three eyes, and was short of stature, holding a citron fruit in his trunk.

One should meditate upon Vighnavināyaka, who holds a noose and a goad in his left and right [hands], a discus and a boon-granting gesture in his upper [hands], and a lotus seat in his lower [hand], adorned with serpents. (8–10)

(In the Śāradā-tantra: [One should meditate on the deity] having the luster of vermilion, three-eyed, with a broad belly, holding in his lotus-hands a tusk, a noose, a goad, and the *iṣṭa* (desired object), and beautiful with a citron fruit shining in his great hand.

Worship Gaṇapati, whose crown is radiant with the crescent moon, who has the face of a lordly elephant with temples half-filled by the flow of ichor, whose head is bound by the king of serpents, and who is adorned with red garments and unguents.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount.
However, in the *Śāradātilaka*, it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; thereafter, one should perform oblations ten times that number"—so it has been said.
Likewise:
"With sweetmeats, flattened rice, parched grain, barley meal, and stalks of sugarcane... (8.12).
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) separately with coconuts, sesame seeds, and plantains,
numbering one thousand, two hundred, and fifty respectively.
The fire-oblation (homa) with petals smeared with the three sweets is for specific desires; now it is described:
an oblation with milk-rice mixed with ghee bestows the desired fruit. (8.14)
One desiring prosperity (lakṣmī) should likewise offer coconuts on the fourth lunar day;
"mocha" refers to the plantain fruit.
Now, the mantra for Lakṣmī-Gaṇeśa is as follows.
O gods, I shall now describe Lakṣmīgaṇapati according to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
This yoga, endowed with the fortune of an elephant, is exceedingly rare;
having first uttered "Śrī Gaṇapataye Saumyāya," one should likewise [invoke] Mahāgaṇapati.
Having spoken the near-mantra and having spoken "O bestower of boons," one should address all people:
"Bring them under my control, svāhā! This consists of twenty-nine syllables. (8.17)
The inner controller (Antaryāmī) is the sage, the metre is Gāyatrī accompanied by Nivṛt, and the deity is Lakṣmī-Gaṇeśa; here, however, [the application] is by means of the first two seed-syllables.
p. 632) One should cause the limbs to be fashioned together with the six long vowels and endowed with the [seed] syllables of their respective families.
Now, the meditation:
"Golden-hued, clad in yellow garments, [holding] the wheel, conch, boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness" (8.19).
Beginning from the upper right hand and ending with the lower right hand, he holds a golden jar upon a lotus with his trunk. || 8-20 ||
He is embraced by Lakṣmī seated on his left lap and by [the Goddess] with his right arm.

Regarding his preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it is stated in that very same source: "One should perform one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) and offer oblations (*homa*) of *vilva* wood-samids soaked in honey. (8.21)
Then, having performed the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites, one should accomplish the desired ritual (kāmyakarman) and so forth;
one should offer four thousand oblations of bilva fruits soaked in honey.
The fire-oblation (homa) brings about great fortune and bestows sons, friends, and a wife.
Now, the mantra of Śaktigaṇeśa from another Tantra:
Pañcāntaka [the letter *ha*] situated in Vahni [the letter *ra*], possessed of the left eye [the vowel *i*] and the half-moon [the bindu]. (8.23)
The three-syllabled mantra of the Lord of Ganesha, encapsulated by Māyā, consists of these syllables;
its metre is Virāṭ, and the sage is said to be Bhārgava. (Merutantra, 8.24)
One should perform the worship of the deity, Śakti, Gaṇapa, and the six limbs;
then, by means of the syllable *ga* joined with the six long vowels, one should meditate upon the elephant-faced one.
As for the meditation: in the upper right hand he holds a goad, and in the left a noose; in the lower left hand a citron, and in the right his own teeth; he is golden in color. (8.26)
Holding a sweetmeat (*modaka*) in his lotus-hand and long yak-tail whisks at his ears;
the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra is stated in that very same place:
"One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (8-27)
One should perform a fire sacrifice with ten parts of that [number] using cakes soaked in clarified butter;
thus, the practitioner whose mantra is perfected shall accomplish the rites for desired ends. (8.28)
Now, the mantra of Gaṇeśa for swift propitiation (as stated in the Nibandha):
Saṃvartaka joined with the two eyes (netra), situated on the side with fire as the seat;
enriched with its own seed-syllable, this ten-syllabled heart-mantra is for the purpose of propitiation. (8.29)
In the Merutantra:
The seer is declared to be Gaṇaka; the meter is said to be Virāj;
the deity is stated to be Vināyaka, who bestows swift grace. (8.30)
One should perform the ritual assignment of the mantra's limbs (aṅgakriyā) using the seed-syllable (bīja) that possesses the six long vowels.
Now, regarding the meditation (as described in the Śāradā-tantra):
[He] holds a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, and a tusk,
with a citron fruit placed upon his excellent trunk.
May the elephant-faced one—red-hued, with three eyes, bearing the young moon upon his crest, and radiant with a necklace—protect you. 8-31.
Regarding its *puraścaraṇa* (as stated in the *Merutantra*):

one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets, or else with the eight substances previously mentioned; thereafter, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. (8.32)
Now, the mantra of Vakratuṇḍa is given in that very same place:
"Vakratuṇḍāya hūṃ" is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra.
This short armor-mantra (kavaca) should be recited by women; it bestows all accomplishments. (8.33)
The sage is declared to be Bhārgava, the meter is cited as Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Vakratuṇḍa, who is saluted by gods and demons. (8.34)
One should fashion the six limbs by means of the six syllables contained within the mantra. Now, the visualization:
[He] has the luster of the rising sun, and holds a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness. (8.35)
One should meditate upon the red-complexioned one with a smiling face, holding [attributes] in his hands, within the heart.

Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it is said: one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (*varṇalakṣa*) and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount. (8.36)
With the eight substances previously mentioned, anointed with honey, according to the prescribed rite.
Now, the mantra of Heramba (in the *Śāradā-tantra*): "The ender of the five [letters], joined with the bindu, adorned with the left ear [vowel]. (8.37)
This mantra of Heramba is proclaimed to begin with *tāra* (om) and end with the heart (*hṛdaya*);
consisting of four syllables, it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life upon men. (8.38)
In the Merutantra, it is declared that the sage is Gaṇaka, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī,
and its deity is Heramba, who has five faces and rides upon a lion. (8-39)
The ritual of the six limbs is proclaimed as being joined with the six long seed-syllables.
In the *Śāradā* [Tantra], however, the meditation [is as follows]:

one should visualize Heramba, who has three eyes, whose vehicle is Hari, who bears the moon, and who possesses the luster of pearls, gold, blue lotuses, jasmine, and saffron; he has the faces of serpents and the radiance of the sun.
I worship Him who holds in His arms a proud gift, a fearless joy-bestowing sword, a chisel, a rosary consisting of heads and eyes, a mallet, a goad, and a trident.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this has been stated in the *Merutantra*:

"Having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds in a tenth part [of that number], and then perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites combined with the three sweets. (8.41)
Thus, once the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner of mantras should then perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*).
Now, the mantra of Haridrā-Gaṇeśa is found in another tantra:
"The ender of the five, situated on the earth (la), with its head adorned by a bindu. (8.42)
The single-syllable great mantra bestows the fruits of all desires;
or else there is another mantra.
O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra). (8.43)
Having extracted the seed-syllable *Indra*, one should extract one's own seed-syllable, adorned at its head with the fourteenth vowel (*au*) and the bindu. (8.44)
The single-syllable Great Vidyā was taught by the Lotus-born One; the ritual placement on the limbs and hands is performed with the seed-syllable conjoined with the long vowel. (8.45)
Other mantras have been omitted for fear of prolixity.
Now, as for meditation: one should meditate on the Lord, who has the hue of turmeric, four arms, and is clothed in yellow garments. (8.46)
The deity holds a noose and a goad, and possesses a sweetmeat and a tusk.
His *puraścaraṇa* is stated [in the *Merutantra*]:
having recited [the mantra] one million four hundred thousand times, at the end, with [offerings] mixed with turmeric powder... (8.47)
Having offered one-tenth of the portion as oblations with rice grains, one should also feed the Brahmins.
Now, regarding the Mahāgaṇapati mantra (in the *Merutantra*):
"In the Ūrdhvāmnāya, I shall proclaim the Gaṇeśas who bestow success. (8.48)

Listen now to the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation: the syllable *Tāra* (Om), the seed-syllable of Śrī, Hṛllekhā, Kāma, and the seed-syllable of the Earth (Laṃ). (8.49)
The seed-mantra of Gaṇeśa is "Gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā. (8.50)
This consists of twenty-eight syllables; the sage (ṛṣi) is considered to be Gaṇaka; the metre (chandas) is Nivṛt-gāyatrī; and the deity (sura) is Mahāgaṇapati. (8.51)

Ga is the seed-syllable, and hrīḥ is the power (śakti); the letter ga, joined with the six long vowels, should be performed by being separately conjoined with the six seed-syllables beginning with Oṃ. || 8.52 ||
One should perform the six limbs of this mantra joined with the *jāti* [svāhā], or else preceded by the *tāra* [oṃ] and joined with the six long vowels. (8.53)
One should perform the placement on the fingers with one's own seed-syllable and the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): On an auspicious island of nine jewels in the sugarcane ocean... (8.54)
On that cool surface of the earth, washed by the waters flowing with the play of its waves, and frequented by fragrant breezes mingled with those masses of water— (8.55)
On that ground, beautifully adorned and graced by wish-fulfilling trees, strewn with various flowers and resplendent with diverse birds. || 8.56 ||
It was filled with various fruits, frequented by throngs of apsarases,
and suffused with the light of the rising morning sun as well as the moonlight of the moon.
Upon a ground made crimson by a mosaic of shimmering clusters of rubies,
it was made melodious by the humming of bees over the blossoms of the wish-fulfilling tree.
In its center, one should visualize the Pārijāta and Kalpavṛkṣa trees, inlaid with six pairs of jeweled bands and adorned with flowers. (8.59)
One should visualize beneath that a lion-throne made of the nine gems;
in its center is the syllable-lotus, and in the middle of that is a six-spoked wheel.
One should meditate on Gaṇeśa in the pericarp and the Great Gaṇa situated within it;
(according to the Śāradā-tantra), one should contemplate Mahāgaṇapati located within a triangle inside a hexagon. (8.61)
I bow to the one whose face is like a lordly elephant, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, who possesses a ruddy luster and three eyes;
who is eternally embraced by his beloved, who holds a beautiful lotus in her hand and rests upon his own lap;
and who is endowed with a citron, a mace, a bow, a trident, a discus, a command-seal, a noose, and a blue lotus.
I worship him who carries in his hands a grain of rice, the tip of his own tusk, and a jewel-filled jar.
He repeatedly warded off with his two ear-flaps the bees whose minds were eager to drink the ichor flowing from the hollows of his temples.
Intoxicated with joy, he gratifies the practitioners with showers of jewels issuing from the mouths of ruby jars held in the tips of his hands.

Adorned with a crown of rubies and decorated with jewel ornaments—(in the *Merutantra*), the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra is stated: having recited it eleven times ten thousand times, plus one thousand, with devotion. (8.65)
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten times the [required] portion with the eight substances prescribed for the single-syllable mantra;
then, having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) ten times that portion, one is consecrated by means of the mantra.
One should properly feed the Brahmins with food of six flavors and give abundant sacrificial fees;
having given these and bowed down, one should dismiss them, and thus the mantra becomes perfected.
(In the *Śāradā-tilaka*, however,) it is stated:
"The practitioner of mantra, being composed, should meditate on the mantra and recite it four hundred thousand times,
together with four thousand [additional recitations], totaling forty thousand."
Now, the mantra of Viriñcigaṇanāyaka (in the Merutantra):
"Next, therefore, I shall fully declare the lords of the Gaṇas according to the Eastern Tradition."
Virañci and Vighneśa said:
Now I shall describe another [liṅga] worshipped by Brahmā, located in Kāśī within the vicinity of Brahmeśa, known as Viriñcigaṇanāyaka. (8.69)

Having uttered "Hrīṃ" and the word "Viriñcipada" ending in the dative case (Viriñcipadāya), followed by "Gaṇapati," and then "Varavara" and so forth as before, this is the twenty-six syllable mantra. (8.70)
The six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) are stated by [the letters] numbering four Vedas, five arrows, five arrows, and two syllables.
Likewise:
"I shall now describe its meditation; indeed, in the hands raised upwards... (8.71).
In the right hands he holds a citron, a mace, a bow, a discus, and a garland;
in the left, a lotus, a noose, arrows, a tusk, and a jar rich with jewels.
She has two lotuses in her hands, is nourishing, and rests upon his lap; she possesses a ruddy luster and embraces the ruddy one, whose cheeks are trickling with the intoxication of passion.
One should meditate upon the elephant-faced god, who has three eyes, wears yellow garments, firmly raises his banner, and is adorned with a crown and earrings. (8.74)
p. 638) The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] is as follows:
it is declared that for all [mantras], the preparatory service consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
One should perform oblations with the previously mentioned eight [substances] combined with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*). (8.76)
"Of all [these]" refers here to the mantras of Viriñci, Vighneśa, and others, which have been omitted for fear of prolixity.
Now, the mantra of Vighnagaṇeśa is found in that very same source:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare those [mantras] which bestow success in the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya)."
The leaders of the Gaṇas residing in Kāśī, who perform various wonders.
The sixty-four Vināyakas, who are portions of Mahāgaṇapati,
each take for themselves a Yoginī and even a servant girl in private.
Having reached the Golden Land (Svarṇabhūmi), as far as my inner chamber,
eight bestowers of supernatural powers (siddhi) are stationed within the eight enclosures.
There, eight [sacred sites] are situated on the heavenly ground outside Kāśī;
that perimeter extending one yojana outside of Kāśī is thus proclaimed.
"Ga" is declared as the six-syllable mantra for Vighna;
it is remembered as the means for accomplishing all eight [deities] and is equal to Kṣipraprasādana.
Regarding the specific requirements for *puraścaraṇa*, that same text states:
"One should recite the mantra ten thousand times more than the Vedas (forty thousand), and perform fire oblations with ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
In this practice, the ritual applications are swift, and the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are likewise swiftly attained. (8.82)
Now, regarding the mantra of Ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa, it is stated in that very same place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantras that grant success in the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya).
One should utter 'Hastipiśācī' and write 'svāhā'; this is the nine-syllable [mantra]. (8.83)
The skeleton is its sage, the Virāj is its metre, and the deity is said to be Gaṇeśa, the bestower of all prosperity; this is the one named Ucchiṣṭa. || 8.84 ||
The five-limbed ritual for this [deity] is said to consist of two, three, two, two, and two [limbs].
His meditation is described in another tantra: "One should meditate on Gaṇeśāna, red in form and adorned with all ornaments. (8.85)
He is clad in red garments, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a red lotus throne;
he has four arms, a massive body, two tusks, and a smiling face. || 8.86 ||
Holding the *iṣṭa* (desired object) and the *abhaya* (fearlessness) mudrā in his right and left hands respectively,
and holding a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*) with two other hands, he is adorned with a mass of matted hair (*jaṭāmaṇḍala*).
One should meditate upon Ucchiṣṭagaṇanāyaka, whose forehead is enriched with the crescent moon, who is adorned with all ornaments, and who bestows all desired objects. (8.88)
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] is said to be nine hundred thousand recitations on Mount Meru; now I shall describe the rites for specific desires.
Another mantra is stated in that very same place:
Now I shall declare to you another great mantra of his, consisting of twelve syllables.
"Oṃ hrīḥ ga hastipiśāci likha svāhā"—this is the mantra.
All practices, such as meditation, worship, and recitation, are to be performed just like those for the nine-syllable mantra. (8–90)
He states the *puraścaraṇa*:
"The *puraścaryā* shall consist of one hundred and twenty thousand [recitations]; the ritual applications (*prayoga*) and so forth are as before.
Thus ends the section on Gaṇeśa.
Now, the mantra of Sūrya (according to the Śāradā-tantra): Tāra, Ghṛṇi, and Bhṛgu, followed by [the letter] adorned with the left ear. (8-91)
The eight-syllable mantra of the Sun, which bestows desired objects, is proclaimed as follows: VAHNI (3), ĀSANA (4), MARUT (5), ŚEṢA (1), SANETRA (3), ADRI (7), TYA (2), PAŚCIMA (6). (8–92)
The sage is declared to be Devabhaga; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is declared to be Āditya, who bestows both seen and unseen fruits. (8-93)
The heart is declared for Satya; the head is said to be for Brahmā;
the tuft (śikhā) belongs to Viṣṇu; and the armor (varma) is proclaimed for Rudra.
The eye is declared for Agni; the weapon is cited as being for all [deities]. Tejas, Jvālā, Maṇi, Huṃ, Phaṭ, and Dviṭha are said to be uttered separately at the end [of each]. (8–95)
Other nyāsas should be consulted in that very same source. Now, for the meditation:
[one should visualize the deity] with hands holding a pair of red lotuses and granting protection.
I praise the Lord of Day, adorned with armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and earrings; wearing a crown of rubies,
possessing the luster of the Bandhūka flower, and with three eyes shining brightly.

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] is stated in that very same [text]: "One who has conquered the senses should mutter the mantra eight hundred thousand times and offer a thousand oblations with fuel-sticks from milky trees, anointed with milk. (8–97)
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"Ākāśa" (ha), conjoined with "fire" (ra) and the "long moon" (ī), is Bhuvaneśvarī;
conjoined with the "emission" (ḥ), it is the three-syllabled mantra of the Sun, declared as *ghṛṅ*. (8-98)
One should sequentially place the three seed-syllables from the Foundation (ādhāra) up to the tip of the feet, from the throat down to the Foundation, and from the head down to the throat. (8–99)
One should fashion the limbs with the middle [syllable] joined with the six long vowels. || 8-99ef ||
Now, regarding meditation: I worship the Sun, who sits upon a seat of red lotuses, the sole ocean of all virtues, and the sovereign lord of all the worlds.
Holding a pair of lotuses and the gestures of fearlessness and boon with his lotus-like hands, he has Māyā upon his crown, possesses a reddish bodily luster, and has three eyes.

Now follows its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one who has conquered the senses should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with food and clarified butter (*ājya*), or with sesame seeds sprinkled with the three sweets (*madhura*), using a tenth part [of the total count]. (8–101)
(p. 641) (In the *Merutantra*) Next, I shall declare another mantra, a six-syllabled one for the [deity] of the day:
*Ha Kha Khakholkāya*, or else *Khakholkāya* with the consort of Agni (*Agnigehinī*). (8–102)
The sage is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Savitṛ;
this mantra for the wife of Agni in her subtle form is considered to be the heart. (8–103)
The head [armor] is with the mantra "sūkṣmākārāyāgnivadhūḥ," and the armor, together with the eyes, is with "sūkṣmabālāya svāhā. (8–104)
The subtle body is formed; "phaṭ" is prescribed as the fifth limb.
With the syllables of the mantra, there shall be the six limbs; now its meditation is described. (8-105)

One should meditate upon Ravi, who holds a pair of red lotuses in his hands, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, has the luster of a bandhūka flower, possesses three eyes, and is beautifully adorned. (8–106)
Now, regarding his preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it is as follows:
With self-restraint and senses subdued, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should then perform oblations with a tenth part of that number using wood from the *vilva*, *aśvattha*, and *palāśa* trees. (8–107)

Then the wise practitioner should perform the libation and other rites with the best fuel-sticks produced from the *udumbara* tree and smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), according to the procedure previously described. (8.108)
Now, another mantra (from the Śāradā-tantra):
"The sky [Ha], adorned with a crescent moon [Ā], followed by that [S] and joined with the letter of creation [Sa];
this two-syllabled mantra, known as Ajapā, is declared to be the celestial wish-fulfilling tree. (8–109)
The seer is remembered as Brahmā; Gāyatrī is declared the metre;
and the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain (Śiva), the origin of the worlds, is proclaimed the deity. (8-110)
One should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) of the mantra by means of the syllable *hasa* joined with the six long vowels.
Meditation: O Mother, [I meditate upon] Him whose head has the form of a flashing lightning-bolt from the rising sun,
and who holds in his lotus-hands the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, the boon-granting mudrā, and the axe.
May the moon-crested, three-eyed one protect you—his body both gentle and fiery, the root of the universe, adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels. (8.111)

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one million times; one should properly offer oblations (*homa*) with milk-rice mixed with ghee amounting to one-tenth of that number; thereafter, the sage becomes perfected (*siddha*). (8.112)

Now, regarding the mantra of Mārttaṇḍabhairava, it is stated in that very same place: "The letter Ā, followed by Kha (the sky), Ra (fire), Va (wind), Sa (the beginning), Ya (the end), Arghīśa (Ha), and the Bindu—this is declared to be the seed-syllable named Mārttaṇḍabhairava. (8.113)

Enclosed by the seed-syllable of the *bimba*, it bestows the fruit of all desires; that which is joined with the letter at the end of the *ṭha*-group, fire, the eye, and the moon is thus described. (8.114)
One should install the five forms using the five seed-syllables beginning with the short vowels,
placing them in sequence upon the fingers from the middle finger to the little finger.
Sūrya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and then Ravi and Divākara;
these [names] are again [assigned] to the regions of the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet.
One should assign the limbs of the eyes using the seed-syllable joined with the long vowel;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka) with the root seed-syllable.
Meditation: [One should visualize the deity] whose innate luster resembles a golden lotus and coral sprout, holding a beautiful khaṭvāṅga and a lotus,
a discus, a spear, a noose, a very beautiful trident, a rosary, and a skull-cup.

We worship the Sun-god, who holds [the world] with his lotus-like hands, who is beautiful with three eyes and the shining face of the Vedas, who is worthy of his beloved’s offering, who wears a jeweled crown, and who is radiant with necklaces. 8-117.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
the practitioner of mantra should recite the seed-syllable enclosed by the two *vimbha*-syllables three hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with ten parts of that number using full-blown lotuses sprinkled with honey.
Thus ends the section on Sūrya.
Now, the mantras of Viṣṇu. (From the Śāradā-tantra, page 643)
Now I shall proclaim the great mantras of Viṣṇu, which accomplish all goals;
by the mere remembrance of which the virtuous have reached the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.

First the syllable *tāraṃ*, then the word *namaḥ*, followed by the two letters *na* and *ra* endowed with long vowels, and then *pavanaḥ*; this mantra, consisting of eight syllables, has thus been declared.
Nārāyaṇa is declared to be the object of attainment (sādhya), the sage is proclaimed, and the meter is stated; Gāyatrī is the goddess of the mantra, and the deity is the imperishable Viṣṇu.
The heart-mantra is declared for Kruddholkā; the head-mantra is remembered for Maholkā;
the crest-mantra is proclaimed for Vīrolkā; and the armor-mantra is considered for Vyulkā. (8.122)
This arrangement of the limbs is considered to be the discharge of weapons from the thousand-spoked wheel;
one should perform the six limbs with the six syllables of the mantra that have more phonemes.
Furthermore, one should place the two remaining syllables on the belly and the back.
Now, regarding meditation:
[One should meditate on Him] who constantly bears a conch, mace, lotus, and discus, shining like a million rising suns, with His two sides graced by Indirā and Vasumatī.

I worship Him who wears a crown, armlets, necklaces, and earrings; who is clad in yellow garments; who is radiant with the Kaustubha gem; who sustains the universe; and upon whose chest shines the mark of Śrīvatsa.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): with a concentrated mind, one should recite this mantra one million times;
one-tenth of that number of lotuses, soaked in honey, should be offered as oblations.
The characteristic of the transformation is sixteen lakhs. Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"Oṃ" (Praṇava), "Hṛt" (Heart), and "Bhagavate Vāsudevāya" (to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva) are proclaimed [as the components].
In the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, this twelve-syllable mantra is indeed preeminent.
The seer is Prajāpati, the meter is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī;
Vāsudeva is declared by the wise to be the deity of this mantra. (8.127)
The heart-mantra is said to consist of the syllable *tāreṇa*; the head-mantra is declared with *namasā*.
The crest-mantra (*śikhā*) is said to consist of four syllables, and the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) is considered to consist of five syllables.
By means of the whole [mantra], the assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) as a weapon (astra) is said to be performed. || 8-128ef ||
Now, the meditation:
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who resembles ten million autumnal moons, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus,
who dwells upon a white lotus, and who fascinates the world with his splendor.
I bow to Him who is praised by the lords of sages, who wears armlets, necklaces, earrings, and a great crown, whose bracelets shimmer, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem.

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): Having been initiated and having conquered his senses, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable; he should then perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) of one thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter.
Now, the mantra of Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva is given in that same place:
"The pair of *hṛllekhā* seed-syllables, followed by the pair of *ramā* seed-syllables;
then 'to Vāsudeva' at the end of 'Lakṣmī', ending with 'the heart' (*hṛt*), and preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ). (8.131)
This mantra, consisting of fourteen syllables, is said to lead to the state of the gods.
The heart is declared to be formed by the two seed-syllables of Śakti, and the head by the two syllables of Ramā.

The *śikhā* (crown) is declared by Lakṣmī; the *varma* (armor) is uttered as "to Vāsudeva"; "obeisance" (*namaḥ*) is prescribed for the *astra* (weapon); one should arrange all [these] beginning with the *tārā* (the syllable Om).
Meditation:
A body resembling lightning and the moon, attained through the power of affection as the union of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, adorned with a profusion of ornaments shimmering with jewels.
May He, who bears these—the mirror of the lotus of knowledge, a jeweled pitcher, a lotus, a mace, a conch, and a discus—always bestow upon you boundless prosperity. (8.134)

Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable, and perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with a thousand blossoming lotuses mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratra*). (8.135)
Worship should indeed be performed upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the method of the twelve-syllable mantra;
a fire-oblation made with milk-rice bestows the subjugation of Lakṣmī.
Having offered oblations with sesame seeds smeared with honey, one shall accomplish all undertakings.
[Regarding Viṣvaksenā: Now I shall declare another mantra of Viṣṇu that accomplishes all purposes. (8.137)

Having extracted the inner meaning of Viṣṇu, this six-syllabled mantra, beginning with the Unmanifest (A), which has the color of an arrow as its heart, serves as a bridge across the ocean of existence.

The Praṇava is unmanifest. Nārada is its sage; Gāyatrī is its metre; and the imperishable Viṣṇu is its deity. One should fashion the six limbs [of the mantra] by means of the syllables of the mantra. (8.139)
Meditation: One should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; who is surrounded by Lakṣmī; who wears yellow garments; and who is dark as a rain cloud. (8.140)
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable and perform oblations with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets.
Thereafter, one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites; in this way, the mantra becomes perfected.
Now, in the Matsya-mantra (of the Merutantra), there was but one incarnation of the Fish in the first kalpa;
I shall proclaim its mantra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (8.142)
*Tāraḥ*, *namo bhagavate*, *ma*, and *matsyāya*—one should utter *ramām*.
This twelve-syllable mantra is declared to have Brahmā as its sage (*ṛṣi*). (8.143)
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre; the deity is the Lord in the form of a Fish.
That Blessed One, the Lord of Ramā, is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Śrī is the pin (kīlaka). (8.144)
The ritual assignments of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) should be performed with the mantra-words. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[The deity] is like a red fish below the navel, and human in form up to the neck.
Dark as a rain cloud, with four arms, he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
His head resembles that of a horned fish; his chest is adorned with the mark of Lakṣmī;
all his limbs are marked with lotuses; he is handsome and possesses beautiful eyes.
He describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

One should recite [the mantra] twelve thousand times and offer oblations with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), daily during the months of Vaiśākha and Kārtika, using one-tenth of that number as the portion for each day. (8.147)

Having begun on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one who has conquered his senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) for sixteen days during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Māgha [attains the fruit].
One should daily recite this Lakṣmī-mantra one hundred times;
likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed, as well as on other days.
One should satisfy one thousand two hundred [deities] with sesame seeds, rice, and sandalwood;
likewise, one should satisfy Śrī with one hundred and eight [offerings] at the beginning and at the end.
Or with red lotuses, or with lotuses, or with fragrant flowers such as mālatī;
when this is performed for one year, the accomplishment of the mantra arises. (8.151)
He should always feed twelve Brahmins and a married woman of auspicious appearance, and he should perform its worship constantly at a reservoir of water.
Likewise:
"In this way, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Endowed with this, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. (8.153)
On the day of its presiding deity and so forth, proficiency arises from the book alone;
for one whose applications are unimpeded, there is no further need for refinement.
O Pārvatī, when these [mantras] are sprouted [with this prefix], my mantras become effective;
all Vedic mantras, when encapsulated by these, bestow success in the Kali age. (8.155)
Strung together and recited in this manner, [mantras] belonging to the Kaula tradition grant swift accomplishment;
likewise, those of the Ganesha, Vaishnava, and Saura traditions grant success when they are interlaced (vidarbhitāḥ).
By whose power the accomplishment of all mantras arises spontaneously, for that reason it has not been stated [elsewhere], nor is it found in other tantras; it is revealed in the Merutantra. (8.157)
Now, regarding the Kūrma-mantra, it is stated in that very same place:
"Next, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the most wonderful Kūrma-mantra.
A single incarnation as Kūrma appeared when the great ocean was being churned. (8.158)
*Tāra*, *namo bhagavate*, *ku*, *kūrmāya*, *dharādhara*, *dhurandharāya*, followed by *ṇa*—at the end of which is the perfected syllable (*siddhavarṇa*); this is considered the mantra. (8.159)
The meter is said to be Prakṛti; Kaśyapa is considered its sage (ṛṣi);
and the Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a tortoise, is held to be its deity. (8.160)
The power (śakti) beginning with "dharādhara" is the syllable *ku*; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is for the attainment of one's desired goal.
The application (*niyoga*) is the deity, whose meditation consists of bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (8.161)
Wearing yellow garments, adorned with a tail placed upon the back of a tortoise, long-necked, possessing great jaws, and having blood-red eyes, he was swallowing [the enemy]. (8.162)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the syllables of the mantra, recite it four hundred thousand times,
and perform an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) along with libations (*tarpaṇa*) using water mixed with sandalwood and blue lotuses.
Now follows the mantra-weapon of Varāha. Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the auspicious mantras of Varāha;
the four classes [of beings] born in the Kalpa are the incarnations of the Lord of Ramā. (8.164)
One should utter "Tāro namo bhagavate varāhāya," and then "rūpāya bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ pataye bhūpataye. (8.165)
"Give to me, cause [him] to give—svāhā"—this is the mantra with the color of a god.
(In the *Śāradā-tantra*) the sage is declared to be Bhārgava, and the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh. (8.166)
The deity of this mantra is said by the wise to be Varāha;
"ekadaṃṣṭrāya" is declared to be the heart, and "vyomolkāya" is remembered as the head.

One should arrange the five limbs as follows: "To the Lord of Splendor" for the crest-lock (śikhā), "to the one of universal form" for the armor (varma), and "to the one with great tusks" for the weapon (astra). || 8.168 ||
Now, as for the meditation:

from the feet to the knees it is like excellent gold; from the region of the navel downwards it has the luster of pearls; from the region of the throat it is like the rising sun; and from the head it has a blue radiance.

I praise the primordial Boar, who holds in his hands a discus and a conch, a sword and a shield, a mace known as the Śakti, and the gestures of generosity and fearlessness, and whose tusks shine as they support the earth.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] is described in that very same source:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) with lotuses smeared with honey;
one should perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount, and worship [the deity] upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*) of Viṣṇu. (8.170)
Now, other mantras (from the *Merutantra*):
Next, I shall fully declare another supreme eight-syllable mantra of Varāha:
*Oṃ bhūr varāhāya namaḥ*. Brahmā is declared to be the sage (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra. (8.171)
The Jagatī meter is prescribed, and Varāha is remembered as the deity;
one should fashion the five limbs with all the words of the mantra. (8.172)

Meditation: One should meditate upon [the deity] who has a dark body, a blue face, and is soiled, seated upon a lotus, joined with the Earth-power (Pṛthvīśakti), and holding a conch, a discus, a lotus, and a mace. (8.173)
Surrounded on all sides by Bhū, Lakṣmī, Kānti, and Rati, and by those bearing armor and swords, it bestows swift accomplishment in the Kali age. (8.174)
One should perform all rites such as recitation (japa) and worship for this [mantra] as previously described. Whoever worships this mantra shall become a lord of the earth. (8.175)
The single-syllable mantra "Im" is proclaimed as that of Varāha;
Hayagrīva is said to be the sage (ṛṣi), the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and he is the deity. (8.176)
The boar-form [deity] has its limbs assigned by means of the seed-syllable joined with the long vowel;
one should meditate upon him as red in color as before, and the worship and other rites should be performed as previously described. (8.177)
The single-syllable seed-mantra "Bhūḥ" is declared to be everything as previously described;
one should always meditate upon it as yellow in color, for it bestows swift accomplishment in the Dvāpara age. (8.178)

Now, the mantra of Dharaṇī (according to the Śāradātilaka): "The heart-mantra for the Blessed One, Dharaṇī, should follow that; at the end of 'Dharaṇī,' one should place the dual [vocative] ending, and this [mantra], beginning with the syllable *dhru* (om), ends with *svāhā*. (8.179)
The Heart of the Earth (Dharāhṛdaya) is said to consist of nineteen syllables;
Varāha is declared its sage, and Nivṛt is cited as its metre.
The deity of all beings is considered to be the Earth (prakṛti). It is declared that [the mantra] consists of three [syllables] for the heart and four [syllables] for the head. (8.181)
The crest-lock (śikhā) is taught with three [syllables], the armor (kavaca) is considered to consist of five;
the eye (netra) is declared to have two, and the weapon (astra) shall likewise consist of two.
One who knows the ritual procedure should thus perform the six-limbed protection with the syllables of the mantra. (8.182ef)
Meditation: [One should visualize] a dark-complexioned goddess, adorned with variegated garments and jewel ornaments,
seated upon a lotus throne, with full breasts and a beautiful face.
We worship the blue lotus, the two, the cluster of fresh rice, the parrot, the grain, and the earth. || 8-183 ||
(p. 650) He describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
"The practitioner of mantra should recite this *Dharāhṛdaya* with devotion one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform oblations (*homa*) with milk-rice mixed with ghee in a tenth part of that amount. (8.184)
One should worship her on the pedestal of Viṣṇu according to the procedure to be described;
[thereby] Nṛhari, the Lord of the worlds and the ocean of compassion, grants his blessing. (8.185)
Those who have taken refuge at his feet consider the ocean of existence as no more than a cow’s footprint;
indeed, he is a bridge for crossing over the otherwise insurmountable sea of saṃsāra.
The uncommon causes for the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha), which have been revealed in the tantras by the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva), are now being stated. (8.187)
The mantras of Śrī Divyasiṃha were worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods. (From the Merutantra:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the auspicious mantras of Nṛsiṃha. (8.188)
In every Manvantara, this incarnation of Hari occurs;
indeed, among the fourteen forms, he appears as Nṛsiṃha in another continent.
He dwells there until the end of the kalpa, bestowing grace upon his devotees;
now, Nṛsiṃha, who was born in the first Manvantara, shall be described.
Since this thirty-two-syllable [mantra] is secret and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, [it is taught] in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada concerning Vaiṣvaksenī:
"O Sage, listen attentively as I proclaim the King of Mantras. (8-191)
By whose grace I create the entire universe in its completeness,
having first raised up Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who was situated within Bali.
Thereafter, one should raise Bhūmibālaka together with Pradyumna;
then, one should raise Balarāma together with Govinda, endowed with affection.
At the end of Vaikuṇṭha, one sees Varāha together with Nārāyaṇa, and the bull named Samādhava-vṛṣaghnākhya who has gone to Naraka-jit. (8.194)
One should extract [the mantra] beginning with Śaṅkarṣaṇa and ending with Madhusūdana, together with Bālastha and ending with Muśalin, along with Balānuja. (8.195)
One should extract Hari joined with Vīrabhāga, Niruddha, and the others;
then Haṃsa at the end, overcome by Bala, and then Bhūdhara and Hari.
Accompanied by Vāsudeva, ending with Viśvamūrti, joined with Viṣṇu,
together with Aniruddha, bearing a mace, enriched with a trident, and possessing the three strides.
[The mantra] joined with Bindumādhava, ending with Haṃsa-Haṃsa, [and] Induka;
[then] the pair Govinda, Viśvamūrti, beginning with Vṛṣahari, and Induka.
Then [he offered] the true offering ending with Bhūdhara, together with Pradyumna,
along with Ādya-Vaikuntha and Hari, together with Puruṣottama.
Having twice extracted both of these along with Viṣṇu, one should place the head at the end;
thereafter, one should give [the mantra] ending in Sāttvata and preceded by Puruṣottama.

Having extracted the tenth [syllable] along with Keśava and Antya, one should extract Vaikuṇṭha and Puruṣottama; then the two Yogins and the Viśvamūrti, and finally the tenth [syllable] together with the Moon (Indu).
This king of mantras, consisting of thirty-two syllables, is a celestial tree;
it is marvelous, serving as the seed for virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (8-202)
But today it becomes the destroyer, the conflagration that burns heaps of cotton;
that which is celebrated as the abode of the Great Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman. (8.203)
O Sage, know that very thing to be this form of the mantra: self-luminous, pervading the universe, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. (8.204)
There is no god higher than Nṛsiṃha; there is no mantra higher than this mantra;
there is no meditation higher than meditation upon Him for the destruction of the fear of saṃsāra. (8.205)
This great mantra is to be worshipped by those who know the true essence of devotion to the Blessed One;
it must not be disclosed by you, my child, for it is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
This mantra is the crest-jewel among many millions of mantras,
just as the Lord Nṛsiṃha is the crown jewel of the deities.
If even by the mere remembrance of his name one is not born again into existence, how much more so for those who worship his lotus feet with faith and devotion? (8.208)
Why would the messengers of Dharmarāja look upon the face of one by whom the three syllables "Nṛsiṃha" have been uttered even once? (8.209)
Indeed, the essential meaning of all four Vedas is but one:
the chanting of "Nṛsiṃha, Nṛsiṃha, Nṛsiṃha. (8.210)
(Merutantra) Due to the excess of greed in the Kali Yuga, there is neither guru nor deity;
the roaring of the name of Nṛhari alone is declared to be the means to the highest good. (8.211)
(In the Saṃhitā: Now hear, O Nārada, the seer and other [elements] of the aforementioned King of Mantras:
I am declared to be the Seer Brahmā, and the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh. (8.212)
The deity of this [mantra] is Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the God of gods and the teacher of the world;
*dhruva* and *māyā* are the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*), while the Nārasiṃha [syllable] is the pin (*kīlaka*).
The accent is declared to be udātta (acute), and the color is cited as white;
its application is proclaimed to be for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 8-214 ||
In the *Merutantra*: "The six limbs [of the mantra] consist of four, eight, six, and six [syllables], with the syllables of the Vedas.
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*) [is described] in the *Saṃhitā*.
One should meditate upon the forest of Kalpa trees on the White Island in the Ocean of Milk.
It was strewn with various flowers and fruits, raining down showers of pearls and heaps of jewels, and was enchanting with the fragrance of blooming young *mandāra* blossoms. (8.216)
It was filled with swarms of bees enjoying the sweetness of honey within the flowers,
resonant with the warbling of cuckoos, and inhabited by various flocks of birds.
It is a source of happiness enjoyed simultaneously by the six seasons,
abounding with blooming lotuses, kahlāras, kumudas, and utpalas.
It was surrounded by lakes filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks;
in their midst stood a pavilion of jewels, shimmering with radiant light.
Upon that ground, red with a pavement of heaps of padmarāga gems within it,
and atop a golden lion-throne illuminated by the radiance of various jewels— || 8.220 ||
One should visualize an eight-petaled lotus upon a couch formed by the coils of the lord of serpents;
one should contemplate Śrī Nṛsiṃha seated upon its pericarp. (8.221)
Resembling ten million moons, clothed in radiant yellow garments,
and difficult to approach due to a garland of flames resembling the blazing fire of cosmic destruction.
The Sudarśana discus, the bow with its arrow, the excellent seal-ring, and likewise the seal known as Abhaya, which is meaningful for his own devotees. (8.223)
Holding [the trident] with his four sprout-like hands, the long-armed one, whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, and whose lotus-face is slightly inclined in meditation. (8.224)
His lotus-like face was adorned with a tongue like a flashing lightning bolt and teeth that were wondrous; he was graced by a mass of matted locks resembling molten gold. (8.225)
Wearing a golden crown blazing with clusters of radiant jewels,
his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and adorned with shimmering crocodile-shaped earrings.
His limbs are bound by a yogic cloth and he is adorned with a forest garland; he is further embellished by necklaces, armlets, anklets, and shimmering waist-bands. (8.227)
Adorned with divine ornaments fashioned from various jewels, and illuminated by the rows of hoods of the lord of serpents, which blazed with the crests of flaming gems.
Having formed a canopy with his own splendors, he illuminated the ten directions with [rays] that mimicked the mass of flames from the fire at the end of the eon.
With the flames from the eye on his forehead, he was difficult even for the gods to behold;
he beheld Lakṣmī, who sat upon his left lap and possessed the luster of molten gold.
Clad in pure linen garments and adorned with various ornaments,
she holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a pair of lotuses, in her lotus-like hands.
[He saw her] whose face was like the full autumn moon, whose lotus-like mouth bore a gentle smile, embracing him with eyes wide open with bliss as he embraced her in return. (8.232)
Indeed, in the southern region of Bhārata, he is constantly being praised by those adorned with forest garlands, who hold the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and water-vessel.
He was surrounded on all sides by heroic attendants resembling sapphire,
as well as by hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā and great sages beginning with Sanaka.
It is frequented by yogis, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases;
its face is exceedingly serene, and it bestows the boons desired by its devotees.
One should meditate in the heart upon the divine lion, the infallible Supreme Self, who is of such a nature—indescribable and beyond the reach of speech and mind. (8.236)
Having thus meditated upon the omnipresent Mahāviṣṇu, who possesses divine manes,
one is completely liberated from the bondage of karma and attains the body of Viṣṇu.
Having meditated upon Nṛhari within the lotus of the heart—He who consists of intense bliss, is peaceful, and is the embodiment of eternal consciousness—one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person. (8.238)
(Blank p.
657) Or else, it resides within the first sixteen wheels (*cakra*), devoid of the *bindu*;
it is beginningless, undivided, accessible to yogins, and beyond the reach of the senses. (8-239)
Higher than the highest, eternal, free from limiting adjuncts, and untroubled;
self-luminous, the witness of the world, and stainless. (8.240)
Having meditated upon Narahari, who is composed of light, one becomes identical with Brahman;
or else, one should contemplate the entire universe as the body of Narahari.
One becomes immediately liberated while living, free from mental anguish and fear from any quarter.
The Intermediate Dhyāna has been described [in the Śāradā-tantra] as having a luster equal to a mountain of rubies, terrifying the hosts of Rākṣasas with its own radiance,
with lotus-like hands placed upon the knees, three-eyed, and adorned with ornaments shining with jewels.
I bow to the omnipresent Lord Nṛsiṃha, who holds the conch and discus in his two arms, whose fierce fangs and mouth shine with a tongue like a blazing flame, and whose mass of hair stands erect.
In the *Merutantra*:
"On the left [he holds] the conch-enemy, with his right arm placed upon his knee;
he devours the king of the Daityas with a splendor like that of fire. (8.243)
He beheld him with a blazing face, a flickering tongue, and three eyes,
being praised by the gods, the sages, and Lakṣmī, who stood with palms joined in reverence.
The distinctions among meditations according to the distinctions of desire have been stated in that very same place:
"For the sake of accomplishing the practice of specific desires, I shall describe the various types of meditation:
[one should meditate on the deity] possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns, three-eyed, and of terrifying form. (8.245)
With eyes like a vajra, possessing the luster of fire, and surrounded by various arms;
the Lord who has torn asunder the Daityas with his claws, his body smeared with streams of blood. (8.246)
In matters concerning cruel deeds and the like, one should meditate upon the terrifying Lord;
now, the meditation on Hari as consisting of the universal form (viśvarūpa) is being proclaimed.
That Nṛsiṃha was most terrifying, with a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction;
he held a rosary, was fierce, and his throat was adorned with a necklace. (8.248)
He has a serpent as his sacred thread and is beautifully adorned by a five-faced lion;
he has the moon as his crest-jewel, a blue throat, and three eyes in each face. (8.249)
He was adorned with ten arms resembling iron clubs,
holding a rosary, a mace, a lotus, and a conch shell white as cow's milk.
Holding a bow, a mace, and an excellent discus,
as well as a sword, a trident, and an arrow— this is Nṛhari, the protector of Rudra.
Having the luster of sapphire and deep blue, shining like the moon and resembling gold;
with its face upward, rising in the east and blazing toward the north, it possesses all colors.
Thus one should meditate upon the fierce Lord for the cessation of all diseases;
when there is a great task to be accomplished, He should be meditated upon as having sixteen arms.
Nṛsiṃha, the lord of all worlds, adorned with every ornament, has two [hands] suitable for the act of rending and two capable of lifting up. (8.254)
Two others hold a discus and a conch; two others hold an arrow and a bow;
two others hold a sword and a shield; and two others hold a mace and a lotus. (8.255)
The other two [hands] hold a noose and a goad, placed upon the crown of the enemy;
thus one should meditate on the all-pervading Lord Nṛhari, adorned with sixteen mighty arms.
One should meditate with undivided mind upon the one of fierce deeds, who has the luster of a blue lotus;
when a most great task is to be accomplished, he should then be visualized as having twenty-six hands.
Nṛsiṃha, richly adorned with all ornaments, the Lord who grants all perfections,
holds in his right hands a sword, a discus, an axe, and a noose.
A plow and a pestle, as well as a shield, a goad, a sharp-edged spear, a slingshot, a shield, a javelin, and a mallet. (8.259)
With the hands on the left side, he holds a conch, a sword, a noose, a trident, fire,
a boon-granting gesture, a spear, and a well-fashioned earthen water-pot.
With his pairs of hands, he [holds] in sequence a bow, the jarjanī mudrā, a mace, a hand-drum, and a serpent against the enemy's knees, head, and chest.
With his two upper hands he holds a rosary of mantras,
and with his two lower hands he performs the rending of Hiraṇyaka.
One should meditate upon the divine Nṛsiṃha, who brings joy to his devotees and strikes terror into the Daityas, and who removes the great fear of death. (8.263)
Now, another supreme meditation is described, which removes diseases of the mouth, removes the effects of poison, removes death, and brings fear to enemies. (8.264)
Seated upon Garuḍa, who resembles a mass of gold, he has the complexion of the full moon;
he is fair-faced and resplendent with three eyes that shine like lightning.

Beautifully adorned and wearing yellow garments, he holds a conch, a discus, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness with his four hands; he is the destroyer of Kṣveḍa and other demons.
One should meditate upon Nṛhari, who destroys the great calamities of untimely death.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Narahari, possessing the splendor of ten million rising suns, radiant with a crown and necklaces, his face terrifying with fangs, and endowed with many long arms whose nails gleam like tips of claws;

I worship Him who has crushed the lords of the Asuras, whose three eyes are the nature of fire, the moon, and the sun, who is terrifying with his mass of matted hair resembling a cluster of lightning, and who vomits forth fire. (8.267)
One should contemplate a gentle mantra for a gentle [deity] and employ this fierce one for a fierce [deity].
Regarding the *puraścaraṇa*, [the Meru-tantra] states:
"The initiated one, having conquered his senses, should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times. (8.268)
One should offer that thousand-fold oblation into the fire with sacrificial food smeared with clarified butter;
then, having performed the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and likewise the honoring of Brahmins. (8.269)

One who has perfected the mantra should then perform the ritual applications; according to the *Śāradā*, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and then offer oblations with ghee-soaked [fuel] one thousand times. (8-270)
"One should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) according to the rules into the fire duly consecrated;
when this is done, the practitioner of the mantra becomes one whose mantra is perfected and endowed with majesty"—thus it is said.
Now, the divisions of mantras (from the *Merutantra*):
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the second [form], the all-pervading Lord Nṛhari.
(In the Saṃhitā: Now I shall declare the supreme mantra of Nṛsiṃha in its seed-form:
the syllable *Saṃ* (*sa*) mounted upon the fire-syllable (*ra*), adorned with the vowel of Manu (*u*). (8-272)
The mantra, pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Atri is declared its sage, and Gāyatrī is said to be its metre. (8.273)
The deity is declared to be Nṛhari, who is saluted by gods and demons;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.
One should perform all the meditations, worship, and other rites prescribed for the King of Mantras.
Regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra], it is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"Eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and having controlled the senses, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (8.275)
One should properly perform the oblation with auspicious milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee, using a tenth part of that [number];
then, having performed one's own consecration, one should satisfy [the deity] with pure water.
Having properly propitiated the brahmins, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra should perform all the ritual applications (prayoga) proclaimed by the King of Mantras. (8.277)
In that very [text] (*Śāradātilaka*), it is said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the third mantra of Nṛhari. (p.
The noose is Śakti, the goad is Nṛhari, and the armor-mantra is Phaṭ.
The six-syllabled mantra of Narahari is said to grant all desires;
Brahmā is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and the Paṅkti meter is proclaimed as its metre (chandas). || 8.279 ||
The deity of this [mantra] is Narasiṃha; the assignment of the limbs is performed with the six seed-syllables.
Now, the meditation:
[one should visualize] his tongue flickering in anger, his own mouth wide open, with eyes of the moon, sun, and fire;
from his feet to his navel, his luster is red, while above it is white, and he has torn apart the body of the lord of the Daityas.
I praise Nṛsiṃha, who bears the conch, the discus, the noose, the goad, the thunderbolt, and the mace; who is formidable with sharp-pointed fangs, and adorned with various ornaments made of jewels.

He describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): "One should recite this [mantra] one hundred thousand times per season and then offer oblations of ghee; thereafter, one should satisfy the Guru with wealth in a well-kindled fire. (8.281)
(Merutantra) Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantra of Jvālāmālinṛsiṃha, which arose during the Turya Manvantara and destroys the origin of all beings. (8-282)
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
The seed-syllable is "namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya," followed by "jvālāmāline" and then "dīptadaṃṣṭrāya. (8.283)
One should utter the word "agninetra" (fire-eyed), followed by "sarvādirakṣoghnāya" (the destroyer of all beginning with the Rākṣasas).
At the end of "sarvabhūtavināśa" (destruction of all beings), there is the letter 'na' with a long vowel, which is Marut.
Thus, at the end of the destruction of fever, there is the seed-syllable of the Leader (Nātha), followed by a pair of *dah*,
a pair of *pac*, a pair of *rakṣa*, and then *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, beginning with the eternal syllable (*dhruva*).
The great mantra of Jvālāmālin is said to consist of sixty-seven syllables;
the heart is said to consist of thirteen [syllables], and the head is declared to consist of ten.
The *śikhā* is said to consist of eleven syllables; the *varman* is considered to consist of eighteen syllables;
the *netra* consists of twelve syllables; and the *astra* should consist of the *karaṇa* syllables. (8.287)
Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-vinyāsa*), one should contemplate the deity of the mantra. [This is] the meditation:
blazing incessantly with the appearance of the fire of universal destruction, possessing three eyes... 8-288.
Resplendent with the crests of his mane, his lotus-like face was adorned with fangs;
terrifying to the rākṣasas, he was formidable with his scattered mass of manes.
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa):
with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then, one should offer oblations into the well-kindled sacrificial fire using the clarified butter of a tawny cow, numbering one-tenth of that [recitation].

(Merutantra) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain [the fate of] that powerful one who is born during the fifth Manvantara; he, endowed with Lakṣmī, is served by those established in the householder stage of life. (8-291)
(In the Saṃhitā:
Now I shall declare the mantra of Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, which is very difficult to obtain: Tāra, Indirā, Śakti, and Ramā [preceding] the Wielder of the Trident, the Supreme Person. (8.292)
Having uttered the word *lakṣmīpriya* in the dative case (*ṅe*), followed invariably by *āmudita*, and having likewise uttered *cetasaṃ*, followed by the word *lakṣmīśrita*. (8.293)

The mantra is declared to consist of the word "ardhadeha" in the dative case, followed by "Ramā," "Māyā," and "Hṛt"; it is composed of six syllables and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. (8.293)
The sage is declared to be Prajāpati; the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
and the deity of this [mantra] is proclaimed to be the Blessed Lord Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with one's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*), one should perform another placement (*nyāsa*).
As it was stated previously in the *Merutantra*: "May Keśava, the wielder of the discus, with the luster of refined gold, protect [me]. (8-295)
Behind him is Nārāyaṇa, bearing a conch shell, resembling a dark blue cloud;
Mādhava is dark as the petal of a blue lotus, holding a mace above him.
On the right side was the great Govinda, the wielder of the bow with the luster of the moon;
on the left was Viṣṇu, the bearer of the plow, resembling the filaments of a lotus.
In the southeast is Aravindākṣa, holding a mace; Madhusūdana is Trivikrama, with a sword in hand and possessing a radiance like fire in the southwest.
In the northwest is Vāmana, the wielder of the thunderbolt, radiant like the rising sun;
in the northeast is Puṇḍarīkākṣa Śrīdhara, whose weapon is the paṭṭiśa.
Vidyutprabha Hṛṣīkeśa is the mallet-bearer in the northwestern direction;
Padmanābha, possessing a brilliance equal to a thousand suns, is my heart-lotus.
Possessing all weapons, all powers, all-knowing, with faces on every side,
resembling an indragopaka insect, holding a noose in his hand, he is unconquered.
Pervading the body both internally and externally, Dāmodara remains;
thus, everywhere, the cage of the twelve names is without any gap.
"Having entered [this place], I have no fear whatsoever at any time";
having first made this assignment (nyāsa) in this manner, one should meditate upon Lakṣmīnarahari.
As for the meditative absorption (dhyāna):
He reclines upon the coils of the serpent king, possessing the parasol of the serpent king’s hoods;
embraced by the radiant Ramā, he resembles the moon. (8.304)
Holding a lotus, a wheel, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and having three eyes with the moon as his crest-ornament;
however, in the *Saṃhitā*, the meditation described for the King of Mantras alone is stated.
He now describes the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
One should recite three hundred and sixty thousand times, or a thousand times that [number].
The best of those who know mantras should offer oblations with mallikā flowers smeared with honey;
having worshipped the God in the water, he should then satisfy him with the mantra.
One should sprinkle one's own head [with water] and then feed the Brahmins;
thereafter, the practitioner should perform the rites for his own desired goals. (8.307)
In that very same work:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantra of Nṛsiṃha which existed during the sixth Manvantara; together with Lakṣmī, it grants all desires. (8.308)
Oṃ Śrī! The eight-syllabled mantra for Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha is considered as follows:
the sage is Prajāpati, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Lakṣmī-Hari. (8.309)
