The seed-syllables *kṣrau* joined with the six long vowels are declared as the procedure for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
All [aspects] such as meditation and worship are declared to be like those of the six-syllable mantra. (8.310)

Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable; he should then offer oblations of milk-rice soaked in ghee amounting to a tenth part of that number, and thereafter perform the libations and other rites.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare that which was born as Hari in the seventh [manvantara]:
"Victory! Victory! O Śrī Nṛsiṃha!"—this is considered the eight-syllabled mantra.

The mantra beginning with "Ṛṣi" is said to consist of eight syllables; its worship is performed according to the six-syllable rite, and the applications are according to the one-syllable rite; a pure householder should accomplish [these]. (8.313)
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare who is born as the eighth [incarnation]:
Nṛhari, the tenth incarnation, during the interval of Dakṣasāvarṇi.
Oṃ kṣrau! Salutation to the Blessed One, Nṛsiṃha; let him speak. Oṃ kṣrau! And [salutation] to the one in the form of the Fish and the one in the form of the Tortoise, from those two. (8.315)
Oṃ kṣrau! Then one should utter the two seed-syllables for the one in the form of a boar (Varāha).
Then, for the one in the form of Nṛsiṃha, one should utter "vedādi" (the beginning of the Vedas) followed by kṣrau. (8.316)
Having spoken [the name] for the one in the form of Vāmana, one should utter the two seed-syllables three times;
then those same [syllables] for Rāma, and those two for Kṛṣṇa, and one should speak them for Kalki.
At the conclusion of the two words "jaya," having said "to the dweller of Śālagrāma" and "to the divine lion," one should thereafter say "to the Self-born."
"Obeisance to the Puruṣa, Tāra, Kṣraum"—this mantra consists of ninety-nine syllables.
However, for one who has not yet attained the twice-born [twice-born] status, it should be addressed to the Buddha, preceded by the seed-syllable. (8.319)
Then the mantra is declared to consist of four hundred syllables;
its metre is said to be Atijagatī, and Atri is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi).
The deity is Nṛhari of the ten incarnations, the granter of all desires;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
Like that of the King of Mantras, his meditation, worship, and so forth should be performed;
at the conclusion of the six-limbed worship, one should worship the incarnations beginning with Matsya.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; thereafter, one should offer oblations with clarified butter and sacrificial food (*havis*) numbering one-tenth of that amount, and then perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other subsequent rites.

Indeed, O Brahmins, by the practice of all rites performed for specific desires, just like this king of mantras, even those who have fallen away from celibacy and other vows [attain their goals]. (8.324)
Having assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha, they became the Sthānanṛsiṃhas;
when properly worshipped, they enter into the body and act perfectly. (8.325)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice of him who is born in the ninth [house], Narasiṃha, whose name is Vīra; listen to that sādhana, O beloved. (8-326)

For the sake of practice among the young, the middle-aged, and the old, three mantras have been taught; and for the one who accomplishes [the goal], when the mouth is purified, all three are indeed perfected. (8.327)
*Tāra*, *namo bhagavate*, and at the end of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should utter the word *nara*;
then, having spoken *siṃhāya*, one should utter the word *jvālāmālā*. (8.328)
Having said "to him whose limbs are bound," one should address him as "fire-eyed";
having said "O destroyer of all beings, burn," one should cause him to be burned in two ways.
*Pa-ca*, *ya-g-ma*, *ra-kṣa-yu-g-ma*, *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *rakṣāgni-gehinī*.
This mantra of fifty-four syllables is declared to be the first. (8.330)
One should state the syllables of the sixteenfold [mantra] in the line, followed by the word *dīptapada*;
then *daṃṣṭrāya*, *agninettrāya*, and thereafter the word *sarvarakṣa*.
Having uttered "ghnāya," one should say "sarvabhūta" in the dative case (ending in -e) followed by "vināśana";
then for the destruction of all fevers, one should utter "hana" twice and "daha" twice.
"PA CA YUGMAṂ BA NDHA YUGMAṂ HUḤ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ KVA GĀRṆAKAḤ. Now I shall explain the third [mantra], whose initial syllables are "GA JA BĀ HA VAḤ. (8.333)
For the purpose of destruction, at the end there should be the word "sarva" (all) preceded by [the name] in three ways;
in the middle, one should join the three words "bhūta-jvara-doṣa" (element-fever-defect).
The mantra is considered to consist of nine syllables, equal to *haṃ*, the four ends beginning with *na*, the pair of *rakṣa*, *ca*, *māṃ*, *ca*, *mām*, *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *svāhā*. (8.335)
The worship, meditation, recitation, and so forth for this [deity] are to be performed as prescribed for the King of Mantras.
These are known as the garland-mantras (mālāmantra), which bring about swift accomplishment. (8.336)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is born in the tenth [day]:
Oṃ Kṣrauṃ, ending with "namo mahānṛsiṃhāya," consisting of ten syllables. (8.337)
The sage is Vāmadeva, the metre is Virāj, and the deity is Nṛsiṃha;
one should perform the ritual assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using one's own seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels. (8.337)

The meditation, worship, preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*), and fire-oblation (*homa*) are like those for Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha. One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables; the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as declared for the eight-syllable mantra. (8.338)
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra of the eleventh [form]:
Oṃ Kṣrau/! Homage to the Blessed One Narasiṃha; this is the mantra. (8.339)
It is taught as having thirteen syllables, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
Vāmadeva is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), and Jagatī is said to be the meter (chandas). || 8.340 ||
Here, the deity Narasiṃha is to be conceived with his own seed-syllable for the assignment of the limbs;
the visualization, worship, ritual application, and so forth, are declared to be like those of the six-syllabled mantra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the one who is born in the twelfth [lunar mansion]:
he dwells eternally in Kāśī, agitating the minds of the wicked. (8.342)
*Tāraṃ sahasrārajvālāvarttine kṣrau hanadvayaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this nineteen-syllable mantra has been proclaimed. (8.343)
The sage is said to be Jayanta; its meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha is proclaimed as its deity. || 8.344 ||
The heart is said to belong to Cakrarāja, while the head belongs to Jvālācakra;
the crest-lock (śikhā) belongs to Gajacakra, and the armor (kavaca) is likewise considered to belong to him.
"Phaṭ! To the weapon, the discus that ends the Asuras"—this mantra for Sudarśana is declared to be the five-limbed [mantra]. (8.346)
Now, regarding the meditation:
In the midst of the assembly of the wheels, one should meditate upon Hari, who has a radiance like the fire of time (kālāgni),
four arms, a wide-open mouth, and who holds four wheels.
One should meditate upon the primordial form, which resembles molten gold, possesses three eyes, destroys all suffering, and is accompanied by Lakṣmī of similar appearance. (8.348)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):

one should recite the mantra one million times; then, one should offer oblations with auspicious sesame seeds numbering one-tenth of that, and subsequently offer forty thousand oblations with flowers.
Furthermore, one should offer oblations with clarified butter a thousand times and perform prostrations;
then, having performed the libations and other rites, one should carry out the ritual applications.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the deity Nṛhari is born in the thirteenth [position], and the *kṣau* syllable is the enclosure. (8.351)
Through *māyā* one may be a bestower of enjoyments, and through the *praṇava*, a bestower of liberation.
The ritual application for its worship and so forth shall be equal to that of the single-syllable [mantra]. (8.352)
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the omnipresent Lord who appeared during the Manvantara;
this one named Abhaya-Nṛsiṃha is the destroyer of all fears. (8.353)
One should utter the Tāra, "Namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya," at the heart; then, having said "Tejas tejasas" and "Āvir āvirbhava. (8.354)
O Vajranakha, O Vajradaṃṣṭra, pierce the two storehouses of karmic impressions! O Fire, you who consume darkness, speak of fearlessness within yourself.
The mantra consisting of sixty-two syllables, beginning with "bhūyiṣṭhā oṃ kṣraum," is considered [the following]:
Śuka is the sage, Atijagatī is the meter, and everything else is as previously stated. (8.356)
The means for accomplishing the fourteen forms of Nṛsiṃha, as revealed by the Vedas, has been described here, O gods; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now, the mantra of Vāmana (in the *Merutantra*):
"Henceforth, I shall fully declare the auspicious mantras of Vāmana.
One mantra burns for an entire Manvantara, while another afflicts the Lord of the Waters. (8.358)
Furthermore, that King Bali gave the three worlds to Hari;
for one *manvantara*, Śakra himself became Bali. (8.359)
Thus, I shall declare the mantras of those six Vāmanas in this Kalpa;
and the six Vāmanas are mentioned in another Tantra as follows:
Dadhivāmana, Yajñeśavāmana, and Bhogavāmana. || 8.360 ||
The Child, the Dwarf, the Universal Form, and another, Valivāmana;
therein is the mantra of Dadhivāmana (according to the Śāradā-tantra): the Tāra (Om), then "Hṛd" (Namaḥ), then "Viṣṇave," followed by "ṅentaḥ" (Vāmanāya), and then "Surapatiḥ" (Svāhā). || 8-361 ||
The mantra of eighteen syllables for Mahābalā consists of two *ṭha* sounds and the word *manu*.
The seer is Indu, the metre is Virāṭ, and the deity is Dadhivāmana. (8.362)
The heart-mantra is said to consist of one syllable, the crest (śikhā) of two, the armor (kavaca) of three, and the eye (netra) of that same number of syllables [five]. (8.363)
The wise have declared that there are two methods for the ritual of the limb (aṅga), namely "the weapon" (astra). || 8-363ef ||
Now, the meditation: [One should meditate on the Lord] white as a pearl, adorned with excellent ornaments of fresh jewels, seated upon the moon,
his lotus-face beautified by clusters of locks of hair shaped like bees.
With the tips of his hands, he holds a golden pitcher filled with pure water and a golden cup rich with curd-rice; let us worship him. || 8.364 ||

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one million times (*guṇalakṣa*), and then perform a fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rule, offering oblations of milk-rice or curd-rice soaked in clarified butter, amounting to one-tenth of that number.
The various divisions of the Vāmana-mantras are to be seen [in the Meru-tantra].
Now, regarding the Trivikrama-mantras [in the Meru-tantra]:
"Henceforth, I shall fully proclaim the supreme Traivikrama-mantra."
One should utter the syllable *tāra*, *namo bhagavate*, and the three *vyāhṛtis*.
To the Pervasive One (Vyāpaka), then *paraṃ*, followed by *ṅe* at the end, and also *trivikrama*:
this great mantra of twenty syllables bestows the kingdom of the Gatas. (8-367)
The six-limbed rite is declared by means of all five feet; the sages are the Vālakhilyas, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. (8.368)
This deity is Viśvarūpa, proclaimed as Trivikrama. Meditation:
His right foot pervades the netherworld (pātāla), and his left foot pervades the surface of the earth.
Then, raising his right hand again, Hari caused it to overflow with the water, kusha grass, and sesame seeds offered by Bali, thereby effecting the pervasion of heaven.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods, who bestows fearlessness with his left hand,
whose lotus-feet are washed by the torrent of the Gaṅgā, and who is praised by Brahmā and the other deities.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra two million times and subsequently perform oblations (*homa*) with sesame seeds, rice, and mustard seeds smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
One should then carry out the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. (8.372)
In this way, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra obtains the desired fruit.
Now follows the mantra of Paraśurāma; regarding that very point:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the most wonderful mantra of Rāma. (8.373)
For an entire kalpa, this alone was the son of Jamadagni, possessed of great strength;
we meditate upon him as the field of Brahman, we meditate upon him as the end-maker of the Kṣatriyas.
May that Rāma inspire us—
this is the most wonderful Gāyatrī of the illustrious Paraśurāma. || 8.375 ||
The sovereign of those adorned by the Kali age, concealed in all tantras, is declared to be the sage Bharadvāja; the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter. (8.376)
The glorious Paraśurāma, who is affectionate toward his devotees, is its presiding deity.
The six ancillary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are said to consist of [mantras] of eight, five, three, two, four, and four syllables respectively. (8.377)

Now, regarding meditation: [One should meditate on] the Sāttvika form, white in color, with its body smeared with ashes, seated at the site of the Agnihotra sacrifice, and surrounded by various hosts of sages. (8.378)
Seated upon a woolen rug, with fingers adorned by golden rings and kusha grass,
he was clothed in two white garments, offering oblations with a tranquil mind.
And one should meditate upon Rāma in his rājasa form, with a body reddish like saffron,
wearing a crown and earrings, and holding a battle-axe, a lotus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding [the moon] with his rays, youthful, surrounded by a multitude of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas,
wearing yellow garments, capable of assuming any form at will, and gazed upon by children.

And he should meditate upon that [weapon] belonging to Tamas, smeared with the blood of a Kṣatriya, resembling an axe, with reddened eyes, the sacred thread resting on the ear, and possessing the luster of Yama. (8.382)
The three worlds were terrified by the thunderous roar of his bow;
he possessed four arms and held a mace, accompanied by his enraged brother.

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable; then, having performed the fire sacrifice with white sugar, clarified butter, ghee, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and having concluded with the feeding of Brahmins, the mantra becomes perfected.
He who is constantly devoted to the rites of Brahman and intent upon the recitation of the Gāyatrī—he alone becomes a perfected one, and never any other brāhmaṇa. (8.385)
Likewise:
"The Franks, the Yavanas, the Cīnas, the Khurāsānīs, and those born in Calendra—upon seeing a devotee of Rāma, these tremble and bow down. (8.386)
Now, the Śrī Raghunātha-mantra (from the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā):
[He meditated upon] Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, his guru, the son of Satyavatī, the sage established in samādhi, peaceful, and possessing the radiant splendor of the gracious sun. (8.387)
Having prostrated with all eight limbs before that treasure of asceticism who was seated on the highly meritorious bank of the Ganges, Śaunaka questioned him.
Śrī Śaunaka said: O you whose face is gracious with favor, turn your mind toward me;
by your grace, many great mantras have been mastered by me.
Behold me with eyes filled with the essence of compassion;
you have realized the eternal Brahman, the Self that is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. (8.390)
Now I wish to hear the mantra, along with its ancillaries and the method of worship,
of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor who has descended as the soul of Rāma.
"Tell me everything, O Blessed One, if I am worthy to hear it;
for this world is afflicted by misfortune and by poverty. (8.392)
By means of which a man may obtain incomparable good fortune, the attainment of great sovereignty, knowledge of the scriptures, poetic talent, and omniscience. (8.393)
Śrī Vyāsa said: Well asked by you, O Brahmin; I shall relate it all to you—just as it was formerly told by Brahmā to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha also gave the Manu to my father, his own son;
my father was pure-hearted, gracious, and a treasury of compassion. (8.395)
At the highly meritorious Kurukṣetra, during a solar eclipse, he bestowed it;
and by me, the mantra has been mastered through recitation, burnt offerings, worship, and other rites. (8.396)
Until now, I have not spoken this king of mantras to anyone.
Listen with devotion to this mantra, which has been handed down through such a lineage. (8.397)
"O Sage, this king of mantras must not be given by you to one who is unworthy. Guard this secret with effort; it bestows the glory of success. (8-398)
Having described the characteristics of a disciple: "One should bestow the mantra upon such a disciple, and not otherwise;
for if one were to speak otherwise regarding him, the deity would become a giver of a curse. (8.399)

He states the extraction of the mantra: "Having extracted this seed-syllable, which ends with the letter *ma*, is joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), and is adorned by Nārāyaṇa; and then that same [syllable] again, deprived of the nasal drop. (8.400)
One should extract the syllable *bhāṃ* joined with the form [of the deity], ending with *māṃ* and concluding with *na*.
This six-syllabled mantra bestows all sovereign powers. (8.401)
O Sage, it generates all good fortune, brings all the worlds under one's influence, grants the accomplishment of vidyās for men, and carries out great commands.
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā, its meter is said to be Gāyatrī,
and the deity is proclaimed to be the Vaiṣṇava abode known as Rāma.
One should first know the phoneme, the seed-syllable, the power, and likewise the salutation.
Regarding the meaning of the mantra, it is said in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*:
"The correct meaning of the King of Mantras of Śrī Rāma is now being declared. (8.404)
The letter *ra* signifies fire and culminates in luminosity;
its ultimate meaning is said to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
The consonant is the partless Brahman, and the vowel is the vital breath (prāṇa) and illusion (māyā).
Know that the union of the vowel with the consonants is the conjunction of the vital breath with that [Brahman]. (8.406)
Therefore, the letter *ra*, which consists of light, is joined with the form of *ka*;
and because it signifies arising (*abhyudaya*), the letter *ma* is said to have the nature of *māyā*.
Therefore, by this seed-syllable, Brahman is said to be identical with the Self.
(In the Rāmopaniṣad:
It is self-luminous, its own light, consisting solely of consciousness through its own experience. (8-408)
That very king of mantras is remembered as the two-syllabled sovereign mantra;
it is the unbroken bliss of a single essence, the savior, and the designator of Brahman. (8.409)
"Rāmāya" is easily understood as being of the nature of truth, bliss, and consciousness;
the word "namaḥ" is easily understood as the singular embodiment of perfect bliss. (8.410)
All gods who seek liberation always bow within their hearts [to this].
Due to the division of the primordial seed-syllables (*ādyabīja*), this mantra is sixfold; as it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain those [mantras] which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (8-411)
That Blessed One appeared as the Rāma-mantras in every Manvantara; through the revolution of the Yugas, he became the incarnation of Śakra in the Kalpa.
Therein, I shall first proclaim the six-syllable king of mantras: "Rāmāya namaḥ"; this is preceded by Rāṃ, Klīṃ, Hrīṃ, Aiṃ, and Tu. (8.413)
The six-syllabled mantra beginning with Śrī-Tārā is proclaimed to be of six kinds: Brahmā, Sammohana, Śakti, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (8.414)
Agastya is declared to be Śrī Śiva; these are the sages in their respective order. The meter is known as Gāyatrī, and Śrī Rāma is considered the deity. (8.415)
Many further subdivisions of the six-syllable mantra itself are taught in that very same [text]:

"The fifty letters of the Mātṛkā-mantra, preceded by each [of the syllables] individually; beginning with Lakṣmī, or beginning with Vāgbhava, or beginning with Manmatha, or beginning with Dhruva. (8.416)
Likewise, there are two hundred such varieties of Rāmacandra;
and by the term "Rāmabhadra," there are likewise two hundred varieties.
Viśvāmitra is considered the sage for those [mantras] beginning with the seed-syllable *ramā*; however, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is said to be the sage for those preceded by the seed-syllable *vāk*. (8.418)
The sage of those [mantras] preceded by *kāmabīja* and so forth is considered to be Sammohana;
however, for those preceded by *tāra* and so forth, the sage is declared to be Śrīśiva. (8.419)
When the single seed-syllables of Śrī, Māyā, and Manmatha are placed at the beginning and end [of each], Rāmabhadra and Rāmacandra are said to be sixfold, consisting of six syllables. (8.420)
The sixfold [mantra] ending with "namaḥ" was previously taught; indeed, that same [mantra] ending with "phaṭ" is also sixfold.
That same [mantra] ending with "vahnijāyā" (svāhā) is likewise considered to be of six kinds. (8.421)
Four hundred and twenty-four varieties have been described by him; likewise:
"For this [mantra] beginning with *tāra* leads to liberation, while that beginning with *ramā* leads to enjoyment. (8.422)

For the perfection of speech, one should employ the mantra of Vāgīśvara; for the subjugation of all, the mantra of Manmatha; and for the sake of all goals, one should recite the mantras encased by the Tārā-mantra and others. (8.423)

Likewise: "The procedure for the six limbs is declared [to be performed] with the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels, at the aperture of Brahmā, between the eyebrows, in the heart, the navel, the genitals, and the feet. (8.424)
(In the *Vaśiṣṭhasaṃhitā*):
One should contemplate the Śakti, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, within the Ādhāra;
the Ādhāra is like the rising sun and consists of its radiance. (8-425)
O best of sages, having thus cultivated the foundational meditation,
one should then contemplate the splendor that has arisen from it in the form of a flame.
Resembling ten million flashes of lightning and as cool as ten million moons, one should open the mouth of the *suṣumnā* and cause [the breath] to reach it through instruction. (8.427)
One should lead [the breath] upward by way of the path of Brahmā to the lunar orb at the end of the twelve;
having reached it, one should, according to the rule and with focused intellect, cause that nectar of immortality to flow down.
Then, one should contemplate one's own body and the entire world as having become one, enveloped by streams of pure nectar flowing forth from it. (8.429)
It is free from conceptual proliferation, formless, blameless, and stainless;
it is the cessation of both the non-empty and the empty, devoid of the states of existence and non-existence.
O best of sages, one should contemplate the Self as indivisible bliss;
one should contemplate the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra with one's own self.
The practitioner of mantras should contemplate in this way and recite the mantra every day;
having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, he shall at the end attain the supreme state. (8.432)
Having withdrawn that splendor into the lotus of the heart, one should meditate upon Rāma, who consists of light and is the sole witness of all the worlds. (8.433)
Hari, who brings about the emergence, the existence, and the dissolution of the world,
is served by gods, asuras, humans, and hosts of yogins.
Now, the meditation: [One should meditate on Him] as four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and jeweled earrings. (8.435)
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra six thousand times day after day;
having become the lord of speech and prosperity, one becomes a poet within a year.
He describes the intermediate meditation (dhyānāntara):
"O Sage, one should meditate upon a golden pavilion at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa);
in its center is a divine and supreme celestial chariot (vimāna) named Puṣpaka. (8.437)
In its center is a lion throne adorned with various jewels;
in the middle of that is an eight-petaled lotus, resembling the rising sun.
O great sage, [one should meditate upon] this Śrī Rāma seated in their midst,
holding in his right hand the mudrā consisting of perfect knowledge.
The left [hand] is for illuminating splendor, and the other is upon the crown of the knee;
[he meditates on] the Lord who is the beloved of Jānakī, possessing a radiance equal to sapphire. (8-440)
O King, [he beheld] the delighter of the Raghus, who was devoted to the garden, possessed of two arms,
and surrounded by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva.
Seated on her left side is Sītā, who resembles gold;
she eternally grants the desires of those who worship her, holding a red lotus in her lotus-like hand.
Lakṣmaṇa was at the rear, holding the parasol and the fine whisks;
on both sides were Bharata and Śatrughna, both holding palm-leaf fans.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra, becoming a vessel for both wisdom and glory.
(Also in the Śāradā-tilaka:
He whose lovely luster is like that of a dark rain-cloud, who constantly sits in the vīrāsana posture,
and who holds in one lotus-hand the mudrā consisting of knowledge while resting the other lotus-hand upon his knee.
I worship him who gazes at Rāghava, with Sītā standing by his side, her hand like a lotus, resembling lightning, and whose limbs are radiant with various ornaments such as a crown and armlets.
(Situated) upon the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), adorned with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*), his hand resting on his left thigh, and accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. (Merutantra 8.445)
In another tantra, after describing the aforementioned meditation:
"By this very meditation alone, one is liberated from all sins—[meditating on] Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, with eyes as broad as lotus petals. (8.446)

But for those great-souled ones who, having meditated upon the lotus of the heart, recite the six-syllabled mantra, liberation is to be known as being like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. (8.447)
(In the *Vaśiṣṭhasaṃhitā*):

"O Sage, for those wise practitioners who recite the mantra while engaged in the yoga of recitation, knowledge of the scriptures and the power of poetic composition arise within six months. (p. 678, 8-448)
This mantra bestows its fruit even without the performance of *puraścaraṇa*.

Its *puraścaraṇa* is stated [in the Merutantra]: "One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable, and then perform the *daśāṃśa* [homa] with oblations soaked in sweet substances. (8-449)
One should offer oblations with bilva leaves, fruits, flowers, sesame seeds, or lotuses.
Now, regarding the *mālā-mantra*, it is stated in that very same source: "Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantra worshipped by Lakṣmaṇa. (8.450)
The syllable *tāra* (om), *namo bhagavate*, followed by *ṅe'ntaḥ* (dative case ending), then *raghunandanaḥ*,
then the words *rakṣoghnaviśadāya* and subsequently *madhurāya*.
"To him of the serene countenance," then "to Amitatejas," "to Bala," "to Rāma," and "salutation to Viṣṇu"—this is [the mantra]. (8.452)
The garland mantra is declared to consist of forty-seven syllables;
the sage is Pitāmaha, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is [the same]. (8.453)
"Rājyābhiṣikto rāmaśca, bījaṃ śaktir namo 'stu"—with these [mantras] numbering seven, six, seventeen, and six, one performs the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*). (8.454)

Likewise: "Dhyāna is declared to consist of ten syllables; one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with bilva fruits, flowers, or leaves, or with sesame seeds combined with the three sweets. (8.455)

One should perform the fire oblation (homa) ten times the number of mantras recited, using milk-rice mixed with the three sweets or lotus flowers; likewise, the ritual libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed in every case.
One should perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*) and feed the Brahmins, following the preliminary procedures as before.
The ten-syllable mantra will now be stated.
The different forms of the Śrī Rāma mantra according to the various *manvantaras* have been described in that very same [text].
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the origin of Svārociṣa.
The single-syllable mantra of Rāma is proclaimed as *rāṃ*.
Brahmā is the sage (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and Rāma is its deity (*devatā*). (8.458)
One should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) known as the "Cage of the Embodiments" (mūrttipañjara),
and likewise the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) using the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels and the half-moon.
One should perform the meditation, worship, and so forth as before, and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each sun (bhānu).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure for the third internal mantra.
"O Rāma, this two-syllabled mantra has been declared as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Its seer and other [limbs] should be as stated for the one-syllabled mantra, and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) should be performed with the first syllable."
All practices, such as meditation and worship, should be understood according to the six-syllable mantra.
In this same way, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is also to be understood.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the fourth internal mantra. (8.462)
By means of the seed-syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, *ramā*, *anaṅga*, *vāk*, and *svabīja*, it becomes sixfold;
thus the two-syllabled king of mantras arises as three syllables.
One should perform all the rites, such as the placement of mantras (nyāsa) and worship, as previously described.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the five internal mantras.
The two-syllable [mantra] ends with Candrabhadra; the four-syllable [mantra] is of two kinds.
One should perform everything, such as the placement of the ṛṣis and worship, exactly as before.
This Manu is considered especially bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the origin of the sixth Manvantara.
"Salutation to Rāma"—this is considered the five-syllabled mantra.
Viśvāmitra is declared its sage, the Paṅkti its metre, and [Rāma] its deity. (8.467)
Rāmabhadra, the seed-syllable, and the power-syllable, along with the first letter,
he should sequentially place as the mantra upon the space between the eyebrows, the heart, below the navel, and the two feet.
The six-limbed [protection] is as before, or else the weapon-mantra is formed with the syllables of the mantra. (p. 680) He describes the visualization:
"In the center, at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree in a grove, upon a seat of flowering creepers... (8.469)
Lakṹṣmaṇa, having fixed an arrow with the corner of his eye,
was fanning the Lord as he gazed at Jānakī.
With his head radiant with a mass of matted locks, dark-complexioned, and surrounded by hosts of sages,
he was seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot while Lakṣmaṇa held a parasol over him.
One who specifically desires victory should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the peaceful destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, together with Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa.
One should perform the fire sacrifice, libations, and other ritual applications as previously described.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mantra originating from Sāvarṇika.
Combined with the six [syllables] beginning with Tārā, the seven-syllable mantra is twofold;
the eight-syllable mantra is twelvefold, and it is celebrated as bestowing fame and sovereignty.
Everything—meditation, worship, recitation, and so forth—is to be understood as being like the six oceans.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mantras born of the ninth [ocean]. (8-475)

The syllable *tāra* (om), followed by *rāma* in the dative case (*rāmāya*), then *krodhaḥ*, *astraṃ*, and *vahnivallabhā* (svāhā)—this is another eight-syllabled mantra; its sage and other attributes should be the same as those of the six-syllabled mantra.
The destroyer of all defects and the bestower of victory in battle—now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mantras arising from the tenth [letter]. (8.477)
Oṃ hrīḥ, namaśca rāmāya hrīḥ—this is the supreme eight-syllable mantra.
Sadāśiva is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chanda). (8.478)
Śivomārāmacandra is proclaimed as its deity;
the limbs [of the mantra] are formed with the long *māyā* (hīṃ) joined with the five syllables of the *tāra* (oṃ).
"Oṃ, salutation to Rāma; Hrīḥ, salutation to the heart," and so forth. Regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of meditation, he says:
"Rāma, three-eyed, bearing the crescent moon, holding a trident, and granting boons."
We worship him whose entire body is smeared with ashes and who wears his hair in matted locks.

One should meditate upon her who is delightful to Rāma, the pinnacle of beauty, adorned with the moon as her crest-jewel, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and possessing three eyes. (8.481)
One should recite the mantra of Rāma’s power known as Sītā one hundred thousand times;
all rites such as fire-offerings (homa) and worship are declared to be like those for the six-syllabled mantra.
He is especially a bestower of enjoyments and a granter of victory in battle.
Now, I shall describe the Rāma-mantras arising from the eleven [syllables].
O gods, the two Mantras consisting of seven syllables, as well as those beginning with *tārā* (om) consisting of six syllables each,
when joined together in a *saṃpuṭa* fashion, constitute the twelve nine-syllabled Mantras.
For them, all [the merit of] meditation, worship, and so forth, becomes equal to seven oceans.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which arises from the interval of twelve.
The ten-syllable mantra of the Beloved of Jānakī begins with *huṃ*, ends with *svāhā*, and has *ṅe* at its conclusion; Vasiṣṭha is its sovereign sage (*muni*). (8.486)

Chanda is the deity; Rāma, who has taken Sītā’s hand in marriage, is the primary seed-syllable (bīja); Dviṭha is the power (śakti); and the six long vowels are considered the limbs (aṅga). || 8-487 ||
One should place the ten syllables of the mantra upon the head, forehead, space between the eyebrows, palate, throat, heart, navel, genitals, knees, and feet. (8.488)
He speaks of the meditation: "In the city of Ayodhyā, within a golden pavilion studded with jewels, where canopies of *mandāra* flowers are fastened and which is adorned with archways. (8.489)
Rāghava was seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot on his lion-throne,
surrounded by Rākṣasas, monkeys, and auspicious gods traveling in divine vehicles.
He was being praised by joyful sages and attended upon by them;
his left side was adorned by Sītā, and he was graced by Lakṣmaṇa. (8.491)
Meditating thus upon [the deity] who is dark-complexioned, with a serene countenance, and adorned with all ornaments,
one should recite the mantra for one hundred thousand syllables with undistracted mind.
The entire practice, including recitation and worship, for this [mantra] is the same as that for the six-syllable [mantra].
Now, in the thirteenth [chapter], I shall declare the Rāma-mantra which has arisen. (8.493)
Rāmaṅge'nta-dhanuṣpāṇi, likewise Vahnisundarī;
this ten-syllabled mantra has Brahmā as its sage, Virāṭ as its meter, and Agni as its deity. (8.494)
Rāma, the destroyer of Rākṣasas, is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (bīja); Svāhā is the power (śakti). One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable. || 8-495 ||

One should perform the placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa), as well as the meditation and the preliminary rite (pauraścaraṇika-vidhi), just as described for the ten-syllable mantra; one should meditate upon [the deity] holding a bow and arrows.
Moreover, this [mantra] is specifically victorious and bestows the restoration of lost sovereignty.
Thus, the mantras practiced by Hanumān and others are to be seen [in the section on] Meru.
Now, the Rāma-gāyatrī is in that very same place.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme [mantra] worshipped by Śatrughna.
We know the Gāyatrī of Rāma, the bestower of victory, which is to be worshipped by those born of the Solar dynasty;
we meditate upon the Beloved of Sītā; may that Rāma inspire us.
This is the Gāyatrī of Rāma, which grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to his devotees. (8.498)
Whatever sin has been committed since birth, which would otherwise remain inexhaustible for ten recitations, is destroyed by a hundred, or even by a thousand recitations. (8.499)
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this [mantra] consists of reciting it four hundred thousand times;
whatever else is required, such as worship and so forth, one should perform all of that exactly as before.
This Gāyatrī beginning with *tārā* bestows liberation itself;
that beginning with *māyā* bestows sovereignty; and that beginning with *ramā* bestows supreme fortune. (8.501)
Even when united with Madana, he deludes the earth.
Now, regarding the mantra of Sītā (from the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā):
having first uttered the Śrī-bīja, one should extract the word "sītāyai. (8-502)
The mantra, joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess), is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it;
its progenitor is declared to be the Seer (Ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (Chandas).
She who is named Sītā, the Mother of the World, is the deity who consists of the universe.
(In the Merutantra) it is said: "The Goddess Sītā is proclaimed; the Śrī-bīja and the two final [syllables] are her power (śakti). (8.504)
One should fashion the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the first [syllable] joined with a long vowel;
one should worship on the Vaiṣṇava pedestal and meditate upon her united with Rāghava.
[One should meditate on her] golden-hued, with lotus-like hands, intent upon gazing at Rāma.
Now, the mantra of Balarāma from another tantra: At the end of the *tāra* (om), [the name] Balabhadra, followed by the heart-mantra (*hṛdayam*) and the eight syllables (*vasuvarṇa*). (8.506)
The mantra is that of Jaimini, its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deity is Balarāma; by repeating the words of the mantra twice, one performs the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
Now, the meditation: I take refuge in Balarāma, who is as fair as a bright cloud, who wears blue garments dear to Revatī, and who holds a plow and a pestle. (8.508)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount.
Now, the mantras of Śrī Kṛṣṇa (from the *Merutantra*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the most wonderful mantras of Kṛṣṇa;
that very Lord Kṛṣṇa resides at the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages.
He shall increase the dharmas of the Kali age for the sake of delivering his devotees;
appearing in seventy-one forms, he shall manifest in every Manvantara. (8.510)
Liberation results from practicing what has been taught therein, while downfall results from practicing what is contrary to it;
thus has the reality of both worldly manifestation and existence been fully explained. || 511 ||
Born at the beginning of the Kali Yuga, he was devoted to the various amorous sports with the gopīs;
by manifesting his power, he brought about the downfall of those who performed such acts.
In the Kali age, however, birth occurs for those devoted to their own duty;
I shall proclaim its mantra, which brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The ten-syllable mantra "Gopījanavallabhāya Svāhā" is as follows: at the end of the word *gopījana*, [the word] *vallabhāya* is added, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā). (From the Gītāmṛta) 8-513.
This ten-syllable mantra bestows both visible and invisible fruits;
O Sage, the recitation preceded by its seed-syllable is declared to be its secret. (8.514)
Because its nature consists of the elided seed-syllable, it is called the "ten-syllabled" here; as stated in the *Bṛhadgautamīya*:
"The ten-syllabled mantra, whose seed-syllable is elided, is the sole abode of both enjoyment and liberation. (8.515)
But when extracted separately by him, O Great Sage, the seed-syllable of desire becomes a mantra that yields fruit through my yoga; not otherwise, even in tens of millions of eons.
In the Merutantra, Nārada is declared to be its sage; Virāṭ is cited as the meter;
the deity is the Son of Nanda (Kṛṣṇa); the seed-syllable is *klīṃ*; and the power is the beloved of the Fire-god (Svāhā). (8.517)
One should proceed with mantras beginning with *āviśuḥ*, followed by terms such as *trailokyarakṣaṇa* and so forth, ending with words like *asurānta* and *cakra*, and concluding with *svāhā*.

One should likewise perform the five-limbed rite with [mantras] joined by their seed-syllables (*jāti*) upon the five fingers, as well as upon the heart, the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the armor (*kavaca*). (8.519)
Having performed the other nyāsas in sequence on the two sides of the weapon (astra), on the hips, the back, and the head, he describes the meditation:
"Having thus performed [the ritual] according to the rule, the practitioner [becomes] a body of mantra. (8.520)
One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the universe, who is eternal and realized through the three Vedas;
first, one should remember the beautiful Vṛndāvana, which shone forth in the past.
It was endowed with an abundance of fruits and an overflow of fresh sprouts,
resounded with the humming of bees and the cries of parrots and other birds.
In that forest, he saw a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), adorned with fresh sprouts and cooled by droplets from the waves at the side of the daughter of the Sun (Sītā).
Joined with golden branches at its tips and endowed with fruits of the nine jewels,
it rises high above the universe, flowing with a downpour of a divine stream of nectar.
The practitioner of mantra should visualize the earth beneath that [seat] as being set with blazing jewels, adorned with the pollen of flowers, and free from the six waves of existence. (8.525)
There, one should visualize a jeweled floor of rubies as the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha),
upon which is an eight-petalled lotus of the color red, as previously described.
In its center, one should meditate with undivided mind upon Kṛṣṇa seated comfortably—the all-pervading Lord, whose face is serene and who resembles the rising sun. (8.527)
Resembling a sapphire, with smooth and long hair,
his head was radiant with a beautiful peacock crest.
His head was beautified by the flowers of the Kalpa tree, which were being visited by bees;
his forehead shone with curling locks of hair, and he had blue lotuses placed upon his ears.
One should visualize [him] with a tilaka mark smeared with gorocana, resembling the full moon, with lotus-like eyes, and earrings shaped like makaras made of blazing jewels. (8.530)
(686) His cheeks surpassed a clear mirror in their loveliness;
his nose was most wonderfully prominent, and his lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit. 8-531.
His teeth were like pomegranate seeds, his neck was as beautiful as a conch shell,
and he possessed the splendor of a necklace fashioned from forest shoots and flowers.
His broad and elevated chest was radiant with the luster of the Kaustubha gem;
his breast was marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, and he was charming with shoulders like those of a bull.
His staff-like arms hang down to his knees; his abdomen is marked by the three folds of skin;
his waist is bound with a small girdle, and he is resplendent with a neck-ornament.
His clear soles are marked with signs such as the wheel, the chain, the lotus, yellow garments, and so forth, as well as the vajra and other emblems. (8.535)
His fingers were placed in the holes of the flute fixed to his lotus-like mouth,
and his mind was captivated by listening to the divine and beautiful melodies arising from it.
Constantly enchanting the multitude of living beings with his side-glances, his mind was filled with an abundance of supreme bliss. (8.537)
It was surrounded by cows whose eyes were fixed intently upon the lotus of his face,
moving slowly as they were weighed down by the burden of their full udders.

[The world was filled] with the sounds emerging from their mouths, which were filled by the drinking of their breasts as they were offered, even though they had completely abandoned every trace of the milk they had swallowed.
With milk joined with masses of foam, enchanting to the sight, and longing to hear songs accompanied by the sounding of flutes; (8.540)
And by the young calves, who had pricked up the pair of their ear-holes and whose heads were scratching at the itch arising from between their horns. (8.541)
For the sake of mutual playfulness, with their hooves touching the ground, they were glossy and heavy, with uplifted tails and beautiful dewlaps. (8.542)
Immediately thereafter, it was surrounded by herds of calves and young bulls,
making lowing sounds like thunderclouds, with heavy, long, and magnificent humps.
With the nectar-like sounds of the flute drunk in by their upturned ears,
they were accompanied by their peers who were singing and dancing, all adorned with identical ornaments.
He was surrounded by cowherds wearing various costumes who were offering praises,
as well as by children of sweet appearance whose speech was indistinct and wonderful.
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should remember the multitude of cowherd women adorned with throat-ornaments fashioned from tiger claws.
One should visualize the host of deities outside, who have brought the god of love back to life with the surging waves of their mutual passion, and who consist of cowherdesses, cowherds, and cows.
In the presence of the God of gods, there was a host of sages desiring an accumulation of wealth, as well as Dakṣa, who was devoted to the study of the Vedas.

Those seeking the Dharma should later remember Sanaka and the others; likewise, on the left, they should remember the lords of yogis with their consorts, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
He also saw perfected beings, vidyādharas, cāraṇas, and hosts of apsarases,
all intent upon playing the vīṇā lute, which was filled with manifold melodies.
One should meditate upon Nārada, the best of sages, free from pride, in the sky.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
then, having been initiated according to the previously mentioned rule, one should mutter the mantra. (8.551)
Abiding by the rules and with senses subdued, the mantra-practitioner should contemplate the meaning of the mantra forty thousand times using a rosary of white lotus seeds. (8.552)
Thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra, the wise practitioner should recite it one million times;
he should then perform one hundred thousand fire-oblations with red lotuses soaked in white ghee, honey, and sugar. (8.553)
One should offer oblations with sacrificial materials mixed with sugar and ghee,
or one should satisfy [the deity] with pure waters scented with camphor and sandalwood.

Then, having performed the self-consecration (ātma-abhiṣeka), one should thereafter worship the Brahmanas with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, betel leaves, and ritual fees (dakṣiṇā). || 8.555 ||

Then, having prostrated correctly before his own guru according to the prescribed rite, he should honor him with wealth, grain, garments, and so forth, while remaining free from any stinginess regarding his resources.
One should propitiate [the deity] with supreme devotion for the sake of accomplishing one's own task;
thereafter, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected may perform the ritual applications (prayoga) desired by himself.
Endowed with devotion and delighting in the obligatory and occasional rites,
one should properly perform [the worship] at that time [of the deity] born of Devakī, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Meditating upon the beautiful one, who wears yellow garments and possesses the luster of the sky,
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times on the fourth night.
One should offer a tenth part of that [number] as oblations with *kiṃśuka* blossoms smeared with the three sweets;
having attained vigor, wisdom, and memory, one shall become the foremost among poets. (8.560)

Now, another mantra (from the Śāradā): having first uttered the word *kṛṣṇāya*, then *govindāya*, and after that the word *gopījana*, it ends with *vallabhāya* followed by the two *ṭha*s (svāhā). (8.561)
The eighteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), is proclaimed;
Nārada is said to be its sage, and the Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter. (8.562)
The deity Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the fruits of all desires, was described by Devatā according to the sequence of syllables numbering four, six, four, four, and two.
One should perform the five limbs of the *mantra* together with the knower of mantras and the relatives.
[The limb of] meditation: one should contemplate him incessantly enchanting within the beautiful Vṛndāvana. (8.564)
Thousands of cowherd girls, with their bee-like eyes sent toward the lotus-face of Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, [gazed upon him]. (8.565)
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, they long painted [their lovers] with eager longing;
their faces were burdened by full, high breasts shimmering with pearl necklaces.
With their braided hair and garments loosened, their speech slow and faltering,
and their lower lips glistening and curved, illuminated by the radiance of their rows of teeth.
They enticed him with various amorous gestures full of passion and pride.
With the splendor of a blooming blue lotus, a moon-like face, and a fondness for peacock-feather ornaments;
bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the magnificent Kaustubha gem, clad in beautiful yellow garments;
his body honored by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds—[I bow to Him].
I worship Govinda, who is intent on playing his flute and adorned with divine limbs.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite this mantra twenty thousand times according to the rule,
and with a well-composed mind, one should offer oblations with reddish lotuses in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that recitation.
Now other mantras are described (in the *Merutantra*):
"Henceforth, I shall duly declare those mantras of ten syllables that have appeared sequentially throughout the three ages (*yuga*), which bestow spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (8.571)
The ten-syllable king of mantras consists of Kāma-Māyā-Indirā (Klṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ) preceded by Māyā-Śrī-Kāma (Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klṃ), and Lakṣmī-Māyā-Smara (Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klṃ) preceded by [the same]. (8.572)
These three mantras consist of thirteen syllables each throughout the three ages; their procedure regarding the beginning and end with the sages and so forth is as prescribed for the *paṅkti* meter.
"In the *paṅkti* [meter]" means that it consists of ten syllables.
The meditation for the third mantra is declared to be like that of ten syllables;
however, that which was stated for twenty syllables applies to the second, while now it is being explained for the first. (8.574)
Holding a sword, a bow, an arrow, and a mallet in his lotus-like hands, he joyfully plays the flute with both hands. (8.575)
One should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa as situated within the solar disc for the attainment of desired fruits.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
having recited the mantra one million times, one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire ten thousand times.
Then, having performed the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites, one who has mastered the mantra should proceed.
Now, another mantra is given in that very same place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare [the practice] for the twenty-seven-fold [mantra] in the Kali age. (8.577)
One should utter "Tāraṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya";
this is declared to be the twelve-syllable mantra, and Nārada is considered its sage (ṛṣi).
The Gāyatrī is said to be the meter, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is considered the deity; the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed with [the syllables] numbering one hundred and eight.
He speaks of the meditation:
"Seated upon a beautiful and auspicious jewel-throne at the foot of a lovely wish-fulfilling tree is Nandana, endowed with all the primary and secondary marks. (8.580)
One should meditate on Him who is dark as a rain cloud, accompanied by a herd of cows with full-grown udders,
and likewise holding two staffs in His two hands.
The imperishable Viṣṇu should be meditated upon as being sprinkled by the stream of nectar from the frontal globes of Śakra’s elephant, which has eyes as long as lotuses.
He describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
"Having thus meditated upon the Lord of Gods, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables;
then one should offer oblations with cow’s milk ten thousand times and perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (8.583)
Now, another mantra from another tantra: *Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *hṛt* (Namaḥ), *bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya*, and the two *ṭha*s (Svāhā).
Nārada is declared its sage (*muni*), and the *anuṣṭubh* meter is proclaimed for it. (8.584)
The Lord, the beloved of Rukmiṇī, [is worshipped] with five limbs by means of the mantra words. (8.584ef)

Meditation: [I meditate on] my beloved, whose complexion is like the *tāpiccha* tree, who possesses a golden luster, whose left hand rises up from a lotus, and who, her heart filled with wonder, embraces me with her vine-like arm.
May Hari protect you for a long time— he who embraces her while holding a golden staff that gleams in his other hand, wearing garments dyed with saffron, and adorned with various ornaments.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
having thus meditated upon the Lord of Rukmiṇī, one should mutter this mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should offer ten thousand oblations of red lotuses soaked in honey.
Now, another mantra (on Mount Meru): Now, therefore, in that which is called the Mountain-Veda, *klī*. *Kṛṣṇā* is the wife of Agni.
This six-syllable king of mantras is to be recited and meditated upon as before. (8-587)
The meaning is "ten oceans. Thus, many varieties of mantras have been omitted for fear of prolixity.
Now, the Buddha-mantra is mentioned in that very same [text]:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the Buddha-mantra of great fruit."
Because it is true, there is never any eligibility for the twice-born and others at all.
These Brahmins, devoted to the left-hand path, are of the Kuṇḍaka class and have fallen from their caste;
deprived of Vedic consecrations, they have through negligence succumbed to their own whims. (8.589)
Likewise, the Golakas by birth, as well as the Kayasthas and others,
having propitiated Viṣṇu-Buddha, attain worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Homage to the Blessed One, the Buddha, who ferries one across the ocean of saṃsāra! Fearing the Kali age, I have come for refuge to you, the worthy protector. (8-591)
By means of the first four words and by the pair of feet, the ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared; with the complete [mantra], the pervasive [protection] is performed three times.
Now, regarding meditation:
One should meditate upon him seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) upon a lotus, with both hands placed upon his thighs;
he is fair-complexioned, with all his limbs shaven, and his eyes are motionless in deep concentration. (8.592)
Adorned with books, seats, and hands, and graced by various disciples,
he was praised by the world-protectors beginning with Indra and was clothed in white garments.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable and perform fire oblations (*homa*) with rice cooked in ghee.
One should also satisfy the Blessed Lord with water mixed with *tulasī*.
Now, the *kalki* mantra is mentioned in that very same place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the *kalki* mantra of great fruit.
'Kaḥ kalkine'—this six-syllabled mantra is said to end with the heart [seed-syllable]. (8.595)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the syllables of the mantra, and perform the pervasive ritual (*vyāpaka*) with the complete mantra.
Now, the meditation: One should meditate upon [the deity] mounted on a blue [bull], resplendent with a white turban. (8.596)
With a great goad in his hand and a magnificent breastplate of kaustubha stone,
he was crushing the hosts of mlecchas, his eyes rolling with rage.
Hari was praised by gods, sages, and gandharvas who had vanished from sight.
Now follows the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times and offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with sugar. (8.598)
One should satisfy [the deity] with pure waters and also gratify the Brahmins;
thus propitiated, the mantra bestows victory in battle. (8-599)
Beholding this means of accomplishment from afar, the lords of the earth bow down, and likewise, their enemies who act according to their own whims fall into doubt.
Day by day his prosperity increases, and upon death he shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Now, the Hayagrīva mantra is declared (in the Merutantra): "The Hayagrīva mantra bestows all forms of abundance. (8-601)
Joined with the syllable *hasau* and adorned with the *bindu*, this seed-mantra (*bījamantra*), served by the Brahmins, is the first of Hayagrīva. (8.600)
For a Kṣatriya, however, [the mantra consists of] the two syllables *ha* and *sa*, joined with *e* and provided with the *bindu*;
for one born as a Vaiśya, it consists of the two syllables *ha* and *sa*, joined with *ai* and provided with the *bindu*.
The *triṣṭubh* is the meter, Brahmā is the sage, and Hayagrīva is the deity;
the ritual for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is declared by means of the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels. (8.602)

Now, the meditation: [He holds] a lotus, a rosary for recitation, the gesture of fearlessness, and a book; he is seated upon a white lotus, fair-complexioned, and adorned with white garments and unguents. (8.603)
I bow to Hayagrīva, the beloved of his devotees, the destroyer of the Dānavas.

Now follows the *puraścaraṇa*: one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for each Veda; at the end, one should offer oblations of clarified butter in quantities amounting to a tenth part of that total. (8.604)

Through satiation with fragrant substances and the like, through purification, and through feeding the Brahmins, the perfected mantra becomes fit for application, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (8.605)
Now, another mantra [is described] in the *Śāradā*:
having uttered the word "udgirat," followed by the words "praṇava" and "udgītha," one should then recite up to "sarvavāgīśvarā," and then "īśvarā. (8.606)
At the end of the inconceivable state consisting of all the Vedas, one should utter "sarvam.
This mantra, beginning with "tārā" (om) and ending with "bodhaya," is proclaimed as having "dvitaya" at its conclusion. (8-607)
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Brahmā as instructed; the meter (chandas) is declared to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity (devatā) is the all-pervading Hayagrīva, the bestower of mastery over speech. (8-608)
One should assign the five limbs [of the mantra] using the syllables of the mantra preceded by the *tāra*.
Now, as for meditation:
[one should visualize] the horse-faced one, possessing the luster of the autumnal moon,
adorned with ornaments made of pearls.
We worship him whose pair of arms is adorned with the wheel and the conch, and who has placed both hands upon his two knees.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable.
For the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, one should offer oblations in the Vaiṣṇava fire ten times the number of recitations, using *kunda* flowers soaked in honey. (8.610)
Now, another mantra (from the Merutantra):
Now I shall declare another excellent mantra that bestows sharp intelligence:
"To the one whose nature is consciousness and bliss, whose form is the self transcending the universe. (8.611)
Salutation to you, Hayagrīva, the King of Vidyās, Viṣṇu. Svāhā! I am that very one; this is the thirty-eight-syllable mantra beginning with "Haṃsa. (8.612)
In this context, the ritual of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-vidhi) is declared to be performed with the syllables of the Tāra-mantra.
The meditation (dhyāna) is as before. Now follows the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
The preliminary practice (puraścaryā) consists of thirty-six lakhs [of recitations], while the rest is considered to be as previously stated.
Now, the Cakra-mantra (according to the *Śāradā-tantra*):
Tāra, Bhṛgu, Viyat, and Bhū again; joined with Vahni and its long vowel at the beginning; followed by Pāvaka, ending with Kavaca and Astra—this is remembered as the seven-syllabled mantra. (8.614)
The sage is declared to be Ahirbudhnya, and the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is proclaimed by the sages to be Hari himself in the form of the Cakra.
To Ācakra, that which is called the heart is declared; to Vicakra, the head is remembered;
to Sucakra, the tuft (śikhā) is proclaimed; and to Dhīcakra, the body-covering (armour).
The eye-mantra is remembered as *saṃcakrāya*, and after that, *jvālācakrāya*;
each of the six limb-mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) is joined with these and ends with *svāhā* (*dviṭha*).
Now, the meditation:
[One should visualize the deity] whose brilliance is like that of the sun at the end of an aeon, filling the entire three worlds with light;
red-eyed, with tawny hair, inspiring fear in the host of enemies, and possessing a terrifying laugh with formidable fangs.

One should meditate in the mind upon the primordial enemy of the gods, known as Cakra, who holds in his arms a discus, a conch, a mace, two lotuses, a broad pestle, a bow, a noose, and a goad. (8.618)

p. 695) Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform one thousand oblations (*homa*) with sesame seeds, mustard seeds, lotuses, wood-apples (*bilva*), and milk-rice, respectively. (8.619)
Now, the mantra of Ananta is in that very same place:
"Next, I shall fully declare another mantra that causes pleasure to Viṣṇu; 'Obeisance to Ananta'—this is declared to consist of six syllables. (8.620)
Vyāsa is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and Ananta is the deity;
the application is for the purpose of destroying disease, otherwise it is the same as in the case of Govinda. (8.621)
Now, regarding the mantra of Gopālasundarī, it is stated in that very same source:
"Next, I shall describe Gopālasundarī, who is to be worshipped through two paths.
One should utter the seed-syllables of Māyā, Śrī, and Kāma, followed by the words 'to Kṛṣṇa'. (8.622)
The twenty-ninth letter, as well as the vowels *ru* and *de*, the fifth [vowel], and the seed-syllable of *trapā*: by these, the seventh peak (kūṭa) is formed.
After that, [one should worship] Govindāya, followed by the peak-mantra beginning with Citra-aiśvarya;
then Gopījanavallabhāya, and after that, Sakalatrapām.
Having uttered the *kūṭarūpa*, one should speak the wife of Fire;
this twenty-three-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. || 8.625 ||
The sage is Vidhātṛ; he is Dakṣa when [the meter is] even, but when uneven, he is Ānandabhara.
The goddess of the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Gopālasundarī. (8.626)

The procedure for the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared by means of syllables consisting of three, three, four, and four [units], excluding the *kūṭa* syllables; one should assign these mantra-syllables upon the body.
Having stated other nyāsas, he describes the meditation:

"One should meditate upon Hari, who is accompanied by Kamalā and Vasudhā, residing within the Śrīcakra, in the Ocean of Milk, on the White Island (Svetadvīpa), amidst forests of wish-fulfilling trees and the like. (8.629)
When that [space] has been pervaded, one should visualize a jeweled pavilion made of gold;
therein, in the center of the Śrī-pīṭha, stands [the Lord] praised by the faces of Brahmā and the others. (8.630)
Holding an eight-petalled lotus, a conch, the [four] primary colors, and a flute with his right hands, and likewise a bow, a noose, and a goad with his left hands. (8.631)
He holds a lute of reddish hue, adorned with various ornaments,
wears yellow garments, and is surrounded on all sides by throngs of cowherd girls.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Thereafter, one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites; thus, the perfection of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) arises. (8.633)
Now, the mantra of Śrīdhara is given in that very same place:
"Next, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme mantra of Śrīdhara:
one should utter the seed-syllable of Kāma mounted upon Ramā, and then say 'to Śrīdhara'. (8.634)
The sixteen-syllable mantra ending with "namas" for "trailokyamohanāya" has Brahmā as its seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī as its meter (chandaḥ), and Śrīdhara as its deity (sura). || 8-635 ||
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable *Śrī* conjoined with the six long vowels. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*):
Having opened [the door] upon a white island where trees bear fruit in all seasons... (8.636)
There, beneath a wish-fulfilling tree, upon a seat prepared by the Lord of Birds,
[he saw the Lord] with conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands, possessing the luster of refined gold.

One should meditate in the heart upon Śrīdhara, the bestower of the goals of human existence, who wears a crown and earrings, whose chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa, and who holds Lakṣmī in his heart. 8-638.

Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): the best of practitioners should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations of clarified butter ten thousand times; thereafter, he should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites as previously described. (8.639)
Then the best of practitioners should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites as before.
Thus ends the section on Viṣṇu. Now follow the Śaiva mantras.
(From the *Śāradā-tantra*): Now I shall declare the mantras of Maheśvara, which bestow the accomplishment of all aims. (8.640)
By those [mantras] previously proclaimed by the sages, one easily attains union with Śiva:
the Heart [syllable], the supreme Vapara [syllable], the witness [syllable], the one ending in *la*, and the one joined with the infinite wind (*ananta*).
This six-syllabled mantra, beginning with *Tārā*, is declared to be five-syllabled.
The meaning of this mantra is stated [in the Vāmadevasaṃhitā]:
"The syllable *Oṃ* is traditionally held to be the designator of the all-pervading Brahman. (8.643)
The word *namaḥ* is proclaimed to be expressive of salutation;
salutation is described by the ancients as having the characteristic of humility. (8.644)

Devotion (*prahvatā*) is the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), which—though appearing as distinct from Śiva due to *māyā*—is in every respect identical with Him who is characterized by truth and other such qualities. (8.645)
He calls the relationship "Name," characterized by identity with Śiva; consciousness (cit), whose nature is truth, knowledge, and supreme bliss, is the other aspect (kalā). 8-646.
The Śāmbhavī [power] is to be known by the word "Śiva" because of its extreme clarity;
therefore, this word is the designator of Brahman, whose nature is the digit of consciousness (citkalā). (8.647)
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the Ṛṣis and others:
"Vāmadeva is the sage, Paṅkti is the meter, and Īśa is its deity;
the preceptor should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the mantra with six syllables. (8.648)
Now, regarding meditation: One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa— resembling a mountain of silver, adorned with the beautiful crescent moon,
his limbs radiant with jewel ornaments, holding an axe, a deer, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and being gracious in countenance.
Seated, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, wearing a tiger skin, the beginning of the universe,
worthy of universal homage, the remover of all fears, five-faced and three-eyed.
(p. 698) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
Initiated according to the Śaiva path, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each of its constituent principles (*tattva*).
One should likewise offer oblations of auspicious milk-rice (*pāyasa*) for as many thousands of times.
Then the mantra becomes perfected, bestowing the desired accomplishments of the practitioner.
Now, another mantra is mentioned in that same place: the six-syllabled mantra, conjoined with Śakti, is said to be the eight-syllabled mantra. (8.651)
The seer and the meter were proclaimed of old; the deity is the Lord of Umā (Śiva).
The ancillary limbs have been mentioned previously; one should meditate upon Soma and Īśa.
Now, the meditation:

I worship Him who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, who is three-eyed, who bears the crescent moon, whose face is smiling, and who holds in His hands a trident, a skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, adorned with beautiful necklaces.
[He beholds] his beloved, whose body is embraced by his hand, her left thigh paralyzed, a beautiful red lotus shimmering in her palm, and her limbs adorned with glittering jewel ornaments. (8.653)
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one thousand times with the best twigs of the *āragvadha* tree, sprinkled with the three sweets (*madhura*).
He states another mantra:

"The mantra known as Prāsāda consists of the letter *sa* with a final *visarga*, joined with the end of *sadyojāta* (the letter *ja*), its head adorned with a *bindu*; it is declared to bestow all accomplishments upon those who worship it. (8.655)
The ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is proclaimed by means of the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels;
Vāmadeva is the sage, Paṅkti is the meter, and Sadāśiva is the deity. (8.656)
The preceptor should assign the forms beginning with Īśāna to the thumbs and other fingers;
first the one named Īśāna, then Tatpuruṣa, and immediately after that Aghora.
They know the first seed-syllable (bīja) as Vāmadeva, and the next as Sadyojāta, in due order.
(p. 699) Now, the visualization (dhyāna): Then, having become composed, one should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva. (8-658)

I bow to the Lord who is adorned with five faces—the colors of a pearl, yellow, white clouds, a pearl, and the *japā* flower—each with three eyes; who wears a crescent moon as his crown and possesses the luster of ten million full moons;
and who holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, fire, a lordly serpent, a bell, and a goad.
One should meditate upon him holding a noose that removes fear, resplendent with immeasurable ornaments.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times;
one should then perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with *karavīra* flowers soaked in honey, consisting of a tenth part of that [recitation].
He states another mantra:
"The Tāra, Māyā, and the Sky [letter] endowed with the Bindu and the Anusvāra;
joined with the five syllables, this is considered the eight-syllabled mantra. (8.661)
The wise practitioner should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and other rites as described for the five-syllable mantra.
Meditation: I bow to the Lord, who is the color of vermilion, whose beautiful moon-ornament shines upon his jeweled crown,
whose eye rises upon his forehead, whose lotus-face is graced with a smile, and who is adorned with divine ornaments and unguents.

He placed his hand upon the rounded, high breasts of his beloved, who rested her hand on her left thigh while holding a young blue lotus; he held his sacrificial ladle against the edge of the sacrificial altar.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): the best among those who know the Vedas should thus recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times;
he should then offer oblations of milk-rice soaked in ghee one thousand times.

Now, the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra is described in that very same place: "The syllable Om (Tāra), the letter Sthirā (Ṣ) together with the ear (r) and the moon (bindu), followed by Bhṛgu (b) adorned with emission (visarga)—this six-syllabled essence is declared to be the mantra consisting of Mṛtyuñjaya. (8.664)
The seer is Kahola, the deity is said to be Devyādi, and the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī; Mahādeva Mṛtyuñjaya is proclaimed as its presiding deity. (8-665)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual with the long-combined *bhṛgu* mantra.
Now, the meditation:
[He is] three-eyed with the moon, sun, and fire; his face is smiling; he stands within two lotuses;
his hands shine with the mudrā, the noose, the deer, and the rosary; and he has the luster of the moon.

One should meditate upon Paśupati, the conqueror of death, whose body is bathed in nectar flowing from the moon on his crest, who is radiant with ornaments such as necklaces, and who captivates the entire universe with his splendor. (8.666)

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one of great intelligence should recite the mantra one million times; then, with a tenth part of that number, he should offer oblations of pieces of *amṛtā* soaked in pure milk and clarified butter. (8.667)
Now, regarding the mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, it is stated in that very same place:
"O lords of sages, I shall now declare the jewel of a mantra which bestows all human goals; by reciting it until one is filled [with its power], divine knowledge is attained. (8.668)
First, [the word] "to Dakṣiṇāmūrti," then immediately after that, the word "to you" (tubhyam),
and at the end of the word "at the root of the banyan tree" (vaṭamūla), the word "to the dweller" (nivāsine).
To the one whose limbs are solely devoted to meditation, one should subsequently utter the word "namaḥ";
this [mantra] addressed to Rudra, the source of bliss, is said to be conjoined with the power of Tārā.
The thirty-six-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of all desires; Śuka is declared to be the sage, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh.
Its presiding deity is said to be Śambhu, named Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
the heart is declared to consist of six syllables, and the head is said to consist of two.
The *śikhā* is prescribed with eight [syllables], the *kavaca* is considered to consist of eight syllables (*vasu*),
the *netra* is said to have five, and the *astra* is declared to have three.

p. 701) These six, beginning with Tāraśakti and ending with Tārā, are the members of the same class; they have been correctly declared as the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) by the most excellent of teachers. (8.674)

Now, concerning meditation: On the delightful slope of the Golden Mountain, frequented by perfected beings and kinnaras, where the heat of the sun is warded off on all sides by the branches of various trees. (8.675)
In that place, where flowering trees were embraced by networks of vines in full bloom,
and which was cooled by the breezes from waterfalls issuing from rock crevices.
Where swarms of female bees were singing, flocks of peacocks were dancing,
and the quarters of the sky were made resonant by the warbling of throngs of cuckoos.
In that place frequented by deer free from mutual envy, where the ancient sages such as Śuka and others constantly resided; (8.678)
It was beheld by the gods, headed by Purandara, who had come for service—
a banyan tree of great height, radiant with fruits like rubies.
It was adorned with dense leaves made of emeralds and embellished by hanging ornaments fashioned from the nine precious gems.
It was adorned with fragrant flowers born of both water and land,
and frequented by flocks of parrots reciting the Vedas and the Śāstras.
Having contemplated that wonderful ground skilled at severing the torments of saṃsāra, [one should contemplate] upon the auspicious and excellent lion-throne situated at its base.
He was seated, possessing immeasurable splendor, with a face like the autumnal moon,
being praised by hosts of sages who longed for divine knowledge.
One should remember the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the primordial source of the worlds.
Resembling Mount Kailāśa, adorned with a mass of matted hair flashing like a crescent moon, intent on gazing through his nose, three-eyed, seated in the *vīrāsana* posture,
his hands graced by the *mudrā*, the *ṭaṅka*, the deer, and the knee, and possessing a serene countenance—
I bow to the supreme Maheśa, who has serpents bound upon his shoulders and is surrounded by sages.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra twenty thousand times more than a hundred thousand (i.e., two hundred thousand).
One should then perform a fire oblation (*homa*) with pure sesame seeds mixed with milk, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"The Praṇava is the heart; after that, the word 'to the Blessed One' (bhagavate); joined with the dative suffix [ṅe], one should utter 'Dakṣiṇāmūrtti'; then 'medhām' for me. (8.686)
Bestow [this]: this mantra consists of twenty-two syllables ending with two *ṭha*s.
Its sage is the Four-faced One (Brahmā), its meter is Gāyatrī, and it is the deity of the mantra. (8.687)
He is known as Dakṣiṇāmūrtti, intent upon the exposition of the Vedas;
one should fashion the six limbs using the six long vowels conjoined with the syllable *tāra* (Om).
Alternatively, one may construct [the mantra] sequentially with syllables derived from human speech;
one should then contemplate the Lord of Mantras situated at the foot of the banyan tree as previously described.
Now, the meditation:
[He is] the color of crystal or silver, with the tips of his hands holding a rosary of pearls,
a jar of nectar, and the mudrās of knowledge and wisdom.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who wears a serpent as an armlet, who has the moon upon his crest, who possesses three eyes, and who is adorned with various ornaments.
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
