remaining established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should then offer oblations into the consecrated fire with lotuses mixed with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
p. 703) Now, the mantra of Nīlakaṇṭha is given in that same [work]:
First is the red [syllable] seated on fire (ra), followed by the first [seed-syllable] adorned with a bindu;
then the second [syllable] situated in the seed of fire (ra), elongated, ending in the letter śa, and adorned with the moon (bindu). (8.692)
The third is the mantra of Lāṅgalī-sargī, endowed with the three seed-syllables.
He is declared to be the essence of Nīlakaṇṭha, the supreme remover of the two kinds of poison.
The two syllables "hara" followed by the fire-born wife (svāhā) are proclaimed as the heart mantra;
"kapardine" followed by a pair of "ṭha" syllables is declared to be the head mantra.
The mantra for the crest (*śikhā*) is declared to be "nīlakaṇṭhāya" followed by two *ṭha*s;
at the end of the word "kālakūṭa," one adds "viṣabhakṣaṇam" joined with the feminine suffix *ṅī*.
"Hūṃ Phaṭ" is prescribed as the armor (kavaca) for Nīlakaṇṭhin by the learned; "Svāhā" at the end is the weapon (astra). The wise know these to be the five limbs (pañcāṅga) of the mantra.
Now, the meditation:
[One should meditate on the Lord] possessing the brilliance of ten thousand rising suns, radiant with the crescent moon bound within his matted locks,
adorned by the lords of serpents, and holding in his hands a rosary, a trident, and a skull-cup.

I worship the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, who holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), who is beautiful with three eyes and five radiant faces, who is clothed in a tiger skin, and whose abode is the primordial ignorance (māyā).
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and duly offer oblations into the consecrated fire with clarified butter and sacrificial food (*havis*) in quantities amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Now, the mantra of Ardhanārīśvara is given in that same place:
"Agni, Saṃvartaka, Āditya, Ra, Anila, and the sixth [letter] with the bindu—this seed-syllable, known as Cintāmaṇi, bestows all prosperity. (8.699)
The sage is declared to be Kaśyapa; the metre is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is proclaimed to be Ardhanārīśvara, the Lord of the worlds. (8.700)
One should perform the six limbs in sequence by means of the consonants beginning with the letter *ra* and the six [syllables]. (8.700ef)
(p. 704) Now, for the meditation:
[He is] beautiful with a blue radiance, sporting three eyes, and holding in his hands a noose, a red lotus, a skull-cup, and a trident.
I perpetually bow to that form which bears the Lord of Ambikā upon half [of its body], whose ornaments are distributed [between the two halves], and whose crown is bound with the crescent moon.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa): the practitioner of mantra should recite the seed-syllable one hundred thousand times while contemplating thus;
he should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains sprinkled with honey.

Now, the Śarabha mantra (in the Merutantra): having uttered "Oṃ kha khā kha phaṭ," [one recites] "he twice swallows the vital breaths," and "huṃ phaṭ, O Śarabha, for the destruction of all weapons. (8-702)
Huṃ phaṭ svāhā for Śālva, the king of birds; this is the mantra of Antaka.
It is remembered as consisting of forty-one syllables, with Vāsudeva as its sage (muni). || 8.703 ||
Kālāgnirudra is proclaimed as the deity;
the meter is Jagatī, Svāhā is the power (śakti), and the void (kha) is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja). || 8-704 ||
The arrangement of the limbs [of the mantra] consists of six, seven, nine, six, and nine syllables. Now, the visualization:
[She has] three eyes like the moon, sun, and fire, and two faces, those of Kālī and Durgā. (8.705)
[He saw] Vidyujjihva, Vajranakha, and likewise Vaḍavāgnudara;
[he saw] Vyādhimṛtyuripughna and Caṇḍavātātivegina.
He possesses the form of a heart-trembling Bhairava who destroys hosts of enemies;
with half his body he is a deer, and with two wings he is a twice-born bird with a beak.
With his face turned downward, he has four feet; with his face turned upward, he has four arms.
He resembles the fire at the end of time and possesses the roar of a dark blue cloud.
(705) He whose strength and prowess were destroyed merely by the sight of him—to him, who possessed a fierce form with a mass of matted hair and who scattered mountains with his wings. (8.709)
"Salutation to Rudra, who has eight feet and whose form is that of a Śarabha.
Regarding the *puraścaraṇa*, he says:
"Meditating thus, one should mutter [the mantra] a thousand times and offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as an oblation. (8.710)
By practicing daily for six months, the perfection of the mantra is produced.
Now, the mantra of Kṣetrapāla (in the Śāradā-tantra): The final letter of the alphabet joined with the nasal bindu, followed by "to Kṣetrapāla" and the heart-mantra (namaḥ), is the spell. (8.711)
This [mantra] beginning with *Tārā* and consisting of eight syllables is proclaimed as that of Kṣetrapāla;
one should apply its six limbs using the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.
Now, as for the meditation: [one should visualize the deity] resembling a mountain of blue collyrium, with tawny hair rising upward,
possessing round and fierce eyes, and holding a mace and a skull-cup.
I bow down to the Lord, the Master of the Field, who is clothed in space, adorned with serpents, possessing fierce fangs, and endowed with a wondrous body.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with *caru* mixed with clarified butter amounting to one-tenth of that number; thereafter, one should worship the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśa*).
Now, the mantra of Vaṭuka for rescuing from calamity is given in that same [text]:
"One should extract 'Vaṭuka' ending in the dative case, and likewise 'Āpaduddhāraṇa'.
Then one should extract 'Kuru' twice, again ending in the dative case, and then that 'Vaṭuka'. (8.715)
The great mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables, conjoined with Śakti, is proclaimed as the celestial wish-granting tree for the complete attainment of one's desired fruits. (8.716)
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) and the Anuṣṭubh the meter;
the deity is Bhairava, the one who uplifts from the waters, as stated by the wise. (8.717)

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms upon the fingers, the body, and the face as before, preceded by the seed-syllable of Śakti and enriched with the five short vowels beginning with *sa* (Sadyojāta), etc. (8.718).
One should join the letter *va*, enriched with the five short vowels, to the [faces] beginning with Īśāna;
likewise, one should join it with the Śakti endowed with the six long vowels and with the letter *va* possessing those same vowels.
One should conceive of the limbs as being endowed with their respective births, beginning with the *praṇava*.
Now, for the meditation (*dhyāna*): its meditation is said to be threefold, according to the distinction of *sāttvika* and the other [guṇas]. (8.720)
I bow to the Child, who resembles crystal, whose face shines with earrings, who is adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels and richly decorated with tinkling bells and anklets;
who is radiant in form, clad in pure white garments, exceedingly gracious, and possessed of three eyes.
[He is] constantly holding a trident and a staff in his two hands and commands.
Resembling the rising sun, with three eyes, red unguents and garlands, and a smiling face; bestowing boons, holding a skull, granting fearlessness, and bearing a trident in his hands;
blue-necked, wearing magnificent ornaments, and radiant with the crescent moon upon his crest.
One should always meditate upon the God who wears garments as red as the bandhūka flower and who removes all fear. || 8-722 ||

One should meditate upon Maheśa, who is as beautiful as a blue mountain, who bears a crescent moon and a garland of skulls, who is clothed in the directions (naked), whose hair is tawny, and who holds a *ḍamaru* drum,
a goad, a sword, a noose, a serpent, a bell, and a skull-cup in his lotus-like hands, possessing fearsome fangs.
He has the form of a serpent, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with jeweled, shimmering tinkling bells and anklets.
This is declared to be sattvic meditation, which wards off untimely death,
generates longevity and health, and bestows the fruit of liberation.
The rājasa meditation is said to grant the accomplishment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
the tāmasa meditation subdues enemies and removes the effects of magical spells, spirits, and planetary influences.
(p. 707) Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable.
One should then perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with honey amounting to a tenth part of that number. (8.726)

Now, the mantra of the Pāśupata weapon (according to the Śāradā-tantra): The Tāra (Om), followed by the letter Vānta (Ś), situated on Dharā (L), adorned with the left eye (I) and the moon (bindu); then Pārśva (Pa), Vaka (Va), joined with Karṇa (Ra), ending with Varma (Hrīṃ) and Astra (Phaṭ)—this is the six-syllabled [mantra]. (8.727)
The *mantra* known as Pāśupatāstra wards off minor planetary influences;
its six limbs consist of the six syllables ending in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*). (8.728)
Now, as for the meditation:
[one should visualize the deity] possessing a radiance equal to the midday sun, bearing the moon, blazing with a terrifying laugh,
three-eyed, adorned with serpents, and having hair, beard, and a topknot shimmering like the crest of a flame.

One should meditate upon Paśupati, the omnipresent Lord, who holds a trident, a mallet, a sword, and a spear in his hands; who has four faces made terrifying by his fangs, and whose form consists of divine weapons.
Regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable and perform oblations with cow’s ghee in the consecrated fire in an amount equal to one-tenth of that.
Now, regarding the mantra of Hari-Hara in another tantra: Having first extracted Māyā (the syllable Hrīṃ), one should then extract Prāsāda (the syllable Hūṃ).
Then follows "Śaṅkaranārāyaṇāya," preceded by the Heart-mantra (Namaḥ) and the Praṇava (Oṃ). (8.731)
The thirteen-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
Nārada is declared its seer (ṛṣi), and Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas). || 8.732 ||
The deity Hariśaṅkara, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the three worlds,
should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) enriched with the six long vowels and the syllable Māyā (Hrīṃ).

Now, the meditation: I worship Hari-Hara, who holds a trident, a discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, whose half-body is dark blue and adorned with their respective ornaments. (8.734)

p. 708) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform an oblation (*havana*) with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) soaked in clarified butter, in a consecrated fire, consisting of one-tenth of that number. (8.735)
Thus ends the section on Śiva.
Now follows the mantra of Gaurī (from the Siddhāntasaṃgraha): Hrīṃ! O Gaurī, beloved of Rudra, O Mistress of Yoga—[one] should utter this word.
Hu Phaṭ Svāhā; this sixteen-syllable mantra of Gaurī is thus proclaimed. || 8.736 ||
The sage is Aja, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and Gaurī is its deity;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of Māyā joined with the six long vowels.
We worship the goddess Gaurī, who possesses a golden luster, who holds in her hands a mirror, collyrium, a noose, and a goad, and who is adorned with divine ornaments. (8.738)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with clarified butter ten thousand times.
Then, having performed the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites, one should accomplish the desired actions. (8.739)
Now I shall declare another mantra: one should extract the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), utter Bhavānī ending in the dative case (Bhavānyai), and at the end, one should proclaim "Namaḥ. (8.740)
The net of nyāsas has been taught previously; one should meditate upon the Goddess with a concentrated mind.
As for the meditation:
she has the luster of the rising sun, possesses three eyes, and holds a sword, a shield, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. (8.741)
One should always meditate upon Bhavānī, seated upon a lion and holding [attributes] with her arms.
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), as previously described.
Thus ends the section on Bhavānī.
Now, I shall describe the Gāruḍa mantra (from the Merutantra): the mantra of Garuḍa begins with *kṣipa tāra* (om) and ends with *agnigehinī* (svāhā). 8-742.

The mantra consists of five syllables; the *paṅkti* is considered the meter, Ananta the sage (*muni*), Garuḍa the deity, the *Tāra* (*oṃ*) the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the goddess Dahā the power (*śakti*). (8.743)
Ending with *svāhā*, the mantra "Jvala jvala mahāmate rudracūḍānana svāhā" should be placed upon the heart; it should be placed on the head at the end of the limb-mantra.
"O Śikhin, svāhā at the end of Garuḍa"—this is declared as the mantra for the crest-lock (śikhā).
As for the armor-mantra (varma), one should utter "Garuḍa prabhañjaya" twice. (8.745)
"Split twice! Terrify the row of the wicked! Crush them!
Svāhā! This thirty-seven-syllable mantra of the eye is now described.
Having uttered "Ugrarūpadhare" and "Sarvaviṣahare," one should then speak the pair "Bhīṣaya" and the pair "Dahaya."
"Bhasmīkuru kuru svāhā" is considered the mantra of the color of ivory; and "Apratihatavalāpratihatā" is the weapon-mantra (astramantra). (8.748)
At the end of the teaching, one should say: *dhūḥ phaṭ svāhā*; this is the eighteen-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā*. Now, the visualization:
[He holds] a serpent with its hood moving at the tip of its beak, its coils adorned by a crown. (8.749)
I worship the poison-destroying mantra whose true sāman-chanting is proclaimed in the [Vedic] Pakṣa [sections].
Its *puraścaraṇa* consists of five hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), because it is stated in that very same source: "One should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times."
Likewise: having performed the libation and other rites with sesame seeds, the mantra becomes perfected. || 8-750 ||
Upon seeing him, the two kinds of poison of the serpent are destroyed;
he shall become devoted to Viṣṇu and himself a destroyer of his enemies. (8.751)
"In this world he shall be happy, long-lived, and honored by kings;
in the next world he goes to Vaikuṇṭha... and so forth.
Now, the mantra of Kārttavīrya is found in that very same place.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the twenty mantras for the right side.
In the sacred tradition (āmnāya), the eight accomplishments (siddhis) are attained by practitioners without effort:
the twenty-second and the fourth [syllables] beginning with *Tā* on the right, and the same two beginning with *Tā* along with the fourth on the left. (8.753)
In the remaining traditions, that [mantra] shall be endowed with the fourteen vowels;
however, the first seed-syllable is joined with the bindu and conjoined with the fourth vowel.
The thirty-sixth and the fourth [consonants], enriched with the bindu, are said to be the second seed-syllable;
the third shall be the Kāma-bīja, and the fourth consists of twelve syllables.
The fourth seed-syllable is said to be conjoined with the sixth vowel, the *svaram* (the letter *u*), and the moon (*indu*).
This constitutes the noose (*pāśa*), the *lajjā* (the letter *e*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the *lakṣmī* (the letter *śrīṃ*), the armor (*kavaca*), and the weapon (*astra*). (8.756)
The ten seed-syllables ending in *ṅe* are "Kārtavīryārjunāya namaḥ";
this [mantra] is remembered as having nineteen syllables, with Dattātreya as its sage (*muni*). (8.757)
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is proclaimed to be Kārtavīryārjuna.
"Phrāṃ" is the heart-mantra, and "Klīṃ Bhrīṃ" is remembered as the head-mantra. (8.758)
Oṃ hūṃ is declared to be the crest-lock (śikhā); kre śre is said to be the armor (kavaca);
huṃ phaṭ is declared to be the weapon (astra); with the remainder, one should perform the pervasive application (vyāpaka). || 8-759 ||
Having stated other nyāsas, he describes the meditation:
"He who has the luster of the sun, adorned with a golden necklace around his neck, wearing a red garment and a turban, and decorated with various ornaments, is to be meditated upon. (8.760)
Bearing five hundred arrows and five hundred bows with his five hundred arms,
he terrified all the wicked with the twanging sounds of his bowstring.
He was firmly mounted upon his bow, the lord of the earth consisting of seven continents;
his lotus-feet were rubbed by the crowns of kings, and his eyes were wise.
He has a massive body, is exceedingly formidable, stands upon a chariot, and is affectionate toward his devotees. (p.
711) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and a fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed with milk-rice. (8.763)
Or else, one may perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) on the bank of a river using sesame seeds, clarified butter, and rice;
thereafter, one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites, whereby the perfection of the mantra (mantrasiddhi) arises. || 8.764 ||
Now, the variations of the mantra:
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the variations of the *Kārtavīrya-manu*. This [mantra] consists of nineteen syllables, begins with *Tāra* (Oṃ), and contains twenty digits (nails) as its phonemes.
The placement of the *chanda-ṛṣis*, worship, and all other rites have been described as before.
This second division has been taught, which bestows what is desired upon those who practice it. (8.766)
"Kārttavīryārjunāya" is the nine-syllable root mantra;
preceded by "Phro," this ten-syllable [mantra] is declared to have the Virāṭ meter. (8-767)

And for the sake of accomplishing all goals, his application [is prescribed], while everything else—such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship—is as before; this, however, is the third variety.

The eastern [mantra] consists of nine syllables, but it becomes eleven syllables; as before, all [its attributes], such as the sage and so forth, are the same, and its metre is said to be Triṣṭubh. (8.769)
For the purpose of paralyzing the command of these thieves who steal wealth, the fourth division has been described, beginning with the ritual application of worship as previously stated. (8.770)
The nine-syllable mantra beginning with *phro klī* becomes eleven syllables;
it is employed for the purpose of enchanting men, women, and kings. (8.771)
The sage [should] accomplish the *chandomukha* as before, and also the ritual applications (*prayoga*s). Thus, the fifth division of the mantra has been fully described. (8.772)
The sixth division consists of nine syllables beginning with *phro* (or *bhrū*), as before;
it performs the rites of delusion, driving away, eradication, hatred, and killing. (8.773)
p. 712) PHRO / HRĪM—these are the nine syllables; this shall be the seventh division.
It always extends subjugation, the destruction of evil, delusion, and auspiciousness. (8-774)
Phro, mā, and the nine-syllable mantra—thus the eighth [mantra] begins with *arcā* as before;
this application is proclaimed for the purpose of attracting thieves. (8.775)
Phro / Kro: the ninth division consists of nine syllables; worship and other rites are as before.
Its application is proclaimed for the purpose of paralyzing speech or paralyzing movement. (8.776)
"Phro Śrī Navākṣara"—thus is the tenth variety described.
The *triṣṭubh* meter is used; all other [details] are as in the nineteenth [variety]. (8.777)
PHRO / the seed-syllable of speech (VĀG) and the nine-syllable mantra; this is recorded as the eleventh division.
HU / PHAṬ and the nine-syllable mantra; the twelve-fold worship and so forth are as before. (8–778)
The third variety is the eleven-syllable mantra beginning with Tārā;
this thirteenth variety is declared to be entirely as described previously.
Thus, there are seven variations beginning with the fourth, preceded by the *praṇava*;
these seven mantras, beginning with the twelfth, are considered to have the *jagatī* meter.
The entire ritual procedure, beginning with the sages and so forth, is considered to be as before;
these twenty mantras are proclaimed as belonging to the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya).
Now, in the Ūrdhvāmnāya:
*Oṃ namaḥ kārttavīryārjunāya varmāstra ṭha ṭha*. This fourteen-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the eighth.

The five limbs of this [mantra] consisting of nineteen syllables are formed by the letters corresponding to the earth (1), the eyes (2), the seven-eyed one (7), and the eyes (2); it is considered that the entire [mantra] begins with the sage (muni) and so forth. 8-783.
Now, the garland mantra (*mālāmantra*):
First is the *tāra* (Oṃ), then *namo bhagavate*, and thereafter one should utter the word *śrī*.
Then [the words] *kārttavīryārjunāya* and then the word *haihaya*. (8.784)
One should recite "Nāthāya Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna" a thousand times, as well as "Karasadṛśasarva" from the verse beginning with "Duṣṭāntaka-pada. (8.785)
One should announce to those who wish to come from all directions—that is, from every ocean—the place desired by all the learned, which is the site where our wealth will be plundered. (8.786)
"Repel the hosts of thieves with your thousand hands;
obstruct them with thousands of nooses and bind them!"—thus [spoke] the Goad. (8.787)
Then, having produced [the mantra] from his own bow, he should draw it with thousands [of arrows];
he should say "Strike! and speak repeatedly, "Pierce! Pierce! with thousands of arrows.
With thousands of swords raised by his own hand, he cuts the pair;
with thousands of maces produced from his own hand, he crushes the two.
"Terrify the two with thousands of sounds produced from your own conch;
cut the two down with thousands of wheels produced from your own hand! (8.790)
One should say "terrify" twice for the rite of others; then "attract" twice; "cause to wander" twice; "delude" twice; and one should utter the pair "expel. (8.791)
Madden twice, heat in two ways, destroy twice;
split in two ways, paralyze twice, and cause to yawn twice. (8.792)
Having uttered "Māraya dvitayam" (slay the pair), [say] "vaśam kuru vaśam kuru" (bring under control, bring under control),
"uccāṭaya uccāṭaya" (expel, expel), and "vināśaya vināśaya" (destroy, destroy).
One should recite "at the feet of Dattātreya," "O you who are most dear to the feet," "O Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna," and "the all-pervading one" by the ocean. (8.794)
One should speak out against those who desire to come as plunderers of our wealth; one should properly address these bands of thieves so that they may be utterly uprooted. (8.795)
"Huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this mantra consists of fifteen syllables, numbering [the sequence] five, four, and three; it has been declared that its meter is Gāyatrī, and the rest is as before. (8.796)
One should place "dattātreyapriyatama," ending in the genitive case, in the heart;
the mantra for the head consists of eight syllables: "māhiṣmatīnāthāya. (8.797)
The *śikhā* is considered to be "and Revatī, who is intent on water-sports";
the lord of the Haihayas, ending with the word *ṅe*, is proclaimed as the *kavaca*. (8.798)
The weapon-mantra for the Thousand-Armed One is thus declared as five-limbed.
Now, the visualization: [One should meditate on him] holding uplifted arrows and bows, resembling the sun in brilliance. (8.799)
One should meditate upon King Kārtavīrya, who fills the entire universe with the twanging sounds of his bowstring, and whose cheeks are adorned with beautiful earrings.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should accomplish all rites.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
three thousand recitations are prescribed; the remainder one should perform as previously described.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*).
With one hundred and eight [recitations] for each of the right and left hands, he should discharge these weapons:
the discus, arrow, sword, mace, axe, and the noose. (8.802)
[He saw] spears, shields, bows, and conchs, resembling the midday sun—
powerful, ruddy, and terrible— mounted upon palm trees and elephants.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] with red garments and red eyes, one should mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times at midnight for the sake of attaining lost wealth. (8.804)
If one recites [the mantra] eight hundred times for six months while standing on one leg in silence,
and then makes a request to the mantra-practitioner, the thieves will surrender all their wealth.
When a mantra-practitioner wishes to lead back animals stolen by thieves, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and meditate on the deity as devouring the kings. (8-806)
Having visualized all the sacrificial animals that have come toward the house as being correctly [bound] at the throat, they will arrive, having been liberated, within twelve days.
One should offer as an oblation at night the remainder of rice and other grains that have been carried off by thieves;
for what has been stolen is revealed by the terrified thieves immediately, and not otherwise.
Intent on meditation, one should discharge arrows with the bow at night;
by reciting the mantra in the ten directions, the protection of the kingdom and so forth shall be secured. (8.809)
And earthen dust consecrated with mantra, when scattered by the practitioner wherever it may be, provides protection during the night. (8.810)
He states another mantra:
"Phroṃ" is the single-syllable mantra of Kārtavīrya;
the worship of the sage and so forth is as before, with one hundred thousand recitations as the preliminary rite (puraskriyā). (8.811)
By means of this [mantra] joined with the six long vowels, the ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is proclaimed;
the applications are as before—thus is the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) celebrated.
The mantras of the western direction have been declared in the Āravva language;
through the accomplishment of these eight hundred and eighty [mantras] in the Kali age, [success is attained].
Five Khānas, seven Mīras, and nine Śāhas of great strength, who will be destroyers of the Hindu dharma, shall arise as universal emperors (cakravartins). (8.814)
In the Pūrvāmnāya, nine hundred and eighty-six mantras are proclaimed; through their accomplishment on earth by means of the Phiraṅga language, [great results are attained].
The lords of the Mandaras are undefeated in battles;
nine, six, and five are the Iṅgrejas, and the Landrajas are also cultivated.
p. 716) Regarding the five Vidyās that I have proclaimed in the *Bauddhanidāna*, all mantras preceded by their respective seeds bestow the accomplishments of the Left-hand path (vāmasiddhi). (8-817)
King Kārtavīryārjuna bestows the fruits of right conduct,
while in this world he grants the fruits of left-hand practice to the Śūdras.
One should not employ the Kārtavīrya rite for the benefit of those who are hostile;
otherwise, the twice-born would incur poverty for seven births and attain the state of a Piśāca.
Thus ends the section on Kārtavīrya.
Now, regarding the mantra of Hanumān, it is stated in that very same source:
"Next, I shall fully declare another mantra consisting of eighteen syllables."
Having uttered "Homage to the Blessed One," one should address Āñjaneya.
"Mahābalāya svāhā"—this is remembered as its mantra; the Sage is its lord (Īśvara), the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Hanumān, and 'ha' is the seed-syllable (bīja). (8-821)
Svāhā, Śakti, Añjaneya, Rudramūrti, Marutsuta, Agnigarbha, Rāmadūta, and Brahmāstravinivāraka. || 8-822 ||
With these [mantras] ending in *ṅe*, one should likewise place the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the thumbs and other fingers.
Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*): [He is] resembling molten gold, with his hands joined in reverence at his heart. (8.823)
One should meditate upon the leader of monkeys, who wears a crown and earrings.
Now follows the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds amounting to one-tenth of that number.
By first performing the complete gratification of Brahmins and other rites as previously described, the mantra becomes perfected.
Now, for other methods: one who has conquered the senses and eats only at night should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for each [deity]. (8.825)
Having performed the recitation, one is freed from minor ailments within three days;
one should perform it in this manner for the destruction of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth. (8.826)

To ward off a major disease, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times for three days; eating moderately, one should constantly recite it ten thousand times while meditating upon the Lord of Monkeys (Kapīśvara). (8.827)
Remembering the monkey [Hanumān], who together with Sugrīva was swiftly conquering his enemies and destroying the flood of Rākṣasas, he meditated upon Rāma.
Having recited the mantra ten thousand times, one should effect a reconciliation between two adversaries;
while meditating on that burning of Laṅkā, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
The practitioner shall burn down the villages of his enemies in no time at all;
at the time of setting out on a journey, he should meditate upon Hanumān and recite the mantra.
He who goes shall soon accomplish his own desired aim and return home;
he who, intent on recitation, always worships the Lord of Monkeys in his home—8.831.
Longevity and prosperity attend him, and his afflictions perish;
this mantra is remembered as one that protects against tigers, thieves, and other such dangers. (8.832)
At the time of departure, from thieves and even from a venomous serpent, one is certainly protected by a well-made cloth in the shape of a tail, fashioned with a pen made from a cuckoo's bone.
One should draw the beautiful form of the King of Monkeys using the eight fragrances;
in its center, one should write the eighteen-syllable mantra and ten thousand names of the enemies.
By binding the head with that [cord] consecrated by the mantra, the ruler of the earth certainly conquers the entire host of enemies merely upon seeing it. (8.835)
Alternatively, a king desiring victory should have the previously mentioned [mantra] inscribed on his banner;
having taken up the banner during an eclipse, he should carry it until its release from contact.
Thereafter, one should have the mantra recited by a master of mantras and perform an oblation with a tenth part [of that number] using mustard seeds mixed with sesame seeds in the consecrated fire.
Upon seeing that banner bearing an elephant, enemies flee in an instant.
Now, another mantra is stated in that very same place:
"Now I shall proclaim another supreme eight-syllabled mantra. (8-838)
The syllable *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ) joined with six long vowels and encapsulated by the *praṇava* (oṃ) is proclaimed as this eight-syllabled king of mantras (*mantrarāja*) of Hanumān. || 8.839 ||
The ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared by means of the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels.
Its seer (ṛṣi) is Śrī Rāma, its meter (chandas) is Jagatī, and its deity (devatā) is Hanumān. Now, the visualization (dhyāna):
The three worlds, shining like the rising sun, [saw] all the rākṣasas who cause agitation.

One should meditate upon the son of the Wind (Hanumān), who terrifies with that very [strength], who is served by Sugrīva and others, and who is beautiful through his meditation on the feet of Rāma. (8-841)
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of twelve thousand recitations, because it is stated that everything for this [mantra] is like that of the twelve-syllable [mantra].
The twelve-syllable mantra is also found in that very same place:
"Now I shall proclaim another great twelve-syllable mantra."
Having correctly uttered the seed-syllable and the previously mentioned five-fold peak (kūṭapañcaka), || 8.842 ||
The mantra is "Hanumate namaḥ"; Rāmacandra is considered the sage (ṛṣi);
Jagatī is specified as the meter (chandas); and Hanumān is regarded as the deity (devatā). || 8.843 ||
The fifth peak-syllable is the seed, while the first peak-syllable is the power (śakti).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) with the first six seed-syllables is proclaimed as its six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga).
As for the five peaks (*kūṭapañcaka*):
they consist of the first and last syllables, the Vedas, and the number of phonemes, joined with the *bindu*, Rudra, and the vowels.
O practitioner, one should utter this first peak of Hanumān. (8.845)

The second *kūṭa* consists of the letters of the *prakṛti*, the *ākṛti*, the Vedas, and the vowels, joined with the *bindu*, *rudra*, and the *svara*; its initial and final letters are those of the *ākṛti*.

The third peak (kūṭa) is said to consist of [the letters] endowed with the visarga, the moon (i), and the vowels (svaras); it comprises forty-two syllables, beginning and ending with the perfected forms (siddhākṛti), and is joined with the vowels of Īśa.
p. 719) The fourth *kūṭa* is with the *anusvāra*; the fifth is considered to be *sādyah sauḥ*.
Now, regarding meditation and the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
the meditation for this is exactly as previously stated; one should recite it one thousand times [per day] for twelve days. (8-848)
One should offer oblations ten times [the number of recitations] using grains mixed with milk, curd, and clarified butter.
Now, regarding the *mālā-mantra*, it is said in that very same source:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *mālā-mantra*; one should certainly recite it. (8.849)
One should utter "Vajrakāya Vajratuṇḍa Kapilapiṅgala";
one should proclaim "Ūrdhvakeśa Mahāvega" and "Raktamukha. (8-850)
Having uttered "taḍijjihva mahāraudra daṃṣṭrotkaṭaka hadvayam," one should say "karāline mahā" and then "dṛḍhaprati" followed by "hā. (8.851)
"O Lord of Laṅkā, having said 'I know,' speak further with great resolve, O sky-walker, you who possess the power to move the great mountain that forms the bridge! (8.852)
Having uttered "Come, come, O Blessed One," and "O you of great strength and prowess," one should say the words "Bhairava, give the command" followed by "Come, come. (8.853)
Having uttered the "mahāraudrapada" mantra, one should encircle [the target] with a long tail;
then, possessing the color of the sun and arrows, one should utter "vairiṇaṃ bhañjaya dvandvaṃ huṃ phaṭ."
The entire procedure for the worship of Munīśvara and others is considered to be according to the Sūryārṇava.
Now, another mantra [from the Sādhanasamuccaya]: Having extracted "Namaḥ" along with the bindu, and then "Hanumanta" ending in the dative case (ṅe). (8.855)
This mantra, consisting of a single syllable—namely "Kavaca" and "Astra"—is of the nature of Rudra;
it was formerly bestowed by Hari upon the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Having performed the ritual application (*sādhana*) of this, one attains victory in battle. Another mantra:
having first uttered one's own seed-syllable, [one utters] the son of the Wind-god (Hanuman) ending in the dative case (*ṅe*). (8.857)
This mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), is declared to be the celestial tree;
the ritual assignment of its limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed by means of the syllables of the mantra conjoined with the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels. (8.858)
One should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the vowels and the consonants beginning with 'ka' and 'pa';
then one should meditate upon Hanumān in battle, accompanied by ten million monkeys.
Seeing Rāvaṇa rushing forward to conquer, and the great hero Lakṣmaṇa having risen quickly and fallen upon the surface of the battlefield; (8-860)
Having aroused great wrath toward his guru and seized the mountain that was his guru, he caused the three worlds to tremble with his cries of "Alas! Alas! and his arrogant displays.
Having pervaded everything up to the realm of Brahmā and having assumed a formidable body,
one should perform worship upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal and carry out one hundred thousand recitations.
Then, having mastered the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should achieve supreme accomplishment.
Likewise: "Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed his daily obligatory rites, the twice-born [should proceed]. (8.863)
Then, having gone to a river and bathed, one should invoke the sacred site (tīrtha) in eight ways;
thereafter, having recited the root mantra, one should sprinkle [the water] as many times as there are suns (twelve).
Having worshipped Hanumān, one should perform six thousand recitations;
thus, at the end of seven days, the Lord of Monkeys arrives.
When one-third of the night remains, he grants the desired boon—
whether it be knowledge, wealth, a kingdom, or the subjugation of enemies.
"It bestows [the fruit] upon the foremost of practitioners; this is the truth, the truth, most certainly so.
Thus ends the section on Hanumān.
Now, the Kāma-mantra (in the Śāradā-tantra):
Brahmā is seated upon the earth, adorned with the *śānti* bindu.
The seed-syllable of the Mind-born (Kāmadeva), which deludes the three worlds, has been proclaimed;
Sammohana is declared the Seer (Ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī metre is stated [to be its meter]. (8-868)
The god Makaradhvaja himself is the direct deluder of all;
the ritual of the six limbs is proclaimed by means of the seed-syllable conjoined with the long vowel.
Now, for the meditation:
[He is] rosy-red like a hibiscus flower, richly adorned with jewel ornaments, bearing a fish-banner, and having beautiful unguents applied to his limbs.
I worship Him who holds in His lotus-like hands the goad, the sugarcane bow, the flower-arrow, and the noose.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; then, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with one-tenth that number of blossoming *kiṃśuka* flowers mixed with the "three sweets" (*madhuratraya*).

Now, another mantra is found therein: having extracted the seed-syllable of Love (Mānmatha), one should utter Kāma ending in the dative case (Kāmāya). This six-syllabled mantra, ending with "Hṛdayāya," is capable of enchanting the entire world. (8.872)
For this mantra, the procedure from the visualization of the heart and so forth up to the final meditation should be performed as before.
Regarding the specific details for the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times per syllable, and perform the fire oblation with offerings soaked in honey amounting to one-tenth of that number.
One should perform the fire-oblation with *palāśa* flowers or with mango sprouts.
Thus ends the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the Kāma-mantra.

[This work] is highly esteemed as a confluence of rivers consisting of well-composed treatises, which possess streams of nectar and are variegated with the wonderful power of words that purify all beings.
In this *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by Nepālendranarendra, the eighth wave—exalted by the luster of a multitude of clearly manifest pearls of sound reasoning—has arrived. || 8.874 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "An Analysis of the Purification Rites for Mantras such as that of Gaṇeśa," in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha Sāh.
